News.title: Dog owners reminded of 8-week law as pet thefts increase across UK
News.content:
Dog owners reminded of 8-week law as pet thefts increase across UK

Freedom of Information data gathered from police forces across the country identified the five breeds most commonly stolen

View 3 Images Owners should act if they have not done so already (Image: Getty)

Dog owners in the UK may want to act now before it's too late. The reminder comes as owners of five popular dog breeds are warned to remain alert amid rising pet thefts across the UK.

‌



‌



Criminals are snatching family pets directly from their own homes and gardens. We recently reported that fresh statistics show dog thefts climbed by 5% in 2025 to nearly 1,200 incidents. This was despite new legislation being introduced to treat companion animals as more than just property.

‌



If owners do not have their dog microchipped yet, they may want to have this done as soon as possible. Gov.uk states that "all dogs in the UK must be microchipped and registered by the time they’re 8 weeks old."

‌



Failure to do so will result in a fine. Officials add: "You can be fined up to £500 if your dog or cat is not microchipped when they need to be."

Owners may not know you need to register with an approved database

View 3 Images You could face a £500 fine (Image: Getty)

Your pet’s microchip contains a number that will appear whenever your dog or cat is scanned. This means if they are stolen or go missing, they should be reunited with their owner if found.

‌



But that's not the only fine some owners could receive. Government officials further state: "You can be fined up to £500 if your dog or cat is not registered" on a specific database.

You must make sure that your dog or cat is registered on one of the following databases (they all meet government standards):

‌



Gov.uk notes: "You’ll be asked for your address and contact details when you register your pet on one of these databases. Track Your Paws does not meet government standards and has been removed from the list of databases. If your pet’s details are registered with Track Your Paws, you should register with another database from the list."

‌



Which five dog breeds are more at risk of theft?

According to The Pet Database Pet Theft and Abduction Report 2026, compiled by Dr Daniel Allen of Keele University, certain pedigree and family-favourite dogs continue to be prime targets for thieves.

Freedom of Information data gathered from police forces across the country identified the five breeds most commonly stolen:

‌



Staffordshire Bull Terrier French Bulldog Dachshund German Shepherd Cocker Spaniel

View 3 Images Owners must make sure their dog is registered on a specific databases (Image: Getty)

Article continues below

Indy Sangha, CEO of Pet Database, said: "Owners are doing everything they can to protect their pets on walks, while the data shows thieves are coming to the front door.

"When a pet is taken, the microchip is often the clearest proof of who it belongs to, yet a fifth of owners don't know it's their job to keep those details up to date. We back Dr Allen's call for police to record microchip status in every pet theft case, so we can finally see how many stolen and abducted pets could have come home."

News.title: New dementia study reveals unexpected medication link to better brain health
News.content:
New dementia study reveals unexpected medication link to better brain health

A study has suggested a surprising link between certain medications and healthier brain vessels. Here’s what Alzheimer’s Research UK says you need to know

View 3 Images More research is needed, but the study could be promising (Image: Getty)

A new study has found a link between brain health and oral contraceptives as well as menopausal hormone therapy (MHT). Following its release, Alzheimer's Research UK - the UK’s leading dementia research charity - has said that the findings are "interesting" but more information is needed.

‌



‌



The study, published in Neurology, states that "women are disproportionately affected by Alzheimer disease (AD), a vulnerability that may relate to estrogen fluctuations across the lifespan. Estrogen has neuroprotective and vasoprotective effects, suggesting that lifetime estrogen exposure may influence both AD-related neurodegeneration and cerebrovascular health."

‌



The research, involving 352 women who had a mean age of 70, found that a longer reproductive lifespan was associated with fewer signs of damage to the brain's small blood vessels. Women who had used oral contraceptives or MHT also showed some signs of better brain health.

‌



View 3 Images Dementia is caused by diseases that damage the brain and interfere with its normal functioning (Image: Hispanolistic via Getty Images)

This included stronger, healthier links between different brain regions and, among MHT users, fewer signs of damage to the brain’s small blood vessels. Because this is an observational study, it can’t prove cause and effect.

The study's discussion reads: "Greater lifetime estrogen exposure, both endogenous and exogenous, was associated with lower cerebrovascular pathology in women and, among APOE-ε4 carriers, greater cortical thickness in AD-vulnerable regions. These findings support the potential role of cerebrovascular mechanisms linking estrogen exposure to brain ageing. Limitations included observational design and self-reported, binary estrogen exposure. Potential cognitive effects require further studies."

‌



This means that more research is needed to clarify what these findings might mean for women’s brain health as they get older.

'These findings are interesting' Alzheimer's Research UK says

Dr Honorine Lebraud, Senior Partnerships Manager at Alzheimer's Research UK, said: “This study builds on growing evidence that reproductive and hormonal history may play a role in brain health as women age.

‌



"Researchers found that women who had a longer reproductive lifespan and therefore experienced a longer period of natural oestrogen exposure, from their first period to menopause, tended to show fewer signs of damage to the brain's small blood vessels. Meanwhile, women who had used oestrogen-based oral contraceptives or menopausal hormone therapy were more likely to exhibit additional signs of improved brain health.

View 3 Images 'While these findings are interesting, further research is needed to understand these patterns' the chairty says (Image: Getty/Dazeley)

‌



"While these findings are interesting, further research is needed to understand these patterns, especially as nearly two-thirds of people with dementia are women. As an observational study, it cannot show that hormone exposure directly improves brain health or reduces dementia risk.

"For now, our advice remains unchanged. Women should not start or stop taking the contraceptive pill or HRT to reduce their dementia risk based on these findings. Decisions about hormonal treatments should continue to be made with a healthcare professional, based on individual health needs."

Article continues below

You can find the study - Reproductive Lifespan and Hormonal Therapy in Relation to Later-Life Neurovascular Health in Community-Dwelling Older Women - here.

News.title: Russell Brand will 'be a target' as he faces lengthy prison sentence
News.content:
Russell Brand will 'be a target' as he faces lengthy prison sentence

The nature of his offending along with his wealth and followers online will likely contribute to what his time in jail will look like, according to one expert

View 3 Images (Image: Metropolitan Police)

An investigative journalist has lifted the lid on what Russell Brand's prison sentence might look like, saying the disgraced star will likely 'be a target his whole time in jail'.

‌



‌



Mark Williams-Thomas, the investigative journalist who helped expose Jimmy Saville's abhorrent crime, who has amassed nearly 100,000 followers on Tik Tok has given his thoughts on what Brand now faces as he was told by a judge he will receive a lengthy jail sentence.

‌



On Thursday, a jury found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault - he will be sentenced on Monday.

‌



Williams-Thomas said on a video on Tik Tok: "On Monday he's going to be sentenced, and it's going to be a very lengthy sentence. He will go to jail.

"But what's going to happen to him, and how is he going to stay safe? Well, he's a man of great wealth, and as a result of what he's done, he offended— but also he'll be a target for other prisoners who will want some kind of potential recognition in relation to attacking him.

View 3 Images Court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Russell Brand appearing in the dock listening to his third accuser in a pre-recorded police interview, played to jurors, at Southwark Crown Court, London (Image: Elizabeth Cook/the Press Association)

‌



"So he's going to be a target his whole time in jail.

He then added: "I've seen his wealth estimated around 20 million. He's got 10 million followers on X, 6 million on YouTube, 4.8 million on Instagram, and platforms can earn you a lot of good money. And those followers— that size of followers— will earn him money."

‌



"He's cleansed himself of all his past behaviour," he continued. "But here is the problem: it depends on what you've done in the past, because your past can very quickly become your present."

It comes as prisoners are said to have been banned from speaking to Brand after he was transferred to prison ahead of his sentencing.

‌



One source, who had just visited her son inside the jail, said: “My son said Brand is downstairs from him. He said no one is allowed to see or speak to him.”

Another female visitor added: “Apparently Brand requested to go on the main wing, but they decided to put him in isolation.” Another source said she was told: "Brand doesn't like the food and is struggling to eat it. It's slop."

‌



Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, who led the Metropolitan Police investigation, paid tribute to the “extraordinary courage, resilience and determination” of the women who spoke out against Brand.

He said: “Despite intense media and public scrutiny, they relived deeply personal and traumatic experiences and placed their trust in us. Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible.

‌



View 3 Images Russell Brand was convicted of rape this week (Image: Getty)

“Brand used his influence, status and fame to prey on and exploit women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be.”

Article continues below

In September 2023, an investigation by journalists from The Sunday Times, The Times, and Channel 4 Dispatches published accusations from women who said they had been raped, sexual abused, and degraded by Brand.

The revelations prompted four women to come forward to accuse Brand of criminal offences, while another two women came forward once Brand had been charged.

News.title: 'Urgent action' needed as strokes cost the UK nearly £250,000 every five minutes
News.content:
'Urgent action' needed as strokes cost the UK nearly £250,000 every five minutes

EXCLUSIVE: Research from The Stroke Association found that every five minutes - the frequency with which someone has a stroke - the cost to the taxpayer is £244,600, nearly the price of a house

View 2 Images The cost of supporting people with strokes is set to skyrocket (Image: Getty)

The cost of supporting people with strokes is set to skyrocket within the next decade unless urgent action is taken to improve diagnosis and treatment, a new report has warned.

‌



‌



Strokes currently cost UK taxpayers £25.7billion a year or £70.4million a day, with over half of this spent on social care.

‌



Research from The Stroke Association (SA) found this equates to £244,600 every five minutes - the frequency with which someone has a stroke.

‌



With people living longer, the charity says without streamlining the process of diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation, the cost of strokes will increase by 40% to £35.9billion a year by 2035.

Former Labour MP calls for more testing after stroke on New Year's Day READ MORE :

View 2 Images Adebisi Desalu-Odiase became a carer for her husband Alex when he had a stroke in 2022 (Image: The Stroke Association)

The brain injury caused by stroke can leave survivors having to relearn basics such as being able to walk, talk or swallow. Around a third of stroke survivors also experience depression.

‌



Despite this, new figures from the Sentinel Stroke National Audit Programme (SSNAP) show that only 7% of stroke patients get the amount of rehabilitation set out by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

Instead of the recommended three hours a day five days a week, their data shows that the average amount of hospital rehabilitation a stroke survivor receives is just 40 minutes per day.

‌



Mum of two Adebisi Desalu-Odiase, 36, from Bedford became a carer for her husband Alex when he had a stroke in 2022. She said: “I lost myself for the year of Alex’s stroke and it took a long time to recover.

“Everything changes after a stroke. Our time together became about me being his carer, and I also took on all the family responsibilities. There is no ‘i’ in stroke – medically, it happens to just one person, but it affects the whole family.”

‌



Alex added: “The moment people understand that each stroke is different, it makes everything else easy. It’s not the same for everybody.

“There needs to be a level of grace to people like myself. I am trying to get better. I hope to get better. People just need to understand that it's not the same anymore.”

‌



The pair are now finalising a book about Alex's stroke and the impact it had on their family, to be released at the end of the month.

The SA is now calling on the Government to treat stroke as a major health, research, social care and economic priority.

‌



Juliet Bouverie OBE, CEO of the SA, said: “The brain injury caused by stroke changes a person’s life in an instant with far-reaching repercussions for both themselves and their loved ones.

“It is the leading cause of adult disability, and survivors must get the right intensity and frequency of rehabilitation for as long as they need, alongside emotional support, to make the best possible recovery.

‌



“This simply isn’t happening so the cost of stroke is extortionate and, as our report illustrates, this is only going to get worse.”

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "Hundreds of people every day suffer a stroke, and the NHS is working hard to get them the rapid support and long-term rehabilitation they will often require.

Article continues below

“In our 10-Year Health Plan last year, we pledged to reduce premature mortality from heart disease and stroke by a quarter within a decade, and our Cardiovascular Disease Modern Service Framework, published in July, aims to accelerate that progress.

“The NHS is also working to increase the delivery of thrombolysis and thrombectomy rates as a key intervention to support improved outcomes in patients who have had a stroke.”

News.title: Donald Trump insists he has 'total control' after launching fresh missile strikes on Iran
News.content:
Donald Trump insists he has 'total control' after launching fresh missile strikes on Iran

The US president launched new strikes on Iran just days after he was told by the American voting public that they did not want his administration to continue the war

View 4 Images Trump claimed the US 'hadn't lost anybody in seven months' when the most recent US servicemember lost their life in July (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump has claimed he is in "total control" after his administration resumed strikes on Iran, just days after he was dealt a shocking defeat at home.

‌



‌



The president's administration announced on Friday that it had carried out what it said were limited strikes on the nation. Trump himself told journalists the strikes were "minor" and directed at Iranian air defence systems on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, after claiming “a lot of progress” was made in talks with the regime.

‌



The lame duck president went on to claim the ongoing Middle East conflict "can't be a war", because the US "hasn't lost anybody for months".

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Trump begs UFC boss Dana White to become his new press secretary in bizarre post READ MORE :

View 4 Images The US targeted Qeshm Island - seen here in the background - during its latest strikes (Image: AP)

‌



Trump told members of the press that the US has "total control" over the situation after his administration launched attacks on what he said was a "little bit of an anti-aircraft device". He claimed: "We knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five."

The president went on to add: “It can’t be a war when for five months nobody is hurt, killed or anything else. It’s not a war. You know, in Russia, Ukraine, they lose 25,000 people a month. We haven’t lost anybody in seven months. So I don’t think that’s a war. We have total control, but we’re dealing with the Iranians. We’ll see how that all works out.”

‌



View 4 Images Trump's war in Iran has been widely rejected (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The US has sustained 21 military fatalities since it launched into war with Iran. The first service member deaths came more than eight months ago on March 1, with nearly two dozen occurring over the following summer.

‌



The most recent deaths were reported on July 1, just over four months ago. A total of 865 servicemembers have been injured during the conflict. The resumption of strikes in Iran comes in spite of Midterm results which last week suggested the public roundly rejected the conflict, on which Trump embarked early this year.

View 4 Images Trump has vowed to continue attacking Iran (Image: AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

Article continues below

Republicans were soundly defeated at the polls, with voting Americans installing Democrats in key swing positions, including across typically deep red states and districts in Texas and Ohio. Conflict in the Middle East was cited among the key concerns of voters, who said Trump's strikes - which closed the critical Strait of Hormuz oil transportation route - hurt them in their wallets.

The issue was acknowledged by senior administration figures, including Vice President JD Vance, who said it was "the reason we lost". But Trump has indicated he has no intention to scale back the war, which he called a "thing", telling reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday: "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we’re very much locked in."

News.title: Netanyahu faces being ousted as rival given chance to form new Israeli government
News.content:
Netanyahu faces being ousted as rival given chance to form new Israeli government

Opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot will get the first opportunity to form a coalition government, Israeli President Isaac Herzog has said

View 2 Images Gadi Eisenkot is a retired Chief of Staff of the Israel Defense Forces and leader of the 'Yashar' party (Image: Getty Images)

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on October 27.

‌



‌



Mr Eisenkot, a former military chief who ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is now a step closer to ousting Israel ’s longest-serving premier.

‌



“This is the time to establish a national emergency government. I will do anything possible to prove us worthy,” Mr Eisenkot posted on his X account just after the presidential announcement.

‌



He has up to six weeks to form a coalition, a challenging task in a deeply divided country reeling from the October 7 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the three years of wars that have followed in Gaza and beyond.

In discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel’s main parties recommended Mr Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government.

View 2 Images Israel's President Isaac Herzog (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



But putting together the parliamentary majority needed remains fraught and any possible coalition would require candidates to make tough compromises that could outrage their own voters.

Mr Netanyahu and his allies lost their majority in parliament in last month’s elections. But the bloc led by Mr Eisenkot also did not win a majority. That left Arab-led parties, which made historic gains, as potential but politically fraught kingmakers.

‌



An Arab party has been part of a governing coalition just once in Israel’s history. Forming such an alliance could be especially divisive for Mr Eisenkot after more than three years of war in Gaza.

Mr Netanyahu has been on a campaign to head off any alliance between Mr Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties, including unsubstantiated claims that Arab parties “stole” the elections.

‌



Shortly before Mr Herzog’s announcement, he called for a “national unity government” in a video statement and warned against “hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters” – language he uses to refer to the Arab-led parties.

Mr Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly portrayed the Arab-led parties as a threat to national security, while Mr Eisenkot has indicated a willingness to partner with them under certain conditions, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed.

‌



Mr Eisenkot and Mr Netanyahu, whose Likud is the single largest party in parliament, could seek to create a broad unity government with major Jewish parties.

However, the men have deep differences over many issues that will be difficult to bridge. That includes Mr Netanyahu’s reliance on religious parties that demand draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men, as well as Mr Netanyahu’s opposition to a formal investigation into the security failures surrounding the October 7 attacks.

‌



Mr Eisenkot could also seek to create a “minority” government — shored up by external support from Arab parties that are not formal members of his coalition. However, other members of his bloc have said they would reject such an alliance.

Mr Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, slammed the prime minister’s video with a statement posted on X and urged members of his party, Likud, to disavow their alliance with “radical parties”, in an apparent reference to the far-right parties in his religious-nationalist base.

Article continues below

The statement argued that Mr Eisenkot would only include parties and parliament members who support his party’s principles.

News.title: Veterans shouldn't sleep rough this Christmas, Burnham says
News.content:
Burnham will ask local authorities to use part of the additional Â£874m already announced to tackle homelessness specifically for housing veterans.

"People who stepped forward prepared to put their lives on the line for the rest of us should never lack a roof over their head," Burnham said in a statement issued on Saturday.

"When they need help, the country owes them more than warm words. It owes them a bed every night, a proper plan and someone in their corner from day one."

The PM will ask councils to work with local organisations and charities to tackle homelessness amongst veterans.

Downing Street said an additional Â£8.7m in funding would be allocated to eight organisations across the UK to help housing providers offer assistance to veterans with complex needs, including those with health or addiction problems.

Among them are Veteran Housing Scotland, Launchpad and SSAFA, the Armed Forces Charity.

The pledge, announced ahead of Remembrance Sunday, is part of Burnham's wider plan to offer everyone currently sleeping rough a bed this winter.

The most recent official figures estimated that there were 4,793 people sleeping rough, external on a single night in autumn 2025 in England - a record high. The number of people recorded as sleeping rough has been on the rise since 2021.

The government has committed Â£4.4bn in total to end rough sleeping.

Burnham previously faced criticism from the Conservatives for failing to end rough sleeping while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester.

He argued that Manchester's scheme attracted rough sleepers from the surrounding regions, adding that "it's only if everywhere does it at the same level that you can actually end rough sleeping".

Liberal Democrats defence spokesman James MacCleary MP said the funding was an "important first step" but that "a one-off cash injection won't fix a crisis years in the making".

He urged Burnham to guarantee long-term funding for councils to tackle homelessness "for good" and to put in place measures to prevent veterans "falling through the cracks in the first place".

The prime minister is urging any veterans who are sleeping rough, or those supporting them, to call a UK-wide helpline on 0800 9520774 to be connected directly to housing and other specialist support.

Separately on Sunday, the culture secretary set out the UK's renewed participation in the EU's Erasmus programme of educational and cultural exchanges for young people after six years.

The UK will rejoin the programme in January, enabling students and other young people to study, train or get work experience in the EU.

In the announcement, Nandy added: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."

Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake responded by saying veterans had not fought for a "student exchange scheme".

He argued that it was "tone deaf and frankly shameful" to announce this on Remembrance Sunday.

"It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," the Tory chairman added.

News.title: Royal Family join veterans and families at Festival of Remembrance
News.content:
King Charles III led senior members of the Royal Family as they paid tribute to British service personnel at this year's Festival of Remembrance.

The Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales, joined the King and Queen Camilla at London's Royal Albert Hall to commemorate those who lost their lives in service, on the eve of Remembrance Sunday.

The audience stood and a fanfare played as the royals entered the concert hall for the annual event, which was also attended by bereaved families and serving personnel.

The King will lead the nation in two minutes of silence on Sunday to remember those who died serving in the two world wars and other conflicts.

News.title: Two seriously hurt in 30-vehicle crash on the M20 in Kent
News.content:
More than 30 vehicles were involved in a crash which left two people seriously injured on the M20 in Kent on Saturday evening.

The crash happened in foggy conditions just after 18:40 GMT on the London-bound carriageway between junctions eight (Ashford) and nine (Maidstone).

Paramedics attended to 11 people, and two were taken to hospital, Kent Fire and Rescue Service said.

The road was shut in both directions early on Sunday, but has since reopened.

An air ambulance crew, three fire engines and a "technical rescue unit" were sent to the scene, where National Highways said "thick fog" had been confirmed.

Kent Police said one of the two people seriously injured had been taken to a hospital locally, and the other to a London hospital.

"Other drivers have sustained injuries not believed to be serious," it said in a statement.

The force has asked anyone with information about the incident or dashcam footage to come forward.

News.title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
News.content:
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.

Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.

Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.

But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.

Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-UniversitÃ¤t (LMU).

But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.

News.title: My parents chose to die together and I was left to grieve alone
News.content:
Some people might find this article upsetting.

Early one morning in June 2024, Bas pulled up next to his parents' campervan, parked on a sunny marina in the north of the Netherlands.

His father and mother, Jan and Els, had spent most of their married life on water. Now in their 70s, they could no longer manage a houseboat. Their campervan, positioned close to the yachts and dinghies, was the next best thing.

Jan and Els got into their son's car. Bas started the engine. This would be the final time he drove his parents anywhere. For Jan and Els, this journey - to the local hospice - would be their last.

At 10:30 that morning they would be administered lethal medication by doctors and die together in what is known in the Netherlands as duo-euthanasia. It's legal and it's rare, but every year more Dutch people choose to end their lives this way.

News.title: Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn't expect a smooth ride
News.content:
First, Burnham inherited the broad deal that's likely to be signed. The UK and EU were originally meant to mint a new and, they hope, improved agreement back in May, then in July, and well, political upheavals mean one thing for getting things done â delay.

But that means the outlines of a new agreement have been clear for many months, an approach based on "closer alignment" as Sir Keir Starmer proclaimed to us at the start of the year.

So if the prime minister hails agreement, spare a thought for those who started the work to get it this far many months ago.

One source familiar with the negotiations told me, "They are 90% there", with agreements designed to make life easier for food producers, a deal on emissions trading which could help manufacturers, and new arrangements for youth visas (although it's understood there is still haggling over putting a cap on the numbers).

An EU source close to the process said: "The bone of contention is a cap â we proposed 150,000, the UK proposed 50,000 â but we would expect to reach a compromise", even though it has been "very tense" on both sides.

A last-minute call from the EU to cut tuition fees for its students is expected to be parked for now with more months of discussion to come. Another fine tradition - agree what you can, but file some tough stuff away for future chat.

There are dilemmas too on the EU's so-called "Made in Europe" plans â draft laws to protect its industries from being hammered by Chinese competition. The purpose is clear â to help the economy grow, with the prime minister quoting figures that suggest closer ties to the EU without going back in could add 0.4 percent to GDP.

But as the tabloid-friendly row over salty snacks illustrates, making it easier to do business with the bloc doesn't come without a cost, and a political awkwardness.

News.title: Labubu hype seemed unstoppable, now the fluffy monster mania is fading
News.content:
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.

Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (Â£11) or more.

Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.

The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.

Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (Â£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".

He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.

But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."

Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.

It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.

Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.

The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.

News.title: Ambika Mod says the 'glass ceiling is always getting higher' for South Asian actors
News.content:
She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles.

Fans have questioned why she hasn't gone on to appear in as many roles as her One Day co-star Leo Woodall, who's since appeared in major films including Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and A24's Anthony Bourdain biopic, Tony.

Addressing this remark, Mod tells Newsbeat she thinks "there's definitely an issue in this industry with systemic racism".

"I think it is really hard for South Asian actors to really push through.

"I feel like the glass ceiling is always getting higher and higher and higher."

A report from the Creative Diversity Network, external suggested that representation of minority ethnic groups on and off-screen dropped slightly last year, after a few years of improvement.

And similar research from media watchdog Ofcom , externalfound people from certain backgrounds are less well-represented across the UK broadcasting industry.

It said "people from minority ethnic groups (across the industry as a whole) only account for 11% of those in senior management roles".

It also found under-representation in creative, production and on-screen roles.

Mod says she doesn't know if on-screen representation is changing, but says she "won't engage" with a role if she thinks its tokenistic or stereotypical.

"I've been very, very lucky in my career so far from very early on to play really complex, meaty roles and to have changed the narrative in many ways," she says.

"And I'm not looking to regress."

And when it comes to considering what to take on next, she says she tries to follow advice Dame Emma Thompson once gave her: "There's no such thing as a career, there's only what you do next."

"I'm always just trying to focus on what the new challenging thing is going to be, or cool people that I want to work with," she says.

"And also what's going to be fun, as well."

News.title: Briton among six killed in 'far-right' shooting in Krakow
News.content:
A gunman believed to have been inspired by far-right ideology has killed six people and injured more than a dozen others in an attack in the busy centre of Poland's second largest city.

Police said the attacker drove on to Main Market Square in Krakow, a popular tourist attraction, on Saturday afternoon and fired randomly at people.

Four women and two men were killed. Three were Polish, one was British and two have not been identified.

Among the 16 injured are five foreign nationals from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain.

Another three bodies were found when counter-terrorism police searched the suspect's home around 125 miles (200km) away, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.

A massive armed police presence was deployed across Krakow on Saturday evening, as security measures were ramped up in the capital Warsaw and elsewhere.

A period of mourning has been declared in Krakow until 11 November.

Two police officers are also among those injured, one critically.

The suspect, who was equipped with military-style weapons and attire, is a 25-year-old Polish man - described by a minister as "ultra-nationalist".

Police shot and arrested him and he remains in hospital having undergone surgery.

Tusk said there were "strong indications" the two women and one man found dead at the suspect's home in Ostrowiec ÅwiÄtokrzyski were his immediate family members.

He said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism... that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "I'm shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in KrakÃ³w today."

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in the historic centre of Krakow, an ornate square which has long been a draw for tourists.

Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.

The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.

Images from the scene show overturned tables and scattered belongings left behind as people ran for their lives.

Armed police officers pursued the attacker's car until it crashed, at which point they engaged him in a firefight.

Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify captured the moment a police officer confronted the suspect as he lay on the ground.

The officer, who is visibly injured, can then be seen falling to the ground.

News.title: Thousands watch elaborate carnival cart procession
News.content:
Rock shows, Del Boy and his three-wheeler from Only Fools and Horses, and a circus big top were among the themes showcased during a spectacular illuminated carnival procession.

Thousands of people watched the event in Bridgwater, Somerset, where clubs spend the entire year preparing carts for the show.

Dan Prosser from the Renegades Carnival Club said the preparations were "more like a lifestyle than just a hobby," adding his non-carnival friends think his devotion to the event is "absolutely nuts".

The carnival ended with 210 people - including local MP Sir Ashley Fox - taking part in squibbing, where a large firework, strapped to a solid block of wood on the end of a pole, is lit.

News.title: Two men arrested after boy injured in sword attack
News.content:
Two men and a boy have been arrested after a teenager was injured in an attack involving a sword near two schools in Gloucester.

St Peter's High School and Willow Primary Academy, in Tuffley, were put into lockdown after the incident at 08:50 GMT on Friday.

Police said a 17-year-old suffered a wound "believed to have been caused by the sword".

A 19-year-old was arrested overnight on suspicion of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. An 18-year-old was held on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. Meanwhile another 17-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

News.title: Roman settlement dating back 2,000 years found under new-build estate
News.content:
Homes have now been built over the excavation site on Gladstone Way, but not before dozens of items including pottery, coins and the jewellery were removed.

The area was also mapped and showed the settlement extended underneath the village of Mancot, which sits between Hawarden and Queensferry.

Matthews said, in spite of its position overlooking the important Roman city of Chester, very little associated archaeology had been found in north-east Wales until recently.

He said it meant that archaeologists and historians in the area had long debated whether it reflected a "poor relationship" between the Romans and the native population of the time.

But finds such as this one and others in Greenfield and Rossett in Wrexham, were making them realise it "probably wasn't the case".

Matthews said the Mancot site "possibly" originated in the Iron Age period, before the arrival of the Romans, and "continued to have successive occupation for a very long period of time".

This idea was strengthened by two coins found there - one from the reign of the emperor Commodus, who was in power from AD 177 to 192, and another depicting Constantine, who reigned about 200 years later.

News.title: Rob Brydon's battle to stay in character playing Peter O'Toole
News.content:
Actor and comedian Rob Brydon has said it was difficult to stay in character while playing the role of a legendary actor portraying a man who was frequently too hungover to do his job.

He was speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme about his role in new radio drama, Peter O'Toole Is Unwell.

It encompasses O'Toole's critically acclaimed stage role in Jeffrey Bernard is Unwell in the West End in 1999, along with his universally panned performance of Macbeth in 1980.

Brydon, who grew up in Baglan, Port Talbot, said taking on the role "felt like a challenge once we got into the studio" and he battled "to stay on the saddle" to remain in character.

The 61-year-old, known for his role as Uncle Bryn in Gavin and Stacey, said he initially thought "I could probably get close to his voice but there were a lot of words" written by award-winning playwright Terry Johnson.

The title of the audio drama is a riff on Keith Waterhouse's play Jeffrey Bernard Is Unwell, in which O'Toole played the title role of journalist Jeffrey Bernard to rave reviews in 1999.

It is said to derive from the words used by The Spectator magazine when the journalist had missed the deadline to file his column.

News.title: Evacuations in Liverpool city centre after car crash causes gas leak
News.content:
A gas leak caused by a car crashing into a restaurant in Liverpool city centre has led to road closures and the evacuation of neighbouring buildings.

The incident happened at about 12:30 GMT on North John Street when a Peugeot car hit the window of Tiger Rock Restaurant, Merseyside Police said.

The driver stayed at the scene and there is no indication that this was a deliberate act, the force said.

Three people who had been in the restaurant at the time of the crash were assessed for minor injuries, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.

A spokesman said the impact caused a gas leak so a cordon has been put in place by firefighters and the police, with a structural engineer and a gas engineer due to attend.

Neighbouring buildings have been evacuated as a precaution and road closures are in place at the junction of Dale Street and North John Street, and also the junction of North John Street and Lord Street.

Buses have also been temporarily diverted with all Wirral Metro services terminating at Whitechapel, and starting their return journey from Sir Thomas Street.

News.title: Victims in rape cases must not feel like they are on trial, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure that victims in rape cases do not feel like they are on trial.

His comments come after Metropolitan Police boss Sir Mark Rowley told the BBC that what he heard reported from Russell Brand's trial came very close to "victim blaming".

The government needs to "constantly look" at how rape trials are conducted to better support alleged victims in court, the prime minister told Times Radio, although BBC News understands there are no plans to change the law around rape trials.

Actor and comedian Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault after a four-week trial in London.

During an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, it was put to Sir Mark that Brand's defence barrister Ian Winter KC "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".

Sir Mark replied: "I think what I've heard reported heads towards, it's getting very close to victim blaming, which is something we've thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don't do."

He said he would support a call from the Victims' Commissioner for a legal duty that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

"It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark explained.

In a Times Radio interview on Saturday, Burnham said he would "look closely" at the police chief's comments.

He said the government needed to look at how to "make sure they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court".

"[I'm] always prepared to make changes," he said. "We need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape, we need to get the conviction rate up.

"All of this is part of our broader agenda as a government combatting violence against women and girls."

Pressed on whether this might lead to a change in the law, the prime minister replied: "I wouldn't rule anything out... I will study what's happened here in great detail."

Brand, who has starred in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall, will be sentenced on Monday and is expected to face substantial jail time.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault after the jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.

The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody.

It has since been revealed that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Met said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Sir Mark told BBC Breakfast he "wouldn't be surprised if many more came forward".

In the wake of Brand's trial, Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman said rape trials must be conducted "in a way that challenges myths and misconceptions about sexual violence".

In a social media post, Waxman wrote that "victims need confidence that the justice process is fair and based on evidence, not myths and false assumptions about rape and trauma".

Speaking to the Today programme on Saturday, director and founder of the Centre for Women's Justice Harriet Wistrich agreed that juries need to understand "underlying behaviours" without "running to judgement" over how a victim behaved in a particular way.

But former Conservative MP Anna Soubry, who has now returned to her work as a barrister where she often defends rape and sexual offence cases in the Crown court, told the BBC "people are being misled" by Sir Mark's comments.

"Every single judge in those cases must give, and does give, a very firm direction to the jury on exactly these points," she said.

As a result, she said she was " really disappointed" in the police chief and stressed "we've got to trust our juries" who are able to have an understanding of the nature of sexual offences.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

News.title: We thought mum abandoned us - then we discovered she'd been murdered
News.content:
"We didn't have anyone to support us really in our lives. We struggled growing up," added Mehmet.

They were unaware that their mother had been beaten to death by her partner before hiding her body in the cellar of their home for about a year before disposing of her remains in household waste bins.

The court heard Dunkley had maintained his account that Lashley had disappeared for decades, despite being spoken to by police multiple times.

He said she had left her youngest child, who was not Dunkley's son, alone in their flat. Dunkley took the nine-month-old to social services and he was later adopted.

Judge Chambers said the "most significant aggravating factor" in the case was that Dunkley had killed the mother of a baby, who she had still been breastfeeding.

Mehmet said Dunkley killed his mother "in such a horrible way and then lied to us for 27 years", and that learning about her death had made him feel guilty about the resentment he had felt in the past.

"I feel bad in a way now that I felt that way towards mum," he said.

News.title: Briton among six killed in horrific mass shooting at Polish tourist spot
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A British national was one of six people shot dead in Krakow on Saturday by a gunman authorities suspected was inspired by far-right ideologies.

Polish defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz described the horrific attack in the city’s main market square as an “act of terror”.

Police said the gunman drove into Krakow’s historic quarter and began randomly firing at people, killing four women and two men. In addition to the Briton, the victims included three Polish citizens. The other two were still to be identified.

Armed officers rushed to the scene and engaged the gunman in a shootout. Two officers were injured in the shootout and one remained in critical condition after suffering three gunshot wounds.

The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish man from Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, a town almost 120 miles north of Krakow, was shot and detained by armed officers.

A regional spokesperson told Reuters the gunman was in a “stable but very critical condition” following multiple surgeries.

In all, police said, 17 people were injured in the incident.

Following the attack, police discovered the bodies of two women and a man at the suspect’s home. Prime minister Donald Tusk announced the discovery and said they were likely the shooter’s close family members.

“We are undertaking activities at the place where the perpetrator lived, so I think we’ll know more about what those investigations bring,” police commander-in-chief Marek Boron said.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwinski said the attacker held “very radical views” and “was fascinated by far-right ideologies”.

open image in gallery Emergency services arrive at the scene following the shooting ( AFP/Getty )

After it emerged that a British citizen was among the dead, prime minister Andy Burnham paid tribute to the victims of the attack. “I am shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Krakow today,” he said. “My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured, and those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland.”

The FCDO advised British nationals in Krakow to “follow the advice of local authorities and monitor local media”.

In a statement, foreign secretary Ed Miliband said the government “deeply mourns the British national and other victims who have died after the appalling attack in Krakow”.

“All of my deepest condolences go to the families of the victims. The UK stands resolutely in solidarity with the people of Poland,” he said.

open image in gallery Investigators at the scene of the shooting on Saturday night ( Reuters )

Police said the suspect wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest and used a military-grade gun. They did not give a motive for the attack.

Polish media reported that the suspect’s 52-year-old father had 11 registered firearms and he owned the car, a black Subaru, that was used in the attack.

Police found a military-style backpack, magazines and a bayonet in the boot of the car, Radio Kielce reported.

Defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, however, said the suspect wasn’t a soldier and had no links to the military.

According to local media, neither the suspect nor his father had a criminal record. The Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime was analysing the attacker’s online activity to see whether he belonged to radical groups.

Mayor Łukasz Gibała said Krakow would observe an official mourning period until Wednesday, but vowed that the city would remain open to visitors despite the tragedy. “The square will belong to us again,” he said.

open image in gallery A police officer stands guard at the site of the shooting ( Reuters )

Footage posted on social media by witnesses showed people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims.

In one video, a police officer was seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse himself to the ground.

The Krakow market square is typically busy with horse-drawn carriages and is popular with tourists.

News.title: Who is the Krakow shooting suspect ‘influenced by far-right ideology’?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Six people, including a British national, were killed in a shooting in the Polish city of Krakow on Saturday.

The attack occurred at around 3pm local time when a gunman opened fire in the city’s main square.

The victims include four women and two men. At least 16 people were injured, including two police officers, one of whom was reported to be in a “very critical condition”.

The gunman was detained after he was wounded in an exchange of fire with police officers. He remained in hospital as of Saturday evening.

Follow the latest updates here

open image in gallery The shooting occurred in Krakow's main market square ( Getty )

Who is the suspect?

Authorities say the suspect is a 25-year-old Polish man.

Police said in an X post that “the only known perpetrator of the incident is in custody”. They did not give a motive for the shooting.

Police spokesperson Katarzyna Cislo said the suspect wore military-like clothes and used military-grade weapons, Reuters reported. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said he was not a soldier and had no connection with the military.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwinski told reporters the shooter was influenced by “far-right ideologies”.

“Everything points to the fact that the shooter was influenced by far-right ideology, a matter that will also be subject to investigation,” Mr Kierwinski said.

“It looks like he had very radical views. Many guns were found in the car he was driving. A search is still being carried out.”

The suspect likely took guns for the attack from his family home, with the interior minister revealing his father owned several firearms.

Police officer Andrzej Fijolek told TVN 24 that the gunman used an AR-15 rifle and held a firearms licence.

open image in gallery Polish prime minister Donald Tusk says suspect’s connection to far-right ideology will be a point of investigation ( AP )

Three people found dead at suspect’s home

Three people were found dead at the shooter’s home. They included two women and one man, who prime minister Donald Tusk said were assumed to be the suspect’s “close family”.

“It looks like they are members of his close family,” he said, confirming the discovery. It’s unclear how the victims are related to the shooter, and their identities and ages are yet to be disclosed.

What are police doing?

Authorities are currently searching the suspect’s home. Mr Tusk said police expected to find an extensive cache of weapons there.

"There could be quite a lot of arms, quite a lot of guns in this house," he said.

The suspect’s connection to far-right ideology would be a point of inquiry, Mr Tusk said, adding that "possible supporters of the perpetrator" should expect to be detained “very quickly”.

“Police officers are on-site, as are agents from the Internal Security Agency, both here at the scene and at the individual's family home,” the interior minister said.

News.title: ‘We heard about 20 shots’: Witnesses describe terror of Krakow shooting that left six people dead
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Terrified witnesses described the moment a gunman opened fire in Krakow’s market square, killing six people, including a British national, on Saturday.

Police said the man drove a car into the market square in Krakow, Poland’s second-largest city and a popular tourist destination, just before 3pm, and started firing randomly at people, who fled in panic.

Armed officers rushed to the scene and engaged the gunman in a shootout. Two officers were injured in the shootout, and one remained in critical condition after suffering three gunshot wounds.

Four women and two men were killed, Poland’s police chief Marek Boron told reporters in the evening. In addition to the Briton, the victims included three Poles. The remaining two were yet to be identified.

At least 16 people were injured, including the suspect, the two police officers, and five foreigners from Britain, Germany, Austria, Portugal and Russia, the interior ministry said.

Follow the latest updates here

The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen who was shot and taken to hospital, had been “influenced by far-right ideology”, Polish interior minister Marcin Kierwinski said.

Police said in a post on X that “the only known perpetrator of the incident is in custody”. They did not give a motive.

open image in gallery A shooter opened fire in the main market square of Krakow, Poland, on 7 November 2026 ( AP )

The shooter was wearing military-like clothes and used military-grade weapons. “Many weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle too,” Katarzyna Cislo, a local police spokesperson, said.

The gunman was in a “stable but very critical condition” after multiple surgeries, a spokesperson for the Lesser Poland Voivodeship office, the regional authority for southern Poland, told Reuters.

Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said that two women and one man were found dead during searches of the suspect’s home. They were believed to be his close family, Mr Tusk said.

Witnesses of the shooting recalled the moment they heard gunshots and ran for cover. One person reported hearing “about 20 shots”.

The market square is typically busy with traditional horse-drawn carriages and is popular with tourists.

“We were walking to the store and heard gunshots. We turned around, people started running, tourists from other countries didn’t know what was happening,” a witness identified as Aleksander told Poland’s Faktowi. “We heard about 20 shots.”

He said he “ran into the store, the lady closed the door, and we waited a moment”.

“I’ve never witnessed such panic. People were running into stores to hide,” he said.

Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle flew to the city on Saturday and said she heard the shots ringing from her hotel.

“We heard shots from hotel room but didn’t realise what it was until we received a call from the hotel confirming there had been a shooting,” she told the BBC.

She said police were outside the hotel “barricading” the street.

open image in gallery Police guard the access to an area in the historic centre of Krakow ( AFP/Getty )

Some witnesses told TV Republika they saw a black Subaru drive up to the market square. “I saw the guy, he started loading his machine gun,” one witness told the news station. “I don’t think he was firing blindly, these were deliberate shots. He had a sort of police mask on and goggles on. Then he shot at the church and fled towards Grodzka Street. Everyone was running away, people in horse-drawn carriages.”

One man described how several people cowered for safety in a police station after the shots rang out.

“I saw shots being fired from the driver’s side window, and smoke was coming out,” the man, who said his name was Konrad, told Interia.

“I ran to the police station in the main market square; when I burst inside, it was full of people hiding on the floor.”

A 67-year-old man called Julek told Reuters that he narrowly missed being shot himself. Julek saw a dark car appear suddenly before the driver started shooting at a group of people and drove off.

“If we had been two minutes earlier, we might have been shot,” he said.

open image in gallery A woman reacts at the site of a shooting near the main market square of Krakow ( Reuters )

Mr Kierwinski told reporters on Saturday evening that the suspect was interested in far-right ideology.

“Everything points to the fact that ‌the shooter ‌was influenced by far-right ideology, a ⁠matter that will also be subject to investigation,” he said.

“Police officers are on-site, as are ‌agents from ​the Internal Security ‌Agency, both ⁠here at ⁠the scene and at ‌the individual’s ​family ‌home.”

Police spokesperson Andrzej Fijolek told private broadcaster TVN ⁠24 that the assailant used an AR-15 rifle and that he had a firearms licence.

The mass shooting is the largest Poland has seen. It has shocked a country that has long viewed itself as safer than the western European nations that have suffered similar attacks.

It follows a string of school stabbings in October that Mr Tusk said were fuelled by online glorification of violence.

Poland will observe a period of national mourning on Sunday and Monday.

News.title: France facing fly half crisis for Springboks clash after Romain Ntamack injury
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

France are facing a fly half crisis for their clash with South Africa after losing Romain Ntamack to a shoulder injury.

Ntamack was forced off in the first half of the 54-17 win over Fiji in Lyon grasping his left shoulder, with head coach Fabien Galthie confirming afterwards that the issue was “pretty serious” and likely to rule him out of the remainder of the Nations Championship.

Galthie is already without Matthieu Jalibert and Thomas Ramos, with Antoine Hastoy another of his playmaking options sidelined.

Stade Francais fly half Louis Carbonel, who has five caps, has been summoned to the squad to prepare for the Springboks, while uncapped youngster Axel Desperes has begun the season in good form for Pau.

It appears likely, though, that Galthie may pair captain Antoine Dupont and Maxime Lucu in the halves in Paris on Friday.

The two scrum halves are each capable at No 10, with Lucu starting there recently for Bordeaux Begles in the Investec Champions Cup against Gloucester.

open image in gallery Antoine Dupont could be paired with fellow scrum half Maxime Lucu ( Reuters )

Veteran centre Gael Fickou has meanwhile been recalled to the France squad as he looks to add to his 98 caps, with wing Teddy Thomas is rewarded for his form for Toulouse more than five years on from his last international appearance.

Julien Marchand also bolsters the hooking options having made his Top 14 return on Saturday..
