News.title: Greg Wise: ‘Being there at the end of someone’s life is an exquisite privilege’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Greg Wise is not, he stresses, an “expert” on grief. “I’m not a therapist. I’m not a grief counsellor. I’m not an academic. I only know the stuff that I know, that I have felt,” he says.

Expert or not, the Crown actor has unexpectedly found himself occupying a space in which grief is his bread and butter, the water in which he swims – something he spends far more time thinking and talking about than his next potential starry TV or film role.

The catalyst for this evolution was arguably Not That Kind of Love, the book he co-wrote with his late sister Clare and published in 2018. Based on the blog she began when she was diagnosed with breast cancer five years earlier, it charts the highs and lows of the last few years of her life; Wise became her carer in the three months preceding her death in 2016, and took over writing when she became too weak to type.

“That was published eight years ago now, and I feel so privileged to, in the interim, have got to know so many extraordinary people in the dying, death and grief world – and I think I’ve learnt quite a bit,” says Wise, now 60. “I’m still getting people stopping me on railway platforms and talking about death.”

We may not be on a railway platform, but we are nonetheless here talking about death – the subject of his new book, Grief Talking, a memoir of sorts in which Wise explores the various losses of his life and the lessons he’s learnt as a result. He describes himself as “a narrator of various different grief stories”, the aim being “to just set myself up as the storyteller of: this is what happened, this is how I reacted, and this is what I’ve learnt – and that’s all.”

“I’m grateful,” he says, “that I was able to write a book without, I think, giving a single piece of advice.”

This foray into literature is the latest move in a 35-year career that has always prioritised variety above all else. After studying drama at the Royal Scottish Academy of Music and Drama, Wise starred in a slew of TV and film roles in the Nineties, with a penchant for playing classically handsome heartthrobs in period dramas like The Buccaneers and The Moonstone. But while acting may have been his first love, it’s never been his only one.

“I’ve always had a reasonably fluid relationship with acting,” he says. “I haven’t done that much over the years; I’ve always been too interested in too many other things.” These “things” include making documentaries, writing screenplays, and his work as a Patron for End of Life Doula UK. He also spends a lot of time up in Scotland, mountaineering, cider-making, and tending to his beloved collection of chainsaws and power tools. “I have an appetite for lots of different things,” Wise says.

open image in gallery Greg Wise and Emma Thompson in ‘Sense and Sensibility’ ( Columbia Pictures )

Grief Talking encompasses Clare’s death, of course, but Wise writes equally movingly about various other bereavements including the sudden death of his university friend in an accident, the intergenerational grief passed down in his family that resulted in cold and distant fathers and narcissistic mothers, and the death of both his parents.

“There is an exquisite privilege of both the journey and the bearing witness of the end,” Greg says of the fact he has been there for all three of his immediate family members at the end of their lives. “I would be very happy for more people to have this experience.”

All this talk of pain and death has swept away any need for small talk. “I may cut to the chase now,” Wise observes about himself. “There’s not a lot of foreplay – we don’t really have time for foreplay.” It’s true that the actor has a “straight to the point” quality about him, and given the sombre topic of conversation, it’s a wonder that the mood is not remotely gloomy. Joining me over video call from his home, Wise is instead lively, his face expressive and animated as he talks about how looking death squarely in the face can be the key to unlocking life’s deep joys; “The most raucous laughter I’ve ever heard was in a hospital,” he observes.

open image in gallery Greg Wise with his adopted son Tindy Agaba, wife Emma Thompson, and daughter Gaia (left to right) ( AFP/Getty )

His voice is deep and resonant, still instantly recognisable, more than 30 years on, as that of Wise’s most famous role: Mr Willoughby in director Ang Lee’s beloved 1995 adaptation of Sense and Sensibility. (He hasn’t seen the new film starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and is therefore unable to comment on how it compares; “Your words, not mine,” he responds wryly when I gush that his was the definitive version and that, as far as I’m concerned, there was no need to make another adaptation ever again.)

It was on the set of the Jane Austen classic in 1995 that Greg met his future wife, Emma Thompson. The celebrated actor, writer and director had both written the screenplay and was playing Elinor Dashwood; he was cast as the caddish love interest of her on-screen “sister” Marianne (Kate Winslet).

Thompson had just ended her marriage with fellow actor Kenneth Branagh following his very public affair with Helena Bonham Carter, and Wise was Thompson’s knight in shining armour, ready to all but whisk her away on a white horse, he writes in Grief Talking. They married in 2003.

I’m still getting people stopping me on railway platforms and talking about death

Both came into the relationship with their own traumas, but it wasn’t until later, when the pair started trying for a family, that they encountered a new form of grief as a couple. After attempts to conceive naturally failed, they were forced down the IVF route. The first round was successful, resulting in their daughter Gaia, now 26; the subsequent rounds were not. “It was a mesmeric grief for the two of us,” Wise recalls. “It is a really isolating experience, especially as a man – the woman is going through most of that, and you’re on the outskirts, doing very little, but still so invested.”

When a second pregnancy didn’t materialise, both Wise and Thompson mourned the child they had hoped to have. The individual ways they each grieved, though, were so different that it became “very atomising”.

“You split into two separate bits,” he says. “You’ve got these two different forms of grief playing out, where it’s quite hard to connect… I felt that I had to be supportive and not look in on the pain that I was feeling, but also unable to connect with Em’s grief. It took us quite a while to navigate through that.”

The couple eventually found their way back to each other, and in 2003 adopted Tindyebwa Agaba, or “Tindy”, a Rwandan orphan and former child soldier.

open image in gallery Greg Wise as Lord Louis Mountbatten in ‘The Crown’ ( Netflix )

It was this difference in grieving styles that inspired Wise to write his book. While much has been published on grief, there is “a dearth of books for men,” he argues. Through his own experiences and research, he found that men and women tend to grieve differently.

“We are all intrinsically individual, but there’s a tendency for women to be able to grieve emotionally, and there’s a tendency for men to keep it cerebral,” he explains. “It’s all part of the schtick that we’re brought up with as boys: big boys don’t cry. Be in control. Be protective. Be proactive. Men generally treat grief as a challenge to be overcome.”

That perspective means men often retreat inwards instead of seeking help. And help is crucial: “Asking for help saved my life,” Wise says simply. He thinks everybody could probably use a bit of therapy; “I absolutely do think professional help is essential.” There are some things that can’t be “walked off” or solved by chatting to your mates, however well-meaning or lovely they are.

My family and I have had some wonderful discussions about how we want to die

Doing his own extensive therapy has, Wise tells me, enabled him to live in a much more expansive way. “I don’t want to get all hippy about it,” he laughs, “but I know that by having done my grief work, that by having sat in the pain and listened to it and learned from it and been given help with it, I am more compassionate. I’m more loving. I’ve got more gratitude. I’m more empathic. I’m kinder. I’ve got joy.”

It’s also made him more fearless. Wise credits his sister’s death for giving him the no-f***s-given courage to compete on Strictly Come Dancing in 2021. “It helps you put things in a little bit of perspective,” he says. “You know, I crashed spectacularly in front of however many million people watching Sunday night live telly. Great! I’m not going to die.”

open image in gallery Greg Wise competed on ‘Strictly’ in 2021 ( BBC )

Wise and his partner Karen Hauer were eliminated in the fourth week, but not before he paid tribute to Clare with a poignant couple’s choice dance dedicated to his disco-loving sister. Now, he’s ready to test life’s limits some more. “I want to see what happens and give it a go. What’s the worst thing that can happen? Ritual humiliation on Strictly? That’s fine! That’s the gig.”

Greg may not be an “expert” on grief, but he does have a couple of words of wisdom he wouldn’t mind passing on. Firstly: address the practicalities around death while you’re still hale and hearty. Wise is a big advocate for putting together a “death box” of all relevant documents and details, such as lasting power of attorney (LPA), an advance plan for end of life, funeral preferences or arrangements, and details and passwords for various accounts.

“My family and I have had some wonderful discussions about how we want to die,” he says cheerfully. “It’s not maudlin because we’re all going to die, and we want to try to do it as well as we can – not just the person dying, but all the people around them. You know, it’s a communal endeavour, a good death.”

Secondly, he implores people to actually engage with their grief, in all its forms and complications. “Do the work. Sit in it. Face into it. Listen to it. Ask for help, but do the work. The rewards are boundless: it’s all about living better, living more fully, being more present, being more grounded and grateful, and compassionate, and empathic with yourself as well as the wider world.”

“I think it’s a world game-changer, grief work,” he says. “I really do.”

‘Grief Talking’ by Greg Wise is published by Bluebird, an imprint of Pan Macmillan (hardback, £18.99)

News.title: The 15-minute exercise trick a busy retired athlete uses to stay in shape
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The article below is an excerpt from my newsletter: Well Enough with Harry Bullmore. To get my latest thoughts on fitness and wellbeing, pop your email address into the box above to get the newsletter directly to your inbox.

Athletes Mat Fraser and Tia-Clair Toomey have been dubbed the “fittest man and woman in history”.

At the Rogue Invitational fitness competition, both discussed a pivotal moment in their lives that changed their approach to staying in shape: becoming parents.

When he was competing as a CrossFit athlete, Fraser would say that, if staying in shape meant enough to someone, they would find the time. “Then I [retired from competition,] worked a regular job and had kids,” he says with a sheepish grin.

After the birth of her second child earlier this year, Toomey is prioritising her kids while getting back to daily training, balancing umpteen business endeavours and deciding what she wants to do next.

“There’s the reality of feeling guilty for not putting all of my time into one sole thing, because there are just so many things that I’m trying to do,” she tells me.

The fitness feats of both athletes are hard to relate to – they can rip hundreds of kilos from the floor and perform gravity-defying gymnastic stunts. But many will recognise the struggle of balancing busy work, family and social lives with the extra commitment of staying fit and healthy.

So, I decided to ask Fraser and Toomey – two vocationally fit people – how they make exercise work for them. That is the theme of this week’s newsletter.

open image in gallery Tia-Clair Toomey: ‘I’ve just been trying to take as many steps as I can’ ( Pliability )

“For the last four weeks we’ve been travelling around Europe for work, so I haven’t been [training too consistently],” Toomey says. “I’ve just been trying to take as many steps as I can. I have a competition with my husband, my sister and her boyfriend.”

After the birth of her first child, Toomey returned to competition after five months. This time, she is looking to “do things a little bit differently,” taking a slower approach.

“It’s still very important for me to be moving my body – it makes me feel good,” she says. “I’ve been doing strength work, but nothing crazy. And some days Shane [her husband] and I will do partner workouts and just have fun with it. Doing it in good company is an easy source of encouragement.”

Fraser, on the other hand, found that retiring from competitive sport and becoming a father flipped his worldview from “I have to train” to “I get to train”.

“Nap time is my training time now,” he says – a far cry from the four-plus-hour sessions he regularly hit during his career.

Fraser uses strength training and CrossFit-style circuit workouts to keep his muscles, heart and lungs healthy. And, on days when time is particularly tight, he employs a 15-minute trick to keep things ticking over.

He picks a piece of cardio kit like an exercise bike, rowing machine, SkiErg or Stairmaster, then uses it for 15 minutes. The first three minutes act as a warm-up, easing his body into the session, then he pushes the pace and gets out of breath over the next 12 minutes. And that’s it – simple, accessible, effective.

Talking to both athletes, I get the impression that the “perfect workouts” social media so often sells us are nigh-on non-existent. But from experience, they both know how doing something, rather than nothing, will only increase their health and happiness.

The same applies to all of us. “Perfect” is an unrealistic goal many of us are guilty of setting. When we fall short, it’s easy to think, “What’s the point?” and return to old ways.

Whereas, if we simply focus on doing “something” on a semi-regular basis, the pressure is off. By giving us more opportunities to play around with different ways of moving, it has the power to be rather fun too.

News.title: This upper eyelid surgery might be why your favourite celebrity suddenly looks so weird
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The trend of celebs getting “work” done is nothing new. It used to be confined to the older contingent, the merry-go-round of botox, fillers and facelifts a mainstay of women (and men) of a certain age desperate to hold back the hands of time.

More recently, we’ve seen the average age for these procedures dropping dramatically. People in their forties, thirties and even twenties are subscribing to a full gamut of regular tweakments and treatments to achieve the same eerily similar “Instagram face” of homogenised hotness.

Within this world of non-stop self “improvement”, specific cosmetic trends go in and out of fashion, from the tell-tale, hollowed out cheeks of buccal fat removal to the sudden uncanny uplift enabled by the deep plane facelift. Now, it’s the turn of the eyelids to get their moment in the spotlight.

Upper blepharoplasty surgery, often colloquially referred to as “bleph” surgery, involves removing excess or sagging skin, muscle, and sometimes fat from the upper eyelids to give a more open and youthful look. It has “100 per cent” become more popular in recent years, according to Dr Rishi Mandavia, a consultant ENT and facial plastic surgeon specialising in facial surgery and rejuvenation.

“One of the first surgical procedures that patients will have for anti-aging and facial rejuvenation is an upper blepharoplasty surgery, because the upper eyelids are really hard to address non-surgically,” he says. “As a result, it’s a really nice first option for surgery where you’re going to have a fantastic result, it’s very safe, low downtime, and most people are candidates for it by a certain stage in life.”

open image in gallery There has been speculation about Emma Stone's upper blephs ( PA )

And indeed, the procedure used to be the preserve of people who were 50+, an age at which the eyes might have naturally become more hooded with crepey, excess skin. However, these days an increasingly young demographic has started enquiring about getting their blephs done.

“We are seeing a higher number of younger patients seeking this surgery,” says Dr Mandavia. He will often steer people away from it: “I’m saying no a lot of the time to those patients if it’s not appropriate for them. What you don’t want to do is remove any extra skin if there’s not enough excess, because that can lead to the horrors of incomplete eye closure, really bad scarring, dry eyes.”

There’s an argument that more young people are interested in this kind of procedure – and are even aware of its existence – because a growing number of young famous faces appear to be getting it done.

In the cult of Hollywood cosmetics, it’s very hard to say for sure who’s had what; most A-listers remain tight-lipped about the amount of “help” they’ve had to stay permanently pert and youthful, often explaining away their newly snatched visage with vague reference to some mythical combination of impeccable sleep hygiene and drinking plenty of water.

But speculation is rife. The latest face to raise eyebrows – pun intended – belongs to Jennifer Lawrence. The 36-year-old Hunger Games actor recently starred in a photoshoot for The Cut; the resulting pictures that have been circulated online, in which J-Law’s lids appeared discernibly taut and her brows lifted, immediately sparked rumours of upper bleph surgery.

There was outcry – Lawrence has always been known for her distinctive brand of beauty and non-cookie cutter features, including sultry, slightly hooded eyes. Any talk of procedures is completely unsubstantiated, however and – who knows? – maybe it’s just a trick of make-up, lighting and Photoshop.

open image in gallery Taylor Swift's blephs have been subject to scrutiny ( AFP/Getty )

Her Silver Linings Playbook co-star, Bradley Cooper, is another member of Hollywood royalty whose appearance set tongues wagging, with claims that he’d “gone too far” in 2023. There was speculation, again completely unsubstantiated, that the then-48-year-old had undergone an op on his blephs (among other cosmetic procedures) during the press tour for his film Is This Thing On?.

On a podcast earlier this year, Cooper appeared to agree with his longtime friends and hosts Jason Bateman and Will Arnett when they vehemently denied any plastic surgery claims, calling the idea “hilarious”.

Fans are also adamant that a number of young women in the public eye have had the procedure, with compelling “before” and “after” photo composites published online of the likes of Taylor Swift (36), Miley Cyrus (33) and Emma Stone (38). It’s important to be clear that all of these claims are also unconfirmed and uncorroborated.

Whether or not these particular performers have had an upper blepharoplasty is almost irrelevant. The mere discussion about the procedure has a knock-on effect on us mere mortals, resulting in an uptick in young people, particularly women, seeking surgical intervention to keep up with the Joneses. Or should that be the Kardashians?

open image in gallery Bradley Cooper has denied plastic surgery claims ( PA )

There is a palpable sadness beneath all of this. “Bleph” content is all over social media; Insta is saturated with before and after surgery posts, while other users are mourning what they see as another blow for individuality, uniqueness and character when it comes to facial aesthetics.

“Nobody appears to have eyelids anymore,” as one podcast host puts it. “Eyelids are over.”

But there is also some push-back. Kyla Cobbler, an Irish stand-up comedian with 1.3 million Instagram followers who has made a heartening amount of content celebrating lines, wrinkles and the natural aging process, posted a video with the caption: “All hail the upper bleph”.

“They’ve now started telling us that this piece of skin above our eyeball, that’s necessary to help us blink, is unattractive,” she says. “I mean really, they’re just pulling it out of their arses at this point.”

She reminds her followers that they have “other options”, and encourages them to spend the money they’ve saved for surgery on a trip to the beach instead. Her rallying cry should perhaps inspire us all: “Get your blephs out for the lads!”

And just remember: as with everything else in life, aesthetic fashions come and go. Why not hang onto your eyelid skin, sit back, and simply wait for the inevitable day that hooded eyes are a la mode once more? You don't know what you’ve got till it’s gone, after all.

News.title: Lando Norris takes pole at Interlagos after chaotic qualifying session
News.content:
McLaren’s Lando Norris claimed pole for the São Paulo Grand Prix for a third consecutive year as he emerged victorious from a marathon, rain-affected qualifying session at Interlagos lasting two and a half hours.

But there was further frustration for his compatriot George Russell, who lashed out at his Mercedes pit wall after being told to abort a push lap in Q3 which he felt would have been good enough to finish qualifying in first place.

Whether Russell was right was debatable, but you could understand his frustration. The Briton has endured a miserable season, dropping from second to fourth in the drivers’ championship in Mexico last weekend after suffering yet another power unit issue.

Russell ended up leaving the Mexico paddock early while team-mate Kimi Antonelli celebrated becoming the sport’s youngest ever champion.

News.title: Man City look to be crumbling after guilty verdict
News.content:
Is this the day the xG gods reward Nottingham Forest? Oliver Glasner’s team sit 19th having won one game all season, but there is no doubt that their performances have been significantly better than results and they might need their luck to turn against Man City team full of firepower.

Despite all of the positive indicators in Forest’s underlying data, Glasner caused some alarm with his comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford.

The Austrian said: “We have to accept it’s not good enough. If we lose four of the last five games, it’s not good enough. And that’s why for me, it’s now time that we change things, that I change things, and that’s what I will do.

“I feel now maybe I made too many compromises in some stuff, and it’s always compromises. It’s a clear way. I will tell [the players] what we want to do, what we have to do, and if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround, and if not, the sixth manager [since the start of last season] will come in.”

Dangerous words perhaps when you work for Evangelos Marinakis, but John Percy reported this week that Glasner was backed by his players in a squad meeting.

City are smarting from back-to-back defeats by Aston Villa and Brighton, but they created more than enough in both games to claim some sort of result. Nevertheless, there is a persistent sense that their defensive unit remains too marshmellow-like over the course of 38 games, and Forest have the counter-attacking threat to test them.

Glasner has happy memories of playing City, beating them in the 2025 FA Cup final with Crystal Palace, but his Forest reign is in urgent need of a signature victory and performance.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Rees-Zammit delivers in best position but work to do for sloppy Wales
News.content:
Maybe it is an indication that Wales are improving that this latest close victory over Japan was greeted with a shrug instead of euphoria.

A year ago, almost to the day, Steve Tandy, the Welsh head coach jumped around and hugged his staff, after a one-point win over the Brave Blossoms and there were reports of red-shirted fans in this stadium crying in joy and relief.

Yet that was Wales’s first home success in 10 Tests and, despite the form since hardly raising itself anywhere near levels of excellence, much more was expected on this occasion.

Yes, Tandy’s men prevailed and it was a huge positive to watch player-of-the match Louis Rees-Zammit in great nick on the wing. Nobody should overestimate the Bristol man’s display because the game knows that he can operate even better, but after this there can now be no doubt that he is a wing rather than a full-back. The 25-year-old conjured five line breaks, beat 13 defenders and made 121 metres.

Yet most notably, Rees-Zammit scored his first try for his country in eight matches and that is exactly what he was put on the green-green grass to do. After assisting in fellow wing Josh Adams’s opening try – this other resurgent British and Irish Lion bagged a brace – Rees-Zammit showed his predatory instincts to go over after a wonderful deft offload from centre Eddie James.

News.title: Odegaard winner spares officials from bizarre VAR row
News.content:
Newly-promoted Hull City stunned Arsenal at the Emirates thanks to goals from Geovanni and Daniel Cousin in September 2008, but you will find long odds on them repeating the feat this afternoon.

With Manchester City playing at Nottingham Forest in the later kick-off, Mikel Arteta’s team have the chance to extend their lead at the top of the Premier League and make it 27 points from a possible 30 going into the international break.

Victory at Anfield last weekend was achieved with steel and resolve, but the more intricate side of Arsenal’s attacking play will be under the microscope against opponents likely to defend deep and in numbers.

With that in mind, it was noteworthy that Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes and Myles Lewis-Skelly started the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on the bench, with only Odegaard coming on.

Declan Rice played the full 90 minutes, and one wonders if this is a rare chance for Arteta to leave him out of a Premier League starting XI.

Hull are 12th and have lost only two league games, a performance which far exceeds the gloomy pre-season forecasts for their chances. However, they are winless since the end of August and have not kept a clean sheet since a goalless draw with Aston Villa on Sept 4.

There is one other three o’clock kick-off: Fulham host Newcastle United at Craven Cottage, with Matthias Jaissle under increasing pressure.

Newcastle were booed off at St James’ Park on Monday after their limp defeat by Everton, and have looked far too easy to play through all season, with their defensive statistics making for grim reading.

Alvaro Arbeloa was in Jaissle’s position a few weeks ago, but Fulham appear to have turned a corner and were impressive in a 1-1 at Villa Park last time out. There were reports of dressing room unrest, but Fulham rank highly for possession and chance creation so it appears the Spaniard is putting his stamp on things.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Spurs to make formal complaint over Jayden Bogle decision
News.content:
Very happy against an in-form side. The first-half was [even], they were in front, we were in front but the second half, it was never in doubt. We were pushing, making chances and we were relentless. After a difficult period with key players out we showed great spirit and unity today. It was a fully deserved win and we are happy.

Sometimes [substitutions] work like this! Noah was a lat call. He has been a whole week out of training. Credit to the physios and our medical department because the doctors said at the beginning of the week that he had no chance of the weekend. In the end they said if I was disciplined and didn’t put him on the pitch for more than 15-20 minutes he could play. And a first assist for Harry [Wilson] and an ice-cold finish from Noah.

If you accept all Tottenham’s invitations to stop the pass with your pressing, this is what they want to bypass you. You have to close the centre and be spot on to allow them possession in areas where they can’t hurt you but be brave when you have the [right] position to press and also in our possession.

I haven’t watched it back. I know there were a couple of situations, a hand ball and this one but I can tell you that Jayden Bogle has no bad intention.That I can guaranteed. It looked unlucky and an unlucky outcome. We hope Mathys [Tel] will recover quickly and we wish him all the best. Jayden is not a nasty player, he is perhaps the softest in the whole league. I call him my butterfly.

We were unlucky at Arsenal and not to get anything at Sundeland and Bournemouth. Against Manchester United we were far the better side but you can see how quickly momentum can slip at this level and for that it’s good to have the winning feeling back and for that credit to my boys.

News.title: Brutal truth is Scotland never looked like beating All Blacks
News.content:
“They [New Zealand] are playing some excellent rugby right now and it is our first game of the season, which is always the toughest challenge for us too. It is a different New Zealand team. It is a team that is playing much more ambitious rugby. They are informed, they are cohesive. They played a lot of Test matches over the summer. We are going to have to find ways to win, find ways to stay in the fight because they will have a lot of possession too.”

New Zealand won all three of their home fixtures back in July in the first half of the Nations Championship, beating France, Italy and Ireland to claim a maximum 15 points. They faced Australia in two Bledisloe Cup fixtures last month, with the All Blacks easing to victory in both matches, scoring 93 points. They will go on to face Wales and England after this game. The All Blacks have travelled to the northern hemisphere without captain Ardie Savea, who is sidelined with a shoulder injury.

“Scotland are a quality side,” New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie said. “They are very well coached and have built a lot of depth over recent years. They play a very similar brand of footy to us and we know we will need to be at our best on Saturday [today]. Murrayfield is an iconic place to play so it will be a special occasion to kick off our northern tour.”

It has been an emotional week for the All Blacks as they continue to come to terms with the tragic loss of their long-time head of security Logan Cadwallader, who died at the team’s Edinburgh hotel earlier this week.

Kick-off from Murrayfield is at 2.10pm.

News.title: Feinberg-Mngomezulu leads Springboks’ nine-try obliteration of Italy
News.content:
What a difference a decade makes. In November 2016, Italy beat South Africa for the first, and so far only, time. Now the Springboks have obliterated Italy – and the roots of this victory can be traced back to that defeat 10 years ago.

That historic result sparked a major rethink in South Africa, a rethink that ultimately led to Rassie Erasmus replacing Allister Coetzee as head coach in early 2018. Erasmus has overseen a remarkable transformation of the Boks since: from an embarrassing loss in Italy to back-to-back world champions.

This win in Turin was built on what Erasmus’s Boks are known for: a potently powerful set-piece and a back line that can deliver mesmerising moments. The one disappointment for their head coach will be how they failed to match the intensity and ruthlessness of their first-half performance in the second 40 minutes.

“It’s almost impossible to put 80 minutes together at 100 per cent,” he said afterwards. “But when you win 66-7, I don’t think you can start nitpicking problems in the second half. That said, we have to play much better than this if we want to be competitive against France and Ireland.”

The Boks were 45-0 up at the break having scored six tries. The majority came off the back of their driving line-out, which they were able to launch to great effect inside Italy’s 22. Morne van den Berg, Malcolm Marx (two) and Siya Kolisi were all beneficiaries of the power of their maul in the first half. Damian Willemse also enjoyed an easy run-in when Jasper Wiese released him into space, but the stand-out finish came from Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu inside 10 minutes.

The 24-year-old fly-half is undoubtedly one of the most exciting players in world rugby and he showed his full repertoire here: deft hands, pinpoint vision and metronomic kicking. The opening try was special, too: his dummy carved out the space for him to break through Italy and he then had the pace to beat any chasing defenders to the corner, where he acrobatically finished one-handed.

News.title: Ireland send out ominous warning with second-gear walloping of Argentina
News.content:
Is it time to fire up the emerald green bandwagon? Not quite yet. But this was not a bad start to Ireland’s autumn; a 42-12 walloping of Los Pumas with Andy Farrell’s team still nowhere near their best. That should be highly encouraging for those of an Irish persuasion.

A year out from the World Cups of 2015, 2019 and 2023, Ireland had enjoyed banner seasons, eyeing up global glory. They never made it past the quarter-finals.

The build-up this time has been tougher going – the Aviva, unusually for this time of year – was not even full for this Nations Championship encounter. But perhaps Ireland will be better for it. They had far too much on a crisp Friday night in Dublin for an Argentina team who were missing a few of their stars, notably Bath’s Santiago Carreras and Lyon prop Thomas Gallo, but still packing 750 caps’ worth of Test experience in their starting XV.

Farrell was missing a few big names himself. Caelan Doris and Jack Conan were out injured, with the Englishman opting to hand Sean Jansen and Nick Timoney starts in the back row. Farrell also chose to start Craig Casey rather than Jamison Gibson-Park – arguably their best player of the last 18 months – at scrum-half, with Sam Prendergast starting again at 10 given Jack Crowley’s absence.

All in all there was a slightly experimental feel to proceedings, making Argentina potentially dangerous visitors. But Ireland had far too much in reserve. Hugo Keenan grabbed a hat-trick and took the player of the match award. Robert Baloucoune was consistently excellent. Mack Hansen’s return on the wing was hugely welcome. Tominey stood out in the back row.

Farrell said he was delighted with the result, if not the entire performance, making special mention of the likes of Keenan, Hansen, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter, all of whom were returning from long injury lay-offs.

“The game’s never going to be perfect. But if you look at the bigger picture, to win 42-12 against a really good side in Argentina, I don’t think too many teams have done that,” Farrell said. “You have to be pleased.”

Asked whether he was happier with the 42 points scored or the meagre 12 conceded, Farrell added that it was probably the latter: “We want to be known for our defence. It shows our mentality.”

Los Pumas scored the first try of the game, Mateo Carreras getting the jump on Casey in the corner to field a Tomás Albornoz crossfield kick.

Sports.title: Valencia vs Real Madrid suspended as players carry stretcher across pitch after medical emergency in stands
Sports.content:
FOOTIE WORRY Valencia vs Real Madrid suspended as players carry stretcher across pitch after medical emergency in stands







Next

REAL MADRID’S clash with Valencia was temporarily halted following a medical emergency in the stands.

The match referee stopped the game so that medical attention could be brought to the spectator.

Players from both teams had the situation explained to them by the official in charge.



Valencia stars Pepelu and Jose Gaya made sure to help as much as they could.



The duo, alongside a pair of medical staff, ran with the stretcher to bring it across to the stand as quickly as possible.

Valencia medical staff and stadium paramedics then gave the fan proper attention.

After a delay of a few minutes, the action was able to get back underway.



Real Madrid had led 2-0 at the time of the stoppage.

Federico Valverde fired Jose Mourinho‘s side into the lead shortly before the half hour mark, with Arda Guler doubling his side’s advantage on 36 minutes.

Not long after the second half delay, Kylian Mbappe notched a third to make the points safe.

Gaya, 31, was sent off on 79 minutes and Real Madrid went on to win 3-0.



The match was always going to be played under an emotional backdrop, as both sides joined forces to pay tribute to Jesus de Miguel.

The late Tenerife striker tragically died aged 30 on Tuesday following an accidental collision during a match the previous evening.

Games across Spain this weekend have been marked by touching tributes.



Stars from Valencia and Real Madrid – including the likes of Mbappe and Jude Bellingham – wore T-shirts honouring De Miguel.

The match was also paused on nine minutes so that players, officials, staff and supporters could come together to take part in a minute’s applause.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick has no idea whether he’ll still be Man Utd boss after Aston Villa clash with sacking season approaching
Sports.content:
Next

MICHAEL CARRICK has not been told he is certain to be in charge of Manchester United after their Premier League fixture with Aston Villa on Sunday.

United could be in the relegation zone at kick-off after one win and four defeats from their nine league matches.



Carrick’s position remains in serious doubt after United resisted sacking him in the wake of the 3-0 drubbing by Bournemouth two weeks ago.

United do not play for two weeks after the Villa match due to the November internationals, which is traditionally a time where clubs change managers.



Carrick revealed that he has received no assurances he will remain the United head coach beyond this week but plans are in place for the period.

He said: “No, no. Just carry on as absolute normal.

“Maybe three or four senior players will be in and around [the training ground], but we’ll certainly train next week and maybe have the weekend off.

“We’ll see how that develops, who’s left behind, who’s with us and what they need. But there’ll certainly be training next week.

“Whatever happens, what’s going to happen is going to happen in terms of the game (against Villa), and we’ve got to prepare right, looking forward to it.

“I said the other night I was really looking forward to the game going into it, I genuinely was. I wasn’t making anything up there for you.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

“Playing at home on the back of the other night, the supporters hopefully looking forward to coming and energised and feeling good about what they might see.

“And we’ve got to repay that.”

Carrick is not planning to get away from the United maelstrom during the pause in the schedule. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer returned to his native Norway five years ago after a stay of execution but was sacked after a 4-1 thumping by Watford in United’s first game back following the autumn internationals.

Carrick and his family have lived in Cheshire for 20 years and both of his children have grown up in the area.

His wife, Lisa, has taught pilates in Alderley Edge, their son, Jacey, is in the United academy while daughter Louise has been in attendance for home games this season.



At the end of last season, Carrick joked a summer holiday was not in the offing due to his children’s school exams. He is not expecting a drastically different break this month.

“Not really different to normal,” he added. “Generally not.

“I think international breaks are always a time when talking about the players that aren’t going away and for the staff, I think there is a little bit to re-energise and freshen up.

“I think some of the players that go away in internationals, they get freshened up in a different environment, so there is an element of that, but I don’t really need it. I’m fine as I am.”

Sports.title: Youri Tielemans’ Man Utd boast has massively backfired as Red Devils host Aston Villa sitting 11 points adrift of them
Sports.content:
Next

YOURI TIELEMANS said after his £35million arrival at Old Trafford three months ago: “There are still clubs above Aston Villa and Manchester United is one of them.”

The Belgium captain’s new side are five points below his former employers Villa in the Premier League, with Michael Carrick’s outfit also 11 places adrift of them in the Champions League group phase.



Tielemans is in line to face his previous club this afternoon but the 29-year-old midfielder’s summer move has epitomised United’s malaise this season.

It was an opportunistic buy when a deal for Ederson collapsed as United prised him away from the Midlands by triggering the release clause in his contract.



A reactionary swoop for a player with plenty of miles on the clock — but it has taken its toll.

Tielemans, who claimed at the World Cup his body “switched off”, was the only United player to start the first 12 games this term.

And his leggy performances did not help the team’s woeful run of results.

United have been accused of a lack of running this season but Tielemans is a calm, composed player rather than a bundle of energy in the middle.

Even his old boss Unai Emery admitted he had to be patient with Tielemans when he joined the Villans from Leicester in 2023 — and the Spaniard has backed his former star in the engine room to be a success due to his “mentality”.

Emery said: “We’ll face Youri Tielemans — and he knows us, of course.

“He’s a fantastic player but when he was here, he needed time to adapt to us.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“After that, he performed well for Villa. Now, at Manchester United, he will maybe need some time to adapt.

“But if he plays against us, he will fight with his qualities and mentality. He has a very strong mentality.”

Tielemans has had several United midfield partners already.

He partnered Andrey Santos on the opening weekend of the Premier League and United were bullied in a 2-0 loss at promoted Hull.

He was then paired with Kobbie Mainoo and it did not work.



Tielemans also replaced Bruno Fernandes as the No 10 amid the United captain’s poor run of form before Tielemans got benched for the games against Chelsea and Roma.

He could be reunited with Mainoo today against Villa, the club he helped qualify for the Champions League twice and scored in their Europa League final triumph over Freiburg in May.

That would ordinarily assure Tielemans of applause from the away end.

But, although he did apologise for calling United a bigger club in those pre-season comments, he may get a mixed reception.

Tielemans was better off the bench in Tuesday’s 3-2 Champions League comeback win over Roma, which ended United’s nine-game winless run.



Boss Carrick has indicated that the past few weeks have taken their toll on players whatever age they are.

Tielemans turns 30 next May and is an experienced campaigner, having made his Anderlecht debut aged 16 and played in three World Cups. This is his ninth season in England.

Yet none of that can prepare players for the intense spotlight and scrutiny that comes with troubled times at United — as Tielemans and his team-mates have found this season.



Asked about how his squad have coped, Carrick said: “As an elite athlete, you know we’re always striving for close to perfection.

“You never get perfection but you always want to be getting to that limit really and playing right on the edge.

“With that, I’d say a huge chunk of that is your mindset, your mentality, your confidence.

“So it is about coping with that, that’s a major part of it.

“But it is something that we have to all take into account. Speaking to the players, from my perspective, of understanding where they’re at with it — for sure, it’s important.



“That feeling, momentum in sport, is massive. Momentum within games, momentum day-to-day, week-to-week, game-to-game, it’s huge.

“Sometimes it’s difficult to quantify where that is but with your feelings and emotions, it’s important.

“Then your memory can click in and you realise, ‘Oh yeah, this is what it feels like, this is how it should be’.

“That’s just a form of why players or teams have good spells then struggle in other spells. It’s all got to come together.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But feeling, confidence, and that emotion — sometimes not even thinking you’re at your best, you just trust and play on instinct.



“And I think we did a lot of that the other night against Roma.”

Sports.title: Regis Le Bris admits Granit Xhaka may be battling a hangover after Xabi Alonso and Chelsea’s failed transfer bid
Sports.content:
Next

REGIS LE BRIS concedes Granit Xhaka may be battling a hangover after Xabi Alonso’s failed bid to lure him to Chelsea.

But Sunderland’s boss insists his Swiss Superman’s warrior spirit remains intact.



Xhaka, 34, was top of Alonso’s Stamford Bridge wishlist following the Spaniard’s arrival in West London this summer.

The Blues chief was desperate for a sensational reunion with the talismanic playmaker who inspired his unbeaten Bayer Leverkusen side to the Bundesliga crown.



Yet the Black Cats dug in their heels and blocked the move, keeping the 34-year-old on Wearside.

The form of Xhaka, who later reiterated his commitment to Sunderland, has nose-dived since that saga with the midfield maestro looking a shadow of his former self.

Alonso instead swooped for Jordan Henderson, a Mackem who came through the ranks at his hometown club before a big-money move to Liverpool in 2011.

With Sunderland sitting bottom of the league, few would begrudge Xhaka looking across the pitch against top-four chasing Chelsea’s Henderson with envious eyes this afternoon.

Asked whether the transfer drama has affected Xhaka and potentially fractured the dressing-room harmony, head coach Le Bris admitted: “[It’s] hard to say. It’s always complex. It’s one element in the equation, so I don’t know, to be fair.”

Opposite number Alonso declined to discuss his pursuit of Xhaka. But the Blues manager acknowledged the key role the midfielder had played in Leverkusen’s success.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Alonso said: “We spoke a lot in that time in Leverkusen with Granit because he was a key part of that team.

“He glued many, many pieces together in the middle with the back three. Mostly with the players around him. It was a very good time together and I’m looking forward to seeing him on Sunday.”

Xhaka struggled previously in tough times as Arsenal skipper, having a run in with fans before being stripped of the armband.

However, he was rehabilitated under Mikel Arteta but Le Bris says he has not needed to perform any such act himself.

He said: “What I know is what I see every day, the involvement of Granit, his standards, training standards, his willingness to play for Sunderland.



“Thursday, we planned to play 60 minutes, but at half-time he told me, ‘I’ll go all the way. I will help the squad.’ This is Granit.

“So after that, he is human, he will have ups and downs. You are not the same player when you are 34 that you were at 23. His game is evolving as well, but his commitment is superb, no doubt about that.”

Meanwhile, Xhaka’s Sunderland team-mate Trai Hume is adamant their current slump has nothing to do with Xhaka’s flirt with Chelsea.



The Northern Ireland defender said: “No, it’s had no effect on us as players. Granit has obviously been a big player for the club since he’s come. He’s our captain, our leader, and just like us, he knows he can be better and we know we can be.

“He demands more from us. We need to step up to the levels we know we can hit but haven’t reached this season. We know as players we are a good team and we have to reach the levels of the Premier League.

“Unfortunately we haven’t reached that so far but that’s what we need to address and improve.”



Xhaka was a statement signing in the summer of 2025 after Le Bris had led Sunderland to promotion. Eyebrows were raised when the Black Cats managed to snap him up for £17m and he proved to be worth every pound of that by leading them to Europa League qualification last term.

However, it could quite easily have been Henderson lining up in red and white this afternoon instead.

The England international was desperate to return to the Premier League following miserable spells in Saudi Arabia and at Ajax.

Despite denials at the time, Le Bris has now admitted that owner Kyril Louis-Dreyfus and director of football Florent Ghisolfi did hold talks with Henderson over an emotional homecoming.

Though he is delighted with how things turned out after they opted for Xhaka instead while Henderson went on to join Brentford before moving to Stamford Bridge this summer.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “Absolutely! Granit is superb as well. Jordan is a great player, first of all. For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo and Kyril, they had conversations.

“I thought that it could have been a good signing for the club, a good symbol, a great player, a great leader. But the market is a market.”

Sports.title: Robbie Savage’s son Charlie scores as Peterborough capitulate in father vs son FA Cup clash
Sports.content:
Next

ROBBIE SAVAGE’S son Charlie delivered a brutal blow to his dad in a sensational first round 5-0 FA Cup tie.

Reading led 3-0 at half-time in the box office clash, leaving an exasperated Peterborough boss Robbie in the dugout.



But nothing could hurt more than the former Forest Green boss‘ own son putting the nail in the coffin after netting the third goal.

Charlie was all grins after receiving the ball inside the box, taking it for a quick walk before bouncing it in at the far post.



Daniel Kyerewaa had already put the frighteners on the Posh with a 26th-minute goal before Jack Marriott doubled their lead 12 minutes later.

And Charlie then delivered the goal that was written in the script in the dying moments of the first-half.



Real salt was rubbed into Robbie’s wounds with Jamie Reid scoring twice to round the a 5-0 thrashing.

Before the game, Robbie waited in the blue corridors of The Weston Homes Stadium to welcome his son into the den.

With ‘Proud to be posh’ emblazoned on the wall, the proud dad held out both arms but his smile was even wider.

When he saw Charlie, Robbie grinned: “Good luck, kid.”



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

While still making time for a hug, the 23-year-old smirked: “I can’t speak to you.”

But the pair have not been speaking all week, Robbie revealed.

As the League One boss plotted the downfall of Reading, both Charlie and Robbie decided that it would be unfair to both sides that they chat away about tactics or anything else.

Speaking to SunSport, Savage Snr said: “Because we’re trying to beat Reading, who’re flying in the league.

“I’ve not been able to speak to him all week. After his last match, as a dad, I’ve not been able to say to him: ‘How did you do?’



“I always speak to him in a positive way.

“And this is only the first occasion since his loan time at Forest Green Rovers where I’ve not been able to speak to him for the week.

“Because it’s not fair on him. I don’t want to put him in a position where something slips out. They might have a game plan. They might have something different.

Sports.title: White: Billam-Smith was stopped too soon
Sports.content:
Chris Billam-Smith finished the fight on his feet, shaking his head in protest, when referee Lee Every halted him in the seventh round against Cheavon Clarke.

No one before had seen Billam-Smith in that kind of predicament. He'd never previously been dropped let alone stopped.

But Cheavon had put him down twice in that round before finishing matters against an old amateur rival.

Billam-Smith wanted to carry on and Zuffa Boxing promoter Dana White agreed, saying: "I thought it was early."

But he added: "Only CBS can answer that question."

Clarke backed the referee's call, convinced he had the former WBO world champion in severe distress.

"If he was blocking the shots he wouldn't have been dancing," Clarke said.

"If Chris had got more time and Chev does what Chev normally does and Chris got knocked down and was then hurt we'd have then had you guys, the media saying: 'Oh the ref didn't do a good job.'

"So did he do a good job or did he do a bad job?"

In his last fight Clarke rose from the canvas twice himself to take out Jack Massey and he pointed out: "Chris was in a worse state than Massey."

Image: Clarke has scored two great consecutive stoppage wins

What next?

Sky Sports boxing expert and former world champion Johnny Nelson said of Billam-Smith: "Even [his coach] Shane McGuigan said he gets hit far too often and he's not happy about it.

"He's got to think: 'What can I change?' if anything can be changed.

"Chris has achieved everything he can do as a professional fighter, so it's now about appetite and direction.

"What does he want to do? Where does he want to go? Does he want to try and get in the ring again with Chev or is Chev his bogeyman for the rest of his life?"

He also thinks Clarke should fight another British opponent next.

Nelson said: "At domestic level he needs to clear it completely to say he's top of the tree as a cruiserweight in the UK.

"Because on the world scene there's some big shapes and sizes that Chev will have hellfire with.

"He's got the energy and the appetite, so let him bask in the glory."

Sports.title: Khawaja: I haven't 'thrown anyone under the bus' with 'Sandpapergate' claims
Sports.content:
Usman Khawaja insists he has not "thrown anyone under the bus" after excerpts from his autobiography claimed the entire Australia team were aware of the ball-tampering scheme on the tour of South Africa in 2018.

Batter Khawaja, who retired from international cricket earlier this year, said he had made a "promise" to David Warner - one of three players banned in the wake of 'Sandpapergate', along with Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft - that he would "tell the truth".

In the Cape Town Test against the Proteas eight years ago, Bancroft was caught on camera trying to rough up one side of the ball with sandpaper to try and make it swing through the air.

The bowling attack for the Cape Town Test - Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood - released a statement in 2021 denying any knowledge of the plot, while Cricket Australia has always asserted only Smith, Warner and Bancroft knew about it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player In 2018 footage emerged of Australia opener Cameron Bancroft using a foreign object to alter the condition of the ball against South Africa

Khawaja said in a video on Instagram: "I haven't ⁠thrown anyone under the bus.

"The guys ‌that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're ‌not the victims.

"[Bancroft, Warner and Smith] took the blame for all of us, and they're the victims - people telling them that they're cheats, getting nailed by the crowd, public humiliation.

"I made a promise to my childhood friend David Warner that I would tell the truth, so he could tell a story. I'm absolutely 100 per cent unapologetic for that. These three guys deserve justice and I haven't pointed fingers at anyone.

"I'm still searching for what I was searching for all those years ago. For us, me included, to take the blame together as a team, so we can all move on from this once and for all.

"You know what? I would do it again in a heartbeat."

Khawaja: Smith talked me out of coming clean

Image: Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins issued a joint statement in 2021 denying knowledge of the scandal

Khawaja said he wanted to come clean in 2018, only to be talked down by Smith, and then again in 2021 after Bancroft said in a newspaper interview that it was "probably self-explanatory" that the bowling attack were aware of the ball-tampering scheme.

The 39-year-old said: "[Smith] being the man and leader he was talked me out of it. He wanted to take the blame. I argued but he was having none of it. That's the first time I tried to come out."

On wanting to fess up five years ago, only to then feel he couldn't once Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon issued their statement, Khawaja added: "I wasn't going to go to war with those guys back then. I just wasn't comfortable. That's the truth.

"How was I ever supposed to bring this up when I knew some of my team-mates didn't want to talk about it? I knew everything I did or said influenced and affected the team.

"I was always conscious of putting my team first. What I say now isn't a reflection of them anymore. Now my words don't influence the team at all. I speak for myself."

Bancroft keen to 'move on' from from ball-tampering saga

Image: Bancroft was one of the three players banned in the wake of 'Sandpapergate'

Another of Khawaja's claims was that fellow batter Bancroft had volunteered to use sandpaper on the ball in the game before the infamous Cape Town Test, which took place in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.

Bancroft - who has only made two appearances for Australia since 'Sandpapergate', both in the 2019 Ashes, and recently said he accepted a Test return was unlikely at this stage of his career - is keen to "move on" from the ball-tampering story, according to his Beau Casson, his coach at state side Western Australia.

Speaking after Bancroft scored 32 for WA against England in Perth, as the tourists warmed up for a three-match ODI series against Australia from Friday, Casson said: "The situation's a long time ago. He's keen to move on and let his bat do the talking.

"You can't control everything. The way he's handled it, over the past couple of weeks, and over the years gone by, it speaks volumes of the way he's done that.

"He certainly sets the example of how to go about being a professional cricketer."

Sports.title: Can Verstappen, Hamilton come from the back in Sao Paulo 'reverse grid' race?
Sports.content:
A mixed up grid and rain on the forecast has set up the prospect of a thrilling Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.

For the third year in a row, Lando Norris will start on pole position in Brazil with new F1 world champion Kimi Antonelli alongside him on the front row.

Unusually though, there will be plenty of attention further down the field as power unit changes for Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton mean they start at the back, while Ferrari's Charles Leclerc starts 14th for a 10-grid place penalty.

And Mercedes' George Russell, who was left frustrated to not qualify first after a strategic error from the team, starts seventh following a five-place grid penalty for a new internal combustion engine, so several of F1's biggest names will begin the Sao Paulo Grand Prix - lights out at 5pm on Sunday with build-up from 3.30pm, live on Sky Sports F1 - out of position.

"It's almost a reverse grid race, no?" Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff told Sky Sports F1.

"Yeah, exciting. I think we want to lock in the points for the Constructors' Championship. But it's all floodgates open, the better. Let's race."

Sao Paulo GP: Top 10 Starting Grid 1) Lando Norris, McLaren



2) Kimi Antonelli,, Mercedes



3) Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls



4) Nico Hulkenberg, Audi



5) Isack Hadjar, Red Bull



6) Oliver Bearman, Haas



7) George Russell, Mercedes



8) Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin



9) Alex Albon, Williams



10) Oscar Piastri, McLaren

How far can Verstappen and Hamilton climb up the field?

Verstappen is no stranger to making his way through the pack at Interlagos after his remarkable victory from 17th in 2024 in the rain.

The Red Bull driver, who has won three times in Brazil, gained 11 places in the opening 11 laps before making the right strategy call to take a crucial victory.

Last year, Verstappen started from the pit lane and impressively charged his way to the podium in dry conditions, but he thinks it will be more difficult to get towards the front this time around.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the best overtakes from Max Verstappen's stellar performance at the 2025 Sao Paulo Grand Prix which took him all the way from the pit lane to the podium

"It's going to be a bit harder to overtake. The Overtake Mode doesn't really do a lot around here. Everyone is draining their battery from the last corner to Turn 1. Everyone has their wings open, so the effect is less than normal," he told Sky Sports F1.

"That will make it a bit harder to overtake once you get to the cars that are similar on lap times. The first few cars are not a problem. The others will be a little harder."

What is Overtake Mode in F1? Overtake Mode has been a replacement for DRS since the start of this year.



It’s a mode the car goes into when you are within one second of the car in front.



It allows the following car a higher car speed while still deploying maximum energy from the electric motor.



On a normal lap, when the car reaches 180mph, it has to, by regulation, ramp down its electric motor power. With Overtake Mode active, that speed tolerance raises to 209mph, so the following car is allowed to go faster.

Hamilton memorably went from 20th to fifth in the 2021 Sprint in Brazil, after he was disqualified from Qualifying, then won the Grand Prix after starting 10th.

However, Hamilton will not have the same car advantage from five years ago with Ferrari struggling this weekend compared to their recent form.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen reflected on a wet qualifying session in Sao Paulo

But, the high chance of rain means Hamilton, and Verstappen, will have the chance to showcase their extraordinary skill and could still find themselves towards the pointy end of the field with a special performance.

"It will be tricky conditions but I love racing in the rain," said Hamilton.

"I was basically using the qualifying as a test to make sure the engine is working, and making sure the car felt good. I feel good for tomorrow."

Leclerc has less cars to overtake from 14th and feels he learned a lot from the wet qualifying by experimenting with set-up tweaks which will benefit him in the race.

"It's going to be very tricky. My biggest strength in the junior categories has been wet driving. Since my nine years with Ferrari, we have never found a way around it," he told Sky Sports F1.

"I still believe if we manage to find the right window of this car, we can fight for much better than top six."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc says he's 'settled' feud with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton after their clash in last week's Mexico City GP

Norris hoping for 'dark, gloomy day' to fight Antonelli

Perhaps quite fittingly, last year's F1 world champion Norris will start on pole from the new world champion Antonelli in the first race since the latter secured this year's title a week ago in Mexico.

McLaren have brought a new front wing, rear wing, beam wing and floor elements to their car this weekend and it appears to have made an immediate performance impact.

Norris and Antonelli traded lap times throughout Friday's practice sessions in the dry but the McLaren driver feels he needs rain to beat Antonelli on Sunday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lando Norris reacted to claiming pole position for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix

"I expect a battle no matter what. If it's dry, I probably expect a bigger battle because I don't think we quite have the speed compared to them," he told Sky Sports F1.

"That's why I feel like we had a very good day today. We made the most of conditions where it's not so much about who has the best car, it's more who can push things to the limit and make the most of that opportunity.

"I'm hoping when I wake up it's a dark, gloomy day because we will have a better chance then."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Torrential rain brings out the red flag a minute after the Qualifying session begins in Sao Paulo

Norris pointed to Antonelli's impressive long run pace in the dry on Friday as the reason he's hoping for rain, whereas the Mercedes driver says he's open to any conditions.

"Hopefully, we can get off the line well, and let's see if it's going to be wet or dry," said Antonelli.

"In the dry, I felt very good over a single lap and on the long run, especially in FP2. So let's see. I'm looking forward to it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell was seething after being told to back off at a time when he believed he could have pushed for P1 during the Q3 session in Sao Paulo

Mercedes have a big opportunity to win the Constructors' Championship with Antonelli starting in second and Russell in seventh, while the two Ferraris are outside of the top 13.

If Mercedes outscore Ferrari by three points, or more, they will seal their ninth title since 2014 but the result of the race itself appears to be more important to the drivers, and Russell is hoping for more rain following his impressive qualifying.

"I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace, along with Lando's, was by far the best out there," he said

"In the rain here, it's always a challenge. I hope it is wet. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet."

Sports.title: Norris claims Sao Paulo GP pole after treacherous rain-hit qualifying
Sports.content:
Lando Norris claimed pole position after a hugely-challenging Sao Paulo Grand Prix qualifying in treacherous wet conditions, for a race that will see Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen start at the back of the grid.

On a rain-hit day at ever-unpredictable Interlagos, qualifying was suspended for over an hour and 20 minutes after a torrential downpour hit the drivers' first laps of Q1.

The rain eventually eased - but never particularly stopped - to allow running to take place, creating a thrilling and unpredictable battle for pole.

In the end it was Norris who impressively came out on top to seal a third successive Interlagos pole position for the outgoing world champion, on a weekend McLaren had already showed improved form in the dry following car upgrades.

Mercedes' George Russell was second fastest ahead of a race he already knew he carries a five-place grid penalty for an engine change, meaning he could not ultimately achieve pole position whatever he did.

He lapped 0.204s slower than Norris in Q3 and from second will drop to seventh on Sunday's grid.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell was seething after being told to back off at a time when he believed he could have pushed for P1 during the Q3 session in Sao Paulo

But the Mercedes driver felt he would have topped the qualifying timesheet outright had he not been advised by his race engineer to back out of what turned out to be his final representative timed lap of Q3, when he came up behind Alex Albon's slower Williams.

Russell's engineer, Marcus Dudley, clearly hoped this would pay dividends by giving the Briton a clearer run on his next lap but the call coincided with the rain worsening, meaning lap times quickly became slower and the final minutes of Q3 inconsequential as all drivers returned to the pit lane.

"I don't want to be P2. I want to be P1!" fumed Russell on team radio.

New world champion Kimi Antonelli qualified third but will move ahead of team-mate Russell to the front row alongside Norris.

Sao Paulo GP Qualifying: Top 10 1) Lando Norris, McLaren



2) George Russell, Mercedes*



3) Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes



4) Charles Leclerc, Ferrari**



5) Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls



6) Nico Hulkenberg, Audi



7) Isack Hadjar, Red Bull



8) Oliver Bearman, Haas



9) Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin



10) Alex Albon, Williams



*five-place penalty to be applied



**10-place penalty to be applied

Charles Leclerc was fourth for Ferrari but he has a 10-place penalty for an engine change to serve so will drop down into 14th on the grid.

His team-mate Hamilton was also originally supposed to serve the same sanction but a problem with his fresh Ferrari engine in final practice triggered a complete power-unit change and locked him in to a back-of-the-grid start.

He will be joined on the back rows by old title rival Verstappen, who has also taken a new power unit in his Red Bull from Saturday's running. Hamilton starts 20th with Verstappen 21st.

Both drivers dropped out in Q2, Hamilton in 11th and Verstappen, who opted not to run in the second phase at all in order to save wet tyres for the race, 16th but neither result mattered given their overriding penalties.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen reflected on a wet qualifying session in Sao Paulo

Ferrari's heavier grid penalties increase Mercedes' chances of closing out the Constructors' Championship on Sunday.

Seven days after Antonelli's drivers' title triumph in Mexico, the Silver Arrows will complete a title double for 2026 with three rounds to spare if they outscore their Italian rivals by three points or more.

Front-running penalties promote midfield runners up grid

The grid penalties for Russell, Verstappen and both Ferraris - which were all confirmed in the sessions ahead of qualifying - mean Sunday's grid has a different complexion to normal in a season otherwise dominated by the 'big four' teams.

Russell and Leclerc's demotions move Liam Lawson - whose future at Racing Bulls remain in huge doubt despite his impressive season - to a joint career-best third on the grid after the New Zealander already impressed in the wet to qualify fifth.

Who has grid penalties at Interlagos? George Russell, Mercedes - 5 places

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari - 10 places

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari - Back of grid

Max Verstappen, Red Bull - Back of grid

Sergio Perez, Cadillac - Back of grid

There were also strong performances in the rain from Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, who will start fourth, and Haas' Oliver Bearman, who will line up sixth.

With Verstappen at the back, Isack Hadjar will be the lead Red Bull driver in fifth.

Fernando Alonso showed his old mastery of the rain to put under-powered Aston Martin into Q3 for the first time this season, while Williams' Alex Albon also made his first top-10 appearance of a difficult year.

Alonso and Albon will line up in eighth and ninth places respectively.

That is just ahead of McLaren's Oscar Piastri - after he dropped out in Q2 following an error on the intermediates at the end of his last lap - and Brazilian debutant Rafael Camara in 11th.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rafael Camara ended his F1 debut in the barriers during Qualifying at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix

Camara, Haas' new signing to replace Esteban Ocon, hugely impressed on his F1 debut to make Q2 before blotting his copybook slightly by crashing into the barriers at the end of that second phase at Turn 12.

Arvid Lindblad will line up 12th after his Racing Bulls car was stopped by technical issues in Q2.

How Interlagos' unpredictable weather created thrilling qualifying

Rain has largely stayed away from the 2026 season but arrived with a vengeance at Interlagos on Saturday.

A big electrical storm following the end of final practice had already drenched the track, but conditions had started to improve, and the rain even briefly stopped, to allow qualifying to begin at its scheduled time.

But just as drivers were starting to queue at the end of the pit lane for the Q1 green light, the heavens opened again and as the cars were released onto the track conditions became treacherous almost immediately, forcing drivers to gingerly complete their out laps amid ever-worsening visibility and grip levels.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Torrential rain brings out the red flag a minute after the Qualifying session begins in Sao Paulo

Race Control swiftly threw the red flag, mandating drivers returned to the pit lane, which would eventually lead to a suspension of one hour and 23 minutes before the track was deemed suitable for F1 cars to return.

And while the rain did start to initially worsen again just as the session resumed, conditions steadily improved thereafter with a drier line eventually appearing around the lap and drivers able to switch from the full wet to the shallower intermediate tyres from mid-way through Q2.

Impressively, while there were spins and off-track moments, only two drivers found the barriers. However, to the disappointment of the home crowd, they were both the Brazilians in the field.

Gabriel Bortoleto slithered off the road in his Audi in Q1, although was able to return to the pits where he stayed due to car damage, while Camara hit the barriers to bring Q2 to a slightly premature end at the start of the final run up the hill.

In the end, despite a frustrated Russell's feeling of what might have been, it was polesitter Norris who tamed the conditions the best to earn the most hard-won of pole positions.

"It was about getting two laps in at the beginning, not making any mistakes, and that's exactly what we did, so it's been a very good day," said the McLaren driver.
