World.title: SERAP to Tinubu govt: Disclose details of ₦50,000 relief payments, beneficiaries, safeguards
World.content:
The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) has urged the Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Dr Bernard Doro “to disclose details of the funding, implementation and administration of the ₦50,000 National Emergency Relief and Stabilisation Intervention (NERSI), including beneficiary selection, payments, contracts with digital financial service providers and safeguards against political interference.”

SERAP’s request follows the Ministry’s public statement of 30 October 2026 announcing NERSI, which is intended to provide ₦50,000 in financial assistance to vulnerable Nigerians. However, questions remain about the programme’s funding, geographical coverage, and engagement of digital financial service providers.

SERAP urged the Minister “to disclose details of the budgetary allocations, funds released and expended, eligibility criteria, beneficiary selection and verification processes, geographical distribution of beneficiaries, and whether the ₦50,000 assistance is intended as a one-off payment or a monthly intervention.”

SERAP also urged him to “publicly invite the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) and the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to monitor the programme’s implementation and expenditure, investigate allegations of corruption, and help ensure that the funds reach their intended beneficiaries.”

In a Freedom of Information request dated 7 November 2026 and signed by SERAP deputy director Kolawole Oluwadare, the organisation said: “Nigerians have a right to know how public funds allocated to NERSI are being spent, who is receiving the assistance, how beneficiaries are selected and whether the programme is reaching those most in need.”

SERAP said, “Publicly funded social assistance must be allocated strictly on the basis of genuine need and objective eligibility criteria. It must not be used to reward political supporters, secure partisan loyalty, finance political mobilisation or influence the electoral choices of vulnerable Nigerians, particularly ahead of the 2027 general elections.”

According to SERAP, “Beneficiaries must not be required or encouraged to attend political rallies, support political parties or candidates, display political materials or demonstrate political loyalty as a condition for receiving assistance. NERSI is a government programme funded with public resources, not a personal gift or political benefit from any office-holder or political party.”

The request, read in part: “Access to the requested information would enable Nigerians to assess whether NERSI is reaching eligible and vulnerable persons, whether public funds are being properly accounted for, and whether adequate safeguards exist against political interference, corruption and misappropriation.”

“Disclosure would also strengthen public confidence in social protection programmes and help ensure that resources intended for vulnerable Nigerians are used for their intended purposes.”

“We would be grateful if the requested information and measures are provided and taken within seven days of the receipt and/or publication of this letter.”

“If we have not heard from you by then, SERAP shall consider appropriate legal action to compel the Ministry and other relevant authorities to fulfil their constitutional and statutory obligations and ensure the proper, transparent and accountable implementation of NERSI in the public interest.”

“SERAP is also concerned by reports that some Nigerians who received notifications of the ₦50,000 assistance have been unable to access or withdraw the funds, while others reportedly encountered messages indicating that they were not eligible.”

“These reports raise questions about the accuracy of beneficiary verification, the reliability of payment arrangements and the effectiveness of mechanisms for resolving failed or disputed payments.”

“The Ministry should urgently investigate these complaints, publish its findings and ensure that all eligible beneficiaries receive the assistance intended for them.”

“SERAP is further asking the Ministry to disclose agreements with the digital financial service providers engaged to administer NERSI payments, including ALAT, MoMo PSB, NairaGram, OPay and Moniepoint, as well as the roles, fees and performance of the providers.”

“The use of the National Social Register and national identity records to identify beneficiaries must be governed by clear rules and appropriate data-protection safeguards. The Ministry should disclose how these records are being used and ensure that beneficiaries’ personal information is protected, while making anonymised and aggregated information available for public scrutiny.”

“SERAP recognises the importance of providing financial assistance and social protection to Nigerians experiencing poverty and economic hardship.”

“However, a programme involving public funds and the personal information of vulnerable households must be administered according to clear and publicly accessible rules, objective eligibility criteria, appropriate safeguards and effective independent oversight.”

“According to the Ministry’s public statement of 30 October 2026, NERSI is intended to provide ₦50,000 in financial assistance to vulnerable Nigerians.”

“However, important questions remain unanswered regarding the programme’s total funding, the number of intended beneficiaries, its duration and geographical coverage, and the criteria and methodology for identifying and selecting beneficiaries from the National Social Register and verified national identity records.”

“The Ministry’s statement describes the ₦50,000 assistance as a monthly payment, while its subsequent FAQ does not clearly specify the frequency or duration of payments.”

“The Ministry has also not provided sufficient information about the selection and oversight of digital financial service providers, the protection and use of beneficiaries’ personal data, the independent verification of payments, or effective mechanisms for addressing complaints, disputed selections and wrongful exclusions.”

“SERAP is also concerned about the need to protect NERSI from political interference, particularly ahead of the 2027 general elections. Clear safeguards are therefore necessary to ensure that beneficiary selection and payments remain impartial and are not influenced by political considerations.”

“These information gaps make it difficult for Nigerians to assess whether NERSI is being implemented fairly and accountably, and whether public funds are reaching those most in need.”

“Nigerians also have the right to know how the National Social Register and national identity records are used to identify and verify eligible beneficiaries, as well as the total number of beneficiaries selected and verified, disaggregated by state and local government area and, where available and appropriate, by ward.”

“The Ministry also has a legal obligation to disclose an anonymised breakdown of the number of beneficiaries and the total amounts paid or scheduled for payment in each state and local government area.”

“The Ministry should disclose any records of the involvement of political actors in beneficiary selection and payments, access to beneficiary databases, the use of public resources to promote the programme, and any complaints or investigations relating to partisan influence ahead of the 2027 general elections.”

“The need for effective accountability is particularly important in light of concerns raised by the Auditor-General of the Federation in the 2024 Annual Report regarding over ₦78.8 billion in public funds allegedly diverted or unaccounted for in the administration of social intervention and cash transfer programmes.”

“The Auditor-General reportedly identified concerns over ₦33.751 billion in cash transfers made in 2023 for which relevant REMITA records, among other supporting documentation, were not provided for audit.”

“These findings underscore the importance of adequate financial controls, proper record-keeping, independent verification and effective oversight from the outset of the new intervention.”

“SERAP notes that section 15(5) of the Nigerian Constitution requires the State to abolish all corrupt practices and abuse of power. Section 16(2)(b) requires the State to direct its policy towards ensuring that the material resources of the community are harnessed and distributed as best as possible to serve the common good.”

“Section 13 imposes a responsibility on all organs of government and all authorities and persons exercising legislative, executive or judicial powers to conform to, observe and apply the provisions of Chapter II of the Constitution.”

“The Constitution also recognises important social welfare responsibilities. Section 17(3)(d) identifies the provision of suitable and adequate food, a reasonable national minimum living wage, old-age care and pensions, unemployment and sick benefits, and welfare for persons with disabilities as matters the State should pursue.”

“The effective and accountable administration of social assistance programmes is important to the fulfilment of these constitutional objectives and the dignity and welfare of vulnerable Nigerians.

“Nigeria has also made legally binding commitments under the UN Convention against Corruption to promote integrity, accountability and transparency in the management of public affairs and public funds.”

World.title: Two waterway accidents kill police officer, woman in Bayelsa
World.content:
By Samuel Oyadongha, Yenagoa

Two separate waterway accidents in Bayelsa State have claimed the lives of a serving police officer and a female passenger, the state Police Command has confirmed.

The incidents occurred in Brass and Sagbama Local Government Areas, according to a statement issued on Saturday night by the Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Musa Mohammed.

The first accident involved a passenger boat that capsized along the Abedigbene waterways in Brass LGA on Thursday while travelling from Yenagoa to Akassa with eight persons on board, including a serving commissioner.

The police said Maritime Union workers in Brass reported the incident, prompting a search-and-rescue operation by personnel of the Nigerian Navy’s Forward Operating Base (FOB) FORMOSO, in collaboration with local divers and members of the Abedigbene fishing community.

Seven passengers were rescued, including the Bayelsa State Commissioner for Trade and Commerce, Dr Ebiere Jones, and an officer of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps.

However, a serving police officer who was initially reported missing was subsequently confirmed dead.

The second accident occurred at about 5:20 a.m. on Saturday, November 7, along the shoreline of Angalabiri Community in Sagbama LGA, when a tanker vessel belonging to Sterling Global Oil Ltd reportedly collided with canoes navigating close to the shoreline.

According to the police, preliminary investigations indicated that the vessel struck and destroyed some of the canoes.

One of the victims, identified as Mrs Victoria Abetnigo, an indigene of Angalabiri, sustained serious injuries and was rushed to Ebedebiri General Hospital for treatment.

She was, however, pronounced dead by the attending doctor. Her remains have been deposited at Ofoni Mortuary, while investigations are ongoing to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Reacting to the two tragedies, the Commissioner of Police, Bayelsa State Command, CP Ajao Saka Adewale, expressed sadness over the incidents and extended his condolences to the families, colleagues and loved ones of the deceased.

The police commissioner particularly lamented the death of the serving police officer, praying for the peaceful repose of the souls of the deceased and strength for their families to bear the losses.

He also commended the Nigerian Navy’s FOB FORMOSO, local divers, Maritime Union workers and members of the Abedigbene fishing community for their prompt intervention during the rescue operation.

Adewale urged boat operators and commercial vessel owners to exercise caution and comply strictly with maritime safety regulations.

He specifically called on vessel operators to maintain safe distances from shorelines and established canoe routes and avoid reckless navigation.

He also advised passengers to wear life jackets throughout their journeys and urged all waterway users to prioritise safety and promptly report emergencies to the appropriate authorities.

The Command reaffirmed its commitment to protecting lives and property across the state.

World.title: Peter Obi congratulates Flamingos on U-17 Women’s World Cup triumph
World.content:
The Nigeria Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Peter Obi, has congratulated the Nigeria U-17 women’s national football team, the Flamingos, following their triumph at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco.

Obi praised the players for their talent, resilience, hard work and dedication, saying their achievement had brought immense joy and pride to Nigerians.

In a congratulatory message posted on his X handle on Saturday, the former Anambra State governor commended the team for representing the country proudly on the international stage.

He said the players had earned a special place in the hearts of Nigerians through their outstanding performance.

“Thank you for raising our flag high and bringing immense joy to our nation. Your remarkable talent, resilience, hard work and dedication have earned you a special place in the hearts of Nigerians,” Obi said.

He added that the team’s accomplishment demonstrated the potential of Nigerian youths and their ability to excel through determination and commitment.

“You have made our nation proud, and we truly appreciate your outstanding efforts. Congratulations, champions!” he stated.

Obi concluded his message with his familiar expression of optimism about Nigeria’s future, saying, “A new Nigeria is possible.”

World.title: Rumbling in Yoruba land: There’s only one Afenifere despite alleged breakup plan – Secretary
World.content:
• Says Adebanjo endorsed Peter Obi in 2023 without telling anybody

• Explains how Fasoranti endorsed Tinubu for president despite supplanting his leadership

By Dapo Akinrefon

Chief Ademola Folarin, a lawyer, is the General Secretary of the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere. Folarin, who is the Agbaakin Maiyegun of Ibadanland, in this interview, speaks on the leadership crisis in Afenifere, reconciliation in the group, and the decision of the Yoruba body to endorse President Bola Tinubu for 2027 among other issues. Excerpts:

There have been issues in the polity ahead of 2027, parties have been trading accusations; there is mudslinging. Do you think this is healthy for our democracy?

Look, adversarial politics is one of the hallmarks of democracy. You have to destroy one party in order for you to rise. It’s one of the pitfalls of democracy that we can’t avoid, which is why some people say democracy is not the best form of government. But we haven’t found a better one. I think we are just being dishonest. There is a better one, it’s not necessarily democratic. We can see it in China, we can see it in the Gulf states, a combination of constitutionalism and monarchy. In China, there is no monarchy, but they have a system of evolutionary leadership, and it is working. The trouble spots in the world are the democracies. Just look around you, everywhere you see a problem, it’s democratic. That’s because it has to be like that. If you want to see the downfall of someone to rise, you can’t have peace, you can’t have stability. The bastion of democracy, Europe and America, are on the decline. It’s consistent with the aims and objectives of the founding fathers of democracy. It was foreseen, but it was unavoidable. If you choose your leaders based purely on numbers, you cannot avoid obvious mistakes. In our country, with the presidential system, it is the same in America. We have simply imported a corrupt system here, presidential system. If you don’t have money, you can’t do anything. That’s what you have. Mudslinging, everything is part of it.

Nigeria has practised the parliamentary system before. Now, it’s practising the presidential system. Which do you think Nigeria can adopt? Do you think it should jettison the two and have another system of government?

It’s a no-brainer which one should prefer between the Westminster parliamentary system and the presidential system. The Westminster parliamentary system is far cheaper and far more representative. Why do I say so? If I want to be prime minister, I don’t need to do a national campaign or whatever. I go to Eti-Osa local government, campaign and win there. Once I win there and my party wins the majority of seats in parliament, I form government. But in presidential, I have to win the majority of votes in the entire country. Then at least 25 per cent of the total number of votes cast in each of at least two-thirds of the number of states in the federation. In this case, 24 states. I have to campaign in the entire country. I need the entire country to vote for me; even without corruption, that is a lot of money. Well, there must be corruption. It’s a no-brainer. We can’t just import a system and think it will work without any modification.

We’ve seen groups, opposition parties, throwing their weight behind preferred candidates. Has Afenifere adopted a candidate for the presidential election?

We announced it about a month ago. We supported President Bola Tinubu in 2023. We have no reason to change our mind now. We have also endorsed him. Look, as far as any discerning, objective person can see, there is no alternative. There is no viable alternative. There are alternatives, but they are not better and they are not viable. On what basis would we jettison the person we support? In any event, personally speaking for myself, I would score him on two fronts. When you combine the scores and find the average, you can decide whether that’s a pass or not. On macroeconomics, I score him 80 per cent. On micro, I score him 40 per cent. Now, 80 plus 40 is 120. Over 200, that’s 60 per cent. On security, we can see progressively there’s improvement. We’re not there yet. On many fronts, what this government is doing is resetting the entire structure. I mean, laying the foundation for a new Nigeria. Now, it comes with pains. No pain, no gain. It comes with pains. Obviously, the macroeconomic aspect of it is still evolving. But you cannot deny the success of the macroeconomics. You cannot.

The numbers are there. You cannot dispute them. There is still a lot to be done. You can point out a few things that they haven’t done right. But show me a government that has been perfect. What’s the alternative? What is the economic policy of Atiku? Do you know? What is the economic policy of Obi? Do you know? Their policy is just to be consistent with adversarial politics, destroy Tinubu. That’s all. Atiku goes to America to probe Tinubu’s certificates. That is what will put food on your table. Or that is what will stop insecurity. Or that is what will stop inflation. All they are doing is to bring the president down. It is well within their right because democracy allows them to do so. So we support Tinubu. I say that categorically because we have already said that. We support President Tinubu for a second time. He deserves it now even more than what he deserved in 2023. In 2023, we supported him based on two things. First was experience. He was the most experienced of all the candidates. Atiku has never held a chief executive position. He was vice president.

What of Peter Obi?

What was his performance compared with Tinubu? The figures are there. There’s nothing to show. They said education was good in his time. His successors said there were some outfits that were not doctoring educational results. Two, what is the educational status of Anambra State today? What is the legacy? Not what you did then, but what survived you. There’s a difference. Tinubu re-engineered the economy of Lagos. That is sustained. You see, there are so many things he has done. You have seen the foundation he laid for Free Trade Zone which has brought in Dangote. You’ve seen what he has done with the Atlantic Ocean. So many things.

You said it that Afenifere has adopted President Bola Tinubu. I have it on good authority that the other camp, which is Oba Oladipo Olaitan’s camp, is backing another candidate…

He is free to do so. You asked me a question and I have answered you. If somebody else wants to adopt somebody else, that is no problem. But I have told you there’s no viable alternative. Be honest with yourself, can Adebayo (SDP presidential candidate) win his own local government? No, but there’s no need to beat about the bush. One thing about Afenifere is that it’s a democratic organisation. Even as I tell you that Afenifere has endorsed President Tinubu, there are members who are supporting other candidates. If Oba Olaitan feels that Adebayo is his candidate, good luck to him.

That brings me to Afenifere itself. The death of Pa Reuben Fasoranti has renewed the eternal rift within your group. Two weeks ago, Oba Laitan announced that he is now the consecrated leader of Afenifere. Is your own group is in support of what he has done?

Although Chief Olu Falae said there should be no talk about leadership succession until after the burial of Pa Fasoranti, isn’t that the sensible, wise thing to do? Why are you discussing leadership? You have not even buried the leader that left. Olu Falae has said the right thing. What is the desperation about?

But he issued a statement…

He can make any statement he likes, but I think it’s a disservice, dishonour, and discredit to the memory of Pa Fasoranti to be discussing leadership while his remains have not been buried. We don’t operate like that. All these things about “I am the leader”, to what end is it really? How does it serve the interests of the Yoruba people that we represent or the unity of Nigeria that we fight for? We don’t engage in such talk.

The last time we met, you hinted that there were reconciliatory moves. How far have you gone about that?

Before Pa Reuben Fasoranti died, we thought that it would have been done…You raised a good point, but that effort has even taken a more dynamic dimension. By the way, Oba Oladipo Olaitan mentioned it in one of his releases that “what a life”. Just a week before Papa’s death, he received a letter inviting him for a family meeting as part of reconciliation. It shows the kind of person Pa Fasoranti was. But we had to step down that meeting because of the burial arrangement. So, it’s ongoing. We will never give up on bringing everybody back under the same roof. Look, at the end of the day, it’s the same Afenifere. We may have misunderstanding here and there, but everybody has agreed that divided we fall, united we stand. That is it. We are more effective. We are more productive. We serve a purpose when we come together. Everybody knows that. Look, you come here telling me “somebody said this”. Is that good for us? It’s not. So we all know. But, you know, as with all human beings, you have to do things gradually. You have to be patient. Delay is consistent with the eventual peaceful outcome. If you want a peaceful outcome, there will be delays. You have to drag some people ahead. And when you want to drag them, it has to be that they are ready to follow you. You must not give up.

Is it true that there are plans to install a former governor as the new leader of Afenifere?

Which former governor?

Otunba Gbenga Daniel…

Everybody is free to have an ambition. There are no plans. Well, okay, maybe he and some people are planning. I don’t know.

It is the Fasoranti camp…

There is no such plan. There is no plan to install anybody. But when we finish the burial, we will all come together and decide who the leader will be. If Otunba Gbenga Daniel is interested, he should declare his interest. If the people, the elders and leaders think he deserves to be leader…

How does a leader emerge in Afenifere?

How do you choose a pope?

It is the conclave of Cardinals…

That’s the way it works too. It’s not elected. It’s not a political party. No. A conclave of elders and leaders. More importantly, if the leader was still alive, he would say this is the person I want. But in the absence of that, a conclave of leaders and elders. You don’t become a leader or an elder simply because you say “I’m Afenifere”. We want to see what you’ve been doing in Afenifere. Are you a force for unity? Or are you a force for division? Or are you a force for yourself? Are you a politically exposed person? If you are fighting in political parties, and you have lost respect in that fray, you can’t be a leader of an organisation that represents the moral conscience of the people. You can’t be partisan, rabid partisan, someone who has been cut apart in different parties and want to be our leader. It’s not possible. Look at Pa Fasoranti. What bad thing can you say about him? Even his enemies loved him. That is the kind of person people will respect. President Tinubu was one of those who tried to supplant the leadership of Pa Fasoranti when he was made leader in 2008. And they went to form Egbe Ilosiwaju. But what did Baba Fasoranti do in 2023?

He endorsed him…

Not because Tinubu asked for endorsement. He called him to be endorsed. Tinubu did not lobby for Afenifere endorsement.

But the late Pa Adebanjo…

That’s the difference between Adebanjo and Fasoranti. You see, Fasoranti was a builder, a unifier, and a team player. Baba Adebanjo endorsed Obi without telling anybody. When they asked him on national TV, “Did you inform the elders and leaders?” he said, “I don’t have to”. On national TV, he said so. Baba Fasoranti would never do that. He was more of a replica of Awolowo. Many people don’t know that Awolowo never took a decision of his own. In Oyo State in 1979, his preference was Pa Alayandeto be governor. But he bowed to the wish of the majority. In Kwara State, his preference was Josiah Olawoyin. But he bowed to the wish of the majority. That’s Fasoranti for you. He attended meetings.

He will not say a word. He was listening to you. If you are taking a decision, and he saw maybe it was going to be a wrong decision, he will talk. Or if you asked about his opinion… Awolowo was exactly like that. Let me tell you my first experience of that, with Awolowo.

Which year was this?

I think it was in 1979. UPN was having a meeting at City Hall in Lagos. And I met Awolowo personally in his house as a student in 1977 or 78. I led a delegation from University of Ife to see him when the Students’ Union wanted to build a hostel. We called it Self-Help Hostel, Annex to Awolowo. We had seen many people, the Fernandes of this world , etc. The first time I met him, and he left a lasting impression. So when UPN was formed, I went there to see, and I heard that they were having a meeting at City Hall. I went there. I wasn’t invited. I wasn’t a member of the party. So I stood at a distance. I was listening to them. I couldn’t hear Awolowo speak. After waiting for about 10 minutes and I didn’t hear him speak, I said, well, maybe he wasn’t there. Then suddenly somebody said: “Now let’s listen to the leader”. I said “that’s him”. Soft spoken. You could hardly hear what he was saying. When we met him in his house in 1978, he asked us to wait. We, about three or four of us, were debating how should we greet him? Should we prostrate? And then we got to his sitting room, sparkling white rock in the middle. Soft spoken. Very nice. Unassuming. Awolowo in all his aura. You know, Fasoranti. It was like that. Baba Adebanjo was good in his own way, but he was not a team player. You attend a meeting with Baba Adebanjo, for one hour, he would speak for 59 minutes. If Baba Adebanjo asked you a question, he would be the one to answer. Before you answer, he would say “no, no, no, no, that’s not it”. But he was a great activist, a great motivator. Everybody has his good parts. For us, it was a no-brainer to support Tinubu.

I was also told that some older members are planning to form what they intend to call Afenifere Independent. What do you say to that?

Follow the truth. That’s what Thomas Jefferson said when he was referring to the founding of the University of Virginia, I think in 1820. Follow the truth, wherever it leads. We are focused on what Afenifere stands for. We are not distracted. There’s a positive to what you are saying in the sense that it is something that is good that is copied. I mean, if Afenifere wasn’t good, you wouldn’t have fake Afeniferes all about. As far as we are concerned, there’s only one Afenifere, and we want everybody to be part of the same family.

How soon is that?

We cannot say how soon or whether in fact it will happen. We can only say we will continue to try. We have seen it before now. We had Afenifere Egbe Ilosiwaju. It is typical of Yoruba. How many Ohanaeze Ndi Igbo do you know of?

I know two…

The second one only recently. How many Arewa Consultative Forum do you know? That’s the way we are. Everybody wants to do his own.

World.title: ADC judgment could cause civil war if not properly managed—Amaechi
World.content:
Former Minister of Transportation, Rotimi Amaechi.

…Says mistake I made in 2023 was listening to Buhari

By Olayinka Ajayi

Vice presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, Mr Rotimi Amaechi, has warned that the Federal High Court judgment against the leadership of his party could trigger unrest.

Last Thursday, the Federal High Court in Abuja nullified the National Working Committee led by former Senate President, David Mark, in a ruling that also invalidated the process that produced former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as the party’s presidential candidate for the 2027 elections.

The judgment, delivered by Justice Peter Lifu, also nullified the emergence of former Minister of Interior, Rauf Aregbesola, as National Secretary, and other decisions taken by the Mark-led leadership, including the nomination of candidates for elective offices. The court further ordered the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, not to recognise or act on decisions taken at the party’s 99th National Executive Committee meeting of July 27, 2025.

The judgment followed a suit, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025, filed by former ADC Deputy National Chairman (North-East), Nafiu Gombe, who challenged the process through which Mark and other members of the caretaker committee assumed control of the party.

Speaking in an interview on Mainland 98.3fm, Amaechi said: “It could cause a civil war if not properly managed. When we heard the news, we quickly met, myself and the presidential candidate and the chairman of the party, and we said: ‘please, lower the tempo’. I am not alleging, as there is a document signed by Nafiu resigning at the same time as Ralph Nwosu. There is a video of him behind David Mark handing over to David Mark. They go to hire, pay money, go to court and compromise some system here and there. There is no internal rift in our party, none. It is just the fear of the All Progressives Congress, APC.

When they saw what happened in Sokoto, they began to cause a crisis that would frighten voters. Looking at things, which other party is opposing the APC other than ADC? The president is from the South-West, and we have three other presidential candidates in the South-West. Even if they don’t get every vote, they would certainly get some votes, and don’t forget the governor of Oyo State, Seyi Makinde, is also running. Let us assume he fails everywhere in the South-West; he will not fail in Oyo, where he comes from. Assuming he wins Oyo State, that is minus one for Tinubu. There is another presidential candidate from the South-East (Peter Obi) who will take away five states from the South-East. Already, he has lost six states from the South. The battle is in the South-South; I am their son. I am running as a vice presidential candidate. Here is a man called Atiku Abubakar, running alone in the North with 19 Northern states.”

On how he lost the 2023 APC presidential primaries to President Tinubu, he said: “Anybody would have defeated anybody. The only mistake I made was listening to the late President Muhammadu Buhari, who told me: ‘don’t campaign, don’t do anything; I will announce you as my candidate’.” He even had it in writing. When he said that to me, I obeyed him because he was my boss, and if he announced such, that would have been a plus for us. I would have gone for the primaries and possibly won because I had the governors on my side. I didn’t do deals, Tinubu did deals, and second, Tinubu played on religion. I will never play religious politics.”

The delegation of Southern Muslims went to see the Northern governors and told them anytime there’s an election, you people support Southern Christians, and when there’s an election in the North, we support you people, and for the sake of the faith, you need to support Tinubu. Nasir El-Rufai was my supporter. He once said in a viral video that this is done for the faith. Imagine how Christians felt that he wanted to prove that Muslims own Nigeria. I would never run such an election. Catholics are 35 million in Nigeria. I wouldn’t want to run that kind of election. So, the Catholics tell all Catholics to go out and vote for Amaechi; by that, you would cause confusion in the country. I wouldn’t do anything at all cost because I want power.”

World.title: Tinubu: Atiku Lacks Moral Integrity, Latitude, Ethics to Hold Public Office
World.content:
*Who built university for him? It’s people’s money, their effort, president alleges

*You won’t regret what you have done, Tinubu tells Fubara on Wike reconciliation

*Your attack a desperate attempt to distract Nigerians from your administration’s failure, Atiku replies Tinubu

Deji Elumoye, Chuks Okocha, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt

President Bola Tinubu and the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, yesterday continued their political fireworks ahead of the 2027 presidential election, with the President questioning the former Vice President’s moral standing for seeking another opportunity serve the country, accusing him of lacking moral integrity, latitude, and ethics to hold public office.

Tinubu alleged that Atiku used public resources to establish his private university.



In a swift response, Atiku described Tinubu’s allegation as a desperate attempt to distract Nigerians from his administration’s failures, saying his investment in education predates his time in public service.

The former vice president explained that in 1993, when a United States court ordered the forfeiture of funds in the president’s bank account, describing the funds as proceeds of narcotics trafficking or funds involved in unlawful financial transactions, he (Atiku) was laying the foundation for his private university.



Speaking yesterday during the APC presidential campaign rally in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, the president challenged Atiku to explain how he funded the establishment of the institution while serving as vice president.

The APC rally, held at the Adokiye Amiesimaka Stadium, was organised by the Rainbow Coalition, a political alliance led by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, to mobilise support for Tinubu’s re-election bid.



He accused the former vice president of using public resources and Nigerians’ efforts to build the university, describing him as lacking the moral integrity and ethical standards required for public office.

Tinubu said that when he took over, 27 of 36 states were unable to pay salaries, which meant a lot for the families and households that depended on them.



He stressed that since then, his administration had reversed the ugly trend, saying the country was on the move toward prosperity.

“To every salary earner, there is a dependent and somebody sharing the food at home. Those people talking of hunger are talking about the mess they created. Atiku was one of them. Ask him how he built a university while in office as Vice President in charge of our economy,” Tinubu said.



“Who built the university for him? It’s your money, it’s your effort. A man without moral integrity, latitude and ethics for the office,” Tinubu added.

The president also accused previous administrations of leaving behind billions and trillions of naira in unpaid pensions and gratuities, saying his administration was working to clear the outstanding payments.

According to Tinubu, the government was addressing the backlog to ensure retired workers received their entitlements and participated in the country’s prosperity.



“The people who governed before us left unpaid pensions and gratuities running into billions and trillions of naira. We are clearing that backlog so that every family is included and we can share in the prosperity,” he said.

He cited retired engineers, welders and teachers as beneficiaries of the payments, claiming that pensioners were receiving their entitlements on time.



Tinubu also praised Wike, describing him as a development partner of his administration.

You Won’t Regret What You Have Done, Tinubu Tells Fubara on Wike Reconciliation

Tinubu also commended Rivers State Governor, Mr. Siminalayi Fubara, for demonstrating maturity, understanding and respect for the intervention by elders during the crisis, which he attributed to a misunderstanding within the political family.

“To me, I intervened on your behalf. Similarly, Fubara, Your Excellency, the host governor today, I want to thank you specifically for your maturity, understanding, and respect for the wisdom of elders.



“When we intervened, you respected our position. You maintained peace. You are a committed democrat, Fubara. You will not regret what you have done as long as all of us are alive,” Tinubu said.

Tinubu urged the youths to collect their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) and participate in the 2027 general election, saying their future would depend on the poll’s outcome.



“It is left for you to use the weapon you have. And that weapon is the PVC. If you have not collected yours, please go ahead and collect it. Please. I beg you. I take God to beg you,” the president said.

He added that the election was not about his personal ambition but about the future of young Nigerians, urging them to use their PVCs to determine the country’s leadership.



In his speech, Vice President Kashim Shetima said the River State was the true definition of political alliances.

The vice president berated those he called political charlatans on the other side of the divide for trying to demonise President Tinubu instead of celebrating him.



Shettima said Atiku and his Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) counterpart, Mr Peter Obi, were no match for Tinubu.

He described Obi’s performance as Governor of Anambra State for eight years and chairman of a bank as mediocre.

Addressing the rally, Governor Fubara promised President Tinubu three million votes in the state.



The governor said Rivers State had thrown its weight behind Tinubu, insisting the state had made its decision and would not turn back.

“Rivers will give you three million votes. We will stand by you. We will work for you. We will deliver for you,” Fubara added.

He also declared that the period of political divisions in the state was over, adding that leaders in the state were now united behind a common political position supporting the president.



For his part, the National Chairman of the APC, Prof. Nentawe Goshwe Yilwatda, described the Tinubu-Shettima presidential ticket as one of the most formidable political combinations in Nigeria’s democratic history.

Yilwatda said the Tinubu-Shettima ticket combined political experience, courage, capacity, and tested leadership, capable of steering Nigeria through its current challenges toward sustainable economic growth and national prosperity.



Also speaking, Wike stated that the people of Rivers State had resolved to vote for Tinubu in the January 2027 presidential election, describing the turnout at the stadium, which he said had a seating capacity of more than 40,000, as evidence of the state’s support for Tinubu’s re-election bid.

APC Targets 2.3m Votes in Rivers

Also speaking, the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Abubakar Yari, said the ruling party had set a target of 2.3 million votes for Tinubu in Rivers State.

Yari noted that the state had approximately 3.3 million registered voters, out of which 2.8 million collected their PVCs.

Your Attack a Desperate Attempt to Distract Nigerians from Your Administration’s Failure, Atiku Replies Tinubu

Meanwhile, Atiku has described Tinubu’s latest attack on his investment in education as a desperate attempt to distract Nigerians from his administration’s failure.



In a statement issued by the Director of Strategic Communication of ADC’s Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC), Phrank Shaibu, the former vice president declared that Tinubu has told Nigerians why they should not allow him to continue as president after his first tenure.



“He also chose to question my investment in education and ask how I built an educational institution while serving as vice president.

“The answer is simple: My investment in education predates my time in public service. In 1993, while a U.S. court ordered the forfeiture of funds in an account in your name, describing them as proceeds of narcotics trafficking or funds involved in unlawful financial transactions, I was laying the foundation for ABTI Academy. That Academy has since grown into the American University of Nigeria (AUN), Atiku explained.



However, information on the university website showed that AUN was founded by the former vice president, in Yola, the capital of his home state of Adamawa.

He first established a private primary and secondary school, ABTI Academy (now AUN Academy) in 2002.

AUN was licensed as ABTI University in 2003, and the ground was broken for the buildings in October 2004.

Atiku further stated, “That moment captures the difference between us. My history is traceable. I can show Nigerians how I built my name, achieved business success and entered public leadership. Your own history remains clumsy and foggy. You cannot erase it by attacking my educational record.



“A president who has plunged the country into a crushing cost-of-living crisis has no business asking Nigerians for another mandate. The real conversation about the 2027 election is how to repair the damage your government has done.

“You say Nigeria cannot return to subsidy and must move forward. But you cannot even tell Nigerians where you are taking them. Forward into deeper poverty, mounting debt, insecurity and mass unemployment?



“Since your inauguration in 2023, your leadership has become synonymous with hardship, pain and despair. Your record is a working example of how a country should not be led. You have created poverty on an industrial scale, pushing more than 79 million Nigerians into extreme poverty.



“Your campaign’s Director-General says hungry Nigerians are simply lazy. He delivered that statement in such bad grammar that it could wake the dead. This government does not even believe Nigerians are hungry. How can you solve a problem you refuse to acknowledge?

“You created poverty, then insult the people suffering from it. You attack my Affordable Life campaign, but the people you are really attacking are the millions of Nigerians desperate for relief from your failed leadership.



“Bola, Nigerians have tested your leadership. The verdict is clear: You are a disaster. In Yoruba culture, I am told, a calabash of pepper represents hostile leadership, while a calabash of honey represents hospitable leadership. Yours is a calabash of pepper.”

World.title: Judiciary Must Protect This Democracy
World.content:
When news broke on Thursday that Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court had sacked the David Mark-led caretaker committee of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and consequently nullified the nomination of Alhaji Atiku Abubakar as the party’s presidential candidate, my initial response was: are we still on this matter? Maybe I slept off along the way. All I had on my mind was that we were now fully set for the epic 2027 presidential election without further drama. I was already doing my permutations on a three-horse race, silently praying for a free and fair process so that we can have something more to celebrate in our democratic journey. My spirit was dampened once again.

The judgment, which the ADC said it has appealed, declared the party’s caretaker committee illegal in the suit brought by Alhaji Nafiu Bala Gombe, the former national deputy chairman (north-east) of the party. The judge also invalidated all decisions taken by the committee. In simplified language, all the primaries conducted by the committee are null and void. That means the party does not have a presidential candidate, much less flagbearers for the governorship and legislative elections. Basically, the ADC, as things stand, will not participate in the 2027 general election. Lifu decided that all the actions taken by the Mark-led committee are illegal, null, void and of no effect. That is massive!

The ADC immediately blamed the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) for the judgment. In a statement, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the ADC spokesperson, described the verdict as a “desperate attempt to cripple the opposition and deny Nigerians the right to choose their leaders in the forthcoming general elections”. He said the judgment’s timing, barely 24 hours after the “massive turnout” at the ADC presidential campaign rally in Sokoto, “exposes the growing desperation of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC)”. Atiku, for his part, said “it is part of a strategy to weaken my support in the north and frustrate a campaign whose message is resonating across the country”.

The APC rejected the ADC allegation. Olorogun Festus Keyamo, the minister of aviation and aerospace development, also issued a strongly-worded statement. “Justice may be slow, but it is always SURE!” Keyamo wrote on X. “You cannot invade a political Party owned and built by Nigerians, hijack it with the connivance of a so-called National Chairman without a PRIOR meeting and approval of a mini National Convention or the National Executive Committee and hope to bluff your way out of such a brazen act by blaming and blackmailing the ruling Party for a misfortune deliberately stoked by you. Sorry, but the law is decided on facts and evidence, rather than sentiments and outrage…”

For those who may be late to the party, trouble started when some opposition politicians joined the ADC last year. Its national officers, led by Chief Ralph Nwosu, resigned. Mark became the chairman of the caretaker committee and Ogbeni Rauf Aregbesola the national secretary in July 2025. Two months later, Gombe filed an ex parte motion before Justice Emeka Nwite of the Federal High Court, saying he did not resign and asking that he be declared the authentic acting chairman following Nwosu’s resignation. He asked the court to stop the committee from “parading” themselves as national officers. The court did not grant the ex parte motion but asked Mark to file a defence.

However, Mark proceeded to the Court of Appeal to challenge the jurisdiction of the high court since the Supreme Court had ruled that a party’s internal affairs should not be determined by a court. Mark also appealed the order directing him to file a defence. The Court of Appeal told Mark that since the matter was still “live” at the high court, he needed leave of the same court to file an appeal, but Mark argued that it was a fundamental right and leave was not needed. Still, the appeal court dismissed the appeal, describing it as premature. The “status quo ante bellum” should be maintained, it further ruled. We started arguing over the meaning of “status quo ante bellum”.

Dissatisfied with the ruling by the Court of Appeal, Mark headed for the Supreme Court. He made the same argument: that the high court had no jurisdiction and that it ought not to have entertained Gombe’s interlocutory application. The apex court partly repeated what the appeal court said: that the matter was still “live” at the high court and Mark needed to seek leave of that court to file an appeal. What was the appeal exactly? The high court had yet to determine the substantive issues before it, so an appeal was not the appropriate course of action. Therefore, the high court must first rule on whether or not it has jurisdiction before Mark could file the kind of appeal he was pursuing.

After the Supreme Court verdict, Gombe’s lawyers asked for the case to be moved away from Nwite but Mark’s lawyers opposed the request, calling it “forum shopping”. In the meantime, Nwite was promoted to the Court of Appeal, and Lifu, whom the ADC did not fancy because of a previous adverse judgment against the party, was assigned to the case. Aregbesola filed a motion asking Lifu to step aside. So did the party’s welfare secretary, Nkemakolam Ukandu. Lifu dismissed the request. Ukandu also sued the National Judicial Council (NJC) and Justices John Tsoho and Lifu. The court struck out the suit and asked him to pay N50 million each to Tsoho and Lifu for failing to pursue it.

Where do I stand on this burning issue? The first thing I want to do is to implore the judiciary to tread carefully. Political tension is already rising ahead of the 2027 general election. Our judges must do everything possible and reasonable to avoid compounding the situation. They must not become part of the problem. The judges must act with restraint and a sense of responsibility in order protect this democracy. I am particularly worried that courts of equal jurisdiction are making contradictory pronouncements on similar cases. Something is terribly wrong and this has to stop. Am I suggesting that because a case is political, the judges should ignore the facts of the matter? No. Not exactly.

While I suspect that the way and manner Atiku and his allies took over the ADC left much to be desired, I am also of the opinion that you cannot abort a child that has been born, as Bashorun MKO Abiola would say. I am a journalist. I am not a lawyer. But I would argue that the Mark-led committee had been functioning with judicial backing. Indeed, on July 2, 2026, Justice Musa Liman of the Federal High Court upheld the emergence of Mark and Aregbesola as ADC leaders in a separate suit filed by Hon. Leke Abejide. He held that it complied with the party’s constitution and the electoral law. The party, therefore, was not acting without legal cover when it conducted the primaries.

The judges, I would add, must seriously consider the question of whether the injury allegedly suffered by Gombe can be remedied without invalidating every decision taken by the party and potentially disenfranchising millions of Nigerians who would ordinarily have the ADC as one of their electoral choices. That is a question worth examining within the limits of the law. As a layman (and I am ready to defer to superior argument), I do not think nullifying every action and every decision of the caretaker committee is the best way to give justice to Gombe, even if that was his prayer before the high court. His grievance can still be addressed through a pragmatic judicial pronouncement.

It is not my place to prescribe to the judges how they should do their job. That is above my pay grade. But I have a fundamental right to air my opinion on matters of national interest. Thus, it should go without saying that this case has to be disposed of quickly. This is what the National Assembly would call “a matter of urgent national importance”. Elections are just 10 weeks away. We do not have the luxury of time. The ADC contributed to the delay by prolonging the litigation through interlocutory appeals instead of allowing the high court to determine the substantive matter earlier. The ADC contributed to the delay by not allowing the high court to rule on the substantive matter.

The judiciary must uphold the law, but justice is not always served by adopting the most destructive remedy available. Where the law permits, courts should consider whether a remedy can address an established wrong without pointlessly undermining the rights of innocent parties and the electorate. To be clear, I am not suggesting that the judiciary should legitimise illegality or shield politicians from the consequences of their actions. That would be another way of undermining democracy. Rather, my appeal is that, in dispensing justice, our courts must also ensure that the remedy does not create a greater problem than the wrong it seeks to correct. Not everything that is lawful is expedient.

AND FOUR OTHER THINGS…

ATIKU OR OBI?

My assumption all along is that if Mr Peter Obi had not left the ADC, the party would have had a very strong chance of unseating President Bola Tinubu in 2027. Splitting the opposition into two would only empower the APC, I argued. Hypothetically, if Alhaji Atiku Abubakar is eventually disqualified from the 2027 presidential race, as a Federal High Court has done pending appeal, will this benefit Obi, candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC)? For one, it will be an all-south affair and fears of the disruption of the power rotation understanding will be allayed. But I am unsure if Atiku’s supporters are transferable to Obi. There may be a recalibration along our other fault lines. Dicey.

SANUSI’S SHOT

Alhaji Muhammadu Sanusi II, emir of Kano, has said President Tinubu deserves credit for bringing Nigeria’s economy back from the brink. He made specific reference to improvements in economic growth, the inflation rate, foreign reserves, and export diversification. “I’m not a fan of politicians, but we need to give credit to President Tinubu’s administration for bringing us back from the brink,” he said at an Oxford Global Think Tank conference. But he said something that Tinubu needs to seriously chew upon: “This government doesn’t express itself properly. It sees every suggestion and contribution it does not like as an attack, and it doesn’t have good spokespersons.” Exactly.

DOWN, NOT OUT

President Donald Trump was taught a political lesson by American voters in the midterm elections on Tuesday, with his Republican Party losing control of the Senate and the House of Representatives to the Democratic Party. It was mostly down to his meaningless and thoughtless war with Iran — which instigated energy inflation across the world and caused a cost of living crisis for billions, including Nigerians. But those who know Trump will not underrate the damage he can still cause in the remaining two years of his presidency. He can keep waging war against America’s friends and foes and use his veto to stall bills passed by the Congress. It is not yet Uhuru. After all, it is Trump. Erratic.

NO COMMENT

Senator Tahir Monguno, senate chief whip and senator representing Borno north, raised a motion on Tuesday seeking a review and enforcement of Nigeria’s bilateral air services agreement (BASA) with China to allow Nigerian airlines to operate direct flights to the Asian country. But it was something else that was troubling Senate President Godswill Akpabio: scarcity of private jets for campaigns. “Watch December and the confusion. Even the private airlines cannot handle. Common campaigns, we cannot see even private jets to hire,” said Akpabio, who makes an average of one outrageous statement per day. Meanwhile, poor Nigerians are busy crying over the price of garri. Wonderful.

World.title: US Midterm Elections and the Rest of Us
World.content:
Postscript by Waziri Adio

US elections have had a global following for a while. But it is doubtful if any other American election, including presidential polls, has been more keenly watched across the globe than the midterm elections of November 3rd, 2026. The reason is simple. The US, in the second coming of President Donald Trump, has become a major source of global anxiety. On Tuesday, the American electorate handed Mr. Trump and his Republican Party a stinging rebuke, to the obvious relief of many across the world who expect this domestic chastening to mark a positive shift in America’s global engagement. They may be right, and they may not be.

It must be emphasised that American voters, including some of the tribally partisan ones, decided to punish a president who was elected just two years ago on the promise of making life more affordable for Americans but who seemed bent on doing the opposite. It must also be noted that most American voters in the midterm elections were preoccupied with local issues, not global ones. But Trump managed to connect the global to the local in the place where Americans are most sensitive: their pockets and their dining tables. With the strong message from the voters and with the Democratic Party taking control of Congress in January, Trump is expected to dial back some of the actions fuelling high prices, and reinvigorated institutions of restraint are likely to provide much-needed checks.

The most obvious point of relief for Americans and non-Americans alike is the likely end of the US-Israeli war on Iran and of Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The Trump-induced crisis in the Middle East constrained the global supply of oil and gas (and fertiliser), and created an energy crisis that put the world at risk and from which US consumers are not insulated. On account of the war and its aftermath, the average price of petrol in the US went from $2.91 per gallon to $4.40, while the average price of diesel jumped from $3.72 per gallon to $6— increases of 51% and 61% respectively within just nine months. Needless to say, this has had implications for the cost of energy and groceries, and Americans did not find it funny. Beyond America’s shores, Trump’s war of choice has increased the risk of another global recession, inflicted pain on consumers across the globe and put governments in different countries under intense pressure.

“The reason we lost is the (Iran) war,” Vice President JD Vance posted on social media the day after American voters delivered their unmistakable verdict. “The president himself said so last night.” The energy markets reacted positively to the outcome of the polls and to Vance’s blunt assessment. The price of a barrel of Brent crude fell from $110.45 at the beginning of the week to $98.32 on Friday, an 11% drop within the week. The expectation of the markets, of Americans and of the rest of the world is that Trump will quickly focus on ending the war with Iran. If this happens, the prices of crude oil and refined products such as petrol, diesel and aviation fuel are expected to fall even further.

The de-escalation will be needed primarily to appease Americans. But the benefits will not be confined to them, just as the consequences of the war have not been restricted to them. The impact of this avoidable energy crisis is being felt across the globe. In Nigeria, the prices of petrol and diesel rose by 40-90% within nine months, with direct effects on transport, food and energy costs for individuals and on operating costs for businesses. This is significant for a country where most citizens are yet to fully adjust to the shocks of petrol subsidy removal and the devaluation of the national currency. If crude prices fall back to $65-75 per barrel, they will still be above the $64.85 oil price benchmark used in Nigeria’s 2026 budget, and they should bring the price of petrol below N1,000 per litre in the country. This will be a big relief for businesses, households and even the Nigerian government, and it is likely to reduce the appeal of the fiscally reckless but populist promise by some presidential candidates to restore petrol subsidy. In that wise, the local decision made by American voters on November 3rd is likely to benefit Nigerians and consumers in different corners of the globe who are reeling from an avoidable global energy crisis.

In addition to ending the war with Iran, Trump may also, in a bid to address high domestic prices, scale back his indiscriminate imposition of tariffs on imports into the US. Trump has operated under the mistaken belief that any country with a trade surplus with the US must be cheating America, and that tariffs would be borne by exporters. However, it is now and always obvious that tariffs are taxes on consumers. Even though exporters may suffer from reduced demand and income, the real losers are the end consumers. Trump’s tariff wars, clothed in nationalistic garb, have imposed a high cost on America and on other countries, some of which have had to impose retaliatory tariffs.

The tariffs have been challenged in US courts, with the US Supreme Court ruling in February this year that Trump exceeded his executive authority in imposing sweeping tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). The administration has since been exploring other statutes to advance Trump’s preferred trade tool. The feedback from the voters may rein in Trump’s appetite for tariffs. But the impact here may not be as consequential or as universal for the rest of the world as ending the war with Iran, since different countries are affected differently by Trump’s tariff wars.

It is important not to read the outcome of the US midterms as a reprimand of America’s interventions in other countries or as a disapproval of Trump’s gruff treatment of American allies and international institutions. As noted earlier, the voters were preoccupied with local issues on November 3rd. Global affairs and foreign policy barely registered during the campaigns or as priorities for voters, perhaps understandably. Even though Americans say they are tired of forever wars, they did not disapprove of Trump’s invasion of Venezuela and are unlikely to bat an eyelid if he decides to invade Cuba next. The only reason they are bothered about the war in Iran is that it made gasoline, groceries and other necessities less affordable for them.

Similarly, while a majority of Americans may not endorse Trump’s hostility towards the United Nations, the International Criminal Court (ICC), Europe and Canada, or his cosiness with Vladimir Putin and other strongmen, those were not the reasons they voted against him and his party on Tuesday. It would be wrong to expect Trump to change his attitude and ways in these areas, precisely because he has no incentive to do so and is unlikely to come under any pressure to. The Democrats in Congress will definitely hold him to account and keep him in check. But they are more likely to focus on domestic issues, and only on those global issues that have a direct domestic impact (like putting America first). Leading members of the Republican Party, including those in Trump’s cabinet, are likely to break ranks with him as they prepare for a post-Trump future. Some of them may occasionally join forces with the Democrats, but likely only on domestic issues with electoral consequences.

One way Trump may respond to his humiliation at home may be to look for those to safely humiliate abroad, and that could include America’s traditional allies. At home, Trump has surely begun his lame-duck phase. But as America’s president for the next two years, he can still do a lot of damage abroad. Besides, those who see the outcome of November 3rd as a possible turning point in how America engages the world may be getting a bit too excited. There is no guarantee that the next American president, even if a Democrat, will depart from the path America has firmly embraced: growing insularity and the weaponisation of dependency. That is a space to watch. The need for a concert of middle powers to rethink and reinvent the global order has not been overtaken by events. The post-WW2 global order was built around undue dependence on America. It should be clear to all by now that this cannot endure forever.

However, one lesson of the midterms that is not discussed enough is that the idea of America as a beacon of light is still very much alive. Within two years of Trump 2.0, America had started looking more like a country firmly under the thumb of one man and less like the greatest democratic experiment of the modern world. To be sure, it will take more than one election to know if some irreparable damage has not been done, but these elections have shown that reports of the death of democracy in America have been somewhat exaggerated.

The voters have shown the way. The culture that underpins democracy has not given way. Some of the vital institutions have held firm. The outcome of the election, with many firsts, is a better reflection of the diversity of America. The mechanisms for restraint and accountability are likely to be re-energised. For the global community that needs the US to continue to be the shining city on a hill, a positive example of democratic ethos and practice, November 3rd is a cheery even if cautious affirmation.

World.title: Obi Challenges Tinubu to Visit 33 States, Account for Loans, Subsidy Savings
World.content:
Chuks Okocha and Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr. Peter Obi, has challenged President Bola Tinubu to visit the remaining 33 states of the federation and account for the over $100billion in loans obtained by his administration and N15.8trillion reportedly saved from the removal of the fuel subsidy.



This is as the NDC has accused President Tinubu’s administration of eroding Nigeria’s commonwealth through excessive borrowing, poor fiscal management and inadequate investment in critical public services, declaring that Obi and his running mate, Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, would reverse the trend if elected in 2027.



Obi said Nigerians deserved to know how the resources accruing to the federal government through increased revenue, taxation, borrowing and subsidy removal had been utilised since Tinubu assumed office.

The former Anambra State governor made the demand in a statement issued yesterday and addressed to the president, titled ‘Good Day, Mr. President: Nigerians Deserve Accountability’.



Obi’s comments followed Tinubu’s recent visit to Akwa Ibom State.

Congratulating Tinubu on the visit, Obi said he hoped it would encourage the president to travel to other parts of the country and engage Nigerians on his administration’s performance.



“I congratulate you on spending a night in one of Nigeria’s states outside Lagos and Abuja. I hope you enjoyed the warmth, hospitality, and delicious cuisine of Akwa Ibom,” he said.

He, however, questioned the president’s foreign travels, alleging that Tinubu had spent over 260 days outside Nigeria since assuming office.



“I sincerely hope this visit will inspire you to travel to the remaining 33 states of the federation, spend time with the people and, more importantly, explain what your administration has done with the N15.8 trillion saved from the removal of the fuel subsidy, the over $100 billion you have borrowed,” Obi stated.



He also asked the president to account for the increased revenues accruing to the government from taxation and other sources, including additional revenues the administration reportedly celebrated last year as exceeding its target.



The NDC presidential candidate said Nigerians deserved measurable evidence of improvements in their living conditions, particularly in poverty reduction, education, healthcare, electricity supply and national security.

He asked the federal government to disclose how many Nigerians it lifted out of poverty under the administration, as well as how many out-of-school children it returned to classrooms.



Obi also demanded information on how many functional primary healthcare centres the government built.

On electricity, he questioned how much the power supply had improved, recalling Tinubu’s promise that Nigerians should not vote for him if he failed to fix the country’s electricity challenges.

“They also deserve to know how much electricity supply has improved, especially given your promise that if you do not fix power, Nigerians should not vote for you,” he said.



On security, Obi called for an explanation of the administration’s efforts to secure the country, noting that Nigeria remained among the most terrorised countries in the world.

He maintained that the government owed citizens an explanation of how it had spent public resources, insisting that Nigerians deserved answers on the administration’s performance.



“Mr. President, Nigerians deserve answers. They deserve to know what has been done with the resources entrusted to your government,” he said.

Obi added that accountability, transparency and measurable improvements in citizens’ welfare should form the foundation of the country’s development.



“The new Nigeria we want to build will be based on accountability, transparency, and the physical, measurable impact of our public resources on the lives of citizens,” he said.

NDC: Obi, Kwankwaso Will End Tinubu’s Borrowing-Driven Governance

Meanwhile, the NDC has declared that the Obi-Kwankwaso ticket was committed to ending what it described as a borrowing-dependent model of governance and replacing it with prudent management of public resources, accountability and productive investments capable of improving citizens’ welfare.



The NDC said this in a statement issued yesterday by its National Presidential Campaign Council spokesperson, Dr. Chiogo Constance Ikokwu, in response to Tinubu’s criticism of Obi over the persistent gully erosion menace in Anambra State.

It argued that the former Anambra State governor’s political ambition went beyond addressing erosion in his home state, insisting that his broader mission was to halt the alleged erosion of Nigeria’s national wealth.



The party questioned the economic benefits of removing the petrol subsidy, demanding explanations for what happened to the anticipated fiscal gains, particularly amid the federal government’s continued borrowing and what it described as inadequate funding of essential public services.



It also expressed concern over the country’s rising debt profile, poor debt-service-to-revenue ratio and the persistent underfunding of healthcare and education.

According to the NDC, Nigerians deserve to know why increased revenue generation and the removal of the fuel subsidy have not translated into improved public services and better living conditions.



“Obi-Kwankwaso will not allow Nigeria to continue borrowing at an alarming rate, without corresponding benefits, while citizens endure worsening poverty, unemployment, insecurity and declining purchasing power,” the party said.

To strengthen its argument on fiscal management, the NDC compared the financial records of Obi and Tinubu during their respective tenures as governors of Anambra and Lagos states.



It claimed that Obi left the equivalent of $500 million in investments and local and foreign currency assets when he handed over power in Anambra State in 2014, including $156 million in dollar-denominated bonds.

In contrast, the party cited Debt Management Office figures which, it said, put Lagos State’s external debt at approximately $190.43 million at the end of 2007, when Tinubu left office.



The NDC also criticised the pension law enacted during Tinubu’s administration in Lagos, which provided lifetime benefits for former governors and their deputies.

It alleged that the law entitled former governors and their deputies to pensions equivalent to 100 per cent of the incumbent governor’s basic salary, houses in Lagos and Abuja, multiple vehicles, furniture and utility allowances, entertainment benefits, free medical care and other privileges.



The party described the provisions as excessive, arguing that they placed unnecessary pressure on public resources.

It further claimed that a subsequent Lagos administration was compelled to review some of the provisions, while Obi did not establish a similar pension arrangement for former governors in Anambra State.



The NDC maintained that the 2027 presidential election would give Nigerians a choice between what it described as Tinubu’s borrowing-dependent economic model and the Obi-Kwankwaso commitment to fiscal discipline and accountability.

Warning against unsustainable borrowing, the party referenced the financial difficulties experienced by countries such as Argentina and Zambia, as well as historical examples involving the Ottoman Empire and 19th-century Egypt.



It argued that excessive debt accumulation, without corresponding productive investments and effective fiscal management, could undermine national development and threaten future generations.

On the erosion controversy that prompted the statement, the NDC defended Obi’s record, saying his administration took steps to address gully erosion and flooding in Anambra State.

It said Obi helped attract and launch the World Bank-supported Nigeria Erosion and Watershed Management Project (NEWMAP) in the state.



The party also cited the former governor’s directive that new state roads should incorporate adequate drainage systems connected to safe discharge points.

It listed concrete drainage and local flood-control projects executed in communities, including Adazi Nnukwu, Amawbia and Umuoji, as evidence of his administration’s efforts to tackle environmental challenges.

The NDC added that Obi regularly engaged the federal government to secure ecological intervention funds for the state, while emphasising accountability in their utilisation.

World.title: NNPC Counters Power Minister, Says Gas Network Not Responsible for Drop in Electricity
World.content:
•Abuja, Lagos, Kwara, Oyo to get improved supply in 24 hours

• TCN rejects grid instability claims

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

The Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited has countered the claims by the Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO), and the Federal Ministry of Power that operational constraints on gas transportation network was responsible for the recent decline in electricity generation.



This is just as the Minister of Power, Mr. Joseph Tegbe, yesterday promised that electricity supply to Abuja, Lagos, Kwara and Oyo states, which were currently experiencing outages would improve within the next 24 hours.

The Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN) has also rejected claims by Ikeja Electric (IKEDC), attributing several Band A feeder outages to “grid instability” and assigning responsibility to the transmission company.



NNPCL’s Chief Corporate Communications Officer, Andy Odeh, said in a statement yesterday that the gas network operated by NNPC Gas Infrastructure Company Limited (NGIC), a subsidiary of the NNPC, remained available to support gas deliveries to power-generating stations nationwide.



“NGIC’s operational records do not indicate transportation-related constraints within its network that explain the current decline in electricity generation,” Odeh said.

NNPC’s clarification followed a November 5 statement by the NISO, which attributed the lower power generation partly to limited gas availability and reduced water inflows into hydroelectric stations.

Specifically, the system operator said the limited availability of “gas has constrained the capacity of affected thermal generating stations to operate at their available levels, while reduced water inflows into reservoirs have impacted the generation capacity of hydroelectric power stations”.



Tegbe also attributed the electricity supply shortfall to planned maintenance at the Egbin Power Station in Lagos and constraints in gas supply to some thermal power stations, which had reduced the amount of electricity available on the national grid.



“Grid operators have, therefore, implemented load shedding in some areas to manage the shortfall. Sabotage of key transmission lines has also restricted the use of alternative routes to supply some locations, especially Lagos,” the minister explained.

But the NNPC said the availability of its gas transportation infrastructure should be assessed separately from gas production, commercial supply arrangements, and actual deliveries to individual power plants.



The company said gas production volumes had grown by about 10 percent year-to-date in 2026, citing efforts to implement the federal government’s gas development and monetisation agenda.

“Gas supply availability is therefore not a challenge as NNPC remains committed to supporting efforts to improve electricity generation through safe, reliable and efficient gas supply and transportation,” it said.



The company said determining the cause of the power shortfall required a broader assessment of the gas-to-power value chain.

According to the oil firm, the review should cover the availability and operational readiness of generating units, plant maintenance schedules, and actual gas offtake, noting that these factors determine whether gas supplied to power plants can be converted into electricity.



“Gas production, commercial supply arrangements and actual deliveries to individual power plants must be assessed separately from the availability of transportation infrastructure,” the NNPC said.

The company called for a coordinated review of operational data by gas suppliers, transporters, power generators, and NISO to identify specific constraints and determine appropriate interventions.

Abuja, Lagos, Kwara, Oyo to Get Improved Supply in 24 Hours

In an update on the power situation, Tegbe said he was aware of the strain the outages had placed on households and businesses in the four affected areas.

Tegbe said his team was working to return the affected generating units to service in phases, with the first units expected to come back online within 48 to 72 hours, counting down from yesterday.



He said the ministry was also working with operators to improve gas supply and accelerate repairs to the damaged infrastructure.

Tegbe also applauded residents of the affected states for their patience.

“I thank everyone affected for their patience and will provide further updates as supply is gradually restored,” he stated.

The current outages, which have lasted several days, have hit the four states, leaving many households and businesses in extended blackout and forcing reliance on alternative power sources.



In the areas impacted by the power cuts, Discos had announced load shedding schedules, with many Band A customers complaining of sharp drops in supply hours.

The situation, the minister earlier said, was compounded by reduced generation from hydro stations due to low water levels, gas constraints to thermal stations, among others, which he stressed limited wheeling to the power distributors.



Meanwhile, the TCN has rejected claims by IKEDC attributing several Band A feeder outages to “grid instability”.

In a statement TCN issued yesterday, the transmission company said the attribution contained in IKEDC’s public notice of November 5 was “inaccurate and misleading.”
