World.title: Trump says he offered UFC's Dana White the press secretary role
World.content:
President Trump says he has offered the open White House press secretary role to UFC CEO Dana White.

The president said Saturday in a Truth Social post, "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States."

"I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris," he said in reference to UFC fighters. "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left."

It was unclear at the time of publication whether White has accepted the position, though he shared an image of himself at the White House press briefing room podium to his Instagram story with the caption, "On to the next chapter."

During a news conference for a boxing event in London Saturday that White was promoting, White was asked about Mr. Trump's social media post.

"I'm flying to Washington, D.C., right now," White said with a smile and a chuckle. "… I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday. So I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

Reporting from at least one media outlet suggested that the post may have been made tongue-in-cheek. CBS News has reached out to the White House and UFC for additional comment.

Dana White, president of Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) and President Trump during an event in Las Vegas, Nevada, on Aug. 5, 2026. Ian Maule / Bloomberg via Getty Images

The president's remarks come days after Democrats swept the midterm elections, taking control of the House and the Senate.

The press secretary role has been vacant since Oct. 16, when conservative commentator Katie Zacharia was removed from the job after just five days. Zacharia was Mr. Trump's pick to fill the role after Karoline Leavitt stepped aside in August, saying she wanted to spend more time with her young family.

As the chief of Ultimate Fighting Championship, running a global league valued at more than $15 billion, White has been a longtime supporter of Mr. Trump and attended his inauguration. The White House also hosted an Ultimate Fighting Championship in July on the South Lawn to mark the nation's 250th anniversary. The event coincided with Mr. Trump's 80th birthday.

"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!" Mr. Trump said in his post.

In an interview with "60 Minutes" last September, White described his relationship with Mr. Trump, saying that when they get together for dinner, they "don't talk politics."

"We talk about … goofy guy stuff that all guys talk about. You know what I mean?" Dana said. "… We talk about 'Rocky' movies. We talk about different fights that have happened."

World.title: 2 licensed skydivers die after midair collision in California
World.content:
Two female skydivers who were taking part in an organized skydiving event in California were killed after colliding midair and plummeting to the ground.

The accident occurred Friday and involved two licensed, experienced skydivers at Skydive Elsinore, the company said in a statement. The Riverside County Sheriff's Department said deputies were dispatched late Friday morning after reports of an air emergency. The skydivers were taken to a local hospital with critical injuries.

They were pronounced dead at the hospital, the sheriff said.

The Riverside County coroner's office later identified the victims as 29-year-old Levi Pimentel of Aurora, Illinois, and 56-year-old Georgia Jean of Box Elder, South Dakota.

Skydive Elsinore said the free-fall portion of the dive and the opening of the parachutes were normal, but as they were preparing to land, the two skydivers collided at about 150 feet above the ground.

"The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground," Skydive Elsinore said in a statement. The company said there was no evidence of equipment malfunction.

The skydivers were visiting from out of town to take part in an organized skydiving event, the company said.

Skydive Elsinore — which says they are the longest-running skydiving operation in North America — is located approximately one hour away from both San Diego and Los Angeles metropolitan areas.

World.title: Mass shooting in Polish market leaves at least 6 dead, 15 injured
World.content:
A man drove into an open market in the Polish city of Krakow and opened fire from his car, killing at least six people and injuring at least 15 others, authorities said. Another three people were later found dead in the suspect's home. The suspected gunman was shot by police and taken into custody.

The shooting happened in the Main Market Square in Krakow around 3 p.m. local time on Saturday. Krakow police said the alleged shooter began firing at random people from his car. Police said the victims were four women and two men.

Two women and one man believed to be relatives of the suspect were later found dead in suspect's home, said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, according to The Associated Press.

Marcin Kierwiński, Poland's interior minister, said there were indications the suspect was fascinated by far-right ideology, according to Reuters. The suspect, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, is fascinated with far-right ideologies and held "very radical" and "ultra-nationalistic" views, The AP reported Kierwiński said at a news conference.

A damaged store display near Krakow's Main Market Square after a shooting that killed six people and injured more than 10 others, in Krakow, Poland, on Nov. 7, 2026. Jakub Włodek/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/via REUTERS

Five foreigners were among the wounded victims, Kierwiński said. He said a foreign national was among those killed.

A spokesperson from the U.S. State Department told CBS News they are not aware of any U.S. citizens being harmed at this time.

Police officers are also among the wounded. The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a confrontation with police a short distance away from the initial violence, and was taken to a hospital for treatment.

The death toll earlier stood at five, but the Malopolski regional government updated it to six in a post on X.

Kierwiński wrote on X that two police officers were wounded by gunfire and one is in serious condition.

"Police officers in Kraków risked their lives to intervene. Immediately. Thanks to their heroic actions, the attacker was quickly apprehended," he wrote.

The alleged black car of the suspect in a shooting stands in the historic center of Krakow, Poland, on Nov. 7, 2026 where a gunman opened fire, killing five people and wounding around a dozen. Bartosz SIEDLIK /AFP via Getty Images

In a social media post, Krakow police said the gunman acted alone.

Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, told TVN24 that the suspected gunman was wearing military-style fatigues and used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police found many pieces of other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car.

Emergency responders gather after a deadly shooting on Nov. 7, 2026, in the Main Market Square of Krakow, Poland. Omar Marques / Getty Images

"I am being kept informed by the Minister of the Interior about the situation in Krakow following the tragic shooting," Tusk wrote on social media, adding that "the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack."

He later headed to Krakow from the capital, Warsaw, a government spokesperson said.

Other details were not immediately available.

Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy.

"The square will belong to us again," Gibała said in a video posted to X.

"We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that's shattered the peace of Poland," Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X. "America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow."

Emergency responders gather after a deadly shooting on Nov. 7, 2026, in the Main Market Square of Krakow, Poland. Omar Marques / Getty Images



Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland, a European Union and NATO member of 38 million people.

"I saw a man shooting at people and walking around the square," Annette, a woman in her sixties, told news wire Agence France-Presse. "It's a tragedy for Krakow; we've never seen anything like this before."

A woman reacts at the site of a shooting near the main market square of Krakow, Poland, on Nov. 7, 2026. Jakub Porzycki / REUTERS

Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said in a statement that the EU stands with Poland and offered her condolences.

"The tragic loss of life in the shooting in Kraków is a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland," she wrote on X. "Poland's strength lies in the resilience of its people. In this moment of grief, Poland does not stand alone."

Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and roughly 155 miles from the capital, Warsaw.

World.title: Israel's president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government
World.content:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27.

Eisenkot, a former military chief, ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leading a bloc of parties seeking to oust Israel's longest-serving premier.

"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," Eisenkot wrote on X in his first reaction to the announcement of his designation.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu's party won a clear majority in the vote. But in marathon discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel's main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government.

Herzog's decision is a setback for Netanyahu, who has leveled allegations, so far without evidence, that some Arab countries interfered in the elections.

The acting director-general of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."

Herzog's announcement, which had been expected on Sunday, came shortly after Netanyahu called for a "national unity government" in a video statement and warned against "hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters" — an apparent reference to the Arab-led parties who have backed Eisenkot.

Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly portrayed the Arab-led parties as a threat to national security. Eisenkot, however, has indicated a willingness to partner with them as long as they meet certain conditions, including agreeing to refer to Hamas as a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed.

Eisenkot's party, Yashar, slammed the prime minister's video with a statement posted on X and urged members of Netanyahu's party, Likud, to disavow their alliance with "radical parties," which is seen as a reference to some of the settler-linked and ultra-Orthodox parties in his religious-nationalist coalition.

The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Netanyahu's bloc won 53, while Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 seats.

Because neither Eisenkot's nor Netanyahu's blocs won a clear majority of the vote, they would need some support from the Arab parties to form a coalition government. The heads of the two largest Arab parties said they would be willing to help Eisenkot's opposition bloc oust Netanyahu, though most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from the Arab parties to form a government.

Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on — Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.

Netanyahu, whom President Trump endorsed enthusiastically, will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

World.title: Pope Leo calls for universal healthcare weeks after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Montevideo - Pope Leo XIV drew on his own recent experience of illness and hospitalization after surgery for lung cancer on Friday to make an impassioned appeal for universal access to healthcare, greater social equality and a society that does not measure people's worth by their productivity or wealth.

"Recently I experienced firsthand the limitations imposed by illness and I received care for which I am grateful," the Pope said in his first speech after arriving in Uruguay, to the country's political and civic leaders.

Pope Leo XIV was released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital four days after removing a cancerous tumor from his right lung. "The experience made me think of the many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis or receive the treatment they need."

"Ensuring that healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of their resources, is a duty that confronts every society," he said.

Uruguay is the first stop of a 12-day trip that also includes Argentina and Peru. Leo's doctors said he needed no further treatment after his operation and was cleared to travel. The trip schedule is the longest international journey of his pontificate so far, with 19,000 travel miles, 14 flights, 36 speeches and approximately 50 events.

Vatican officials told reporters ahead of the trip that the Pope would have a medical team travel with him, as is customary on papal trips, but that no special measures were being taken. "We're speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health," the Vatican spokesman said.

The Latin America journey is Leo's first return as Pope to the country and region that has profoundly shaped his vision, and where he spent decades of his life, first as an Augustinian missionary, and then as bishop of Chiclayo, Peru. The pope holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.

MONTEVIDEO, URUGUAY - NOVEMBER 6: Pope Leo XIV looks on during a welcome ceremony at Plaza Independencia as part of an official visit to Uruguay. Enzo Santos / MB Media / Getty Images

Leo's remarks on caring for the sick were part of a broad appeal for a society where the most vulnerable are protected, and where economic development benefits everyone rather than just the elite.

"The creation of wealth and economic initiative…must also translate into goods and opportunities that effectively reach everyone," Leo said.

While praising Uruguay for four decades of uninterrupted democracy, he stressed that a country's success is ultimately measured by how it protects human dignity and cares for the most vulnerable in society.

Leo also spoke in defense of children, including the unborn. Abortion was legalized in Uruguay in 2012, making it one of the first Latin American countries to do so.

"Their absolute dependence on their mother does not diminish the dignity to which they are entitled or the protection they deserve," the pope said.

Children, he said, must have access to quality education and opportunities to enter the workforce and achieve personal independence. Touching on a subject close to his heart, he said that technological advances and artificial intelligence must serve human beings rather than replace workers.

Leo will remain in Uruguay until Sunday when he will continue his travels to Argentina and Peru. The Vatican spokesman said there, Leo would address a range of issues, including the environment, arms tracking and political instability.

The Pope will also hold meetings with survivors of clerical sex abuse, but no further details are available as of now.

World.title: UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
World.content:
UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.

Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.

Sponsor Message

White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.

When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."

He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."

The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.

Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as "assistants," adding, "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"

Sponsor Message

While White didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.

Trump's post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.

The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.

The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.

Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.

He brought White and the sport to the White House's South Lawn in June for the celebration of America's 250th year of its independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.

Sponsor Message

"It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one," said White afterward.

White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

World.title: Homelessness in the U.S. saw its largest drop in more than a decade last year
World.content:
Homelessness in the U.S. saw its largest drop in more than a decade last year

toggle caption i Damian Dovarganes/AP

After years of increasing to record-high levels , the homeless population in the U.S. dropped more than 6% in 2025. That amounts to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It's the second year in a row that homelessness has declined, with a smaller drop in 2024.

"President Trump's actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release announcing the results of an annual count in communities around the country. The agency had not yet posted a detailed report.

Sponsor Message

A second independent analysis based on the same count, but commissioned by the advocacy group National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline but credited different reasons for it.

"It's good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working," said CEO Ann Oliva.

Both analyses find there's still nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. living in shelters or on the streets, significantly more than before the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Trump administration cited its changes in immigration policy as a key factor in the decline. During the Biden administration, New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw a surge in asylum seekers who turned up at homeless shelters. "That's also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently," said Devon Kurtz, Public Safety Policy Director at the Cicero Institute, an administration ally on homelessness policy.

Kurtz also pointed to declines in cities like San Francisco, which is moving to support more sober-living options , housing that bans drugs and alcohol. But critics say that can send more people back to the street if they relapse, which is common.

The Trump administration argues that the requirement to be drug-free would help more people achieve recovery, and wants to expand such programs. In fact, the administration wants to overhaul several billion dollars in homelessness spending and shift it toward short-term housing with mandated addiction and mental health treatment. So far that's been blocked by courts .

toggle caption i Lynne Sladky/AP

The administration says longstanding federal policy of getting people into permanent housing first, then offering voluntary treatment, has failed, and is to blame for the pandemic spike in homelessness. But Oliva, with the homelessness alliance, said programs that get people off the street without preconditions were a big part of the latest declines, especially among veterans.

Sponsor Message

"Investments in programs like that are much closer to the scale of need for veterans than for any other population experiencing homelessness," she said. Homelessness among U.S. veterans was down more than 7% last year, and has declined nearly 60% since 2010.

By contrast, Oliva said more permanent housing is needed for people who are chronically homeless, and more likely to suffer from mental health problems and addiction. Unlike other groups that saw a decline last year, there was a small uptick in people who've been homeless for a long time.

HUD also credited a crackdown on homeless encampments after the Supreme Court in 2024 said cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public places. Oliva said the analysis her group commissioned showed that cities with such bans "actually did worse than the national average."

Oliva noted last year's decline in homelessness was broad and likely due to a number of factors, including softening rental markets in some places. Even though rents are still high they're down from record peaks during the pandemic, and that could stem the flow of newly unhoused people.

There were also declines in places that saw major weather disasters, like western North Carolina and Hawaii. When HUD and other groups move in to help those displaced, unhoused people also get assistance they did not have before.

World.title: The surprising and often forgotten history of economic populism in Texas
World.content:
The surprising and often forgotten history of economic populism in Texas

Transcript

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

As the votes came in on election night Tuesday, some of the most shocking results were in Texas. The blue wave did not stop at the border of the Lone Star State. Democrats swept the top races in Texas with James Talarico winning a Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa winning the race for governor.

Austin-based political commentator David Griscom was perhaps not as surprised to see his state flip. Earlier this year, he published a book titled "The Myth Of Red Texas: Cowboys, Populism, And Class War In The Radical South." He joins us now. Welcome.

DAVID GRISCOM: Thank you so much for having me. It's been a really wonderful past few days.

SCHMITZ: What great timing, with a book title like that. Texas, obviously, as you've written, has a reputation for being a reliably red state, but as we've seen, it's a lot more complicated than that. How did Texas Democrats pull this off?

GRISCOM: Well, I think in a lot of ways, you saw Texas Democrats returning to our roots here. You know, many people forget this, but Texas was once the hotbed of kind of left-wing, pro-working-class politics. Going all the way back to the 1890s, we were the heart of the populist movement, and it's no accident that James Talarico, Clayton Tucker and Gina Hinojosa all call themselves populists.

Using this kind of rhetoric, I think, really focuses on the billionaires and the folks who are harming our democracy. And I think that gave a lot of people who might have been waiting for an excuse to maybe buck the Republican Party, which has dominated state politics here for so long, the opportunity to do so.

SCHMITZ: Let's go back in history a little. You know, Texas politics are often associated, you know, with oil billionaires, conservative evangelical voters and the Republican establishment. You know, your book, "The Myth Of Red Texas," tells the story of, you know, working-class, populist tradition that oftentimes goes overlooked. Tell us a little bit about that.

GRISCOM: So there's multiple phases of this. It's an entire kind of generation or tradition in Texas politics that has been forgotten. My book opens up talking about barbed wire, which we all associate with Texas. But when barbed wire first comes to Texas, it was fiercely resisted. There was an episode called The Fence Cutting War, and this happened all across the state, where working-class cowboys got together and they started cutting down these new barbed wire fences because they saw these as a tool that was being used to dispossess them.

This then flows into the populist movement, which was born right here in Texas in Lampasas, where a bunch of farmers got together and they started asking themselves why those who work most get least and those who work least get most. And they started to look around and realize that it was the monopoly powers, the power of the banks, and it was the corruption of the politicians.

SCHMITZ: I want to dig in a little bit on that and the populism aspect of this. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has embraced the populist label with open arms. You know, I want to play a clip here from an interview that she did before the election with The New York Times.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GINA HINOJOSA: Populism is about economic power. We see that things are so stacked against working people in this country. Fighting culture wars at this time is not a winnable fight, and that is not the fight of 2026.

SCHMITZ: And that's really interesting. I mean, she's separating her and Talarico's style of politics from Democrats elsewhere, who have sort of engaged more in identity politics. Is there something uniquely Texan about Hinojosa's or Talarico's approach as Democrats?

GRISCOM: Absolutely. So again, you know, Texas has had major swings before where everyday working people - cotton farmers, Black and white - they were able to unite working people, the vast majority of people, on messages about the ways that they can improve their life. And that's what Gina and James were able to do. They didn't run a partisan message, and that is a long tradition that has existed in this state.

I'd also add, if I could, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez - after 2024, she made a very strong point about how effective some of the anti-trans ads that the Trump administration put out were - you know, they are for they/them, Trump is for you. And AOC said, like, this was a problem with Democrats. When a lot of people were feeling economic pain, they felt that the things that Democrats were interested in weren't immediately important to their lives.

And in this election, the table was kind of reversed because all of the ads in Texas were about anti-LGBTQ things, anti-trans. And when somebody's talking about that - in this case being Republicans - when you're really struggling to get by, it does really show that these folks are out of touch with your economic needs, and that really helped Gina and James, for sure.

SCHMITZ: That is David Griscom, author of "The Myth Of Red Texas." David, thank you.

GRISCOM: Thank you so much.
