World.title: Regional gaps in safe sport rules remain a 'major' concern for Canada's sport integrity agency
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More than six months on from a report that rang alarm bells about the prevalence of abuse and maltreatment in sport, the head of Canada’s sport integrity agency continues to have “major” concerns about regional gaps in safe sport rules.

Sport Integrity Canada maintains Canada’s Safe Sport Program public registry, which includes the names of more than 80 people who’ve been sanctioned across more than two dozen different sporting bodies.

The registry captures violations of the Universal Code of Conduct to Prevent and Address Maltreatment in Sport, a set of rules governing behaviour around sport that all national sport organizations in Canada had to adopt as a condition of federal funding. It applies to coaches, volunteers, athletes and other leaders across sport.

A New Game Plan Series

WATCH | Sports commission warns of 'culture of silence': Commissioner of future of sport says 'widespread abuse,' 'culture of silence' exist at all levels | Duration closed caption 2:01 Lise Maisonneuve, head of the Future of Sport in Canada Commission, says BIPOC, 2SLGBTQ+ and para-athletes in particular face a lack of opportunity across all levels of sport in her report to enhance safe sport and improve the sport system in Canada.

The behaviours captured in the registry range from physical, psychological and sexual maltreatment to neglect and retaliation, among others. Some of the people on the list have been convicted of crimes. Some have been banned from sport permanently. Others faced sanctions such as suspensions or additional education.

It’s a snapshot of abuse and maltreatment in sport in Canada, but far from a fulsome picture.

That’s because most provincial and local sporting organizations aren’t required to adopt the Universal Code of Conduct. Details of maltreatment at those levels may not appear on Sport Integrity Canada’s registry.

“We know that individuals who cause harm in this way can move from one sport to another sport at one level to another level, where their names aren’t being appropriately placed on a registry so people know about it,” Sport Integrity Canada president and CEO Jeremy Luke said.

“It's a major concern for us. It was a very clear recommendation coming out of the Future of Sport in Canada Commission report and it needs to be put in place in Canada to protect participants who are participating in these sports.”

It’s also not a new concern. Reporting from CBC’s Shattered Trust project chronicled the problems with implementing safe sport rules at the grassroots level, and the consequences of the gaps that exist there, over the last few years.

The evidence shows that despite growing awareness and policy efforts, maltreatment remains deeply rooted in Canadian sport. Future of Sport in Canada Commission report

The Future of Sport in Canada Commission’s final report, released in March, described a system with a longstanding “culture of silence,” and one where racism and discrimination are major issues.

The commission’s work began after a number of athletes spoke publicly and testified in front of Parliament about the harm they experienced during their sporting careers.

“The evidence shows that despite growing awareness and policy efforts, maltreatment remains deeply rooted in Canadian sport,” the commission, led by former Ontario Chief Justice Lise Maisonneuve, wrote. “It affects individuals at all levels, including at the grassroots. These systemic problems require immediate and sustained government action. Although it is not possible to eliminate maltreatment entirely, governments and sport organizations must work together to strengthen and align prevention and response measures so that all participants can safely experience sport’s benefits.”

There are plenty of rules at the national level, where Sport Canada has the power to withhold federal funding to national sport organizations that don’t follow safe sport rules.

It’s below the national level that a hodge podge of safe sport policies persist, from the education every athlete and coach receives, to something as simple and important as background checks, the commission found.

WATCH | The Norway Model: A New Game Plan: The Norway Model | Duration closed caption 5:43 CBC Sports' Donnovan Bennett explores Norway's sporting system, and how Canada might be able to learn from the Nordic nation.

“Participants noted major inconsistencies in safe sport policies across levels of sport and jurisdictions, emphasizing the need for a shared understanding of maltreatment and consistent standards ‘from coast to coast to coast,’” the commission wrote, describing interviews with more than 1,000 participants in the Canadian sport system. “They supported the development of clear and harmonized expectations and remedies for all participants, regardless of sport or level.”

‘Urgent’ need for harmonization

The Future of Sport in Canada Commission said there’s an “urgent” need for more uniformity when it comes to how maltreatment is handled across the country.

More than seven years ago, sports ministers from provinces and territories across the country signed the Red Deer Declaration , agreeing that sport should be a safe place free from maltreatment and abuse. They agreed to work together on issues like monitoring and education.

The declaration led to the Universal Code of Conduct at the national level, but implementation at the provincial and territorial level has been “uneven,” the commission found. Quebec has its own safe sport legislation, for example, while British Columbia created a non-profit called Sport Safeguarding BC to oversee complaints in that province.

Some jurisdictions still don’t have a centralized place for people to file complaints. Many rely on third parties to handle those complaints, a set-up that the commission described as “costly, inconsistent, and affected by perceived or real conflicts of interest.”

The commission called for a pan-Canadian safe sport program that would harmonize rules, education, and the handling of complaints. But that will “take time and political commitment to build,” the commission said.

Luke envisions a system where Sport Integrity Canada can take a leadership role and provide guidance on sharing information and making sure there are consistent rules.

That includes closing the gaps on the registry.

“I think it's a priority, but I also think we need to get to a place where a priority becomes action and that we can put in place the necessary systems to make it occur,” Luke said.

“There are some challenges around putting in place registries, but what's most important is that we protect people who participate in sport, particularly vulnerable people, and that we agree as a country that we want to have a registry so that we can properly protect participants in sport from the grassroots level all the way through to the national level.”

WATCH | What can Canada learn from Australia's sports system?: A New Game Plan: What Australia can teach Canada about rebuilding its sports system | Duration closed caption 4:41 CBC Sports' Karissa Donkin takes us behinds the scenes of Australia's sporting system, and wonders what Canada might be able to take away from how the nation runs its program.

Funding for safe sport

In the last year, the federal government has earmarked more than $1 billion, spread over several years, to a sport system in transition.

Sport Canada has put $17.3 million into Sport Integrity Canada in 2026-27, up from $12.6 million in the previous fiscal year. The Sport Dispute Resolution Centre of Canada also saw a boost, from $1.94 million, up from $1.5 million.

Adam van Koeverden, Canada’s secretary of state for sport, gather sport leaders from across the country for a national summit in Ottawa next Monday and Tuesday, and safe sport will likely be on the agenda.

“Sport Integrity Canada has been among the strongest organizations in terms of their ability to apply for additional funding and demonstrate very, very clearly where the gaps lie and what they need in order to achieve stronger and safer sport systems,” van Koeverden said in a recent interview with CBC Sports. “They're one of our most important partners and certainly a regulated, mandated organization within the Canadian sport system.”

But the real heavy lifting to close the gap will require a pan-Canadian solution, something the federal government alluded to in an October press release announcing sport funding.

It will take all provinces and territories on the same page with the same vision, and it’s not clear how long something like that might take.

“Addressing maltreatment is a shared responsibility that requires commitment and collaboration from all levels of government across Canada,” the press release from Sport Canada says. “The federal government continues to work closely with provincial and territorial partners to advance safe sport priorities, including independent complaint mechanisms, awareness and education initiatives, and the exploration of a national safe sport registry. Together, these efforts look to build a more coordinated, consistent and effective approach to safe sport from coast to coast to coast.”

Looking abroad

Sport Integrity Canada works with other sport integrity organizations across the world through the International Integrity Group. Canada will serve on the organization’s executive through 2028.

The group includes Sport Integrity Australia, the similarly named organization that has wrestled with many of the same issues as Canada has faced.

More than five years into its existence, Sport Integrity Australia is trying to tackle the fragmentation between levels of government by adding national integrity managers at the state level to help integrate safe sport policies. Australia is also a federation, with powers divided between the federal level and provincial/state bodies.

“It gives us that formal connection from the national to the state level,” Sport Integrity Australia CEO Dr. Sarah Benson told CBC Sports. “By having those integrity managers in place, they'll also be a connection through to the community level.”

Dr. Sarah Benson, CEO of Sport Integrity Australia, is spearheading a review on the effectiveness of national integrity framework that guides that country's safe sport. (Karissa Donkin/CBC)

Australia doesn’t have all the answers. Still a young agency, Benson is spearheading a review on the effectiveness of the national integrity framework that guides safe sport in Australia.

She’s also hoping to use a home Olympic and Paralympic Games in Brisbane in 2032 as a vehicle for culture change in Australian sport.

“How can we do things differently that would actually benefit and put the athlete at the centre of what we're doing?” Benson said. “How can we use sport to actually try and make a difference in those areas that we've really been challenged to really shift the dial on in the past?”

But Australia’s sport integrity framework is rooted in legislation that makes it easier to cooperate with law enforcement agencies that are investigating the same issue as the sport integrity body.

It’s something Luke said Canada is missing. Sport Integrity Canada regulates abuse and maltreatment, as well as doping and competition manipulation.

“They [Sport Integrity Australia] have a lot of authority being a government agency that enables them to be able to cooperate with law enforcement and cooperate with other governmental bodies and be able to investigate matters perhaps in ways that we can't in Canada, given we're not a government agency and we're not founded in legislation in the same sort of way,” Luke said.

“I think that's a model we want to continue to consider the pros and cons of as we look to implement some of these recommendations in Canada and whether that’s a place that we should be evolving to.”

World.title: Israel's president asks Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's rival, to form new government
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has chosen Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition lost its majority in the country's Oct. 27 elections. John Allen, Canada's former ambassador to Israel, discusses how this decision could shape the country's political landscape.

Israel's president on Saturday chose Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's strongest rival, to try to form a new government following a deadlocked election that left neither man ‌with a clear path to power.

Netanyahu, Israel's ⁠longest-serving leader, ⁠is ‌fighting to hold onto office after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an ⁠Oct. 27 election but still emerged as the largest bloc ‌in parliament.

An anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Eisenkot, an ex-military chief, has refused to ​join forces with Arab ⁠parties who could hand it a ⁠majority of seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset.

But Arab leaders, incensed by what they view as the racist policies ​of Netanyahu and his far-right allies, still nominated Eisenkot to try to form a government first — giving him the most endorsements.

"President Herzog has invited Gadi Eisenkot to the President’s Residence, where he will be tasked with ​forming the government tomorrow," said the spokesperson of Israel President Isaac Herzog, whose largely ceremonial role involves nominating a candidate ⁠to form a coalition after ⁠elections.

Israel's President Isaac Herzog, right, receives the results of Israel's elections from Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg at the president's residence in Jerusalem on Wednesday. (Ohad Zwigenberg/The Associated Press)

Weeks of protracted negotiations are ‌expected to follow Eisenkot's nomination. He has 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension.

His potential pathways to power include trying to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside; forming a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties that he and his allies have shunned in the past; or forging a unity government with Netanyahu.

Analysts ⁠say that all three options are unlikely to take shape. If Eisenkot fails, another candidate can try to form a government and if that candidate fails, parliament can nominate another.

There is a deadline for the process of about 100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is ‌held.

An Orthodox Jewish voter casts a ballot at a polling station in Haifa, Israel, on Oct. 27. (Baz Ratner/The Associated Press)

"This is the time to establish a national emergency government. I will do anything possible to prove us worthy," Eisenkot posted on his X account just after the president's announcement.

Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu's wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total, short of a 61-seat majority.

Eisenkot's Yashar party emerged as the second-largest party with 21 seats, while his coalition, spanning four centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led parties, won just 48 seats. Two parties representing Israel's Arab minority won an ​unprecedented 19 seats.

Political newcomer

A son of Moroccan immigrants, Eisenkot, 66, would be the country's first prime minister from Israel's Mizrahi community, Jews who trace their roots to the ⁠Middle East and North Africa.

Reserved and media-shy, Eisenkot only entered politics in 2022. He briefly served in Netanyahu's wartime cabinet following Hamas's ⁠Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel before returning to the opposition.

From opposition, he publicly rebuked Netanyahu over his leadership, including his management ⁠of ⁠the military campaign in Gaza, and has sworn that ​he would not serve in government with him.

Eisenkot's public standing is also bound up with the personal price his family has paid since 2023: a ​son and two nephews were killed fighting ⁠in Gaza.

Eisenkot highlighted his security credentials on the campaign trail, citing his "Dahiyeh doctrine" of responding to attacks with disproportionate force, which he deployed as a commander during Israel's 2006 war with Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon.

Eisenkot has criticized settler violence against Palestinians, which has surged since 2023, raising tensions in Israel’s ties with Western states, and he opposes Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who have both faced sanctions by some Western countries for inciting ⁠violence against Palestinians.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: Pasquale Grasso & Samara Joy– Song of the Day
World.content:
By Circles Robinson

HAVANA TIMES – Today we feature Italian guitarist Pasquale Grasso with US vocalist Samara Joy on the Duke Ellington standard “Solitude”. (2021)

Havana Times Song of the Day features artists mostly, but not only, born in Latin America and the Caribbean. Additionally, artists influenced by Latin American rhythms/sounds and/or are of Latin American heritage but born elsewhere. Jazz is another feature of our posts.

World.title: “Neurotics Anonymous” – a Film Honoring the Role of Movies in Our Lives
World.content:
The Cuban film Neurotica Anonima at the La Rampa Theather in Havana.

By Irina Pino

HAVANA TIMES – Last Saturday, I watched the Cuban film Neurótica Anónima [“Anonymous Female Neurotic”] at Havana’s “La Rampa” movie theater. The film is directed by Jorge Preugorría, who is also an actor, and stars Mirtha Ibarra, the former muse and wife of film director Tomas Gutierrez Alea. The production is an adaptation of a play written by Ibarra and produced in Spain, where it enjoyed great success.

The plot centers on an usher at the [fictitious] Cine Cuba movie theater and is clearly an allegory of the country’s destruction. Together with the other movie theater employees, Mirtha Ibarra’s character is informed in a meeting of the theater’s imminent closure, due to the danger of the entire building collapsing. The employees are told they’ll be reassigned to other venues to continue their jobs.

The first of the group to react is Iluminada, the character Mirna Ibarra interprets. She protests vehemently, since she loves this site where she has worked for many years. The other employees join her. Then, the projectionist has the idea of making a documentary to save the locale.

They fan out to the street to collect opinions. Most of those they interview agree that movie theaters are dying: people don’t go, due to the lack of transportation and a preference for the ease of watching at home.

That’s actually a reality here. Only two movie theaters are still functioning in Havana – La Rampa and Yara, each offering two shows on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. Those that are left from “Project 23” (which included several other theaters on 23rd Street in Havana) are subject to blackouts, making attendance at these theaters very risky.

The neighborhood movie theaters no longer exist, buried by disinterest and destruction. None of the government organizations has been interested in preserving them. This has contributed to people losing the habit of enjoying the cinematic arts in a darkened hall.

But back to the plot of Neurótica Anónima. It’s a bit fantastical, with elements borrowed from “Moscow Doesn’t Believe in Tears”, “Thelma & Louise”, “Throne of Blood”, and “The Passion of Joan of Arc”, as well as “Strawberry and Chocolate” and “To a Certain Extent”—both of the latter starring Cuban actress Mirna Ibarra.

These cinematic winks have their own beauty and are welcomed by the film buffs who detect them, for their artistic value and the feelings they evoke. This technique isn’t new – right now I’m recalling “Stardust Memory”, one of my favorite Woody Allen films, which echoes scenes from Federico Fellini’s “8 ½”.

But in this film, something very peculiar is happening: the protagonist is suffering from a neurosis that causes her to imagine herself playing the heroines from all these films. Her experience is vivid.

The sub-plot involves her real life as a couple. Her husband is an alcoholic who spent three years in prison for a crime at the foreign company where he worked. He now earns money renting out their patio for religious rites where animals are sacrificed, something Iluminada finds intolerable, along with his addiction.

I want to highlight one amusing scene, where she goes to a Research Center for Control of Neurosis. The Center has a series of different treatment rooms for different disorders. It makes me think that Cuba has us suffering from so many kinds of disorders that it would be very difficult to enumerate all of them.

In general, the film features a cast of outstanding actors and actresses, some of them now passed. Mirna Ibarra gives freshness and credibility to her character.

This feature film comes short of being memorable, nor is it as critical as other Cuban films. However, it still represents an interesting option for admirers of cinema from our island.
