World.title: Cuba’s Current Electricity and Longstanding Water Crisis
World.content:
A young man waits for a container used to store drinking water to fill up at an improvised water tap in Havana. Water scarcity in Cuba has been exacerbated by the energy crisis, which hinders pumping through aging water infrastructure that suffers from constant leaks. Image: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

By Dariel Pradas (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – “Water that arrives, trust that stays.” That is how an  on Revolico, a classified ads website for Cuba, ends. It is one of many offering home water delivery by private tanker trucks amid the country’s widespread water shortages.

“The water shortage this year is beyond description. Here in our area, we used to get water every other day. But now I’ve gone about two weeks without it. In desperation, I started looking into how much it would cost to have a tanker truck deliver water to my house, but they’re far too expensive,” Yunaisy Pupo, a 48-year-old human resources manager, told IPS.

Offers advertised on Revolico, social media, and by word of mouth can easily cost more than $15 to fill a household’s water cisterns.

Pupo earns slightly less than the equivalent of nine dollars a month at a public institution, roughly the average salary in Cuba’s state sector, which employs 68.5% of the country’s 4.1 million workers.

Problems caused by breakdowns in water distribution networks, water lost through leaking pipes, power outages, and even fuel shortages have long made it difficult for Cubans to access water, a service historically subsidized by the state and provided at extremely low prices.

Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel said on Wednesday, November 4, during the radio program Criterio Compartido (Shared Perspectives), that the water problem, which he described as “real, serious, and complex,” has “structural roots, distribution networks that have been in operation for decades, and investments we have been unable to make on the scale required.”

Last year, 20% of Cuba’s approximately nine million inhabitants experienced some type of disruption to their water service every day, according to a report presented on December 19 to the National Assembly.

In 2026, with the US oil blockade against the island imposed on January 29, the country’s chronic water supply crisis worsened even further.

During the same radio program on Wednesday, November 4, Antonio Rodríguez, president of the National Institute of Hydraulic Resources, reported that disruptions to the piped water supply affect more than 2.6 million people in Cuba. He said 66% of the problem is linked to the electricity crisis, while 25% is due to failures in pumping equipment.

Rodriguez specified that Havana alone has 536,000 affected residents, twice the number in any other province.

“We don’t have fuel to pump water, and on top of that, we don’t have enough fuel to generate electricity. Without electricity generation, there is no way to distribute water,” the Cuban president said during the radio broadcast.

A man in Havana transports several containers of drinking water using an improvised, rudimentary handcart. Many Cubans must leave their homes to secure a water supply—sometimes by collecting it directly from leaks in the water distribution network. Image: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

The War Over Water

Water shortages force many Cubans to collect and transport water to their homes using wheelbarrows, bicycles, cars, or electric tricycles, sometimes traveling several kilometers in rural or suburban communities.

Yunior Machado, a 37-year-old unemployed resident of Old Havana, used to fill his two 20-liter containers from a nearby leaking pipe whenever he went days without receiving water through the distribution network. The pipe protruded directly from the street and spewed water, attracting dozens of people who lined up to fill their containers.

“They’ve apparently fixed the pipe because they paved the street. Now I have to walk farther away” to find another leak or water source, he told IPS.

In an apartment building in Arroyo Naranjo, one of Havana’s 15 municipalities, located on the outskirts of the city, a silent war began when water started reaching the apartments with much lower pressure and less predictability.

Or perhaps it wasn’t so silent, because everything began in May when the first neighbor installed a noisy “water thief,” as Cubans call the pumps that suck up the limited water flowing through the distribution network and push it into a particular home at higher pressure.

Installing these pumps in the same neighborhood reduces pressure throughout the network, making it even harder for households without such equipment to obtain water.

Because the closest neighbors are the most affected, the other families in the building soon began buying their own water thieves, creating a kind of competition in which the winner is whoever has the most powerful pump and takes all the water.

“This has become a situation where it’s every person for themselves. It’s a war over water. And I still haven’t bought a pump for that. So, I only get water when the electricity goes out, because then none of the pumps work,” said Reinier Sotolongo, a 25-year-old package delivery worker.

The situation outside the capital is even worse because some rural communities are not connected to distribution networks and depend on tanker trucks provided by the state, also at subsidized rates.

Power outages, which last longer outside Havana and commonly extend for 48 or even 72 hours, further reduce water pumping capacity.

In early 2026, Hilda Freyre, a homemaker living in the city of Gibara, in the eastern province of Holguin, went almost three months without receiving water.

“We’ve had to buy more buckets and water containers,” the 61-year-old woman told IPS in an interview conducted in July.

According to Freyre, some neighbors cope with the water shortage by using wells dug in their backyards. In her case, however, she has managed thanks to a large underground cistern roughly the size of her terrace, which never completely empties or fills.

Her cistern came close to running dry during those three months. She did not believe it would ever fill up with the three or four hours of water service she received from time to time.

“I would need at least three days of continuous water supply,” she said.

Workers from the state-owned company Aguas de La Habana are working to repair a breakdown reported in Havana on October 29. Ruptures in water distribution networks have been a recurring problem in Cuba, even before the multidimensional crisis intensified in 2026. Image: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

Solar Panels for Water Supply

On Wednesday, November 4, the same day as the radio program featuring Diaz-Canel, the Cuenca Sur water supply facility underwent an emergency shutdown, disrupting water service in six of Havana’s 15 municipalities, according to the state-run company Aguas de La Habana, which is responsible for the city’s water service.

The incident occurred just days after the company warned, on October 29, of various interruptions at several water supply sources due to the energy deficit, forcing it to extend the intervals between water deliveries in all Havana municipalities.

In recent months, such announcements have become somewhat routine.

The government’s proposed solution is to make water pumping at the capital’s three main supply sources — the Ariguanabo Basin, Cuenca Sur, and El Gato — independent of the national electricity grid.

Rodriguez, the head of the National Institute of Hydraulic Resources, announced that construction of 10 solar parks with a combined capacity of 200 megawatts would be completed by August 2027, along with batteries to provide backup power.

He also announced the upcoming arrival of pumping equipment that will benefit several areas of the country, giving priority to Havana, Santiago de Cuba, Holguin, Matanzas, Artemisa, and Pinar del Rio, the provinces most affected by the crisis.

“The crisis must give us an opportunity to move forward, not only to solve the immediate problems but also to address the accumulated problems we face in these areas of water supply,” Díaz-Canel said.

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posed in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: On Cuba’s North Coast There’s a “Tactical Island”
World.content:
But it’s just for play

From social media promoting Tactical Island

By Angry GenXer

HAVANA TIMES – “Battlefield,” reads the sign above the gate leading into a space covering approximately a quarter of a city block, enclosed by dense black mesh fencing. The sign has a camouflage background, and camouflage is also the dominant color scheme of other signs on either side of the gate explaining what goes on inside the fenced perimeter. Several smaller signs attached to the mesh warn curious passersby to keep their distance because it is a “firing zone” where they risk being hit by hydrogel projectiles.

Geolocation data indicates that the facility is located in Santa Cruz del Norte (Mayabeque Province, Cuba). Isla Táctica (Tactical Island) is a brand or account active on social media platforms such as Instagram and TikTok, sharing content from the site. There is no public information about who runs the project, although everything suggests that it is not operated by military institutions but rather by one of the many private businesses that have recently emerged in Cuba. It is probably the first and only Cuban venture of its kind, at least with the level of professionalism and facilities displayed on social media.

Unlike other establishments with similar names (such as “Isla Táctica” on Margarita Island, Venezuela, which specializes in tactical and military equipment, or a unit in the Canary Islands), this particular brand is associated with geolocated records and posts from Santa Cruz del Norte, a small city whose economy is primarily industrial and fishing-based.

From social media promoting Tactical Island

War Games Across from the Havana Club Rum Distillery

The venue presents itself as a recreational space for children, young people, and adults. In a peaceful coastal area, just a few meters from an old watchtower—now a food market—and a small beach with a club called El Pescador, where neighborhood residents go swimming and dance to reggaeton. The late afternoon and evening air fills with gunfire and shouts of euphoric enthusiasm for mock warfare. People line up to get in and emerge drenched in sweat, debating victories and defeats, wounds and deaths in a make-believe battle.

On the opposite bank of the nearby river stands the distillery that produces the world-famous Havana Club rum. Closer is a Border Guard unit (that military presence is real), while farther upstream are docks for local fishing boats. Inside the perimeter of the “Island,” the surrounding landscape is reproduced on a smaller scale: sand, jagged coastal limestone rocks, and stacks of tires that serve as obstacles and protective barriers for the “combatants.”

For around 800 pesos (slightly less than US$1), each player receives a gun that fires hydrogel projectiles, two magazines, and protective equipment (a mask and vest). Hydrogel is a viscous substance that forms small beads containing more than 98% water. These are superabsorbent polymer beads (usually sodium polyacrylate), the same material used in diapers or to retain moisture in gardening. They do not damage the skin, strike the body with much force, or leave stains, unlike their more hard-hitting counterpart in this type of “warfare” entertainment: paintball. (Paintball activities in Cuba are limited to a handful of amateur clubs and corporate tourist facilities; I have heard nothing about their use in actual military training.)

A tactical game using hydrogel guns imitates real infantry combat, with rifles that fire projectiles. Isla Tactica’s rules expressly prohibit hand-to-hand combat or other acts of personal aggression (a notice warns that such behavior is subject to “zero tolerance”). Its small size also makes it impossible to conduct large-scale or in-depth tactical operations. Although who knows? If the business prospers, other, more extensive make-believe “battlefields” might emerge. But I imagine the price of “fighting” in such “theaters of operations” would be considerably higher.

From social media promoting Tactical Island

Private War Games vs. Official Military Training in Cuba

The perimeter of Isla Tactica features AI-generated images depicting real combat situations, including drones and heavy military equipment. The Cuban flag is always visible on these posters. Even so, they differ noticeably from the graphic propaganda used by the authorities to promote military training among the population. By all appearances, Isla Táctica offers young people a more interesting and appealing option than the usual defense-preparedness exercises periodically organized by government authorities.

Before the 1990s, Cuba had the SEPMI (Society for Military and Internationalist Patriotic Education), which operated clubs sponsored by the Cuban military and supported by counterpart organizations in “friendly countries,” such as the Soviet DOSAAF. Through SEPMI, young people and adults could learn various skills of military interest, ranging from parachuting to military strategy games. During the 1990s crisis of the post-Soviet Special Period, SEPMI disappeared. What remained were dreary, rundown shooting ranges with air rifles, housed in old shipping containers in various neighborhoods and offering little appeal to potential enthusiasts. (They are operated by the ACRC, a veterans’ organization that uses them to raise funds.)

There has also been quasi-mandatory military training for civilians in neighborhoods, schools, and workplaces (not to mention compulsory military service for males beginning at age 16). This training consists of occasional gatherings to assemble and disassemble AKM rifles, practice marching, and, with luck, do some target shooting. In general, students and workers view participation in such “events” as just another political obligation imposed by the authorities.

Against this backdrop, Isla Tactica offers war as a game—with a discreet patriotic aesthetic (Cuban flags appear on promotional posters but are not flown over the “battlefield”) and abundant elements of military style (camouflage, images of real combat, tactical equipment). It is clearly an exciting option in a country with very few entertainment choices, and even fewer spaces for people with specialized hobbies.

The big question remains whether this type of project or business conflicts with the desire of most Cubans to live together peacefully or, on the contrary, contributes to a culture of peace by “sublimating” aggressive impulses and turning fighting into harmless entertainment.

Nor is it clear whether potential gang members or politically violent groups might use such facilities to encourage aggression or social confrontation.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Cuba Begins to Privatize its Tourism Industry and Beaches
World.content:
By Amado Viera

HAVANA TIMES – During its final years under state management, the Punta de Ganado campground was notorious for the neglected condition of its beaches. By the summer of 2025, mounds of sargassum seaweed covered most of the swimming area, and vacationers had to resort to ingenious maneuvers just to get into the water.

Santa Lucía Beach, where Punta de Ganado is located, is particularly hard hit by the arrival of this seaweed, carried by ocean currents from the vast expanses of the Atlantic. For decades, it was common to see tractors in the mornings “plowing” the dunes to collect the sargassum that had washed ashore the night before. Crews of workers would then haul it to designated dumping sites far from the coast. It was laborious work, but essential to keeping this Camaguey beach resort clean.

However, as the economic crisis worsened in 2022–2023, sargassum removal was among the first activities to suffer budget cuts. Before long, only the stretches of beach occupied by hotels and other tourist facilities were being cleaned. Later, not even those areas received attention. With foreign tourism disappearing and domestic tourism falling to a minimum, there was no one to pay for the cleanup. Mounds of rotting sargassum on the sand became the new normal that greeted the few Cuban vacationers who ventured there.

For Now, More Expensive

In mid-October, Punta de Ganado became one of the first campgrounds to be managed by a private business. These facilities are intended primarily for Cubans. Although the Popular Camping Business Group has issued no public statement about the transfer, it is most likely part of a broader process that will affect a substantial portion of the roughly 100 such facilities across the country. An employee of the group’s Camagüey branch said that, at least in the province, the goal is to transfer all seven of its campgrounds to private management before the end of 2027.

Punta de Ganado was leased to a private company that committed to restore its beach, open-air pavilion, and restaurant first; then, in a second phase, repair the cabins, “so that accommodations will be available during next year’s vacation season.” That was the explanation given by one of the sales promoters who advertise day trips there on Facebook and other social media platforms.

The offers are far from cheap. Round-trip transportation from the city of Camagüey costs between 5,000 and 6,500 pesos per person, depending on the private transportation provider hired. Admission to the campground costs an additional 500 pesos per adult and 300 pesos per child or teenager. (With average state salaries under 9,000 pesos a month ($10 USD) these private offers are extremely expensive, while more accessible to those who have private businesses or family remittances from abroad).

That’s how a typical day begins at the new Punta de Ganado, where visitors are prohibited from bringing in food or beverages and can choose from activities as varied as ATV rentals and an inflatable children’s playground. A bubbles party was organized for the facility’s reopening, and “they even hope popular performers will be offering concerts,” the sales promoter highlighted.

The plans are ambitious, but the economic situation presents a formidable obstacle. “The food is as expensive as in the most exclusive private restaurants in Camagüey,” complained Nayara Ramírez, a resident of the provincial capital who attended the facility’s mid-October reopening party.

“It wasn’t bad, but everything has to be put into perspective,” she said. “On the one hand, there were the high prices, and on the other, the beach, which is the main reason you travel all the way there, wasn’t nearly as clean as they advertised. Only the ‘VIP area’ looked as though it had been thoroughly spruced up, but not all customers had access to it. I don’t even want to imagine how much it will cost to stay overnight once they start offering accommodations again.”

This reporter tried several times to contact Punta de Ganado’s new managers, but without success. In general, the businesses beginning to emerge in former Ministry of Tourism facilities follow the principle of attracting as little attention as possible. It is not unusual for changes in management to be made public only after the lease agreements have been signed, and sometimes even after the facilities in question have reopened.

Even the defense of these new businesses is often left not to their owners but to public figures, in what appears to be an attempt to lend the privatization legitimacy.

For example, even Carlos Rene Soriano, director of the Popular Camping company’s Camagüey branch, has come to Punta de Ganado’s defense. Responding to recent criticism of the so-called “VIP area,” he justified the additional 5,000-peso charge for this service by explaining that customers who pay for the service receive “personalized attention, with a waiter who brings them whatever they order; exclusive use of a lounge chair, a table and four chairs; and access to one of the cleanest beaches in the resort area.”

As for the menus costing 5,000 pesos or more per person, he ended the discussion with a blunt remark: “These days, an onion costs 300 pesos.”

Changing the Rules

At first glance, the decision to lease campgrounds and lower-end hotels to private entrepreneurs would seem to be a consequence of the crisis facing Cuba’s tourism sector. As of the end of September, the island had recorded a decline of nearly 40% in foreign visitors compared with 2025, a year that was already considered poor. And the outlook is even worse, mainly because of fuel shortages, which have reduced foreign airline operations to a minimum and, consequently, tourist traffic.

But that circumstance explains only part of the problem. The other fundamental variable in the equation is the peso’s exchange rate against the dollar, which has made virtually all state-owned enterprises unprofitable.

Balancing the books has become practically impossible, explained Yasmani Rabelo, an accountant who worked for years at the Popular Camping Company’s Camagüey branch.

“When Punta de Ganado reopened after the pandemic, there was a certain correspondence between the official exchange rate and the informal market rate, and state-owned companies still sold supplies and provided services at prices that aligned with both. But as the peso continued to lose value, an increasingly wide gap developed between the government’s exchange rate and the real one, which is what private businesses operate with. This happened while virtually all commerce was shifting into private hands, which sell at much higher prices. Popular Camping and other similar companies did not raise their rates to the same extent and began accumulating losses, to the point where they couldn’t even cover their workers’ low salaries,” he explained.

By the end of 2025, the situation had become unsustainable. That year, during the last summer the facility operated under state management, “there were barely enough supplies to serve the campers. The facilities weren’t repaired, the furniture wasn’t replaced, and when it came to food, we reached the point where the restaurant had only one meat option and the cafeteria couldn’t open because there was nothing to offer,” Rabelo recalled. To generate enough income to operate normally, they would have had to double or even triple most of their prices, something government guidelines didn’t allow state enterprises to do.

Private companies, whose only obligation is to their owners, don’t have to abide by that restriction. The clearest reflection of this change in approach can be seen in the prices, which at Punta de Ganado increased between fourfold and tenfold, simply because of the change in management.

Far too much for most Cuban families to afford. It matters little that the beach is cleaner than it was a year ago. Ultimately, many Cubans will no longer be able to enjoy it.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: The US Elections and the Policy Towards Cuba
World.content:
The US Congress and Cuba.

By La Joven Cuba

HAVANA TIMES – The midterm elections will not immediately change US policy toward Cuba, but they open up a two-year horizon. Trump’s electoral setback could be the first step toward a return to Obama’s policy, something political groups on both sides of the Florida Straits should prepare for.

The Democratic Party won majorities in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, where, until now, the Republican advantage had allowed President Donald Trump to carry out his legislative agenda without too many challenges or checks and balances. The Democrats, whose demise many had predicted, are regaining their place in institutional politics, which they will use to try to achieve significant gains as the opposition ahead of the 2028 presidential elections.

The most significant change for Cuba could come in congressional committees. With the new Democratic majority, Gregory Meeks could chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Joaquin Castro the Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, until now headed by Maria Elvira Salazar. Both have questioned the policy of maximum pressure against Cuba, which could translate into greater oversight of the executive branch and more room to discuss alternatives for engagement, although their main priority will be to block and reverse the work of the current administration.

However, the results of these elections, by themselves, have little direct impact on Washington’s policy toward Cuba, since that policy is conducted primarily by the executive branch, requires little congressional approval, and is not a priority issue in election campaigns or domestic politics in the United States.

For now, Marco Rubio, at the State Department, remains one of the principal architects and implementers of US policy toward Cuba. However, according to analyst Carlos Alzugaray, his continuation in office could depend on his own political ambitions ahead of the 2028 presidential elections, potentially opening the door to a less aggressive stance toward Havana.

Alzugaray states: “A US policy against Cuba without Marco Rubio at the State Department could lose intensity. I tend to think Rubio will look for a way to leave the Trump administration while preserving his image as one of the most effective members of the cabinet, without falling into the extremism of others. His path to the presidency, by entering the race next year for the 2028 Republican nomination, could be very risky because he would be up against J.D. Vance, who has certain advantages.

“Rubio may decide that entering that contest is not in his best interest because the chances of losing are high. And even if he wins the primaries, he would enter the 2028 election burdened by Trump’s record, which could be disastrous over the next two years. That is why it would make sense for Rubio to leave the administration. He might even choose to wait until 2032, allowing some time to pass and building a new political platform from which to seek the Republican nomination.”

Meanwhile, in Florida, Cuban-American Republican members of Congress Maria Elvira Salazar, Mario Díaz-Balart, and Carlos Gimenez retained their seats, although by much narrower margins than in 2024. While the state remains a Republican stronghold, these results reveal an erosion of Trump’s support among segments of Latino and Cuban voters, primarily because of his immigration policies, which have affected a historically privileged community whose members could hardly have imagined ending up in detention centers or being deported to third countries.

Midterm elections serve as a measure of public satisfaction two years into an administration. For several months, most reputable polls had been predicting a comfortable Democratic victory, reflecting above all the tremendous dissatisfaction with the rising cost of living, particularly fuel prices.

This will be the central focus of a Congress now dominated by Democrats, who will hold the most combative Republican administration they have faced in decades to account, not only on economic matters but also on social issues, healthcare, immigration, inclusion, and every other major issue on the agenda.

A Democratic Congress will be able to scrutinize and challenge the White House and State Department’s policy toward Cuba more closely, but it will not actually change that policy.

In the short term, this will have little impact on Cubans living on the island. Nevertheless, it should not be dismissed, considering that it could mark the beginning of a change in the political climate, led by a Democratic Party that appears to be keeping pace with a new generation of millennial politicians, people of color, and socialists. Meanwhile, many of Trump’s staunchest supporters are taking note and beginning to retreat from their previous positions in order to be as well positioned as possible for the 2028 presidential elections.

On the other hand, the claim repeatedly made by Trump and Rubio that Havana is “about to fall” has shifted to “that will take some time,” as the Cuban government withstands economic pressure without showing signs of instability so far. This is despite the enormous social and human cost of the maximum-pressure policy, which ultimately falls on the most vulnerable sectors of society.

The most unpredictable period lies between now and January 3, 2027, when the new Congress takes office. For Cuba, the worst-case scenario would be direct military action, although that possibility has also faded following the debacle in Iran. The cost of failure or a prolonged stalemate on the island would represent too great a risk for questionable short- and medium-term benefits, both economically and politically.

Cuba is part of a rather chaotic web of US international relations that has developed in recent months, including the distancing from Ukraine, the fiasco in Iran, strained relations with some NATO allies, the tariff war, and the recent rapprochement with Russia, to mention just a few issues. Amid this seemingly erratic behavior, it is worth asking what either Donald Trump, who presumably does not want another international fiasco before leaving office, or Marco Rubio, who is building momentum for a political future beyond 2028, would consider a victory in the case of Cuba.

Everything seems to indicate that the United States is increasingly willing to wait for Cuba to collapse under economic pressure, while Havana has shown signs that it can hold out for at least the next two years. A Democratic Congress changes nothing at this moment, but it signals the possibility of a less hostile environment toward Cuba in two years and could serve as a barrier against the prospect of large-scale military action, which by now already seems unlikely.

From Havana’s perspective, the Democratic victory should be interpreted as an opportunity to lay the groundwork for future rapprochement. These two years should be used to deepen the economic reforms already announced, expand opportunities for foreign investment by offering greater guarantees to investors, and strengthen the conditions under which the domestic private sector operates.

A more open economy, with clear rules and genuine investment opportunities, could create incentives for business sectors linked to the Democrats — and even Republicans who are not aligned with the Cuban-American representatives — to find commercial reasons to advocate easing sanctions. Along with this, a possible Democratic victory in 2028 — which now seems more likely — would open the possibility of reviving part of the rapprochement initiated by Obama.

What is certain at this point is that both Cuba and the United States will have new presidents in 2028. Washington will have to decide whether to maintain a strategy of economic pressure that has particularly punished the Cuban population, while Havana has two years ahead to implement reforms that encourage greater exchange. The peoples of both countries, especially the Cuban people, who have endured the harshest consequences of this confrontation, deserve finally to be placed at the center of every decision.

First published in Spanish by Joven Cuba and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Paraguay’s prosecutors charge Santiago Peña and seek his pre-trial detention over the Ueno Bank collapse
World.content:
Paraguay’s prosecutors charge Santiago Peña and seek his pre-trial detention over the Ueno Bank collapse

8th Sunday, November 2026 - 01:53 UTC Full article

Peña, who testified before prosecutors on Saturday, is accused of alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator

Paraguayan prosecutors on Saturday charged former President Santiago Peña, removed from office by the Senate on Friday, and requested his pre-trial detention in the case over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which froze the savings of nearly three million customers. A judge must rule on the request. Prosecutors also charged former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, who is in custody.

Peña, who testified before prosecutors on Saturday, is accused of alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator. Carvallo, who had been Ueno’s chief executive before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank, is charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and self-serving administration. According to prosecutors, between 2023 and 2026 the bank received large deposits from public bodies and the pension system while granting allegedly irregular loans to companies linked to its owners, the Vázquez Group. Peña denies any wrongdoing.

The former president, who had been placed under house arrest after his removal, was moved overnight to the barracks of the Presidential Escort Regiment, responsible for presidential security, after protesters threw stones at police and tore down fences near his residence in Asunción. Police dispersed the protest. Dictator Alfredo Stroessner took refuge in the same barracks in 1989 during the military coup that toppled him.

The new president, Pedro Alliana, began his term with cabinet changes. He appointed Ariel Martínez as interior minister, a post he held under former President Horacio Cartes (2013-2018), and Juan Carlos Baruja, also close to Cartes, head of the ruling Colorado Party, as public works minister. Alliana said he would suspend foreign travel to focus on the crisis and promised that all those affected would recover their savings.

Customers with balances of up to about US$1,500 have begun recovering their money, and payouts will later be extended to an initial maximum of 40 minimum wages, about 121 million guaraníes or US$19,300. Banks will open exceptionally on Sunday so that those affected can open accounts and complete the necessary procedures.

Tension remains high. Protesters and the opposition accuse Alliana of failing to act in time to prevent the bank’s collapse and are also demanding his removal and early elections in early 2027.

World.title: Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing
World.content:
Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:55 UTC Full article

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment

Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, will visit the Falklands and South Georgia from Monday, November 9, the day before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on Argentina’s case against the Sea Lion oil project, Buckingham Palace has announced.

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment. The Princess, who will travel with her husband, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence, will begin with a series of engagements in the Falklands: she will meet members of the community, visit Cape Pembroke Lighthouse, Tussac House and the newly completed Falkland Islands National Sports Complex, and attend a reception at Government House in Stanley.

In South Georgia, a territory with no permanent civilian population, she will see the Trust’s work, meet British Antarctic Survey staff and members of the territory’s government, and commemorate the explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton (1874-1922), who sailed some 1,500 kilometres in a lifeboat to the island to seek help for his crew, trapped by ice in Antarctica.

The palace presents the trip as a heritage and commemorative visit. Its timing, however, coincides with a key week in the dispute over the islands: the Hamburg tribunal will hear Argentina and the United Kingdom on November 10 and 11, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies plans to debate the sovereignty defence bill on November 12, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago. Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

World.title: “They all must go”: Peña’s removal fails to calm anger on Paraguay’s streets
World.content:
“They all must go”: Peña’s removal fails to calm anger on Paraguay’s streets

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:50 UTC Full article

Many protesters, mostly young people, turned their anger on the entire Colorado Party government and kept vigil in the city centre with flags, placards and drums

Thousands of Paraguayans celebrated in Asunción on Friday as the Senate removed President Santiago Peña from office, but the joy turned almost immediately to anger among those who wanted a complete change of government. “Out with them all,” hundreds of protesters chanted outside Congress as Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as the new head of state.

Celebrations erupted at the news that Peña, 47, was leaving office without immunity and, hours later, was placed under house arrest accused of breach of trust over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which had more than 2.9 million customers in a country of 6.1 million people. But many protesters, mostly young people, turned their anger on the entire Colorado Party government and kept vigil in the city centre with flags, placards and drums. “If the same people stay, there is no change”, “We want jail” and “Where is the money?” read the signs.

“The people are staying here until they all go,” Celicia Lugo told the EFE news agency, adding that Peña and Alliana “are the same”. “The incoming government is more of the same, because only Peña will be gone, the rest will stay,” said Milda Cuevas, who celebrated the removal and demanded that the former president “be tried” and “go to prison”. For Andrea Gutiérrez, Ueno “was just one example” of what she sees as the ongoing plundering of citizens.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday, when the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank, which had received large amounts of public funds during Peña’s term, and froze its deposits. Those affected include some 32,000 pensioners of the Social Security Institute, according to EFE.

In an attempt to contain the anger, Alliana announced after being sworn in that those affected by the bank’s closure “will be fully compensated”, without saying how. The legal deposit guarantee covers up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes per depositor.

World.title: Leo XIV begins his tour in Uruguay, praising Mercosur and peace and questioning abortion and euthanasia
World.content:
Leo XIV begins his tour in Uruguay, praising Mercosur and peace and questioning abortion and euthanasia

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:30 UTC Full article

Photo: AFP

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Montevideo on Friday, the first stop on his South American tour, and in a speech to Uruguayan authorities praised Mercosur, peaceful coexistence and care for the environment, but also defended life “even that which is still growing in the mother’s womb” and questioned euthanasia, in a country where both are legal and which is considered the most secular in the region.

The pontiff’s plane landed at 4.19 p.m. at Carrasco airport, where he was met by President Yamandú Orsi and the Cardinal Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla. Leo XIV travelled in the popemobile along the waterfront promenade to Plaza Independencia, accompanied by some 3,000 volunteers, received the key to the city and visited the Cabildo and the Cathedral. Orsi welcomed him to a region “where there are no wars between countries”, called him “dear friend” and noted that in Uruguay former presidents sit together “in peace and joy”. Former presidents Julio María Sanguinetti, Luis Alberto Lacalle Herrera and Luis Lacalle Pou attended the ceremony, along with Lucía Topolansky, widow of former president José Mujica.

In his speech, the Pope took up Francis’s ideas on the common good and care for natural resources, and praised the transformation of Uruguay’s energy mix. He stressed the importance of peace and dialogue in resolving differences and praised the role of Mercosur, the bloc Uruguay forms with Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. “Coexistence between people of different origins and traditions is also part of Uruguay’s history,” he said.

Leo XIV also addressed the most sensitive issues for the country. He defended life from conception, a reference to abortion, legal in Uruguay since 2012, and to euthanasia, approved in 2025. “Everyone deserves to receive [care] until the natural end of life,” he said. He also referred to the high suicide rate: “No one should feel like a stranger among their own or think that their absence matters more than their presence.” And he said secularism does not mean religion must be confined to private life.

Uruguay separated Church and State in its 1919 Constitution. Only 36% of Uruguayans describe themselves as Catholic, according to Latinobarómetro, and one in ten of those consider themselves practising. A survey by Usina de Percepción Ciudadana found that 37% of Uruguayans attach importance to the visit and 63% little or none.

On Saturday the Pope will celebrate Mass in Paysandú, visit the Montevideo neighbourhood of Casavalle and the Catholic University of Uruguay, and lead a vigil at the Centenario Stadium. On Sunday he will celebrate Mass in Florida, before the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, the country’s patron saint, and travel to Buenos Aires. After Argentina and Peru, he will return to Rome on November 16.

World.title: Paraguay’s Senate removes Santiago Peña, who is placed under arrest, and Pedro Alliana takes office
World.content:
Paraguay’s Senate removes Santiago Peña, who is placed under arrest, and Pedro Alliana takes office

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:17 UTC Full article

The removal was approved at 6.55 p.m. local time by all 44 senators present out of 45, including those of the ruling Colorado Party, after a trial lasting some ten hours

Paraguay’s Senate on Friday removed President Santiago Peña from office in an impeachment trial for “poor performance of his duties” over the collapse of Ueno Bank, and hours later prosecutors ordered him placed under house arrest over alleged economic crimes. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in before Congress that night as the new head of state and will serve out the term until August 15, 2028.

The removal was approved at 6.55 p.m. local time by all 44 senators present out of 45, including those of the ruling Colorado Party, after a trial lasting some ten hours. With it, Peña loses the lifetime Senate seat and parliamentary immunity he would have obtained had Congress accepted the resignation he tendered on Thursday, which was never considered. Thousands of savers gathered outside Congress celebrated the decision.

Prosecutor Christian Benítez said Peña will remain detained at home until he is placed at the disposal of the Specialised Unit for Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption. According to La Nación, prosecutors are investigating him for alleged breach of trust, influence peddling and self-serving administration. The order also covers former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, according to the Associated Press. Peña denies any wrongdoing.

The Senate rejected the 72-hour extension the president had requested to prepare his defence. Peña, who had said on Thursday that he would appear, ultimately did not attend and sent his lawyers, Adolfo Ferreiro — who in 2012 defended President Fernando Lugo, also removed through impeachment — and Ricardo Preda. Both argued they had not had enough time to prepare a defence and that the trial was moot after the resignation, arguments the Senate rejected.

“I submitted my resignation to avoid further harm to the country and help restore calm to Paraguay. I do not want my presence to be a cause of further division or instability,” Peña wrote in a farewell message. “I say goodbye with gratitude, without ignoring the anguish of those who are waiting for answers today.”

Alliana, 52, born in Pilar, a former governor of Ñeembucú department and former president of the Colorado Party, was sworn in minutes after the removal. Antonio Barrios took over as vice president, according to ABC Color. The opposition accepted the succession, albeit with reservations. “We accept this situation to ensure institutional continuity for the country,” said opposition senator Rafael Filizzola, who called Alliana “complicit” in what happened. Alliana had publicly distanced himself from Peña on the eve of the bank takeover and is expected to make changes to the government and the Central Bank.

The fall of Peña, a 47-year-old economist who took office in August 2023 with a modernising message, unfolded in just four days. On Tuesday, the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank over insolvency and irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, freezing the deposits of nearly three million customers, about 60% of the adult population, as well as hundreds of millions of dollars in public and pension funds. Carvallo had been the bank’s chief executive before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank, and Peña himself was a shareholder in the bank’s holding company until April 2025. On Thursday, the Colorado Party withdrew its support, led by its president, former President Horacio Cartes, who backed the impeachment.

World.title: Peña says he will face his impeachment trial as Argentina denies he has entered the country
World.content:
Peña says he will face his impeachment trial as Argentina denies he has entered the country

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:56 UTC Full article

“We have no record of him being in Argentina.” Javier Milei’s government, a political ally of Peña, has not commented on the Paraguayan crisis.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced on Thursday night that he will appear before the Senate to defend himself in the impeachment trial against him, after Congress failed for lack of a quorum to consider the resignation he had tendered hours earlier, leaving him formally in office. Argentina’s government, meanwhile, denied any record of Peña entering Argentina, following reports that he might have left Paraguay.

“Given the continuation of the impeachment trial, I will appear and exercise my right to a defence,” Peña said in a message released after the joint session of Congress called to accept or reject his resignation was suspended. The session lost its quorum when deputies of the ruling Colorado Party walked out. The Senate called an extraordinary session on Thursday night to set the impeachment trial in motion, on grounds of “poor performance of his duties”, and another on Friday morning to begin proceedings in the president’s presence, according to the Paraguayan press. The Chamber of Deputies had approved the charges by 78 votes to none. A two-thirds Senate majority is needed to remove him.

Uncertainty over Peña’s whereabouts persisted through the afternoon. Presidential spokesman Guillermo Grance acknowledged he did not know where the president was, according to ABC Color, and the speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, Colorado Party member Raúl Latorre, also admitted not knowing. “While we debate, the media are saying that President Santiago Peña has already set foot on Argentine soil,” opposition deputy Johana Ortega said during the session. In Buenos Aires, official sources quoted by La Nación ruled it out: “We have no record of him being in Argentina.” Javier Milei’s government, a political ally of Peña, has not commented on the Paraguayan crisis.

The reports recalled the departure of former Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who on October 27 crossed into the Argentine city of Puerto Iguazú and flew from there to Miami after refusing to accept his defeat by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The dispute between resignation and impeachment has legal consequences. If Congress accepts the resignation, Peña would take a lifetime Senate seat with parliamentary immunity; if the Senate removes him, he would lose that protection. The opposition and much of the ruling party, including Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, back the impeachment. According to the press, prosecutors have announced they are opening proceedings against Peña, although no formal charges have yet been brought.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday with the takeover of Ueno Bank, which froze the deposits of nearly three million customers and hundreds of millions of dollars of public funds. If Peña leaves office, Vice President Pedro Alliana will take over the presidency until August 15, 2028.

World.title: Lula sees his win as “a lesson for the world” after setbacks for Netanyahu and Trump
World.content:
Lula sees his win as “a lesson for the world” after setbacks for Netanyahu and Trump

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:42 UTC Full article

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva described his October 25 re-election as “a lesson for the world” and linked it to the electoral setbacks suffered in recent days by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump. “In the same week, Netanyahu lost in Israel and I think my friend Trump is losing in the United States,” he said on Thursday in a live broadcast on YouTube.

Lula, 81, spent an hour and a half on a livestream with congressman André Janones, the architect of the digital strategy that helped his electoral comeback, watched by some 600,000 viewers. “I am more afraid than in my first term,” he admitted. “My obsession is back: I cannot fail, I cannot betray them. I have to do better.” The president defended some of his priorities, such as ending online betting, the sovereign exploitation of critical minerals and the importance of the university entrance exam, and promised to find ways for people to take part in government decisions.

Lula said he would speak more often through social media. “I will speak more directly to the people through social media. I will no longer allow the press to interpret what I think,” he said. He also invited Janones to accompany him next week on his first official trip since re-election: the UN climate summit, COP31, in Turkey, and a summit with Southeast Asian countries in Manila.

In Israel’s October 27 election, Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority, winning 53 of the 120 seats, although his Likud party came first; Netanyahu has alleged fraud. In the United States, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 5.

World.title: Watchdog publishes a list of 77 clergy accused of abuse in Peru ahead of the Pope’s visit
World.content:
Watchdog publishes a list of 77 clergy accused of abuse in Peru ahead of the Pope’s visit

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:38 UTC Full article

US-based organisation Bishop Accountability on Thursday presented in Lima a list of 77 members of Peru’s Catholic clergy publicly accused of sexually abusing minors, days before Pope Leo XIV, who lived in the country for more than two decades, begins his tour of South America. Victims and the organisation called on the pontiff to take concrete steps, including setting up a truth commission.

The list, published on the website of the organisation, which documents sexual abuse cases in the Catholic Church, includes priests, brothers, seminarians and consecrated laypeople who have worked in Peruvian parishes and schools, as well as Church officials accused of allegedly covering up complaints. It is based mainly on the book Den of abusers or safe Church?, published this year by Reinaldo Nann, a former bishop of Caravelí in southern Peru who has left the priesthood. Those on the list have been publicly accused; not all have been tried or convicted.

“The Peruvian Church is stubbornly putting children at risk by covering up for abusers,” said Bishop Accountability co-director Anne Barrett Doyle. José Enrique Escardó, president of the Peruvian Survivors’ Network and one of the first to denounce the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, the Catholic movement Pope Francis suppressed in early 2025 after abuse allegations, said “victims need comprehensive reparation” and that “the most important thing is prevention”.

The organisations made three requests to the Pope: that bishops and religious superiors in Peru publish the names of clergy accused of abusing minors; that a Truth Commission be set up to investigate the cases; and that a universal zero-tolerance rule be enshrined in canon law.

Leo XIV, who holds Peruvian nationality, was bishop of Chiclayo and chaired the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference Commission for the Protection of Minors, where he worked alongside Nann. According to the former bishop, the current Pope was then “more open to listening to victims than the rest of the bishops”, although he considers him “too cautious a man” who is not driving change fast enough. According to El País, the Vatican has announced that the Pope will meet victims during his visit, although the meeting is not yet on the official schedule. There has been no response from the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference to the list.

The Pope will visit Uruguay and Argentina before arriving in Peru, where he will stay from November 11 to 17.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: INE crisis deepens, economy gains momentum and Latino voters reshape US midterms
World.content:
Plan Michoacán progress report

Wednesday’s mañanera was devoted to progress on Plan Michoacán, the federal response to Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo’s killing in November 2025. Sheinbaum said the plan is 67% complete, with 1,680 of more than 2,500 “actions” finished. Planned investment through 2030 has more than doubled from the original 57 billion pesos to 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion), and 72.43 billion pesos has been spent.

Cabinet members each highlighted a piece of the plan. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said 115 “Well-being Fairs” across all 113 municipalities helped residents complete more than 1.1 million administrative procedures, and that 673 firearms were exchanged for cash. The government, together with the private sector, is investing more than 41 billion pesos in six highway projects covering 411 kilometers, and work on the 9.3-billion-peso Bajío Industrial Park in Zinapécuaro starts this month. Other officials cited scholarships for 795,000 students, 177,000 people aided by the Sembrando Vida reforestation program, electricity coverage reaching 99.99% of homes and a new addiction-treatment hospital in Apatzingán. Tourism is up 10.1% through August. Mexico News Daily noted that not all the investment cited is directly tied to Plan Michoacán funding.

Security was left for a separate update next Tuesday. Homicides in the state fell 40.3% in the first nine months of 2026. At the Uruapan march, Quiroz demanded an “exhaustive” and “independent” investigation into Manzo’s killing, noting that more than 30 people have been arrested, including seven of his bodyguards. She hasn’t decided whether to run for governor.

Banxico surprises with rate cut

The central bank lowered its benchmark rate 25 basis points to 6.25% in a split vote, though 30 of 36 institutions surveyed by Citi expected no change. Banxico raised its fourth-quarter headline inflation forecast from 3.5% to 3.7% and signaled it would hold the rate “for an extended period.” The dollar hit 18.96 pesos before closing at 18.75.

Mexican judge faces extradition

Luis Benítez Alcántara, a Mexico City district judge, was arrested in Colombia on Nov. 1. U.S. officials accuse him of accepting a US $2 million bribe to help free Andrew Clark, second-in-command to ex-Olympic snowboarder Ryan James Wedding’s trafficking organization. Benítez is the first Mexican federal judge indicted by the United States, and he faces nine counts, each carrying up to 15 years. Separately, Édgar Aarón Vázquez, leader of the New Empire Cartel and accused of protecting Wedding, was killed Thursday in a confrontation with police in the State of Mexico.

Phone-free schools

Starting Tuesday, cell phones and tablets are restricted during classes and recess at public and private primary and secondary schools nationwide. High schools will set their own rules with their school communities. The Education Ministry’s slogan was “Turn off the screen and turn your imagination on!”

The rules follow a Sept. 18 decision by the National Council of Educational Authorities, in which officials from all 32 states agreed to the measures. Education Minister Mario Delgado said the goal is to boost focus, encourage socializing in schoolyards and hallways, and promote responsible technology use. The guidelines grew out of expert presentations on the addictive nature of certain algorithms and forums with parents and educators. According to Delgado, 81% of 565,000 educators surveyed backed guidelines for safe device use.

Papal visit confusion

A comment by the Vatican’s new communications chief about the pope visiting “Our Lady of Guadalupe” set off reports of a 2027 Mexico trip. Televisa’s Vatican correspondent Valentina Alazraki reported that a Vatican spokesperson clarified the comment referred to a parish in Casavalle, Uruguay. Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada said she had no confirmation, and Alazraki reported that Leo XIV wants to come but “there is only the intention.”

Mexican-American María Montserrat Alvarado took office as the Vatican’s communications chief on Sunday. The 39-year-old Mexico City native, raised in Miami, is the first laywoman to lead a ministry-level Vatican department.

Mexico’s economy gains momentum

The MND Economy Index™ hit a record 74.5 out of 100 for August, half a point shy of “strong.” Mexico-Canada trade rose 18.3% in the first eight months to 34.42 billion Canadian dollars, while Mexico’s trade surplus with the U.S. jumped 26.1% through September to a record US $184 billion, driven largely by AI-related equipment purchases.

2026 annual growth forecasts improved in both Banxico (1.5%) and Citi (1.8%) surveys.

Mexico City weighs tougher penalties for animal poisoning

After four dogs died from poisoned meat in Condesa’s Parque España, lawmakers proposed tougher penalties. Labor Party lawmaker Diana Barragán’s bill would allow three to nine years when poisoning kills an animal, and other proposals would bar convicted abusers from acquiring animals. A 58-year-old suspect is jailed pending trial.

Travel headlines

Looking ahead

Banxico and Citi both predict Mexico’s economy will grow about 1.8% to 1.9% in 2027, with year-end 2026 inflation near 3.9%. Banxico has signaled it plans to hold its rate steady for an extended period.

One sector that will shape that outlook is data centers. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said last week that companies have announced more than US $8 billion in data center projects, led by Querétaro, with Guanajuato and Nuevo León also drawing investment. Sheinbaum has said Mexico needs data centers to advance in artificial intelligence, but not necessarily to become a hub for the rest of the world, given their energy and water demands.

Data centers were also a hot topic in the U.S. midterms. The Associated Press reported that a campaign season filled with outrage against them ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the facilities. Gina Hinojosa, who won the Texas governorship, campaigned on a moratorium on new data center construction. Whether the issue crosses the border is an open question as Mexico heads to its own midterms on June 6, 2027.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: Is the beach the real Mexico?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — explores whether living in a beachfront community really qualifies as an authentically Mexican experience.

About 15 years ago, when I had my first online job, one of my supervisors lived in Los Cabos. She very much enjoyed telling people “what it was like in Mexico,” and was proud of her knowledge.

“Well, in my experience here, that’s not a problem at all!” she’d say when one of the many other Mexican residents would casually bring up an issue. “Things are pretty easy in Mexico, you know. All you have to do is …”

A friend of mine who worked with me and lived in Mexico City would privately express her annoyance to me. “That’s easy to say if you live in a gringo paradise with low population density. I’d love to see this ‘Mexico genius’ get by in my own barrio.”

Even in Xalapa, where spotting a foreigner is like stumbling upon Waldo, I’ve been on the receiving end of this kind of annoyance. “You live in a bubble in Xalapa; that’s not the real Mexico!” a friend of mine once insisted. She herself had lived for years in a tiny town outside of a fairly dinky and unglamorous city. I rolled my eyes and let it go; it wasn’t something I cared to debate.

Besides, if that was “the real Mexico,” I’d happily leave it all for her.

Where is the real Mexico, and how do I get there?

Chances are that you clicked on this article primed for a debate. It’s a sensitive topic, especially among those of us who consider Mexico home and ourselves to be fully integrated. Whether we foreigners live in beach towns or tiny towns, everyone’s surely got an opinion!

So what is the measuring stick that people use to define the “real” … any place, actually? Because this tendency isn’t at all unique to Mexico.

Think of every Hallmark rom-com you’ve ever seen: a high-powered and glamorous businesswoman travels from her sleek New York City apartment back to her home for the holidays. It’s always a small town in the U.S. Midwest. Everyone knows each other, and her high school sweetheart is there, handsome and single, or perhaps widowed.

That small town? That’s the “real” America, the movie says. Not like New York City, which was actually established first. Similarly, people in Mexico — especially foreigners — often have some strict ideas about what counts as “authentically Mexican.”

I suspect, actually, that Mexicans do not have conversations about this, which is telling: they have nothing to prove. They’re Mexican, and wherever they live in the country is “really” Mexico, period.

Not all beaches are developed equally

Still, beach communities receive special scrutiny. Not all beach communities are alike, though. Living in Cancún or Los Cabos, for example, is very different than living in Chachalacas, Veracruz.

Cancún and Los Cabos are full of fancy beach resorts and the kind of development that could attract royalty. Everyone who works there has to speak at least some English.

Chachalacas is a tiny town that only recently got paved roads. Its fanciest hotels are fancy simply because they have in-room air conditioning and a pool. English can most certainly not be counted on, and beach parking is on the sand … or you can take a bus from a small, unfancy town nearby. Bathrooms are bare toilet seats in the middle of small wooden shacks; 1 star for sure. To flush the toilet, there’s a large tub of water outside and a bucket. But boy, is the seafood good!

So here’s the question: Is Chachalacas more real than Cancún? It’s hard to argue that they share much in common besides the beach. Or perhaps it’s the presence, or not, of foreigners in a place, be it the beach or somewhere else. Does the fact that one might look around and see a sea of one’s paisanos make it less authentic? For some, I think it absolutely does.

We were in the real Mexico all along

And of course, the question might not even be a consequential one. People live where they want to live. Does it matter if they’re adapting or not? Do people even care if where they’re living is authentic in a stranger’s view? But no matter where you are, if you live on or near the beach, expect to get side-eyed when you talk about your knowledge of Mexico.

The word “beach” is practically synonymous with “vacation,” which explains a lot. You hear it in our language: “Time to leave the beach and get back to the real world.” This is a sad phrase to me, since it separates the real world from the kind of world that you’d actually like to live in. So perhaps the rest of us are just jealous?

My daughter has an educational book about sex. It spends some time talking about the differences between boys and girls. It does a good job of emphasizing that things like haircuts and clothing are pretty much never exclusive to one sex. “There are all kinds of different ways to be a boy,” it says, and “there are all kinds of different ways to be a girl.”

This, I believe, is the correct attitude to have with most things. Like everywhere else, Mexico is a very diverse place. There are as many different ways to “be Mexico” as there are different ways to be Mexican.

So wherever you are, maybe don’t worry about it too much. If someone wants to challenge you on it, like my friend above, shrug your shoulders and suggest a Tex-Mex style margarita, or maybe a caguama … you know, depending on where you are.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.
