World.title: Belize and Taiwan strengthen ties at Taiwan International Travel Fair
World.content:
Belize and Taiwan strengthen ties at Taiwan International Travel Fair

By Zoila Palma: This week, a Belizean delegation visiting Taiwan for the Taiwan International Travel Fair participated in a series of meetings and engagements aimed at strengthening bilateral relations and exploring opportunities for continued cooperation between Belize and Taiwan.

The delegation included Minister of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations Anthony Mahler, Devin Daly, Chief Executive Officer Nicole Usher, Chief Tourism Officer Josue Carballo and Senior Liaison Officer Sandra Mahler.

They were also joined by Minister of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs Thea Garcia-Ramirez, Belize’s Ambassador to Taiwan Katherine Meighan, and Belize Electricity Limited Board Member Lawrence Ellis.

During the visit, the Belizean officials met with representatives of Taiwan’s Ministry of Sports and Ministry of Foreign Affairs to discuss areas of mutual interest and opportunities for collaboration.

The delegation also held discussions with representatives of Lion Travel, one of Taiwan’s largest travel agencies, as part of efforts to strengthen tourism connections and explore opportunities for Belize.

The delegation’s engagements also included a special dinner hosted by the Latin American and Caribbean Trade Office, bringing together regional partners and providing another opportunity to build relationships.

World.title: A major milestone for Belize’s conservation efforts – Over 3,500 acres added to the Maya Forest Corridor
World.content:
A major milestone for Belize’s conservation efforts – Over 3,500 acres added to the Maya Forest Corridor

Safeguarding Belize’s forests through responsible harvesting, restoration and sustainable forest management

This article is sponsored by Bulridge Ltd.

By Zoila Palma: More than 3,500 acres of land have been added to the Belize Maya Forest Corridor Trust, marking a major milestone in Belize’s forest conservation efforts and completing a protected connection between key wildlife habitats.

The Ministry of Natural Resources, Petroleum and Mining, in partnership with the Belize Maya Forest Corridor Trust, announced the achievement on November 6, 2026.

The newly incorporated lands connect the Labouring Creek Jaguar Corridor Wildlife Sanctuary with the Manatee Forest Reserve, strengthening the Maya Forest Corridor and providing a more continuous protected landscape for wildlife.

The achievement represents years of collaboration involving the Government of Belize, conservation organizations, landowners and local communities working to safeguard the country’s natural heritage.

Minister of Sustainable Development Orlando Habet highlighted the regional importance of the initiative, noting that the corridor contributes to a broader conservation vision shared by Belize, Guatemala and Mexico under the Calakmul Biocultural Declaration. “Beyond our national commitments, the Maya Forest Corridor contributes to our shared regional vision under the Calakmul Biocultural Declaration,” Habet said. He emphasized the importance of regional cooperation, stating, “Forests do not recognize political boundaries.”

Habet added, “The Maya Forest Corridor demonstrates that conservation and sustainable development can advance together.” He also stressed the importance of community participation, saying, “Communities must be recognized as partners in the corridor’s management and governance, with meaningful opportunities to participate in decisions and benefit from its conservation.”

Minister of Natural Resources Cordel Hyde also welcomed the achievement, expressing pride in Belize’s contribution to protecting its forests and preserving the country’s natural heritage. “All over the world, developed countries are failing to deliver on their conservation commitments,” Hyde said.

He added, “So I’m mighty proud of this that is happening today and to be a part of this initiative to do our small part.”

“To finally connect this corridor and make it complete and in this process honor our ancestors.”

“This is not a sale, this is a vesting for conservation purposes,” Hyde said.

Hyde explained that the newly incorporated lands are being secured on behalf of the people of Belize to prevent future governments or ministers from alienating them for other purposes, as has happened in the past.

The Belize Maya Forest Corridor Trust includes the Belize Zoo and Tropical Education Center, WCS Belize, the Foundation for Wildlife Conservation, the Environmental Research Institute of the University of Belize.

World.title: Minister of Foreign Affairs commends security forces for professionalism in face of acts of intimidation by GAF
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs commends security forces for professionalism in face of acts of intimidation by GAF

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Foreign Affairs Francis Fonseca is commending Belize’s security forces for their professionalism during acts of intimidation by the Guatemalan Armed Forces in the Sarstoon today.

“Belize will always stand up to Guatemalan aggression with courage, dignity and professionalism.

We are committed to peace but the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our nation will not be compromised.

Belize is proud of our Security Forces on the frontline of our national defense,” Fonseca said.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed that today, a Belize Defence Force (BDF) patrol conducting a routine patrol around Sarstoon Island was aggressively approached by two Guatemalan Armed Forces (GAF) vessels that had crossed into Belizean waters, in an evident attempt at intimidation.

World.title: Haiti gang leader killed as Bukele steps up war on gangs, and Belize watches closely
World.content:
Haiti gang leader killed as Bukele steps up war on gangs, and Belize watches closely

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Haiti’s National Police say they have “neutralised” Mathias Saintil, leader of the Boston gang in Cité Soleil, one of the poorest areas of the capital, Port-au-Prince.

Saintil was reportedly hit by multiple bullets during a police operation and later died in hospital. Haiti’s Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé celebrated on social media, writing, “One less gang leader,” and warning that gangs would not be able to sleep.

The killing comes as El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele takes a more aggressive role in Haiti. After four Salvadoran aviation technicians serving with the international Gang Suppression Force were kidnapped on October 18, Bukele sent as many as 2,000 troops to Haiti and warned gang leaders that worse was coming if the hostages were not returned alive.

Belize has its own reasons to pay attention. National Security Minister Michel Chebat recently said he plans to visit El Salvador to study Bukele’s crime fighting strategies and see whether any lessons could apply here.

That approach has strong supporters, but also critics. Human rights groups say Bukele’s crackdown in El Salvador, including mass arrests and mass trials, has undermined due process and civil liberties.

At home, Belize is under a 30 day state of emergency in Southside Belize City and parts of the Belize and Cayo Districts, following the murder of four men on the Coastal Highway.

World.title: Armed gangs backing squatters
World.content:
An aerial view of Flamingo Beach, Trelawny, where some of the land has been overrun by squatters, stalling a proposed development that includes resort and entertainment facilities in addition to a residential component.

Well-known attorney Gordon Brown says armed gang members from outside the community are thwarting his six-year-long effort to curb squatting on sections of 167 acres of land he owns in Flamingo Beach, Trelawny. Even a private security firm, he said, has refused the job of protecting the property from being further overrun.

Brown has submitted plans to the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) and the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC) for an integrated development that includes resort and entertainment facilities in addition to a residential component, but he is unable to proceed as the land is littered with structures at various stages of construction.

In his view, apart from the TMC, which has publicly expressed concern about the stalled development, little has been done by State agencies to help him with his battle.

“Whilst I cannot say exactly how many acres have been squatted upon, what is unequivocal is that, since 2020, both personally and through the several attorneys who have assisted, I have made assiduous efforts to contain the festering squatting problem,” Brown said in a written response to the Jamaica Observer’s Real Estate on the Rock.

“In the supervening five years since filing suit I have respected the rule of law and complied with all orders of the court. Regrettably, my experience has proven yet again that, in our nation, those who abide by the law and show restraint are met with contempt or indifference. Those who flout it are given safe harbour by the authorities, especially if muscular action is visited upon them,” he added.

He listed a litany of failed attempts to arrest squatting taking place on the land, starting with his lawyers’ appeal to NEPA in early May 2020 to use its powers to “require the demolition of all illegal structures on the property”. He said NEPA posted warnings on all the structures on the site, but they were ignored and the squatting continued unabated.

According to Brown, in mid-January 2021, his attorneys served all the squatters with notices to quit, referencing NEPA’s May 2020 warning. In February, he said, his lawyers wrote to the superintendent of police for Trelawny, alerting him that his team may be needed if the squatters got rowdy after being served with notices to leave the property. Then in March 2021 he tried to hire private security to patrol and protect the land in an effort to move the process along.

“They carried out investigations and declined to accept the assignment, as their checks revealed the credible presence of armed gang members from other communities who were in place to resist any efforts to impede the illegal construction,” said Brown.

He said his lawyers then appealed to the commissioner of police, in late March 2021, alerting him to “rampant suspected criminality” in the area and the impact it was having on his property.

“This was copied to several parties, including the chief of defence staff, member of parliament and others, but we received no response, save from the TMC,” said Brown.

“Early April 2021 I met with the TMC to present the estate’s case and its need for coordinated action by the municipality and the police to curtail and demolish the structures. Subsequent to a meeting with the deputy superintendent of works of the TMC on-site, the property caretaker was ambushed by armed thugs who warned him not to erect the signage that we had agreed with the TMC should be put in place to advise the squatters of imminent action,” he added.

Brown then sought help from the courts, filing a suit in May 2021 in which he named all the then-known squatters

— about 10 of them

— and provided a “generic description” of a handful of others who were not known. In the suit, he sought an order for possession of the property. According to Brown, he was “granted an injunction restraining the squatters from damaging the site’s ecology, carrying out further construction activity upon the premises, and other relief”.

However, that did nothing to rein in the squatters, some of whom claim to own the land they occupy.

“Since that time there has been an explosion in the number of occupants. The injunction has been renewed pending final determination of the matter by the court. The occupants have falsely claimed that they have been in occupation of the premises for a period that would give them a possessory title to the parts of the premises occupied by them, but produced no evidence to support their claim. I have tendered video, aerial and geospatial evidence of the state of the premises as of the date of the court action [and before] which prove their claims untenable,” said Brown.

In explaining his claim to the land, he said he was the administrator of the estate of the late Carl Fei, an American who owned several parcels of land in Jamaica, including “approximately 167.25 acres at Flamingo Beach, Trelawny, near to the border of St James”.

“I was registered as the proprietor on November 11, 2005, but have been engaged with the affairs for the estate for many years prior to that date,” Brown told the Sunday Observer.

The Flamingo Beach land issue came to public attention in September when Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager raised an alarm during the TMC’s regular monthly meeting. He cited Flamingo Beach as one example of the growing problem of squatting in Trelawny which has resulted in the municipal authority being inundated with complaints from frustrated landowners.

“There is a submitted plan here for that property that will help to build Trelawny, but we cannot proceed because there is this problem of squatting,” Gager said of Flamingo Beach, naming Brown as the owner of the land.

During the meeting the mayor also referenced significant squatting on sections of 344.5 acres of land in an area called Tilston, Hague, where one acre has been informally settled; and Hague Cave Island, where four acres of the property have similarly been occupied. He also pointed to Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny

— where approximately 12 acres of the property had been informally occupied

— which had made news headlines following an August 11 early-morning demolition of about 20 structures by the private owner.

There is also a major development planned for Cooper’s Pen and the landowner has been fighting a legal battle for years to get squatters off the land. Brown pointed to similarities between that case and his struggles at Flamingo Beach.

“This débâcle bears all the portents of another Cooper’s Pen, only with more visible, painful results,” he said.

He outlined the ways in which State agencies have failed to act effectively.

“The police have been given statements by parties duped into ‘purchasing’ lots at Flamingo Beach by unscrupulous persons and received necessary information to investigate and prosecute same. No one has been charged,” Brown said.

“I have made several overtures to the police in Trelawny and at the level of the high command for their assistance to address the burgeoning criminality, but with only token support, limited to police escorts whenever court orders are posted on-site. Even equipment bearing insignia and markings of the Jamaica Defence Force has been observed on the site, engaged in illegal activity,” he alleged.

Insisting there can be no excuse for squatting, Brown lay the blame at the feet of successive administrations who have skirted around the issue. He said there has been a “collective refusal” to craft plans to install basic infrastructure on the 550,000 acres of land believed to be in the Government’s possession; pursue transparent divestment methodology and pricing; and put in place the technical staff and enforcement personnel needed in municipal corporations across the country to review and inspect building sites.

Pointing out that the bulk of the country’s housing stock is informal but it is “futile” to demolish them because of non-compliance, Brown argued that many squatters genuinely want to be legitimate owners of property, but the State has failed to put the necessary channels in place.

“Many squatters pay for lands which they occupy

— just not the legitimate owner. Squatters spend large sums for palatial homes on lands they do not own. There is clearly no issue of their ability to afford land, which represents 10 per cent or marginally more of the cost of overall development,” he argued.

“Given an opportunity to acquire lands owned by Government legitimately, those in search of lands [who become squatters] would do so. However, the State must make lands affordable, while ensuring that both the subdivisions and intended development of them are orderly and comply with structural integrity for the safety and health of the intended inhabitants. Formal infrastructure in the form of paved roads and electricity are never a feature of communities that have been squatted,” Brown said.

“These services typically follow after an informal settlement has been established and there is pressure on a member of parliament to support it. These become far more costly to implement because there is no planning of these communities; service roads are twice as long, etc. It is therefore only logical for the State to lead with low-cost, basic infrastructure

— serviced lots in locations with sufficient proximity to main/arterial roads, etc,” Brown added.

He made it clear, however, that he was not excusing the behaviour of those who have stalled his plans at Flamingo Beach.

“These [plans] cannot exist nor be pursued in the context of lawlessness and criminality,” Brown told the Sunday Observer.

World.title: Romain Virgo bares his soul on My Woman & I
World.content:
Virgo’s latest single, My Woman & I was released on Friday, October 30, 2026Contributed

For Romain Virgo, vulnerability has never been something to shy away from. Whether through his music or in his personal life, the reggae singer believes there is value in allowing people to see the person behind the performer, even when the emotions being shared are difficult.

That openness is at the heart of his new single, My Woman & I, a deeply personal offering inspired by a period of uncertainty in his own relationship and a reminder that committed love is not necessarily love without struggle.

Written about a year ago, the song emerged at a time when Virgo and his wife, Elizabeth, were navigating some of the challenges that can arise in any relationship.

Rather than suppressing those feelings, the singer turned to music to process them, recording what was on his heart.

“Relationships and everything that comes with it, those moments when it feels like things aren’t going to work, that’s how I was feeling about my personal relationship in the moment,” he told the Jamaica Observer. “Relationships are like a roller-coaster ride and sometimes, as musicians, the best way to handle these things is to put it in the music. I put pen to paper and I just wrote how I was feeling and recorded it.”

For Virgo, the decision to draw on such a personal experience speaks to his commitment to authenticity. He wants listeners to recognise themselves in his music, particularly those who have experienced the uncertainty that can accompany a relationship while still believing in the possibility of working through it.

“The world, by now, knows me and knows that I am not afraid to show the real side of me. Whether through music or in real life, I am authentic always,” he said.

That willingness to be candid extends to the conversations surrounding the song at home.

When Virgo first played My Woman & I for his wife, her response was not quite the enthusiastic reception he might have hoped for.

“If I’m going to be as vulnerable as possible, the first time she heard this song, she hissed her teeth while laughing at the same time,” he recalled. “I would trouble her and tell her this is the song that she will probably hate the most.”

The reaction, however, appears to have softened. Virgo recently caught her singing the song, prompting a laugh when she remembered that she had supposedly disliked it.

For him, the moment reflects a growing understanding of how music allows him to work through his experiences, including those that are deeply personal.

His creative process, he explained, means drawing on what he is feeling in the moment rather than shying away from difficult emotions. More importantly, the song is not about presenting a relationship as perfect. Instead, Virgo hopes it will resonate with people who understand that commitment is sometimes tested by circumstances that cannot be resolved overnight.

“I hope this single will give people who look to music for their peace and to express themselves. I hope it gives them a sense of belonging,” he said. “I hope they hear someone who has been through some tough times when it comes to relationships and now that it just something that comes with the territory.”

His message to listeners is simple: Difficulty does not have to mean defeat.

“When you’re committed to something, you have to find ways to work through issues and keep showing up, don’t give up on love,” he said.

Though written a year ago, My Woman & I is only now making its way to listeners. Virgo explained that the timing was not right for its release earlier, particularly in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, when he delayed the release and promotion of several songs already in the pipeline.

With the time now right, the single will also serve as a precursor to a larger project currently in development. Sources suggest a 2027 release on Ineffable Records.

“This track will lead into something bigger. We working on a project that we can’t give too much details on just yet. Just know this single is a part of a bigger picture,” he said of the track produced by Mr G and revives the classic Dub Fire rhythm made famous on Dennis Brown’s Promised Land.

For now, My Woman & I offers listeners an intimate look at an artiste willing to turn his own experiences into music, with a message that extends beyond romance. Love, as Virgo presents it, is not simply about the moments when everything falls into place, but also the willingness to keep showing up when it does not.

My Woman & I was released on Friday, October 30, and is available on all digital platforms.

World.title: The 15-year challenge
World.content:
Inter Miami’s Lionel Messi (second left) deftly scores past Cavalier’s goalkeeper Vino Barclett (#1) as Jeovanni Laing (left) looks on during the Concacaf Champions Cup second-leg round-of-16 match at the National Stadium on Thursday, March 13, 2025. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

When Mount Pleasant FA and Cavalier FC represented Jamaica in the Concacaf Champions Cup it was a proud moment for local football. However, their participation also highlighted the gap between Jamaican clubs and the region’s top teams.

Clubs in Major League Soccer (MLS) and Mexico’s Liga MX have far greater financial resources, with budgets exceeding US$10 million (over $1.5 billion). This puts them well ahead of teams in the Legend Jamaica Premier League (JPL).

The difference is not just about players’ salaries. It also comes down to facilities, technical support, sports science, preparation, and the cost of competing internationally.

Mount Pleasant have done more than most Jamaican clubs to improve their operations. Under owner Peter Gould, the St Ann club has built its own training academy, hired experienced technical staff, and established itself as one of the leading teams in the Caribbean.

However, even with that investment, Mount Pleasant still have work to do to compete with the best in Concacaf.

Mount Pleasant Sporting Director Paul Christie says the club has made significant progress since 2022, but is still some way from achieving its continental ambitions.

“In 2022, when we were given the privilege of carrying out the mandate by owner Peter Gould, Mount Pleasant was 172nd in Concacaf’s club rating and 35th in the Caribbean,” Christie told the Sunday Observer. “Since then, we’re on the cusp of breaking into the top 50 in Concacaf, and we’re the #1 team in the Caribbean. Until we are able to satisfactorily compete at the Concacaf level, there’s still a lot of work to be done.”

The challenge extends beyond individual clubs. Professional Football Jamaica Limited (PFJL) Chief Executive Officer Owen Hill says the league must address several problems if Jamaican teams are to compete more regularly at the regional level.

One of the biggest challenges is the lack of stadiums that meet Concacaf’s requirements. This often forces clubs to play home matches overseas, increasing their expenses and taking away the advantage of playing in front of their supporters.

Hill pointed to Portmore United’s Caribbean Cup campaign as an example of the problem. He explained that the reigning JPL champions had to play a home match in Trinidad because suitable venues were unavailable in Jamaica.

“That was a home game – in Trinidad, why?! Trinidad is not even close to Jamaica, but the reason they played in Trinidad is primarily because of the economics of it. It’s cheaper to play in Trinidad than Jamaica,” Hill told the Observer.

Hill explained that the National Stadium was booked for the Independence Gala period, while Sabina Park was being used for the Caribbean Premier League. He said Portmore had no other suitable venue available and had to travel to Trinidad to fulfil the fixture.

Playing home matches overseas means clubs miss out on ticket sales and other income that could be used to improve their operations. It also limits the support they receive from local fans.

Hill wants clubs to eventually have their own stadiums that meet minimum Concacaf standards. This would not only give them a suitable home venue for international matches but also allow them to build stronger connections with their communities and generate income.

The PFJL is also working with Concacaf and the Jamaica Football Federation to adjust the domestic calendar around international competitions. However, Hill says clubs must also plan their training programmes and squad depth because fixture clashes cannot always be avoided.

The financial demands of international football are another concern. Hill says the PFJL supports clubs that qualify for regional competitions, while Concacaf subsidies have increased. However, the cost of travel, maintaining squads, and preparing for matches remain major challenges.

“Our clubs and, by extension, our economy, are not about to sustain that consistently, so what we try to do is incentivise the opportunities but also ensure that education happens very early,” Hill says.

The PFJL also wants Jamaican clubs to become stronger brands that can attract investment from the Diaspora and international sponsors. Hill admits that the response from overseas Jamaicans has so far been limited, but believes clubs can become more attractive to investors as the professional product improves.

The league has already reached some important milestones, including an expanded sponsorship agreement with Legend Beer, 360-degree broadcast coverage, and venue partnerships with Independence Park Limited.

Hill also sees the proposed redevelopment of Montego Bay Sports Complex as a model for future projects. He believes Jamaica needs at least 10 stadiums of a similar standard over the next decade to improve the facilities available to clubs and other sporting events.

However, better stadiums alone will not close the gap. Hill says clubs also need proper gyms, recovery facilities, and technical analysts who can study opponents and help coaches prepare their teams.

He believes the lack of those resources also affects how Jamaican football is viewed internationally. While the country’s players are recognised for their speed and athleticism, tactical preparation remains an area that needs improvement.

The long-term plan is to build clubs that can generate enough income through sponsorship, commercial activities, and player transfers to reinvest in their operations.

“When I talk about the vision, I’m saying no less than 10 to 15 years of building and toiling before we see some actual results, such as players being sold for solid amounts of money; transfer fees are now back into the club’s ecosystem to develop the club’s infrastructure at a minimum standard,” Hill says.

World.title: Loyalty At Heart
World.content:
In Citizen Magazine Issue 005, award-winning actress Sheryl Lee Ralph shares the spotlight with her daughter, stylist Ivy “Coco” Maurice, for “Loyalty at Heart”. (Photo: Rasaan Wyzard)

Plus…

For Sheryl Lee Ralph, style is a family affair. The Emmy, Critics Choice and Independent Spirit Award-winning actress joined her daughter, stylist Ivy “Coco” Maurice, for a striking fashion moment in Citizen Magazine Issue 005. World.title: Man suspected of drowning in Alligator Pond
World.content:
People enjoying the river and sea at a beach in Alligator Pond. A no swimming sign is seen in the background. (Photo: Kasey Williams)

MANCHESTER, Jamaica — A man is suspected to have drowned in Alligator Pond, south Manchester on Saturday.

Police identified him as Simon Newman, a resident of Downs near the Manchester/ St Elizabeth border.

Preliminary reports are that about 4:00 pm Newman was swimming in a river when he got into difficulty and went underwater. His body was later removed from the river. Police were called and he was pronounced dead at hospital.

The area, known as River, has been the scene of numerous drowning incidents over the years, especially on holidays.

In August 2023, two people drowned at the location. A local community hero, who saved people from drowning at the same location, also drowned upstream in the river in Alligator Pond, a week after rescuing several people.

READ: Alligator Pond hero found dead in river

A police source said in January 2025 Newman’s twin brother was one of two people who died in a crash on the Buttup main road in south Manchester.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: Manning Cup quarterfinalists decided
World.content:
In this file photo, Kingston College’s Deshawn Byfield (left) and Mona High’s Jermaine Morgan vie for the ball during the ISSA Walker Cup final at Stadium East. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Former champions Jamaica College (JC), Mona High and Wolmer’s Boys were the last three qualifiers to the ISSA Manning Cup quarterfinal following the final set of games in the round of 16 on Saturday.

JC drew 1-1 with Eltham and finished second on five points in Zone 4. Eltham won the group with seven points. Norman Manley defeated Tivoli Gardens 4-2 and grabbed third place with three points. Tivoli Gardens ended with a point.

In Zone 1, defending champions Excelsior came from behind to beat St George’s College 2-1 and consolidated their position at the top with nine points. The Light Blues finished at the bottom with a point.

Mona High booked their spot with a comprehensive 4-0 win over St Catherine High and finished with six points and second spot in Zone 1 as St Catherine were eliminated with a point in third spot.

Wolmer’s Boys blanked Hillel Academy 2-0 and finished second in Zone 3 with six points and into the last eight. St Andrew Technical High School (STATHS) topped the group with maximum nine points after whipping St Jago High 5-0.

Kingston College defeated Calabar 1-0 to top Zone 2 with maximum nine points. Calabar, who had already qualified for the quarterfinal, were second with six points.

The quarter final pairings have been decided with Group A consisting of Excelsior high, Eltham High, Wolmer’s Boys and Calabar High while Group B will have KC, STATHS, Mona and JC.

–Howard Walker

World.title: NWC customers miss out on $50m
World.content:
SOME National Water Commission (NWC) customers missed out on hundreds of dollars in compensation as the utility paid only $23.76 million of the $73.78 million potentially available for breaches of its Guranteed Standards during the 2025–2026 financial year.

The shortfall of approximately $50 million is outlined in the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) 2025–2026 Annual Report, tabled in Parliament on Tuesday.

The report shows that the NWC committed 14,817 breaches of its Guaranteed Standards during the period April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026.

But the utility paid just 32 per cent of the potential compensation its customers should have received.

Among the reasons cited for the non-payment were customers failing to submit the required claim forms and NWC receiving relief from the Guaranteed Standards following Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.

The OUR excused the utility from meeting certain service requirements between October 24 and December 31, 2025, because of the disruption caused by the Category 5 storm.

This meant the utility could avoid paying compensation for breaches covered by that relief during the period.

The report also disclosed that, in March 2026, the NWC requested a further six months of relief, beginning January 1, 2026. At the end of the reporting period, that request was still under review, with the OUR indicating that a decision would be issued in the next financial year.

The Guaranteed Standards are service requirements that utility providers are expected to meet. Where a provider breaches an applicable standard, affected customers may qualify for compensation, subject to the relevant conditions and procedures.

The NWC’s compensation figures form part of wider concerns about customer service and unresolved complaints recorded by the OUR during the financial year.

The OUR said it received 3,558 contacts from consumers about utility services during the period, of which 1,168 related to the NWC. These included complaints, enquiries, and other matters brought to its attention.

At March 31, 2026, the NWC also accounted for 251 of the 625 complaints that remained open across all utility providers, representing 40 per cent of the outstanding cases.

The report found that billing disputes and service interruptions were the leading reasons consumers contacted the OUR, accounting for 48 per cent and 18 per cent of all contacts, respectively.

The regulator also noted that it had secured approximately $21.34 million for customers through investigations of appeals and complaints during the financial year.

The NWC accounted for the largest share, paying approximately $9.45 million for consumers, or 44 per cent of the total. The OUR said it would continue reviewing the NWC’s request for additional relief in the following financial year.

The utility recently applied for a 51 per cent tariff increase which is to be considered by the OUR.

World.title: Labourities riding westJLP forgoes customary public rally at National Arena for scaled-down conference in MoBay
World.content:
The sea of green at the public session of the JLP’s 2023 annual conference which will not be repeated this year as only delegates will be invited to the conference to be held in Montego Bay, St James. Karl McLarty

NO National Arena spectacle, no sea of supporters bussed from across the island, no grand public rally.

The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) will again scale back its 2026 annual conference, opting for a delegates-only business meeting in Montego Bay on November 15.

JLP Deputy Leader Desmond McKenzie, who announced the decision at a media conference at the party’s headquarters on Belmont Road in New Kingston on Friday, said the party recognised that although thousands of Jamaicans had received assistance through the Government’s response in the wake of Hurricane Melissa one year ago, much more needs to be done.

“In that vein of recognising the moment and the mood of a section of the country, in respect of our annual conference we have chosen to forgo the usual spectacle which we have had at the National Arena in Kingston,” said McKenzie.

He said the annual conference will be held at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James, beginning at approximately 10 am, with about 6,000 delegates expected to attend.

The decision means there will be no customary mass public meeting, with the party saying it wants to show solidarity with Jamaicans who are still struggling more than a year after the Category 5 storm, particularly those in western Jamaica which was among the areas hardest hit.

According to McKenzie, the decision to scale down the conference was based on a recommendation from the party’s officers, which was approved by its central executive, with the conference instead taking the form of a business session to address internal party matters, political issues, and its role in the recovery effort.

McKenzie explained that prime minister and Party Leader Dr Andrew Holness is expected to address the conference at approximately 1:30 pm, with his speech to be open to the media and broadcast live.

But, McKenzie underscored that the rest of the conference’s business will take place behind closed doors, with attendance restricted to party delegates.

Meanwhile, JLP Deputy General Secretary Dr Andrew Wheatley told Friday’s media briefing that the party’s constitution requires it to hold an annual conference, which is traditionally a business meeting involving delegates.

He said the large public gathering usually associated with the event is a separate public session. Wheatley said the party had chosen to hold the business meeting in Montego Bay to engage stakeholders and workers in western Jamaica who were affected by the hurricane. “We want to empathise with the people, those affected by Hurricane Melissa, especially those in western Jamaica. So we wanted to forego the celebratory aspect of our annual conference and deal with a private business session that will afford us the opportunity to programme political activities, do a self-assessment as to where we are as a political party, and engage the most important members of the party — the delegates of the party — as we…take decisions for not only the betterment of the Jamaican Labour Party but, by extension, the people of Jamaica,” Wheatley said. He also urged delegates to participate actively as the party prepares for the next local government elections. Leadership changes will also be on the agenda, with the private session expected to include elections for the party leader and deputy leaders. Wheatley said the party understood that supporters would miss the usual opportunity to gather and celebrate its achievements, but argued that the circumstances required a different approach. JLP Chairman Robert Montague defended the decision, saying the party had a responsibility to identify with Jamaicans who were still dealing with the effects of the hurricane. He rejected suggestions that the JLP was copying the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP), which held the public session of its 88th annual conference at Independence Park in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, on Sunday, September 20, after moving the event from its usual venue at the National Arena in Kingston. “As a party that cares and as the national party of this country and the party that forms government, we also have a responsibility — a responsibility to those who are still suffering and who are still recovering from the hurricane. We have a responsibility to provide mature leadership to the country. [We] say, rather than jollyficate with some while some persons are struggling, let us identify with our brothers and sisters who are struggling,” he said. “You will also note that the party leader, who is prime minister, has basically put the country on notice that it is time we as a nation begin to tighten some belts, to cut some expenses in order to bring relief to those who are suffering. So, it’s a mature decision and it’s a decision if we did not take, our members and supporters would have condemned us,” Montague added.

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Bodo Ramelow
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Die Welt spielt verrückt, doch im Präsidium des Bundestages herrscht überraschende Einigkeit. Bundestagsvizepräsident Bodo Ramelow (Die Linke) gibt im Gespräch mit Gordon Repinski einen seltenen Einblick in die überparteiliche Zusammenarbeit, auch bei Nachtschichten. Dabei wird deutlich, mit welcher Strategie das Gremium den Provokationen der AfD begegnet.

In seiner eigenen Partei brodelt es derweil gewaltig. Ramelow findet deutliche Worte zur Antisemitismus-Debatte innerhalb der Linken und kritisiert das taktische Lavieren einzelner Abgeordneter. Warum er trotzdem eine Gesinnungsprüfung ablehnt, aber klare rote Linien beim Existenzrecht Israels zieht, offenbart die tiefe Zerrissenheit seiner Partei.

Zudem verrät er, warum die Wahrnehmung der Linken im Bundestag derzeit auch von der Gruppe der „Silberlocken“ abhängt, wie sich die Silberlocken regelmäßig absprechen und warum er sich trotz aller Krisen nicht verrückt machen lässt.

Mit den Linken, aber auch der SPD und den Grünen beschäftigt sich auch der neue Podcast von POLITICO und WELT. In „Inside Links“ geht es jede Woche darum, wie in Deutschland womöglich eine neue linke Mehrheit entsteht, zu welchem Preis und wer künftig dabei möglicherweise am Regierungstisch sitzen könnte. „Inside Links“ gibt es auf den Podcast-Plattformen zu hören und zu sehen, unter anderem auch hier.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

Für alle Hauptstadt-Profis: Der Berlin Playbook-Newsletter bietet jeden Morgen die wichtigsten Themen und Einordnungen. Jetzt kostenlos abonnieren.

World.title: Merz’s conservatives poised to nominate Germany’s first woman president
World.content:
President of the Bavarian parliament Ilse Aigner arrives at the Christian Social Union party congress in Munich, on Oct. 23, 2026. | Alexandra Beier/AFP via Getty Images

BERLIN — Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner is set to become Germany’s next president, making her the country’s first woman to hold the office, according to two senior conservatives with knowledge of the matter.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) will nominate Aigner to succeed outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the officials told BILD, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. Both officials were granted anonymity to discuss internal party matters freely. Aigner’s nomination will officially be announced Monday, according to the officials.

Aigner, who previously served as agriculture minister under former German Chancellor Angela Merkel from 2008 to 2013, is currently president of the Bavarian State Parliament. She is also a member of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

World.title: Trump’s ‘big, beautiful’ European security plan isn’t convincing Europe
World.content:
The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.

POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.

U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”

“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.

Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”

“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments ... it will not fly with the European allies.”

World.title: NATO faces €7B shortfall on military aid pledge to Ukraine
World.content:
The shortfall comes ahead of an alliance meeting on Nov. 17 where European capitals are expected to examine ways to boost funding and increase the transfer of critical weapons to Ukraine. While new NATO funding pledges are still expected, it’s possible that allies may fail to meet this year’s target, the diplomats said.

A NATO official speaking on behalf of the organization said that “allies continue to provide essential military support to Ukraine” to fulfill the pledge and “are working to ensure that Ukraine has the support it needs now and into the future.”

The target combines bilateral contributions throughout the year and €30 billion drawn from the EU’s €90 billion loan to Ukraine.

Kyiv has repeatedly urged allies to step up their funding as Russia continues its devastating air assaults; more than 40 people were reportedly killed after a school bombing this week.

During a closed-door meeting with allies Thursday, Ukraine’s ambassador to NATO Alyona Getmanchuk “emphasised the importance for Ukraine of NATO Allies fulfilling the commitment made at the Ankara Summit to provide €70 billion in military support this year,” according to a statement by the Ukrainian mission.

“It is essential to mobilise all partners to the fullest extent, accelerate new decisions, and translate previously announced commitments into concrete deliveries of equipment or transfers of funds,” it added.

World.title: Wave of bomb threats target Irish media outlets and more European flights
World.content:
“We have expected a rise in hybrid threats to Ireland because of our hosting of the EU presidency, and the EPC meeting will be by far the biggest set-piece event of that presidency, so one must presume it’s no coincidence that we’re experiencing this spike in hybrid activity now,” the Irish official said.

The Irish government said the threats against media outlets were probably part of a European-wide pattern of threats that have targeted dozens of airlines this week, including Irish carriers Ryanair and Aer Lingus. Hackers also targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

“It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralized or coordinated effort,” the Irish government said in a statement. “However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”

Bomb threats also targeted at least 18 European flights Friday, after at least 22 the day before, raising concerns that the hoaxes may be part of a coordinated campaign to disrupt air traffic.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Friday that the bomb threats affecting flights could be “an attempt at hybrid aggression and war in some psychological way.” He added that “it cannot be a coincidence that so many identical events occur with the same modus operandi throughout Europe.”

Luis Gallego, CEO of airline group IAG, said: “It is clear that what they [the perpetrators] are looking for is to create chaos and disruption in the different airports.”

World.title: EU capitals urge Brussels to ‘swiftly’ sign electricity deal with UK
World.content:
A group of countries are now urging the European Commission to wrap up discussions by the end of 2027, according to an EU diplomat granted anonymity to discuss internal discussions.

Proponents say the plan would unlock new renewable energy investment in the North Sea and could cut electricity prices.

But the EU says the U.K. would have to make a contribution to EU cohesion funds as the price of participating in the market — a politically difficult ask for London.

Clean energy hub

The leaders, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, write that the agreement is “necessary to unlock the full potential of the North Sea” and to “transform it into the largest clean energy hub in the world.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa give a press conference at the end of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

“An agreement will thus enhance Europe’s energy security and contribute to a competitive economy that centres on access to clean and affordable energy,” the letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa states.

“These benefits underline the importance of swiftly concluding the ongoing negotiations. We call on you and the UK to agree during the Summit on a path towards the conclusion of these negotiations.”

World.title: Spain and the Netherlands battle over ECB presidency
World.content:
Exiting European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde gives a press conference in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, on Oct. 29, 2026. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images

Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot are in the hunt for the top job after Christine Lagarde’s exit.

BRUSSELS — The Netherlands and Spain on Friday submitted candidates to succeed Christine Lagarde, who steps down as president of the European Central Bank on Feb. 7.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain's central bank, and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, a former president of the Dutch central bank, were the only candidates to emerge after the 5 p.m. deadline, as expected.

Their candidacies are part of a larger game of musical chairs that includes France and Germany, as Europe’s four economic powerhouses negotiate how to secure their seats on the ECB’s executive board.

World.title: ‘I don’t know if it reassured or worried them’: European envoys quiz Le Pen over lunch
World.content:
The group of ambassadors from the eight countries that share a border with metropolitan France — Germany, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Monaco and Andorra — already met with conservative presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau in September. They are planning to host meetings with the other presidential hopefuls, including far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, at their respective embassies in the coming months.

“I don’t know if it reassured or worried them,” said an adviser to Marine Le Pen who accompanied her to the lunch. “What is sure is that they can now report back to their capitals what the National Rally wants to do,” the adviser added.

Le Pen was mainly questioned about her plans to downsize the EU and on bilateral issues, as well as U.S. President Donald Trump after his seismic defeat in the midterm elections.

While in the past, the National Rally has been supportive of Trump, the party has progressively distanced itself from the U.S. president. The National Rally’s Jordan Bardella on Wednesday said his party was not affected by the result and suggested that Trump’s popularity was undermined by the war in the Middle East and its economic consequences.



Le Pen has also been campaigning for a harsher approach on migration, which would involve stricter checks at the borders, potentially impacting countries whose envoys she met on Wednesday. All of them, apart from Andorra and Monaco, are part of the Schengen free-movement area.

“There is a general interest on what would her stance be on the key issues of mutual interest and cooperation on which we are working with France,” said one diplomat from a participating country.

“It was a very frank exchange. She told them what she says everywhere and she was able to elaborate on a number of topics a little more at length than she would do on TV,” the same adviser said, adding that Le Pen regularly meets ambassadors.

World.title: Trump offers UFC boss White House press secretary role: 'Dana, please take the job!'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he had offered Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White the position of White House press secretary.

 

"I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account, adding that White would be a press secretary "like none other."

"Dana, please take the job!" Trump said.

Speaking to reporters in London on Saturday evening, White did not go into detail but said he was flying to Washington "right now" and that he would meet with Trump on Monday.

"I'm sure we'll have more to talk about after that," he continued, noting that he already had "a lot of jobs."

White had earlier shared an image on his Instagram story showing him standing behind a White House press conference lectern with a caption reading: "On to the next chapter."

Trump and White have forged a close relationship over the years, with Trump a regular attendee at UFC events and White having spoken at a number of the president's rallies, including at an inauguration eve event in January 2025.

The search for a new press secretary comes after Katie Zacharia quit after less than five days in the job following an awkward first press briefing.

Her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, a favourite of the president, had announced in August that she was stepping down to focus on her family.

Trump has called Leavitt one of his "most trusted aides" and said she would continue to serve as an outside advisor.

"Karoline has been one of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office," Trump said in a social media post at the time.

World.title: Where would you go in a time machine? Physicist says time travel only goes forward
World.content:
A question many of us have posed in our minds is: where would you go if you had a time machine?

 

Would you crank the dial backwards like Marty McFly and risk sabotaging your own future? Before you start packing, a physicist has some news that may ruin a few Marvel movies: you may only be able to go one way, and it isn't backwards.

Hongsheng Zhang, a researcher at the University of Jinan in China, has shown that in a broad class of theoretical universes, travelling into your own past is impossible.

The whole argument rests on one fact. In relativity, the direction of light can never sit at right angles to an object’s direction through time.

Imagine spacetime sliced into layers that light itself can travel along. Anything moving slower or faster than light must cross these surfaces in the same direction, like climbing a staircase that never lets you step down.

If you can only ever go up, you can never arrive back on the step where you started.

The argument needs no exotic matter, no quantum effects and no assumptions about what fills the universe. "The whole content is bookkeeping about directions," Zhang told ScienceAlert.

The two loopholes

Physicists call journeys to the past "closed timelike curves": routes through spacetime that loop back to the very place and moment they began. Einstein's equations allow them in a handful of scenarios, such as near the core of a spinning black hole.

Crucially, Zhang's research - which is awaiting peer review - also reveals exactly how a time machine could achieve travelling back in time, and it claims there are only two ways.

The first is twist. Imagine light rays that, instead of travelling side by side, spiral around one another like the strands of a rope. When that happens, the neat surfaces of light can't form, so there is no one-dimensional staircase to keep you climbing.

This is what happens near the centre of a spinning black hole. Einstein’s theory says a spinning mass drags space and time around with it, an effect NASA’s Gravity Probe B satellite measured around Earth in 2011. Close to the black hole’s core the drag is so strong that moving “forward in time” is bent into a circle.

A traveller following that circle would see their clock ticking forward in time as normal, yet their journey would arrive back at the moment they set off. Physicist Brandon Carter showed in 1968 that such loops exist inside spinning black holes.

The second is the shape of the universe itself. The staircase might be perfectly built, but it could lead around the sides of a building, so the top step leads straight back to the bottom, like the impossible staircases in an Escher drawing. You would keep climbing and still end up where you began. Most of the time machines physicists have designed on paper, including those built from wormholes, rely on this trick.

The theorem has its limits, as Zhang acknowledges.

“What it does not do is tell us whether nature permits any of this. That remains open, and it is the question I would most like to see answered,” Zhang explained to ScienceAlert.

Destination: tomorrow

Trips to the future, by contrast, are already well established. Einstein showed that moving very fast, or sitting in strong gravity, slows your clock relative to everyone else's. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station return to Earth a few thousandths of a second younger than they would otherwise have been, according to the European Space Agency.

The work does not settle whether our own universe allows a journey to the past.

For now, though, anyone planning a trip may want to pack for tomorrow rather than yesterday... unless you have the Time Stone of course.

World.title: ‘We’re hardly producing any power’: Can Europe’s solar boom survive a cloudy winter?
World.content:
Europe risks entering its first ‘dunkelflaute’ of the year as cloudy weather dampens the continent’s solar boom and sends energy prices soaring.

 

Solar, which has been described as a “shining star” of the transition away from fossil fuels, is one of the quickest-to-install and cheapest forms of energy in the world. In the right conditions, it can cost as little as €0.024 to produce one unit of power via solar panels – far outperforming coal, gas and even wind.

It has already saved the EU €42.9 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the war on Iran, which broke out on 28 February. It also helped stabilise the grid in the summer when back-to-back heatwaves triggered a spike in cooling-related electricity consumption.

But Europe’s prolonged period of cool, cloudy and windless weather pose a serious problem.

Can solar power perform in winter?

A dunkelflaute – German for ‘dark lull’ – is a term used to describe an extended period when wind and solar power generation are low or non-existent because there is not enough wind or sunlight.

It typically occurs from October through February in Northern Europe, exacerbated by short daylight hours, heavy cloud cover and fog. This coincides with increased energy consumption across the continent, due to chilly temperatures triggering demand for heating.

Multi-day dunkelflauten are rare, but such an occurrence pushes Europe’s energy grid to rely more heavily on expensive backup generation such as natural gas.

According to Bloomberg forecasts, German day-ahead power prices for Thursday 29 October were above €300 a megawatt-hour, about double the average in October, with hourly rates hitting above €500 for the evening peak.

‘It’s extremely disheartening’: Home solar output dips

On an individual scale, households with solar panels are also noticing a spike in their energy bills. One UK resident who has 12 solar panels installed on their roof with a combined capacity of 6.36 kW tells Euronews Earth that on Wednesday (4 November) the panels only produced 10.90 kWh of solar – leaving them to rely on the grid for an additional 27.40 kWh of energy required.

On Thursday (5 November), when their city was overcast for the entire day, the home generated just 2.40 kWh of solar, and imported 20.60 kWh.

This is despite having an 11.52 kWh home storage battery that is charged at night on an off-peak tariff to discharge in the day when electricity consumption increases.

Cloud is expected over the weekend and well into next week, meaning many Brits will be generating significantly less solar than they have during the summer.

“We’re hardly producing any power,” the resident, who wishes to remain anonymous, tells Euronews Earth.

“It’s extremely disheartening to see we’re importing so much energy when we have spent thousands on a solar system. However, we know that the panels will start to perform better when the clouds clear.”

Hydro steps in for solar’s dips

Of course, it is no surprise that solar produces most of its electricity in the summer months. In the EU, solar’s share of electricity generation hit 25.4 per cent in June – but in October this dropped to just 13.2 per cent.

Of course, solar relies on daylight opposed to heat - meaning homeowners with rooftop panels will still produce power even on cold days.

According to green energy supplier Good Energy, home solar systems in the UK can still generate around 25-35 per cent of their annual output in winter, which it says "provides a nice cushion for winter bills".

A dip in solar production also tends to coincide with increased generation of hydropower – which started to rise in the EU last year from October.

Solar is also able to help offset some of the electricity spikes caused by heatwaves, following a sudden need for space cooling, such as air conditioning and fans.

Graph showing share of electricity generation from solar by month in 2025 and 2026. Ember

According to energy think tank Ember, during the late-June heatwave this summer, daily electricity demand rose by up to 28 per cent in Italy, 23 per cent in Hungary, 14 per cent in France and 13 per cent in Spain compared with pre-heatwave days.

It says that as heatwave-driven demand increased, solar was the only major power source to perform “better than usual”. Compared with other days in June and July, average daily solar generation during the heatwaves was 17 per cent higher in France and Hungary, five per cent higher in Spain and the same in Italy.

A typical UK home with rooftop solar generated enough electricity to power an A/C unit for five hours per day during the hot spell, a separate Ember analysis found.

At the same time, water-intensive forms of energy such as coal, hydropower and nuclear struggle during heatwaves – as scorching temperatures and lack of rainfall increase cause prolonged periods of drought.

In August, Poland was forced to reduce output on its coal-fired power plants, which require massive amounts of water for cooling, following critically low water levels in the Vistula River.

The move temporarily removed 1.3 GW from Poland’s power system, enough to power more than one million average households. This is around two per cent of the country’s current energy capacity.

World.title: Cheek kisses, shoes off and punctuality: European social etiquette rules travellers should know
World.content:
A kiss on the cheek, turning up early or leaving food on your plate... little gestures can mean very different things across Europe.

 

Now, new research has revealed the etiquette rules travellers should know before heading to Europe, from greeting strangers to getting dinner right.

Preply, an online language learning and tutoring marketplace, looked at public data sources and surveyed 1,600 people living in 27 countries about European etiquette, and the results challenged some assumptions we’ve all probably been guilty of making.

While it might seem like etiquette isn’t a huge deal, it’s actually an important thing to consider when travelling to a country, where you’ll want to be kind, understanding and respectful of the people you meet.

It seems as though more people are understanding the necessity of the practice – and the proof is in the data.

As of September 2026, the #etiquette hashtag had reached some 4.4 billion views on TikTok, while searches for “how to have good etiquette” have risen by a staggering 373% in the past year alone.

When travelling in Europe, though, etiquette can change as quickly as the borders do, so it’s wise to be aware in order not to put a foot wrong. Here’s what the findings showed.

How to greet someone appropriately

You might associate Europeans with cheek kissing as a greeting, but it’s actually far less common than you might expect.

In 23 of 27 countries, the majority of people surveyed would actually wait for the other person to initiate two cheek kisses.

Across Europe, that figure is 85% and in Denmark, Estonia, Sweden, and Slovenia, respondents said they would reject the gesture outright.

Shoes on or off?

While not every country is as strict as Sweden – which saw 100% of respondents say it’s a must – taking off your shoes is common practice across the continent.

In 24 out of the 27 countries, most people said they would take their shoes off when visiting someone’s home.

Many countries in the north of Europe said indoor shoe removal was a must, and it was just Spain, Italy, and Portugal that disagreed, saying they preferred to keep their shoes on inside the home. That’s possibly down to warmer climates, which means houses have fewer carpets to protect.

Interestingly, there was an age divide, too.

Most respondents aged between 18 and 34 said they always took their shoes off, while those aged 35 to 54 preferred to wait until asked by the host.

To bring a gift or not to bring a gift?

Everyone likes to receive a gift from a visitor, but some like it more than others.

More than half of the survey respondents considered bringing a gift to be standard practice, while a third said they reserve gift-giving for special occasions.

Only Finland saw the majority say they’d never bring a host a gift.

The study found that respondents from 17 out of the 27 countries said they’d likely bring a bottle of wine or a bouquet of flowers when visiting a friend, although nine of that number – including Austria, the UK and Spain – said they’d reserve the gesture for a special occasion.

Make sure to finish your food

While opinions differ on most etiquette topics across Europe, finishing food was considered respectful across all 27 countries.

Seen as a universal marker of respect for the host’s effort, 82% of men said they always finished meals, compared to 75% of women.

Some female respondents said they were more likely to deliberately leave a little left, possibly out of a sense of politeness.

Punctuality is a divisive issue

Online searches for the term “is it better to be on time, early or late?” were, according to Preply, up 66% globally over the past year, and the data reveals a somewhat complicated answer.

In 23 out of 27 countries, respondents favoured arriving on time, with Greece particularly keen on punctuality, while 35% of men said they prefer to arrive early, a higher figure than female respondents who aim to arrive on time.

Respondents in Czechia, Germany, Poland, and France said they preferred to arrive early at a destination.

The survey found that single people were twice as likely to arrive late, and those with children found it particularly hard to keep to a rigid schedule.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 8th, 2026 – Morning
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Poland: Footage shows people taking cover as a gunman opens fire in Krakow
World.content:
Terrified pedestrians fled through the streets of Kraków on Saturday as a gunman opened fire in the historic Main Market Square, killing six people and injuring 16 others.

 

Witness footage captures people running for safety as vehicles race past and shots ring out. Other images show shattered windows, overturned café chairs, ambulances and police cars rushing to the scene, with a helicopter circling overhead.

Police said the attacker, a 25-year-old Polish citizen, fired indiscriminately from a car before exchanging shots with officers nearby. He was wounded, arrested and taken to hospital.

The victims included four women and two men, one of them British. Two police officers were also injured, one critically.

The interior minister said the suspect held ultranationalist views, while the defence minister called the attack an act of terror. Investigators believe he acted alone.

World.title: Ukraine: Russian strikes hit Kyiv region, damaging infrastructure
World.content:
Footage released by Ukraine's emergency services shows crews directing powerful jets of water towards burning industrial structures, with firefighters working among the wreckage as flames spread through the site.

 

The attacks also damaged energy facilities and a major bridge in Kyiv. In the capital, a kindergarten was left severely damaged, with a large crater in its grounds, shattered walls and children's toys scattered among the rubble. Workers began clearing debris from the destroyed building, while nearby residents inspected the damage. Five people were reported wounded in the strikes.

The latest attacks come as Ukraine prepares for another difficult winter, with its energy infrastructure repeatedly targeted by Russian forces. Damage to power facilities threatens to disrupt electricity and heating supplies as temperatures fall, placing further pressure on an already strained network.

The renewed bombardment also comes amid diplomatic efforts to bring the war to an end, with talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States under discussion. Despite these initiatives, strikes on civilian areas and critical infrastructure continue, highlighting the challenges facing Ukrainians as the conflict enters another winter.

World.title: Liverpool FC targets counterfeit pro-Palestinian shirts using altered club crest
World.content:
The organisation "UK Lawyers for Israel" (UKLFI) had on 26 October 2026 alerted four Premier League clubs to possible trade mark infringements and reported on them in an online article. On 5 November the online portal "Jewish News" also carried a report.

 

Liverpool FC has confirmed that it is taking action against the sale of unauthorised football shirts featuring pro-Palestinian messages that display a modified version of the club crest. The club fears that fans could mistakenly take these shirts for official merchandise.

The Premier League club has therefore taken measures against online retailers who are using its protected trade marks without permission. The shirts are being sold via the website "From Palestine to the World".

Crests and sponsor logos deliberately altered

Fake jerseys for several English Premier League clubs with pro-Palestinian messages are being offered online. Club crests, lettering and sponsor logos have been altered to spread political messages. The shirts are not authorised by the clubs concerned.

Manchester United: The club crest has been combined with the slogan "Manchester with Gaza", and the centre shows a dove of peace carrying an olive branch. The club has passed the information on to its brand protection department.

Chelsea FC: The crest has been turned into "Palestine Club", and the word "Palestine" appears on the shirt in place of the usual sponsor logo. The club has referred the matter to the relevant internal department for review.

Manchester City: The official shirt sponsor EtihadAirways has been replaced by the wording "Palestine Airways". The club has confirmed receipt of the letter but has not yet announced any specific measures.

Liverpool FC: The iconic club crest has been modified and marked with the initials "P.L.C.", which stand for the Palestinian legislature (Palestine Legislative Council).

The club has already taken steps and reported the relevant sales offers to website operators and social networks over possible trade mark infringements. Further action is planned.

Legal background

The background to these moves is possible breaches of UK trade mark law (Trade Marks Act 1994). Using protected club crests and logos without permission can constitute a trade mark infringement. Political expression and support for Palestine are generally protected by law, but this does not create a right to use protected trade marks.

There is also a risk that fans may mistake the shirts for official merchandise and thereby attribute to the clubs a political stance they have not adopted.

World.title: As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?
World.content:
Droughts, floods and extreme heat are upping the pressure on delegates at the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey. Can countries move beyond pledges to concrete action?

With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet."

From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.

Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

And in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.

Can shipping adapt as Germany's busiest river runs dry? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

The global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.

Climate talks not enough to save

Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.

"There's no question that we could be doing more," said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

"It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff."

Climate 'clubs' banding together to enact change

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to come to an agreement, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.

"The Paris process is important. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs."

Small states push fossil fuel treaty amid Iran energy crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.

Spark new momentum on decarbonization

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims . One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.

EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.

Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark new momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels."

It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements including phaseout plans.

Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.

Climate financing 'far from what's needed'

Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

Island nations and coastal communities in places like Panama (above) are at risk of rising seas Image: Martin Bernetti/AFP
