World.title: Bulgarian Air Force escorted three civilian aircraft following bomb threats
World.content:
The Bulgarian Air Force scrambled MiG-29 fighter jets on November 5 to escort three passenger aircraft that had been the subject of bomb threats, the Defence Ministry said.

One of the civilian aircraft landed at Plovdiv and the other two at Vassil Levski Sofia Airport, the ministry said.

In cases of a such a nature, under command from the Nato Joint Air Operations Centre, the Bulgarian fighter jets on air policing duty, perform tasks of detecting, recognising and escorting aircraft, the statement said.

Bulgarian media reported that the aircraft that landed at Plovdiv was a flight from London. Three buses were sent to the scene to transport the passengers to Sofia.

The plane landed in a remote area of the airport for inspection. According to the plan for action in such situations, fire engines and ambulances were sent there.

The operator of all three flights for which they received threats is Ryanair.

After thorough checks, no explosive devices were found on board the aircraft, media reports said.

November 5 is the second consecutive day to see numerous bomb threats against civilian aircraft in European air space. Two of those on November 4 were against aircraft travelling to Sofia.

(Photo: Defence Ministry)

World.title: Croatian Promotional Video Starring John Malkovich Wins Award
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – The now famous Croatian promotional video starring the one and only John Malkovich has won a prestigious award.

The now globally known video “Croatia – I Hear It’s Beautiful” was awarded at the City Nation Place Awards in London. Croatian islands won gold and Dubrovnik also took home silver at the Wanderlust awards ceremony. 24sata reports some excellent news for Croatian tourism is coming from London, where the prestigious City Nation Place Awards ceremony was held, at which the promotional video “CROATIA – I hear it’s beautiful”, starring John Malkovich, won the main award in the Best communication strategy: tourism category.

This is another in a series of awards won by the promotional video of Croatian tourism, and this time it is an award given by City Nation Place (CNP), a global platform and professional organisation dedicated to the branding and marketing of cities, regions and countries.

“This year we’ve made a significant step forward in presenting Croatia on the international scene, and we are particularly proud of the new promotional film that presented the country from a different, fresh and authentic perspective, as well as the entire campaign ‘Croatia I hear it’s beautiful’. At a time when it seems that almost everything has already been seen and presented, it is important to continuously find new, innovative ways of communication and promotion, create different stories and highlight what makes Croatia special,” said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport.

Croatia’s popularity on a global level is also confirmed by the prestigious Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards, which are awarded by the respected British travel magazine Wanderlust on the basis of votes from its readers. Precisely the travel lovers and readers of this popular magazine declared Croatian islands the most desirable in the European regions category (gold award), while Dubrovnik was declared the second most desirable European city (silver award)

“We are extremely pleased with this international recognition, which confirm that Croatia has a strong and recognisable tourism story. It is particularly valuable that Croatian islands and Dubrovnik were recognised by the readers and travel lovers themselves. More than 250,000 Wanderlust readers took part in the voting and this year broke the record with as many as 8.2 million votes. The success of the promotional video of Croatian tourism shows that creative, authentic and contemporary communication can further strengthen the visibility of our country on international markets. Our goal is to present Croatia as a diverse and high-quality destination throughout the year, highlighting not only its best-known strengths but also the richness of local experiences, culture, local food and way of life,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board.

Gold for the Croatian islands confirms the allure of Croatia’s island diversity, preserved nature and authentic experiences, while the award for Dubrovnik additionally confirms its international recognisability and rich cultural-historical heritage. Let us add that among others the presentation of the Wanderlust awards was also graced by the presence of Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex.

World.title: First Leg Lengthening Procedure Carried Out in Croatia
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – The very first leg lengthening procedure carried out in Croatia has been performed at Zagreb’s Clinic for Traumatology.

A medical team from the Clinic for Traumatology in Zagreb has performed the first leg lengthening operation in Croatia using a new method that does not use an external fixator. Index reports that the procedure was carried out on a 28-year-old patient for whom a six-centimetre difference in leg length had been making movement difficult for years.

Kristina Sambolek (28) has had a shorter left leg since birth due to a hip deformity. She has spent her entire life in and out of hospitals, and numerous operations are behind her. Because of the difference in leg length she walks on her toes and wears shoes with soles of different thicknesses. “The first thing they did to me was literally tie my legs so they were hanging in the air and try that way to set the hips back into the socket,” Kristina described.

“The biggest problem was that on the left side I didn’t have a proper socket at all, nor a joint, so for years they tried to fix that with operations. I have the feeling that I spent more of my childhood in hospital than at home,” she recalled.

slovenia has been using this method for around a decade

Over time, she learned to endure the pain and accepted the limitations, but she never gave up hope of a better life. “I’ve been through operations and I know what awaits me, so I’ve come to terms with the fact that I have to go through this so that it will be easier for me. My wish is to be able to put on high heels and be like a real woman,” she said. The operation at the Traumatology Clinic is the result of international cooperation with colleagues from Slovenia. “This is one of the most favourable methods for lengthening long bones. It is much simpler for patients than external fixators,” said Prof. Dr. Sc. Matej Drobnič, specialist in orthopaedic surgery from Ljubljana. He added that in Slovenia this method has been used for about ten years and that five to six such procedures are performed annually without significant complications. The two-hour procedure in Zagreb is the first of its kind in Croatia.

“It’s a type of brand new technology where a nail is implanted into the bone. The leg then grows on its own, one millimetre a day. The patient will lengthen the leg herself with magnetic stimulation and we expect that in 50 days we will get the 50 millimetres we are planning,” explained Assist. Prof. Dr. Sc. Tomislav Čengić, head of the 3rd Department of Geriatric Traumatology and Hip Surgery at the Clinic for Traumatology.

The new method will enable patients with a difference in leg length to be treated in Croatia, without going abroad. “Three to five patients a year could certainly be found in Croatia for this type of operation. This procedure is significant for us, but also for the entire orthopaedic and traumatology profession in Croatia,” emphasised Assoc. Prof. Dr. Sc. Srećko Sabalić, head of the Clinic for Traumatology. Assist. Prof. Čengić emphasised that the success is the result of teamwork. “The entire clinic team took part in the procedure, from anaesthesiologists, scrub nurses, technicians to radiology engineers,” Čengić said. For the patient the operation means a step towards easier walking, and for Croatian orthopaedics the introduction of a modern treatment method.

The operation was performed by Assist. Prof. Tomislav Čengić, Prof. Matej Drobnič, Dr Danijel Jurković and Dr Fabijan Čukelj. Also in the team were anaesthesiologist Dr Ajša Muratović, scrub nurses Martina Stivičević, Tihana Krusha and Barbara Funtak, and radiology engineer Dubravko Kamenar.

World.title: Wanderlust Readers Crown Dubrovnik Second Most Desirable European City
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Wanderlust readers have once again crowned Dubrovnik as the second most desirable European city to visit.

The City of Dubrovnik has once again confirmed its position as one of the most desirable European tourist destinations by winning the Silver Award in the Most Desirable City in Europe category. Dubrovacki Dnevnik reports that the city took home the award at the prestigious Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards 2026, which was held on the 4th of November in London. This recognition continues a series of international successes for Dubrovnik, which in recent years has regularly ranked among the best European city destinations according to readers of the respected British travel magazine Wanderlust.

The awards ceremony was held in the impressive Painted Hall, located in the historic Old Royal Naval College complex in London’s Greenwich. The Silver Award was accepted on behalf of the Dubrovnik Tourist Board by its director Miro Drašković. In this year’s selection Dubrovnik competed against some of the best-known European city destinations, including Copenhagen, Madrid, Lisbon, Istanbul, Bordeaux, Genoa and Tbilisi. This success confirms Dubrovnik’s international recognisability, its rich cultural and historical heritage, unique architecture and exceptional tourist appeal.

Wanderlust is otherwise one of the oldest and most respected British travel magazines, which for more than three decades has been promoting authentic travel, the discovery of new destinations and responsible and sustainable tourism. Its annual Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards, which this year mark their 25th edition, rank among the significant recognition in the international tourism industry. Special value is given to the awards by the fact that the winners are decided by the readers and travel lovers themselves.

Croatian islands were declared the Most Desirable Region in Europe. This recognition for the Croatian National Tourist Board, together with the silver award for Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik Tourist Board, additionally confirms the strong position of Croatian destinations on the international tourism market.

Dubrovnik has in recent years been repeatedly awarded in Wanderlust’s selection, including winning the gold award in the Most Desirable European City category. At last year’s ceremony it also received a special recognition from Wanderlust editor-in-chief George Kipouros for outstanding achievements in sustainable tourism management. With that recognition Dubrovnik was highlighted as an example of responsible destination development, thanks to the City of Dubrovnik’s “Respect the City” project and measures for managing tourist flows, regulating cruise ship arrivals, and preserving cultural heritage and the quality of life of the local population.

The continuous recognitions from one of the most respected British travel magazines have special importance for Dubrovnik, especially given that the United Kingdom is one of its most important source tourism markets. They represent additional confirmation of Dubrovnik’s international recognisability as a destination that combines exceptional cultural and historical heritage, authentic experiences and a responsible approach to tourism development.

World.title: Croatia Records Strong Cruise Tourism Growth in 2026
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Croatia has recorded some particularly strong cruise tourism growth throughout 2026, with almost a million passengers arrived at Croatian ports on foreign cruise ships.

Over the first nine months of 2026, almost a million passengers arrived at Croatian ports on various foreign cruise ships. Dalmacija Danas reports that the aforementioned figure is as much as 11.7 percent more than in the same period last year. The latest data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics reveals that Dubrovnik and Split are among the most visited ports in the entire country, while the largest share of cruise voyages took place precisely in two Dalmatian counties.

According to data published by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) this week, in the period from January to September 2026, 80 foreign cruise ships entered Croatian seaports and completed a total of 677 cruise voyages. On those massive vessels, there were as many as 958,109 passengers, which is around 100 thousand more than in the same period of 2025, when 858,066 were recorded. The number of cruise voyages rose by 9.9 percent, and the number of passengers by 11.7 percent. At the same time the number of foreign ships decreased slightly, by 1.2 percent.

Foreign cruise ships spent a total of 1,557 days in Croatian territorial waters, which is an increase of 7.7 percent compared to last year.

dubrovnik and split lead the way

The most interesting data concern Dalmatian ports, which continue to play a key role in Croatian cruise tourism. Dubrovnik is by far the most visited Croatian port, with a total of 505 visits by foreign cruise ships in the first nine months of this year. In second place is Split with 284 visits, while third is Zadar with 191 visits. Among the seven most visited ports are also Korčula with 95 visits, Hvar with 89, Rovinj with 84 and Šibenik with 81 visits. This latest data shows exactly how important Dalmatia is for the arrivals of foreign cruise ships, with Dubrovnik and Split particularly standing out.

According to DZS data, of the total of 677 cruise voyages by foreign ships, the largest share was achieved in Dubrovnik-Neretva County – as much as 46.5 percent. Split-Dalmatia County follows with 25.1 percent. This means that in these two counties a total of 71.6 percent of all recorded cruise voyages by foreign ships in Croatia were realised. Further up north in Dalmatia, the expansive and particularly island-strewn Zadar County accounted for 12 percent, and then further up in Istria County the number stood at 7.5 percent, in Šibenik-Knin County 4.9 percent, and finally Primorje-Gorski Kotar County four percent.

the maltese flag reigns

In the first nine months of 2026, Croatian ports were visited by foreign cruise ships sailing under the flags of 15 countries. The most cruise voyages were made by ships under the Maltese flag – a total of 201, which accounts for 29.7 percent of all recorded voyages. They are followed by ships under the flags of the Bahamas with 174 voyages, Norway with 66 and Panama with 52 voyages. Interestingly, ships sailing under the Bahamian flag carried the largest number of passengers – 294,569 – while ships under the Maltese flag carried 265,838 passengers.

184,000 cruise passengers in september alone

In September this year alone, 132 cruise voyages by foreign ships were realised, carrying 184,523 passengers. Compared to September last year this is an increase in the number of voyages of 18.9 percent and in the number of passengers of 11 percent. The highest number of passengers recorded in one single month was recorded in July – 196,389 – while in August, 186,048 passengers were recorded. DZS data thus confirms the continued growth of cruise tourism in Croatia, with Dalmatian ports, led by Dubrovnik and Split, occupying the leading positions.

World.title: Tourism in Central Dalmatia Up in 2026 – Polish Visitors Top the Charts
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Tourism in Central Dalmatia has seen an increase in 2026, with Polish visitors in particular topping the charts as far as visitor numbers go.

“We’re now entering the final stretch of another tourist year, a period in which we’re summing up the results, but at the same time already directing our gaze towards what still awaits us. Although the tourist rhythm is gradually changing, Central Dalmatia continues to do well through all sorts of events and experiences that give people a reason to visit the area outside the main summer months.

The Advent period is on its way, which brings another new opportunity to present Dalmatian cities, places, islands, as well as the Dalmatian hinterland, their traditions, food scene and special festive atmosphere,” stated the director of the Tourist Board of Split-Dalmatia County Ivana Vladović.

18.6 million overnight stays in central dalmatia

Dalmatinski portal also reports that this year’s statistical data also confirms that the effort has well and truly paid off. In the first ten months of this year, Split-Dalmatia County, according to data from the eVisitor system, was visited by 3.9 million guests. They achieved 18.6 million overnight stays in commercial accommodation, which is 1% more arrivals and 0.5% more overnight stays than in the same period last year. The largest number of overnight stays was achieved by guests from all of Europe, including Poland, Germany, elsewhere across Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Great Britain and the Czech Republic.

“We’re now intensively preparing for 2027, which will be particularly significant for the county because it will carry the title of European Region of Gastronomy. This is fantastic recognition, but also an opportunity to present even more strongly the richness of our gastronomic heritage, local producers, traditional dishes and the people who preserve and pass on the culinary heritage of Central Dalmatia. We’re already working on new promotional campaigns, projects and activities with which we will bring this title closer to domestic and international guests and additionally connect the local food scene with our cultural identity, way of life and year-round tourist offer,” Vladović added.

dalmatia is still aiming to attract visitors throughout november

This November, this region of Dalmatia is also offering an entire series of interesting events that enable visitors to get to know its food, cultural and traditional heritage. In Omiš, the international gastronomic festival Grand Gourmet is being held, in Dugopolje the International Honey Fair Dalmatina, and Kaštela through the manifestation Zinfest – Fešta o’ Crljenka present the rich wine tradition and connection with one of the most famous world varieties.

Lovers of active holidays can participate in or follow the State Championship in rafting on the Cetina and the Hileja Marina Trail, while in Gornji Dolac at the end of the month the popular Christmas Village opens. The Split offer is additionally enriched by Štorije o’ spize, a manifestation dedicated to Dalmatian gastronomy, local producers and traditional flavours, and the Dalmatia Film Festival, which gathers lovers of domestic and international film production.

dalmatia beyond the summer season

Precisely the connection of different experiences and values of the region is one of the directions in which the Tourist Board intends to continue developing and presenting Central Dalmatia. Gastronomy, culture, natural heritage, active holidays, nautical tourism, islands and the Dalmatian hinterland form a diverse offer that goes beyond seasonal frameworks.

“In the period now just behind us, we continued to present Central Dalmatia on important international markets and business events, talk with partners and tourism professionals and monitor the changes that shape global tourist demand. Such meetings are important for strengthening how recognised we are, but also for the timely recognition of new opportunities. I believe that with joint work we will turn the title of European Region of Gastronomy into a strong opportunity for the promotion of Central Dalmatia, its people, tradition and quality offer,” director Vladović said, wishing all stakeholders in tourism a successful end of the year and a lot of creativity and enthusiasm in the preparation for the next tourist year.

World.title: As the European Union Prepares for Crisis, How Prepared is Croatia?
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – The European Union is currently preparing itself and its member states for crisis by encouraging the stocking of food and other supplies, but just how prepared is Croatia?

Just how ready is Croatia for more serious crisis situations, such as major power outages, supply disruptions, natural disasters or security threats? Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this specific question is opening up once again after the European Commission published guidelines in which it recommends that people prepare stocks of food, water, medicines and other basic necessities for at least 72 hours of crisis.

The emphasis is placed on three-day self-sufficiency of the general public. The European Commission recommends that households have basic stocks of food, water, medicines and other necessities ready and prepared, as well as a pre-packed bag or backpack with the most necessary things in case of emergency evacuation. In addition, the guidelines cover three more areas: education of children on how to act in crisis situations already from kindergarten age, with an approach adapted to their age, special protection measures for persons with disabilities, and clearer and much more timely information about possible dangers.

All of this is a continuation of the broader Union Preparedness Strategy, which the European Commission presented back in March 2025. The strategy covers 30 measures by which it seeks to strengthen the ability of the EU and its member states to respond to various crisis situations.

the government hasn’t bothered to show much interest in the eu’s recommendations

The new European recommendations have been intensively discussed in the media in recent days, yet the Croatian Government has so far not publicly presented the new guidelines nor explained whether and in what way it plans to implement them whatsoever in Croatia. Although the guidelines are not legally binding for the member states, the absence of official communication is somewhat surprising. The European Commission, namely, expressly states that it wants with them to encourage national authorities to develop their own preparedness measures, adapted to the circumstances and needs of individual countries.

It should be said that Croatia already has its own recommendations for acting in crisis situations. The Directorate of Civil Protection has published on its pages instructions for preparing a survival kit, which includes food, water, medicines, a battery torch, a radio receiver, documents and other necessary necessities. The existing Croatian instructions recommend stocks of food and water for at least two days.

An inquiry was therefore sent to the government in which an answer was requested specifically to the question of whether it plans to present the new European recommendations to the public. The second question was whether or not it plans to issue its own guidelines and, if it plans them, when their publication can be expected. The question of just how ready Croatia genuinely is for more serious crisis situations, what the current state of the shelters is, how many of them are functional and whether there are plans for their renovation was also posed. Information was also requested on the sufficiency of state strategic commodity reserves in the event of a longer-lasting crisis.

there are serious issues with croatia’s shelters

The state of Croatian shelters is called into question by the finding of the State Audit Office from 2024, which warned of numerous omissions in their management and maintenance. The audit established that of the 476 shelters managed by the 14 covered cities, 306 of them were not regularly used, and the cities did not undertake the necessary activities to put them into use. In seven cities only visual inspections of the shelters were carried out, without minutes on their correctness. The auditors also stated that the Directorate of Civil Protection did not have reliable and updated data on the condition and equipment of the shelters, and inspection supervisions did not cover the checking of the public shelters themselves.

City risk assessments did not cover threats such as wars and terrorist attacks. Due to the established deficiencies the State Audit Office issued a total of 158 orders and recommendations, and assessed the management of shelters in seven cities and the Directorate of Civil Protection as partially effective.

there are also massive problems with medicines…

According to the Government report for 2025, state commodity reserves were distributed at a total of 357 locations throughout Croatia. The total value of state commodity reserves at the end of last year amounted to 93 million euros, which is 6.87 percent more than the year earlier. Particularly worrying is the fact that Croatia at the end of 2025 in the strategic commodity reserves did not have recorded medicines, sanitary or consumable medical material, although their holding is provided for by regulations. Namely, the Act on Strategic Commodity Reserves from 2022 expressly includes among strategic products medicines, vaccines, antidotes and medical material, while the state balance determines the concrete products that need to be secured.

In total, it is a matter of 106 types of products for which it is expressly stated in the report itself that they need to be held in state reserves, but they are not in stock. Their procurement has been announced for years, but even at the end of 2025 that part of the strategic reserves was not filled. According to unofficial information from Jutarnji list, the Ministry of Health has for years not amended the regulations necessary for the procurement of medicines into state reserves. The Ministry of Economy confirmed that there are legal obstacles and that the situation has not changed even during 2026.

In the warehouses there were cereals, oil, sugar, cans, tents and other necessities, but certain hygiene products were missing, including soap, incontinence diapers and means for disinfecting water and space. According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Economy for 2025, the total filling of the planned balance of strategic commodity reserves amounted to only 51.39 percent. The filling of food reserves amounted to 72.4 percent, and of non-food 81.75 percent. This is the realisation of the state stock plan.

risks already faced by croatia

As we have already written, the European Commission warns of a series of threats, from geopolitical tensions and possible military conflicts to cyber attacks, sabotage of critical infrastructure, natural disasters and disruptions in supply. It is clear that such risks do not bypass Croatia either, especially when it comes to cyber attacks, possible supply disruptions and other disruptions that can spread across national borders. However, there are also dangers that the Croatian institutions themselves warn about. According to official data of the Directorate of Civil Protection, among the significant risks for Croatia are earthquakes, floods, open space fires, landslides, extreme temperatures, strong winds and epidemics. Croatia has in recent years already experienced the consequences of devastating earthquakes in Zagreb and in Banovina, large fires and floods.

Such natural disasters can cause longer-lasting interruptions in the supply of electricity and water, damage transport infrastructure and hinder the work of emergency services.

the great power outage of 2024 – a stark warning

How possible such disruptions are is also shown by the example of the 21st of June 2024, when due to a major failure in the electricity system across a lot of southeastern Europe, a large part of Dalmatia was left without electricity, as were large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Albania. The power outage caused problems in traffic, communications and the everyday functioning of people and almost all infrastructure.

According to the report of the Croatian Energy Regulatory Agency for 2024, the supply interruption in Croatia affected almost 200 thousand network users, and individual users were without electricity for almost four hours. The incident showed how quickly a disruption in interconnected electricity systems can spread across state borders. Therefore the question of preparedness is not related only to possible war and security threats, but also to the dangers that Croatia has already faced. The question remains how ready the civil protection system, shelters and state commodity reserves are today to respond to a new major crisis.

World.title: Dinamo Shock Premier League Sunderland With 2-0 Away Win
World.content:
Dinamo produced one of their best European results in years on Thursday night, beating Sunderland 2-0 in the fourth round of the Europa League league phase.

It was a dream debut for interim coach Jerko Leko, who took over only days earlier after Mario Kovačević was sacked. Luka Stojković opened the scoring in the 23rd minute and set up Dion Drena Beljo for the second in the 39th, before Dinamo held firm through a second half in which the Premier League side had a goal disallowed and hit the woodwork.

The win lifts Dinamo to seven points from four matches, level with Sunderland, and brings in €450,000 in UEFA prize money, the reward for every league-phase win in the Europa League. Combined with the earlier win over Anderlecht and the draw with Hapoel Be’er Sheva, Dinamo’s results in the league phase alone have now earned them more than €1 million, and their total European earnings this season stand at close to €16 million.

Lineups

Sunderland: Roefs; Meunier, Danso, Alderete, Methalie; Xhaka, Ahoka; Rigg, Angulo, Fofana; Isidor

Dinamo: Kotarski; Valinčić, Domínguez, Galešić, Goda; Stojković, Mišić, Kačavenda; Lisica, Beljo, Oršić

Dinamo started well. Josip Mišić pounced on a loose ball in the 2nd minute and shot over from 18 meters, while Wilson Isidor’s falling effort from the edge of the box three minutes later was a simple take for Dominik Kotarski. Oršić blazed a shot well over in the 9th minute.

Sunderland’s best early move came in the 11th minute, when Chris Rigg found space on the right and crossed for Jules Ahoka, whose header was gathered by Kotarski. Isidor then headed over from a Nilson Angulo cross in the 17th minute, and three minutes later a scramble from an Angulo free kick ended with Thomas Meunier’s shot blocked by Mišić.

Dinamo almost took the lead in the 22nd minute. Moris Valinčić crossed from the right, and Beljo controlled the ball in the box, but his close-range shot was blocked at the last moment. From the resulting corner, the breakthrough came. Oršić delivered from the right, Sunderland headed it out only as far as Stojković on the edge of the box, and the midfielder took it on his chest before firing a volley into the net for 1-0.

It should have been 2-0 a minute later. Stojković played in Oršić, who rounded goalkeeper Robin Roefs and shot towards an empty net, only for Meunier to clear off the line. Galešić was booked in the 25th minute, and Xhaka followed a minute later after a painful collision with Mišić in midfield that left both captains needing treatment.

Sunderland nearly equalized in the 30th minute. Meunier sent a curling ball from the right into the Dinamo box, and it evaded everyone in the crowd of bodies before striking the post. Kotarski saved an Isidor effort two minutes later, and Kevin Danso was booked in the 36th minute for stopping Valinčić.

Stojković went close again in the 38th minute, forcing Roefs into a save with a low shot from 18 meters. A minute later, Dinamo doubled their lead. Stojković intercepted a Danso pass and immediately slipped Beljo in behind the defense, and the striker lifted the ball over Roefs from five or six meters for 2-0.

Mišić needed treatment just before half-time after being stepped on, but returned after a minute on the sidelines. Three minutes were added, and Dinamo went in 2-0 up.

Sunderland coach Régis Le Bris made four changes at the break. Leko made one, with Stjepan Radeljić replacing Sergi Domínguez.

Kačavenda was booked within 20 seconds of the restart for a foul on Fofana, and after 70 seconds, Sunderland had the ball in the net. Isidor headed in from close range after a Xhaka free kick, but VAR ruled it out for offside.

Sunderland challenged the Dinamo box in the 55th minute: Mišić blocked a Malick Fofana shot, and Hume’s fierce follow-up struck Kačavenda in the head. Hume was booked a minute later for a heavy challenge on Kačavenda, and Isidor shot wide from a Fofana cross. Sunderland’s biggest chance came in the 58th minute. Kotarski saved from Reinildo from close range after a Xhaka set piece, and Danso’s rebound crashed off the crossbar.

Dinamo finally threatened on the counter in the 59th minute, when Valinčić found Mateo Lisica on the right, and his cut-back fell for Stojković, whose 20-meter shot went wide. A minute later, Kotarski saved a powerful effort from the edge of the box.

Brian Brobbey replaced Isidor in the 63th minute, while Ivanušec came on for the outstanding Stojković. Brobbey had his first chance in the 67th minute, when the ball dropped to him after Radeljić misjudged it, but he failed to connect cleanly and caught Kotarski, who needed treatment. Prevljak replaced Beljo in the 70th minute, and Brobbey headed wide from a Le Fée free kick.

Kotarski saved a long-range Xhaka effort in the 76th minute, Galešić produced an excellent block on Fofana two minutes later, and Brobbey’s penalty appeal after going down under a challenge from Radeljić in the 79th minute was waved away. Leko brought on Perez Vinlof and Hoxha for Goda and Oršić, and Sunderland’s attacks grew increasingly toothless. Four minutes of stoppage time passed without incident, and Dinamo held on for a famous 2-0 win.

World.title: Wanderlust: Croatian Islands Most Desirable Region in Europe
World.content:
November 6, 2026 – The season may be over, but the recognition keeps on coming. Croatian islands win big at the prestigious Wanderlist Reader Travel Awards.

Various studies cannot agree on how many there are exactly – some say 1185, others 1244, or even 1246 – but one thing is for sure – Croatian islands are gorgeous, a fact once more reinforced at the 2026 Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards in London earlier this week.

In the category Most Desirable Region (Europe), Croatian islands came away with the Gold Award, accompanied by this glowing tribute:

The rise of the Croatian Islands isn’t about riding a hot trend; it’s more a story of travellers simply discovering what’s there for themselves. With millions of visitors a year heading to Croatia’s Adriatic coast, those escaping its busier spots are realising how much more there is to see offshore. Beyond well-known Hvar, Brač and Korčula lie quiet, car-free communities such as Silba; incredible nature on Mljet, whose entire north-western end is a national park; pristine night skies on Lastovo, a candidate to become an official Dark Sky Park; and history aplenty in island-bound, UNESCO-listed Trogir. Even getting around invites reflection, with sailing trips from Vis aboard traditional sardine-fishing boats offering a recipe for slowing down.

Certain islands such as Hvar are no stranger to international recognition, having also been voted among the best islands in Europe in the 2026 Conde Nast Readers Traveler Awards, home to the first public theatre in all of Europe, and one where no island has more UNESCO heritage. But this was an award for all Croatia’s islands, 50 of which are inhabited, and which provide much of the country’s tourism draw.

While all the islands may look similar on the surface, there is an incredible diversity once you scratch the surface, which reveal some rather surprising facts, many of which I have summarised in this video below, 25 Things You Would Not Expect to FInd on a Croatian Island. These include the first place in the world to abolish slavery (Korcula), the birth of cricket in mainland Europe (Vis), and the birthplace of organise tourism in Europe (Hvar).

World.title: Demand for raw milk leading to supermarket shortages, farmers say
World.content:
Farmers have said there are no milk shortages in Estonia – despite gaps on supermarket shelves – but competition for raw milk has intensified as companies look for ways to make higher-value items, such as protein-rich products.

Earlier this week, ERR reported there were shortages of milk sold in plastic bags in some of Estonia's supermarkets.

Marta Palm, purchasing manager at Rimi Estonia, said around two weeks ago the producer of Rimi Smart milk told the supermarket there were supply difficulties.

"We have been in very close contact with the producer, and the producer has said that the transition to new feed had temporarily made raw milk production more difficult," she said.

One of the suppliers of milk in plastic bags, Maag Food, declined to comment on the issue to Saturday's "Aktuaalne kaamera" evening news show. But Lenno Link, head of dairy farming company Väätsa Agro, said changing feed generally does not affect production, which is usually "very stable".

Bagged milk in an Estonian supermarket. Photo is illustrative. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Raw milk production is actually increasing in Estonia by around 100 tons each year, as processors are competing for raw milk more than before.

"People are consuming more and more protein. This is largely also thanks to weight-loss drugs, and animal protein is being added everywhere, to various products. Whey protein powder, which is produced from raw milk, has become very scarce," Link said.

Prices on the European milk market have risen by around 10 percent in recent months. This gives dairy farmers hope of signing more favorable supply contracts with processors for next year.

The Estonian Chamber of Agriculture and Commerce said the tense period of contract negotiations may be one reason why supplies of milk in plastic bags have been disrupted in recent weeks.

"This competition means that raw material prices are rising, dairy processors have to pay more to obtain milk, and so they are looking for ways to process that milk into higher-value products to add more value to it. The question is rather whether milk in plastic bags can be sold in stores at a price that is also fair to producers," said Ants-Hannes Viira, head of agricultural policy at the chamber.

"Milk in plastic bags is certainly not going to disappear from the mainstream market anytime soon. I have been in the dairy industry for over 20 years, and there has been constant talk about milk in plastic bags disappearing, but today we still see that consumption of milk in plastic bags in Estonia is 100 tons per day," said Valio CEO Maido Solovjov.

According to Rimi's purchasing manager, Maag Food has promised to resume its deliveries of milk in plastic bags next week, and the retailer has pledged not to raise the product's price.

World.title: More migrants caught in Tallinn, 1 foreigner found dead in apartment
World.content:
A 21-year-old man from Pakistan was confirmed dead by police at an apartment in Tallinn on Saturday. Eight illegal migrants who said they had traveled from Latvia to Estonia were also found in the same location.

At around 4 p.m. on Saturday, foreign nationals staying in an apartment on Tehnika tänav called an ambulance for one of their companions. Paramedics who arrived at the scene confirmed the death of a 21-year-old man of Pakistani origin and informed the police. Officers responding to the scene found no external signs of violence on the body.

Inna Toater, operations manager at the North Prefecture, said there were eight other foreign nationals in the apartment, and checks revealed that they were staying in Estonia illegally.

"According to preliminary information, the men arrived in Estonia today from Latvia. According to the men themselves, they were involved in a traffic accident in Latvia last night, when the vehicle transporting them veered off the road. We are currently establishing how the men reached Estonia and under what circumstances one of them died," she said.

Toater said the health of the other foreign nationals in the apartment was also checked.

"Three men were taken to hospital for further medical examinations, while the remaining five were taken to a detention center," she explained.

The body of the 21-year-old man was sent for an autopsy to determine the cause of death. Police are continuing to investigate the exact circumstances of the incident.

According to preliminary information, the eight foreign nationals are from Afghanistan, Morocco and Ethiopia.

Thousands of migrants have crossed the Belarusian-Latvian border into the European Union without the correct documentation this year in what officials say is a "hybrid attack" orchestrated by the regime in Minsk.

The migrants, mostly from Africa and the Middle East, then travel on to other countries in western or northern Europe, using Estonia as a transit country. However, more than 400 people have been caught in Estonia this year after Poland and Germany boosted security checks on their borders, and smugglers changed their routes.

When apprehended, the migrants are usually returned to Latvia under EU rules.

World.title: Mystery orange 'fireball' over Estonia turns out to be aircraft contrails
World.content:
A bright orange object that appeared to fall towards the ground was reported over both in Tallinn and Lääne County on Thursday afternoon, Maaleht said .

However, Taavi Niittee of the Tõrva Astronomy Club said the photographs taken most likely captured planes, or rather their condensation trails lit by low-angle sunlight.

The effect occurs when a contrail left by a high-flying aircraft is lit by the sun low on the horizon, as it is at this time of year, turning a bright orange or red hue ahead of sunset and resembling a burning object.

Contrails consist of small ice crystals formed from water vapor in aircraft exhaust and can persist in the sky for some time depending on weather conditions.

If the aircraft is moving at certain angles relative to the observer, the glowing trail can look as though it is "falling" from the sky.

Niittee said there is nothing unusual about the sighting, describing it as relatively common on clear evenings at this time of year.

A meteor, by contrast, appears when a small body from space enters the atmosphere at high speed and begins to glow, typically lasting only a few seconds.

A contrail can remain visible for several minutes or longer, making this the simplest way to tell the two apart.

Niittee advised anyone seeing something similar to check air traffic, for example the Flightradar24 site, where you can see flights in real time, as well as all flights in the preceding 24 hours.

World.title: Rally car, sword fight and football: President Ülle Madise's Father's Day
World.content:
President Ülle Madise gets into a rally car, plays football with fathers and sons, joins a band rehearsal and takes part in a historical sword fight in a Father's Day show airing Sunday.

The broadcast is called "Isadepäev Vabariigi Presidendiga Mulgimaal" ("Father's Day with the President in Mulgimaa") and follows the president through the villages of Raasilla, Holstre and Mustla, where different generations work together and traditions pass from fathers to children.

Mulgimaa is a distinct historical region of South Estonia, primarily covering present-day Viljandi County and parts of Valga County. Its small villages, the show highlights, have an active community life in which generations take part in shared activities.

The show sees the head of state embark on a forest hike alongside the rally track and the other activities, taking part rather than simply observing.

It will close with a presidential address to fathers across Estonia. The show was pre-recorded, and highlights can be seen in the gallery above.

"Isadepäev Vabariigi Presidendiga Mulgimaal" airs on ETV at 8.30 p.m. on Father's Day, Sunday, November 8, with sign language interpretation on ETV2 and in Russian on ETV+.

World.title: Gallery: PÖFF presents lifetime awards on opening night
World.content:
The 30th Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) opened at Alexela Concert Hall in Tallinn Friday, with lifetime achievement awards given out to three people.

Animator Priit Pärn, composer Sven Grünberg, both from Estonia, plus Icelandic director Hilmar Oddsson were the recipients.

Oddsson, 69, is one of the film-makers who helped put Icelandic cinema on the world map in the 1980s. His most recent film, "Á Ferð með Mömmu" ("Driving Mum"), which involved Estonian film-makers, won PÖFF's grand prix in 2022. Awarding him is also a nod to the Nordic auteurs the festival began with in 1997 — Oddsson was one of them, and his film "Tár úr steini" ("Tears of Stone"), which brought him to Tallinn 29 years ago, screens again in the anniversary program "PÖFF tähistab" ("PÖFF celebrates").

Grünberg, who turns 70 shortly, was honored for his contribution to Estonian film music. He has scored nearly 130 Estonian and foreign films, seen by tens if not hundreds of millions of people. His credits include "Hukkunud Alpinisti hotell", "Leiutajateküla Lotte", and "Naksitrallid"," and the series "Wikmani poisid".

Pärn, who recently turned 80, was honored for his contribution to Estonian animation and is Estonia's most internationally known film-maker. This is his 13th lifetime achievement award. His 1987 film "Eine murul" remains one of the deepest portraits of the oppressive Soviet everyday, and his own teaching system has produced a generation of animators in Finland, Estonia and beyond.

The 30h annual PÖFF festival got underway on Friday and runs until Sunday, November 22, with 230 feature films and 259 shorts from 87 countries being screened during that time.

World.title: Parties still compiling candidate lists ahead of March Riigikogu elections
World.content:
Parties are still recruiting Riigikogu candidates with some list places unfilled. The coalition Reform Party will not announce its lead candidates until late on this month.

The opposition Center Party has yet to decide which electoral district party chairman and former Tallinn mayor Mihhail Kõlvart will head up.

The Riigikogu elections take place in March and final candidate lists are due by mid-January, meaning parties are deep into the process of deciding who to run where, to optimize results.

Due to the d'Hondt proportional representation system used in Estonia, parties usually place their vote magnet candidates, usually leading politicians, high up on their ordered lists – excess votes these candidates have after clinching a seat can be distributed to candidates lower down on the list, who may not win a seat in their own right.

Kõlvart is one such vote magnet, and Center's Secretary General Anneli Ott told "Aktuaalne kaamera": "The party chairman would be a major vote-winner in any constituency. But which constituency he will head the list in remains undecided."

The party's two MEPs Jana Toom and Jaak Madison, will head electoral lists, Center, whose traditional bedrock areas include Tallinn and Ida-Viru County, confirmed.

Center Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

The Social Democrats (SDE) have made more apparent progress. The party leader, Lauri Läänemets, will run in Järva and Viljandi, while new member, former foreign ministry secregary general and prime ministerial candidate Jonatan Vseviov, is to run in Harju and Rapla. "The regional branches have not yet made their final decisions on the order of candidates or who will ultimately stand," said SDE Secretary General Piret Hartmann

The Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) has finalized leading candidates in half its constituencies, with chairman Martin Helme running in Tallinn's Mustamäe and Nõmme. Helme said the party faces difficulty winning votes in the bigger cities, meaning great efforts must be focused there. "A third of the Riigikogu is elected from Tallinn. So naturally, we are focusing on Tallinn," Helme said. EKRE's traditional stronghold has been southwestern Estonia.

Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu is to run in Harju and Rapla, just south of Tallinn and including the capital's commuter belt, with MEPs Jüri Ratas, a former prime minister, and Riho Terras also standing. Secretary General Andres Metsoja said regional branch proposals matter most when making decisions.

Looking for its first ever Riigikogu seats is Parempoolsed, whose chairwoman Lavly Perling is prepared to run in Harju and Rapla, though the party has not completed all its leads and has even turned some aspirants away. Deputy chairman Siim Kiisler said ideological conviction matters to the party more than profile.

Eesti 200, who in summer saw two MPs defect, is still compiling its full list.

Several of the parties have been hit by a wave of departures of high profile candidates who are not running this time around. SDE has lost Raimond Kaljulaid, a prominent MP who sits on the Riigikogu's national defense committee but is returning to the private sector, as well as MEP Marina Kaljurand. Former education minister Liina Kersna (Reform) is not seeking re-election and neither is Hanno Pevkur, defense minister until September and once a challenger for Reform's leadership. Parempoolsed has lost defense and security expert Rainer Saks, who cannot run due to taking up a post as presidential adviser.

High profile candidates may run for a party even if they cannot then take up the seat won, usually because they hold another post which bars that. MEPs and local government leaders fall into that category for instance. Their votes won will be transferred to candidates lower down the party's ordered list.

Polling day is March 7, 2027.

World.title: Priit Reiska: A rare opportunity to increase the number of people with higher education
World.content:
Universities need certainty that funding will be available for the entire duration of a student's studies. A decision on admissions for one year creates a commitment lasting several years to the young people who enroll, writes Priit Reiska.

The 2027 state budget, which has reached its second reading in parliament, will also shape the educational opportunities available to young people who are currently completing secondary education. Will universities have enough places for a larger generation of school graduates, and can the quality of education be maintained while teaching more students?

Parliament has already expressed its position. In its statement "In Support of Higher Education," lawmakers called on the government to ensure that, beginning with admissions in 2027, at least 1,000 additional tuition-free study places are provided annually over several years in fields important to Estonia's development leap. That statement must now be reflected in the state budget.

"Educating the current large generation of young people carries particular importance."

While about 10,100 young people completed secondary education in 2024, forecasts by the Ministry of Education and Research indicate that the number of graduates will reach 12,500 by 2028. This gives Estonia an opportunity to increase the number of people with higher education, but it requires that opportunities to continue studies grow alongside the number of graduates.

Educating the current large generation of young people carries particular importance. If this opportunity is missed, it will become much more difficult to increase the number of highly educated people later because of declining birth rates. Missing out on higher education can limit a young person's opportunities and leave part of their potential unused for the benefit of society.

Education and Research Minister Kristina Kallas has also warned that insufficient study opportunities could increase the number of young people entering the labor market without professional qualifications and slow the competitiveness of the Estonian economy.

University of Tartu Rector Toomas Asser has emphasized that Estonia's move toward a more knowledge-intensive economy depends on how many people possess the necessary expertise. Training the next generation of top specialists requires a strong higher education pathway that begins with sufficient admissions to bachelor's programs.

I have written previously that the scale of higher education and choices of study fields cannot be determined solely by current labor market needs. It is already difficult to predict workforce needs five or 10 years into the future, and the rapid development of artificial intelligence is increasing uncertainty even further, as developments in recent months and weeks have demonstrated.

In such circumstances, the strength of academic university education lies in broad-based knowledge, critical thinking, independent learning skills, and the ability to create new solutions. Highly educated people also create new jobs and help society adapt to change.

New study places require real additional funding

During spring negotiations over administrative agreements, both the ministry and the universities estimated that creating additional study places would require a total of €146 million over the next four years. Of that amount, €19.7 million is needed in 2027, including €13.3 million for first-cycle higher education places.

The increase in higher education funding planned in the draft state budget amounts to only €3.67 million. Compared with the funding needed for first-cycle study places alone, that is nearly €10 million less. The shortfall is intended to be covered by redistributing the existing operating support of universities and professional higher education institutions. As a result, creating new study places would require reducing funding for existing education.

"Efficiency should also be measured by whether students can successfully complete their studies and graduate."

For young people, this creates a real risk that new study places will be established at the expense of current students' learning conditions. If more students must be taught with the same amount of money, the result may be larger study groups, fewer elective courses, and fewer opportunities for individual guidance and meaningful feedback from lecturers. Besides the number of places, it is important to ask what kind of education students enrolled in those places will actually receive.

This is not the first time agreements on higher education funding and actual budget decisions have diverged. In 2023, universities and parliamentary parties agreed that years of funding shortfalls should be corrected over four years and that a sustainable funding model should be developed.

Since then, the planned increase in operating support has repeatedly been reduced. According to the Council of Rectors, operating support for higher education in the 2027 budget falls nearly €50 million short of the level previously agreed upon.

At the same time, universities have increased admissions, improved on-time graduation rates, and developed new forms of study. The administrative agreements signed this spring also included a commitment to educate more young people.

Universities must, of course, organize their activities efficiently and seek ways to teach better with existing resources. Efficiency should also be measured by whether students can successfully complete their studies and graduate. Expanding admissions will not achieve its goal if lecturers have less time to support students and the risk of dropping out increases.

For this reason, universities need certainty that funding will be available for the entire duration of a student's studies if admissions are to be increased. A decision on admissions for one year creates a commitment lasting several years to the young people who enroll.

Parliament can still change the situation

On October 14 of this year, parliament adopted the statement "In Support of Higher Education" with 65 votes in favor. In addition to creating extra tuition-free study places, the statement calls for continued increases in funding for Estonian-language higher education, competitive pay for academic staff, and improvements in educational quality. Parliament has therefore expressed a clear position that educating more young people and ensuring the quality of higher education must go hand in hand.

"Such an opportunity will not come again for decades. Let us make use of it."

Parliament now has an opportunity during the budget process to translate that position into funding decisions. The Council of Rectors' request is that an additional €19.7 million be added to existing higher education funding in 2027 to create new study places. Redistributing existing operating support will not meet that need.

This amount will not solve all the funding problems in higher education, but it would make it possible to increase admissions without reducing funding for existing education. For today's school students, it would provide more opportunities to continue their studies and confidence that a study place also means a high-quality education.

Parliament has supported the creation of additional study places. The 2027 state budget should therefore include real additional funding to create them.

We currently have an opportunity to provide higher education to a larger generation of young people than before. Such an opportunity will not come again for decades. Let us make use of it.

World.title: 400 Estonian students in Russia face recruitment risk, warns KAPO
World.content:
Despite official warnings, nearly 400 young people from Estonia study in Russia, where they risk being recruited by intelligence services or sent to the front, Postimees reported .

The Russian Embassy in Estonia actively promotes Russian higher education on its website, offering scholarships regardless of academic performance and free language courses to help students enrol.

Neither the Estonian Ministry of Education and Research nor the education information system has data on how many Estonians study in Russia, though UNESCO statistics put the figure at 384 in 2023, the year after the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began.

Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said going to Russia to study is "one of the strangest and most incomprehensible reasons for traveling there," warning that Estonia's ability to provide consular and other assistance to any of its citizens who found themselves in danger would be extremely limited.

Taro said a foreign national could be taken hostage for instance to exchange for captured Russian intelligence operatives, or placed in a situation where signing a contract with the Russian defense ministry ended up the only way out for them — followed by being immediately dispatched to the frontline in Ukraine.

The Internal Security Service (KAPO) says Estonian residents traveling to Russia attract the attention of Russian intelligence, may be detained, and face unpredictable application of Russian law.

KAPO bureau chief Marta Tuul said those interested in studying in Russia are primarily from Russian-speaking backgrounds, and that Russian universities host intelligence officers working under cover who identify and recruit students.

Tuul said recruits may not be activated immediately, with intelligence services waiting until they reach positions useful to them, and that the fate of African students who have been sent to the front cannot be ruled out for Estonians either.

In August, Postimees reported that Nikita Kuzmin, born in Estonia, enrolled at a university in St Petersburg, was recruited by the GRU, given the choice of cooperation or the front, and gathered information on military and civilian sites in Narva before being caught and sentenced to four years.

Prosecutor Margaret Beres said Kuzmin had no accomplices in Estonia and was caught early on, so no significant damage was caused to Estonia's security.

World.title: Iran executes three men linked to anti-government protests
World.content:
TEHRAN: Iranian authorities executed three men on Sunday after convicting them of carrying out operations on behalf of Israel and the United States during anti-government protests in January, the judiciary said.

The death sentences against Hassan Divband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh “were carried out this morning after being upheld by the Supreme Court,” the judiciary’s Mizan Online website reported.

It said they were found guilty of “participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups” during the protests.

Mizan said the men threw Molotov cocktails and grenades, used bladed weapons and firearms and set fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran.

Other defendants in the case received sentences ranging from five to 10 years in prison, it said.

The protest movement initially sparked in December by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, attributing the violence to “terrorist acts” orchestrated by the US and Israel.

Foreign-based NGOs, however, have cited higher figures and maintain that Iranian security forces fired on protesters.

The number of executions in Iran has risen since the start of the Middle East war, which was triggered in late February by US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic.

World.title: Saudi defenses intercept Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh, southern regions
World.content:
RIYADH: Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed cruise and ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Houthi militia toward Riyadh and the southern regions, the coalition said on Sunday.

Two cruise missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the Riyadh and southern regions, while two ballistic missiles targeting the capital were also destroyed, coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki said, the latest in a series of aerial threats targeting several Saudi regions since the beginning of November.
