World.title: Dutchman and Spaniard in two-horse race for ECB presidency
World.content:
The choice for European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde’s successor probably comes down to Dutchman Klaas Knot and Spaniard Pablo Hernandez de Cos.

The Netherlands and Spain each nominated their former central-bank chiefs to replace Lagarde when she departs in February, Kyriakos Pierrakakis, who heads the group of euro-area finance ministers, said Friday in a statement. De Cos currently leads the Bank for International Settlements.

“At its next meeting on 9 November, the Eurogroup will take stock of these candidacies,” the group said.

World.title: JCG-discovered “Godzilla” seafloor formation wins heritage status
World.content:
The Japan Coast Guard said that the “Godzilla Megamullion,” a massive seafloor formation discovered during its 2001 continental shelf survey, has been selected for the International Union of Geological Sciences’ list of 100 Geological Heritage Sites.

The JCG announced the designation of the megamullion, located southeast of the remote Tokyo-administered Pacific island of Okinotorishima, on Friday.

A megamullion is a dome-shaped seafloor structure formed when mantle rocks are exposed on the ocean floor through fault activity associated with seafloor spreading.

Located on the Philippine Sea plate, the Godzilla Megamullion measures about 125 kilometers in length and 55 kilometers in width, making it roughly 10 times larger than a typical megamullion. It is believed to be the largest such formation ever discovered.

An overview of the underwater geological formation known as “Godzilla Megamullion” | JAPAN COAST GUARD / VIA JIJI

The megamullion was named after the giant monster Godzilla because of its enormous size and was registered internationally under that name in 2021.

Studies of the Godzilla Megamullion conducted by an international team led by Japanese scientists have produced important findings on mantle structure and the processes involved in plate formation. The site was recognized as a globally significant geological reference point for scientific research, according to the JCG.

This marks the third round of selections for the IUGS geological heritage list. Other Japanese sites previously chosen include the Nojima Fault in Hyogo Prefecture, which triggered the 1995 Great Hanshin Earthquake.

World.title: Azerbaijan welcoming ‘set-jetting’ fans of Japan TV drama ‘Vivant’
World.content:
Some fans of popular Japanese television drama “Vivant” have been flocking to Azerbaijan, hoping to see with their own eyes where the second season of the hit series was filmed.

Hugging the western shore of the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan will likely continue welcoming more Japanese visitors, including growing numbers of “set-jetters,” or people who travel to locations where famous movies and TV shows are filmed. One travel agency has said that package tour sales to the country have been strong.

Among the set-jetters who visited Azerbaijan in late October was Mayumi Kishi, 47, from Tokyo. Standing before the ruins of a bathhouse at the Palace of the Shirvanshahs in the country’s capital of Baku, which appeared in the drama as Jerusalem, Kishi said: “This is it. The character came out from this spot.”

Squealing with delight, she took photos on her smartphone.

Kishi had already planned to visit Azerbaijan even before learning about where the drama series was filmed. After a suggestion by her travel companion, she decided to stop by and pay a visit to one of the places that served as the drama’s filming locations. She said that she watched the drama before the trip to familiarize herself with the filming locations.

“I hope that people who have watched Vivant will visit” the country, she said.

Bukinist, a bookstore in Baku, appeared in the drama as a base for “Beppan,” a purported secret intelligence unit within Japan’s Self-Defense Forces that is at the center of the drama series.

Japanese visitors have become a daily sight at the store crammed full of books. Saying that such visitors walk around the store taking photos and videos, the store manager in his 50s added that the drama has helped create a warm bond between the two nations.

Japanese travel agencies have begun offering set-jetting tours.

In cooperation with Tokyo Broadcasting System Television Inc., which produced the TV drama, Hankyu Travel International launched a travel package to coincide with the airing of the latest season. Some departures between late November this year and October next year already have waiting lists.

“Sales have been strong, thanks to the impact of the TV drama,” an official of Hankyu Travel said, adding that the company is thinking of opening up more booking slots.

The Azerbaijani side has welcomed the rising interest generated by the drama.

Speaking in a recent interview, Rashad Azizov, director-general of Azerbaijan’s Cinema Agency, said that the Japanese drama is making “history” by providing an “opening moment” to create a “bridge” between the two nations.

He expressed hopes for more Japanese tourists to visit his country to enjoy its historic sites, architecture and cuisine.

World.title: Eurovision brings pop and politics to Asia
World.content:
Boasting K-pop and Bangladeshi beatboxing, Eurovision stages its first Asia edition this Saturday, bringing the European song contest’s unique brand of kitsch and geopolitics to the world’s most populous region.

World.title: Magnitude 5.7 quake injures dozens in central Japan
World.content:
A strong 5.7-magnitude earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, injuring dozens of people, shattering windows and disrupting train services, officials and local media said.

The quake struck at 1:04 am in Shizuoka Prefecture, the Japan Meteorological Agency said. No tsunami warning was issued.

Authorities reported no deaths, but the quake shattered storefront windows and knocked items off shelves and caused transport disruption in parts of the country.

An emergency official in Aichi said authorities had received 16 reports of mostly minor injuries.

Authorities in neighboring Shizuoka said at least three women sought emergency medical care, including a woman in her nineties who injured her shoulder after falling from her bed during the shaking.

The local Chunichi Shimbun newspaper and Tokai Television separately reported at least 24 were hurt across the two regions.

In Toyohashi city in the Aichi region, windows of a car dealership were found shattered after the quake.

A large book store in Toyota city, also in Aichi, reported that its merchandise dropping from shelves.

The quake also forced temporary delays and suspensions of regional train services Sunday morning, including the Shinkansen bullet trains.

The quake was felt as far west as Osaka, where a foreign resident was taken to hospital after falling from a second-floor apartment when the shaking startled them, local media reported.

Officials in Osaka couldn’t be reached for immediate comment.

Separately, a 4.3-magnitude quake struck the Kumamoto region at 10:53 am (0153 GMT) Sunday, the Meteorogolical Agency said.

There were no immediate reports of serious damage or injuries from the second quake.

The southwestern region is still trying to recover from a 7.1-magnitude tremor that killed 38 people, flattened homes and left tens of thousands without power in July.

Japan sits on the Pacific “Ring of Fire” and experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year.

The country is haunted by the massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.

World.title: SoftBank and ABB consider China carve-out to salvage robotics deal
World.content:
SoftBank Group and ABB are looking at carving out the Chinese part of a giant robotics deal as they explore ways to salvage a transaction blocked by Beijing, according to people familiar with the matter.

The two companies and their advisers are trying to find a solution after China’s powerful Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review on Thursday halted SoftBank’s move to acquire the ABB unit valued at $5.4 billion.

They are studying how the Chinese business, which is ABB Robotics’ largest single market, could be separated out, the people said. SoftBank is leading the push, people added, asking not to be identified as the talks were private.

World.title: Japan holds nuclear disaster drill simulating Tomari plant accident
World.content:
The government on Saturday conducted a comprehensive nuclear emergency drill simulating a severe accident at Hokkaido Electric Power’s Tomari nuclear plant in Japan’s northernmost prefecture.

The three-day drill, which runs through Sunday, involves the Hokkaido prefectural government, relevant municipalities and the Cabinet Office. The drill includes exercises conducted at the Tomari plant for the first time in 10 years. About 8,500 local residents are expected to take part.

The drill is based on a scenario in which an earthquake off the western coast of Hokkaido causes equipment failure at the plant’s No. 3 reactor, rendering its cooling system inoperable.

On the second day of the exercise, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi declared a nuclear emergency. While some participants transported people assumed to have been exposed to radiation, others held a countermeasures meeting through a video conferencing system.

In 2025, the Nuclear Regulation Authority concluded that the No. 3 reactor at the Tomari plant met the country’s new safety standards, a prerequisite for its restart.

The authority is still reviewing a construction plan covering the detailed design of the reactor’s facilities, and the timing of the reactor’s restart remains uncertain.

In a lawsuit filed by local residents seeking a halt to the Tomari plant’s operation, Sapporo District Court partially granted the plaintiffs’ request and issued an injunction in 2022. Sapporo High Court is scheduled to hand down its appellate ruling in January next year.

World.title: Astellas employee to be released from China prison in December
World.content:
A Japanese employee of Astellas Pharma, who was sentenced to three years and six months in prison for espionage in China, is expected to be released in mid-December and return to Japan, sources said Saturday.

According to sources, final arrangements are being made to release the employee of the Japanese pharmaceutical company in his 60s on Dec. 14.

The employee was suddenly detained by Chinese authorities in March 2023, when he was about to leave China after the end of his Beijing assignment. He was indicted in August 2024.

World.title: Demerit system for contractors ‘not ruled out’, Hong Kong development chief says
World.content:
The Hong Kong government has not ruled out the possibility of introducing a demerit system for contractors, according to the development chief, after an independent inquiry into last year’s deadly Tai Po fire identified unscrupulous consultants and building professionals as the main culprits of the tragedy.

Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said in a television interview on Sunday that authorities were also considering introducing new conditions for homeowners who applied for the government’s building maintenance subsidy scheme, including a long-term plan and fund for property maintenance.

“I do not rule out the possibility of introducing a demerit points system in the next stage if we can formalise the mechanism further. However, we have not considered it at this stage,” Linn said.

World.title: Hong Kong must build ‘reassuring’ environment amid political criticism: Paul Lam

Hong Kong must focus on the “practical work” of building a safe and convenient environment and reassuring the international community amid criticism of its legal system, the justice minister has said, after 10 countries issued a joint statement decrying the latest jail sentence handed to opposition activist Joshua Wong Chi-fung.

“It is inevitable that their criticism will continue … Political realities have to be dealt with, but I do not think we should allow them to distract us from our focus,” Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok told a radio programme on Sunday.

“We must get practical work done, because concrete results are what will attract people to Hong Kong, to support us through action.”

Hong Kong’s former director of health Margaret Chan Fung Fu-chun made history yesterday (November 8, 2006) when she was nominated World Health Organisation director-general in a resounding victory that saw her lead all the way in four rounds of voting.

World.title: Hong Kong must show real remorse for the Tai Po fire tragedy
World.content:
When Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu and seven principal officials bowed deeply before the cameras on October 29, Hong Kong witnessed something rare: a collective government apology.

It came 11 months after the Wang Fuk Court fire claimed 168 lives and uprooted 1,984 households. A minister has resigned . Many reforms have been promised. Yet public reaction remains divided. That division reveals what people expect an apology to achieve, and how differently they understand political responsibility.

A political apology should acknowledge failure, accept responsibility and express remorse. It should also commit the government to preventing a recurrence. The purpose of a political apology is to bring closure. While the chief executive would like closure, he cannot yet declare that it has been achieved.

World.title: Tarmo Peltokoski begins HK Phil tenure with Mahler’s monumental Symphony No 8
World.content:
Gustav Mahler’s rarely performed Symphony No 8, a work requiring such a large orchestra and choir it is known as “Symphony of a Thousand”, finally received its Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra premiere on Saturday, heralding an ambitious new chapter as the 26-year-old Finnish conductor Tarmo Peltokoski officially took the podium as music director.

The 5pm performance at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre involved nearly 600 musicians and singers from six choirs: the Hong Kong Philharmonic Chorus; the Learners Chorus; the London Philharmonic Choir; St Paul’s Co-educational College Senior Mixed-Voice Choir; Ying Wa College Choir; and the Hong Kong Children’s Choir.

The monumental 85-minute piece, with performers pushing the stage to the limit and the choir occupying about a third of the seats on the balcony, formalised the start of the youthful maestro’s four-year contract as the ensemble’s ninth music director.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.content:
As it expands its weather-warning systems across the Global South, China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU — an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration — to Sri Lanka, one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

The device, described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox, was presented to Sri Lanka’s meteorological department on Nov. 1. It will form part of a system designed to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year.

Launched in July 2025, MAZU takes its name from a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It combines AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from the country’s weather satellites.

Conventional weather forecasting relies on supercomputers to calculate how the atmosphere will change using equations based on physical laws. AI models, by contrast, learn from years of weather data.

“Chatbots familiar to the public learn patterns in language, while AI weather models learn how the atmosphere evolves,” Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led the development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, told Sixth Tone. “By training on years of meteorological data, these models can predict future weather conditions based on current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity.”

Once trained, AI models can produce forecasts faster and more cheaply than conventional methods. One model can generate a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods. For forecasts covering 15 to 60 days, AI models can reduce computing costs to one-thousandth of those of conventional methods.

But most of the savings come from running routine forecasts, Niu said. Training models, building datasets, and maintaining systems still require investment — resources many countries in the Global South lack.

MAZU’s cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, according to domestic media, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years.

In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data to develop warnings for heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods. In Djibouti, the model developed by Niu’s team helps provide tailored weather warnings for the East African country’s port.

Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, for which there is little historical data. Local weather in complex terrain also remains difficult to forecast, and it is not always clear how AI models arrive at their predictions.

The models also need to be adapted to local conditions, Niu said. “Our approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, conduct independent evaluations, and make local adjustments.”

Even with AI, he added, “human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: The weather warning system Mazu at the China Meteorological Administration booth during 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. VCG）

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019218/China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.title: China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019218/China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.content:
Traditional Chinese colors have become a popular topic on Chinese social media, with posts sporting catchy headlines such as “Our Ancestors Had the Ultimate Eye for Beauty” and “Out-of-This-World Color Combinations in ‘Dream of the Red Chamber.’” Open one of these posts, and you’ll often find neatly arranged color swatches labeled with evocative traditional names such as tianqing, “celestial blue”; yuebai, “moon white”; qiuxiang, “autumn fragrance”; and yanzhi, “rouge.”

In my opinion, this enthusiasm is undoubtedly a good thing. Traditional colors deserve greater attention and should be made more accessible. Color swatches can also be useful for showcasing the colors of historical artifacts and help modern audiences connect with the past. But this kind of simplification is a double-edged sword. In making something rich and complex easier to understand, it can also reduce it to a crude, one-dimensional representation. What makes information easier to communicate can also obscure or distort its meaning.

In fact, color swatches have significant limitations when it comes to representing and explaining traditional colors. They can only scratch the surface of a much richer cultural history.

Modern color charts emerged from Western industrial and commercial systems designed to control production quality and reproduce specific colors. But this standardized, scientific approach often falls short when applied to traditional Chinese colors. Anyone who has visited an exhibition of antique clothing or textiles and tried to photograph it may have experienced this firsthand. What appears to the naked eye as a beautiful pine green might look mustard yellow on a smartphone screen. Or the various golds and yellows of an imperial dragon robe might lose their distinctiveness entirely. If even digital cameras equipped with sophisticated image-processing algorithms struggle to capture these colors, what chance does a simple color swatch have?

So why do modern industrial color charts fall short in representing traditional Chinese colors?

First, color swatches are designed to standardize colors within specific product categories, whereas traditional Chinese color names developed within particular craft traditions. As these traditions evolved, a color’s name could refer to subtly different hues in different periods.

Several factors contributed to these variations. In the age of traditional handicrafts, differences in materials and craftsmanship could produce markedly different hues. Local production conditions also gave products from different regions their own distinctive characteristics. Fashions changed over time, altering the shades associated with particular color names. Even on a single garment, colors could appear different depending on the lighting, viewing angle, or direction of the weave.

Traditional indigo dyeing offers a good example. Indigo must first be fermented in vats and chemically reduced before it can be used to dye fabric. A single dip produces a pale blue, and the color deepens after each subsequent immersion. As a result, even fabrics dyed in the same vat can emerge in countless different shades.

Second, modern industrial color standards demand precision, assigning each color a numerical value. Traditional color names, however, did not follow this quantitative model. Rather than corresponding to a single fixed value, they generally described a natural range of hues.

Take xinghuang, or “apricot yellow,” for example. The yellowish-red of a ripe apricot is not a precisely defined hue. Yet despite natural variations in its color, people can still recognize the familiar shade of a ripe apricot.

Finally, the meanings and appearances of colors have changed considerably throughout Chinese history. These changes reflected rulers’ preferences, interpretations of cultural doctrines, shifts in folk customs, the rise and decline of craft techniques, and the movement of goods through domestic and overseas trade.

Consider qing, a color term widely used in ancient China. Depending on the context, it could describe the blue of the sky, the green of plants, or even the black of someone’s hair or eyes. By the Ming (1368–1644) and Qing (1644–1911) dynasties, it still encompassed a broad range of hues. People wore qing-colored robes, but their exact shades varied. Although the “Da Ming Huidian,” or “Collected Statutes of the Ming Dynasty,” prescribed shiqing for officials’ outer robes, surviving examples range from reddish tones to bluish-green and darker, more somber shades. Meanwhile, the robe the emperor wore during rituals at the imperial tombs was yuanqing, a shade that appeared almost black.

Another example is zi, or “purple.” Examining the cloud and wave motifs on Qing imperial dragon robes reveals how the color evolved over successive reigns, from dark brownish shades early in the dynasty to mauve hues in the middle period and brighter purples in the late Qing.

Furthermore, in ancient China, color was not simply something to admire or enjoy. It also symbolized divine authority and helped define ritual conventions and social hierarchies, distinguishing the central government from local authorities and the nobility from ordinary people.

Ancient China developed a five-color system associated with concepts such as the five directions and five elements. Qing, chi (vermilion), yellow, white, and black were the five primary colors, while green, red, bi (jade), purple, and liuhuang (“flowing yellow”) were the five auxiliary colors. Successive rulers used these distinctions between primary and auxiliary colors to reinforce social hierarchies.

During the Qing dynasty, for example, the emperor’s ceremonial attire followed a four-color system from the middle of the dynasty onward. He wore tianqing, “celestial blue,” when performing sacrifices to Heaven; minghuang, “bright yellow,” for sacrifices to Earth; dahong, “deep red,” for sacrifices to the Sun; and yuebai, “moon white,” for sacrifices to the Moon.

The Qing imperial court also expanded the use of yellow in imperial dress, a practice dating back to the Sui (581–618) and Tang (618–907) dynasties. Strict rules determined who could wear particular shades. Minghuang, “bright yellow,” was reserved for the emperor, empress dowager, empress, and imperial noble consort. Xinghuang, “apricot yellow,” was restricted to the crown prince and crown princess, while jinhuang, “golden yellow,” was worn by princes, noble consorts, and consorts. Xiangse, “fragrant yellow,” was designated for imperial concubines and various ranks of princesses and princely consorts.

Clearly, color swatches alone cannot convey such rich cultural meanings and historical details. But the problem goes beyond how we reconstruct traditional colors. It also concerns how we understand history itself.

Modern industrial products are generally designed for mass consumption, often favoring simplicity and practicality. By contrast, many of the objects that have survived from ancient China belonged to emperors, empresses, and other powerful figures. The differences between their world and ours, in social context, cultural values, and everyday life, mean that interpreting these objects through a modern lens can easily lead to superficial conclusions or misunderstandings.

This brings us back to today’s enthusiasm for traditional colors on social media. China’s color traditions never formed a fixed, unchanging system, and preserving a tradition involves more than simply reproducing the past. It is a process of critically engaging with what came before, deciding what to discard, what to preserve, and what to adapt or develop further.

But meaningful preservation must begin with an understanding of the historical traditions themselves. That means looking beyond individual colors to examine the contexts in which they emerged, how their meanings and uses changed over time, and the cultural, social, and material relationships that shaped them.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from the Palace Museum, reedited by Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.title: China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
World.content:
Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang pledged to share China’s market with the rest of the world and promote balanced international economic development at the opening ceremony of the 2026 China International Import Expo (CIIE) on Thursday.

“Mutual benefit is at the heart of trade and economic cooperation,” Ding said in his opening address. “Open and connected markets are fundamental for such partnerships.”

Ding also called for deeper investment cooperation, greater collaboration in technological innovation, and stronger dialogue to remove trade barriers.

This year’s CIIE, the ninth annual event and the largest edition to date, welcomes a record 4,142 overseas companies from 162 countries, regions, and international organizations to Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center. The event’s total exhibition area is also its largest, exceeding 440,000 square meters.

The event, which runs Nov. 5 to 10, welcomed more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and global leading enterprises, with 2,000 companies participating for the first time. A record more than 480 products will either make their global, Asia, or China debut at the expo, including a laparoscopic surgery robot by Johnson & Johnson, a cochlear implant capable of 360-degree sound coverage by Swiss hearing care firm Advanced Bionics, and a 6G terminal prototype by U.S. tech company Qualcomm.

This year’s exhibition comprises six main sections covering technical equipment, consumer goods, food and agricultural products, automobiles and smart mobility, medical devices and health care, and trade in services. It also offers a dedicated “innovation incubation zone” for tech startups.

CIIE has also expanded efforts to support African countries, with free exhibition booth space for the “least developed” countries up 17% from last year’s exhibition. The expansion comes as China introduced zero tariffs on imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations in May.

Launched in 2018, CIIE is the world’s first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports. The expo underlines China’s continued efforts to promote inclusive economic globalization and build an open world economy.

In the first nine months of 2026, China’s imports of foreign goods reached 16.7 trillion yuan ($2.5 trillion), up 22.3% year on year, the fastest growth since 2021, according to official data.

(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo’s exhibition center in Shanghai, Nov. 5, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.title: Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
World.content:
Applications aimed at preventing impulse purchases have soared in popularity during this year’s Double Eleven, the world’s largest shopping festival. The apps involve users listing the items they want, along with their prices, then sharing them with friends and strangers who vote on whether they should buy them.

Dozens of such mini-programs have sprung up across major platforms including WeChat and Alipay following the August success of the WeChat mini-program “Still Want to Buy?” (Hai Mai Me in Chinese), domestic media reported last week. Related hashtags have garnered tens of millions of views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Thursday.

Domestic e-commerce giant Alibaba launched Double Eleven, also known as Singles’ Day, on Nov. 11, 2009, as a 24-hour shopping event. The festival has since grown to a monthlong event across all e-commerce platforms and begins around mid-October.

The trend comes as young Chinese consumers become increasingly money-conscious. According to a May report by Ireland-based consulting firm Accenture, 82% of the country’s Gen Z — more than 230 million people — have started saving money or cutting back on non-essential spending.

The rise in anti-impulse-buy apps dates back to the release of Still Want to Buy? in August. Created by a 29-year-old developer under the pseudonym Qiancheng, the app gained more than 75,000 daily active users within three days of its launch, and total registered users exceeded 500,000 as of mid-September. More than 85% of users are females under 24, Qiancheng told local media.

He said the tool came about after his girlfriend suggested using automated office purchase approval systems — which employees must go through to obtain authorization for work-related purchases — to govern shopping decisions. He added that he often personally feels regret after making impulse purchases.

“It’s difficult to make money nowadays, so I think it’s worth letting people we trust help us make better spending decisions,” Qiancheng said.

However, Still Want to Buy? was taken down on Oct. 31, reportedly due to targeted reporting from online trolls. Qiancheng told local media he is applying to have the mini-program relisted and is developing an independent app to expand the program’s function.

WeChat mini-program “Wait Up, Wallet” also offers similar features to Still Want to Buy?, but it allows users to seek advice from total strangers.

This October, Lin Yinjie, a 20-year-old college student from the eastern Fujian province, vibe-coded a similar app, the Alipay mini-program “Hold On a Sec.” The app lets users log items and prices and set a cooling-off period, during which friends help them decide whether to buy. So far, the program is mainly used by Lin and her friends and does not have a wide audience.

Lin told Sixth Tone that she used to place orders mindlessly while scrolling shopping apps and social media. “As a student on a tight budget, I know how easily the desire to buy things can quietly drain my wallet,” she said.

“A 9.9-yuan ($1.50) purchase seems insignificant, but before you know it, you’ve spent hundreds of yuan,” she said, adding that, “A lot of things I think I really want turn out to be things I no longer care about after a few days.”

Over the past week, Lin says her tool has helped her save over 80 yuan, which she used to buy a camera memory card instead. “It’s like trading ‘unnecessary spending’ for something I actually need,” she said.

Public reactions to the apps have been mixed. While many users report receiving practical advice through the mini-programs, others note an unfortunate side effect. “When I review other people’s requests, I end up wanting to buy the items myself,” one user noted on Douyin. “It’s turned into a product recommendation feed.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG and Weibo, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.title: Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
World.content:
For nearly 27 years, Starbucks coffeehouses in China have been a haven for non-paying patrons attracted by its comfortable seating, ample power outlets, air conditioning, and free restrooms.

This stemmed from the American company’s foundational brand concept of making its outlets “third places” — safe, accessible spaces between home and work to relax and connect with friends, whether you intend to spend or not.

Now, it seems, spending is mandatory.

In late October, Starbucks China introduced a nationwide purchase-required seating policy, pledging to be “clear in its rules but warm in its execution,” with staff encouraged to politely stop non-paying customers from hogging tables and chairs. At the same time, it unveiled plans to invest more than 300 million yuan ($45 million) in reshaping the in-store atmosphere.

As the company undergoes major corporate restructuring while continuing to expand, does it risk losing its “third place” image in China?

Stirred up

The first Starbucks on the Chinese mainland opened in Beijing’s World Trade Building in 1999. Today there are about 8,000 outlets across 1,100 counties in the mainland.

Li Kele regularly visits her local store in the southwestern Sichuan province. After walking in and sitting down on Oct. 21, taking a moment to browse various online platforms for discounts, Li was soon approached by a barista brandishing a menu and asking if she needed any help. “The store never used to push customers to place an order,” she says.

Starbucks outlets have been attracting non-paying patrons since the 1980s, and the company officially adopted a worldwide open-door policy in 2018.

However, concerns over disruptive behaviors, alongside the company’s desire to prioritize paying customers and staff’s experience, prompted the global headquarters to reverse the policy in January last year.

The change began at its North American stores, where a new code of conduct stated that Starbucks coffee shops, patios, restrooms, and other facilities were for employees and customers only.

Anecdotal evidence suggests baristas in China began nudging seated patrons to make purchases in early 2026.

One customer shares that in January they observed employees at a Starbucks branch in Beijing’s central Xidan shopping district walking around the store offering table service to people without drinks, which is not typically available, and promoting discount coupons. Sometimes they’d subtly point out that the store was crowded and seating was scarce.

On Oct. 19, social media users in several cities began posting about signs spotted at Starbucks stores that stated customers should “make a purchase before taking a seat.”

When a domestic media outlet contacted Starbucks China for a response that same day, a spokesperson denied any plan to introduce a purchase-required seating policy. But within 48 hours, the company made a complete U-turn, announcing that such a policy would take effect on Oct. 22.

The move has sparked much debate online. Yet in real terms, implementation has so far been limited to advisory measures, such as signage.

“The latest wording is that they (head office) encourage us to ask people to leave,” says Zhang Yi, a part-time Starbucks barista. “They want us front-line staff to persuade non-paying customers to give up their seats in whatever way we consider peaceful.”

However, because the practice isn’t tied to their performance review, employees might be reluctant to enforce the new rules, Zhang adds. “If I’m on shift, I won’t do it. I’ll just work the way I always have.”

In the grind

Starbucks built its “third place” branding concept based on the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg’s 1989 book, “The Great Good Place,” in which he describes the human need for communal, welcoming social environments separate from home (the “first place”) and work (the “second place”).

This positioning requires providing space for relaxed socializing. But when revenues don’t keep pace with increases in rent and operating costs, it becomes a potential pain point.

When Brian Niccol was appointed CEO of Starbucks in September 2024, same-store sales — a metric that measures revenue growth from established locations — were on the slide in the U.S. market.

To reverse the trend, he launched “Back to Starbucks,” a plan aimed at “rediscovering the power of third places” by improving the in-store experience, such as reintroducing old-school ceramic mugs and handwritten names on cups, as well as more comfortable seating. He then scrapped the 2018 open-door policy.

Investor data suggests the changes have already had an effect in North America, where same-store sales were up by 8.1% year on year in the third quarter of fiscal 2026 (Sept. 29, 2025, to Sept. 27, 2026) and same-store transactions grew by 4.5% over the same period.

In China, recent growth in same-store sales has been powered more by product innovation, deliveries, and price adjustments, according to Cathy R. Smith, Starbucks’ chief financial officer.

As online take-out orders increase and in-store spending declines, running a brick-and-mortar “third place” becomes more expensive. In this case, seat-hogging shifts from being a tolerable service issue to an operational problem.

Pressing issue

In April this year, Starbucks completed a $4 billion joint-venture transaction with Boyu Capital, a China-focused alternative asset management and private equity firm based in Hong Kong. The deal gives Boyu a 60% share in Starbucks’ China retail business and transitions all 8,000 coffeehouses into licensed operations.

The U.S. coffee giant says it expects the transaction proceeds, along with the value of its retained 40% stake and licensing agreement, to account for more than $13 billion over the next decade. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, Starbucks’ international segment operating margin increased to 19.1%, up from 13.6% a year earlier.

However, while the deal benefits global headquarters, Starbucks China still faces pressure to expand. At a partner forum in April, CEO Molly Liu confirmed the company is already two-thirds of the way to its goal of opening stores in more than 1,500 counties over the next three years.

With this in mind, the purchase-required seating policy looks more like an efficiency drive, as the company attempts to cut costs.

This also comes amid a major restructuring of Starbucks China’s workforce. As all staff are now part of the joint venture, they can no longer hold Starbucks shares, which trade on New York’s Nasdaq exchange. This means the end of the Bean Stock program in China, which since 1991 has awarded full- and part-time employees shares after a certain tenure.

Liu said at April’s partner forum that benefits would continue through fiscal 2026, with a new long-term incentive plan to be introduced in the fourth quarter. As of Nov. 4, there had been no further announcements.

As social insurance contributions are mandatory only for permanent staff in China, barista Zhang believes the company prefers to hire part-time workers. Jiemian News reported in January that Starbucks China’s official recruitment channels were promoting vacancies in 269 areas, with full-time positions making up just over 20%.

Behind its new seating policy is a contradiction Starbucks China cannot easily escape: the “third place” concept justifies the brand’s premium, yet recent growth has come from deliveries and discounts, bringing sales without a customer ever sitting down.

The joint venture and its target to grow to “as many as 20,000 locations over time” sharpen that contradiction. Smaller markets and leaner per-store costs make it hard to build to the original standard.

Therefore, tightening seating rules, restructuring its workforce, and expansion look less like separate decisions than part of one cost logic.

(Due to privacy concerns, Li Kele and Zhang Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Zhan Fangge.

A version of this article originally appeared in Baobian News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A sign asks customers to make a purchase before taking a seat at a Starbucks. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
World.content:
A Chinese app designed to report hotels that allegedly have bedbugs and other pests has been updated and re-released following controversy over the validity of the claims. The app attracted more than 300,000 users at its peak, flagging over 600 hotels nationwide, according to its creator.

In a Sunday post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, the creator of the app, a WeChat mini-program called “Bedbug Map,” announced that he alone would now review bedbug reports — previously, evidence was approved if a majority of users verified it. He also clarified that users are required to upload photographic evidence of bedbugs. The next day, he also posted a review of nearly 300 rejected bedbug reports, explaining why each had been declined.

Released Sept. 16, the mini-program lets users report hotels with bedbugs, cockroaches, or other pests, resulting in a bug or question mark icon over the hotel’s location. Tapping it reveals the number of user reports.

Controversy arose after reports that multiple hotels were asked by customers for refunds after they reported having found bedbugs via the app after their stay. One hotel was allegedly asked to refund 3,000 yuan ($450) in room charges after a report citing “two bumps” on a guest’s body was posted on the map and approved by users. According to the report, the hotel later asked a third party to inspect the premises, but found no traces of bedbugs.

The creator, a 26-year-old manufacturing industry worker who asked to remain anonymous, told Sixth Tone that in the past few days he had personally reviewed more than 700 pieces of photo evidence submitted over the previous two months.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone revealed that 232 hotels are now marked on the mini-program’s map, down from the more than 600 reported before Monday. The mini-program currently lists 36 hotels as having successfully appealed reports after submitting third-party evidence.

The app has also been taken down twice, most recently in late October, by WeChat parent company Tencent, citing its restrictions on applications run by and registered to individuals.

The creator told Sixth Tone that Bedbug Map was created with the help of AI in under two weeks. He said he got the idea after searching online for bedbug information after he and his girlfriend developed bites following a move, discovering most bedbug posts involved hotels.

On the day of its release, the mini-program attracted over 100,000 users, according to the creator. Under his release announcement on Xiaohongshu, many commented asking him to expand the function to public transportation, which he then added to the app. However, the function was removed in subsequent updates.

“I guess the reason the app was well-received is that it addresses a key pain point for the average traveler: the lack of cleanliness and the resurgence of bedbugs.”

The mini-program previously allowed users to submit reports without photo evidence. However, after users raised concerns about the potential for people to maliciously target hotels without evidence, the program was updated in late September to allow users to upload photographic evidence. Photos can be either uploaded or taken directly via the mini-program — in the latter case, the app automatically adds a watermark showing the time and location.

“I’m simply the initiator,” he said. “The goal is to get everyone involved in managing the mini-program’s data and reviews.”

Hotels can also appeal bedbug reports — indicated on the map by blue semicircular icons above such locations — as well as upload disinfection records, business licenses, and photos of pest-control operations.

The creator said he even recruited volunteers at one point to inspect the hygiene of hotels that filed appeals. However, the function was soon taken down because of concerns about volunteers’ safety, among other issues.

He said that managing the mini-program alone has “brought pressure and criticism,” adding that he hopes the government will “provide professional guidance to improve (the app’s) credibility.”

In an interview with domestic media, Lin Feiran, a lawyer at Beijing King & Capital Law Firm, suggested the company bring in professionals to identify insects reported at different locations.

State media outlet CNR News wrote in a Monday commentary that “a map pieced together by internet users being used to fill the gap in hygiene information shows that formal (reporting) channels are lacking,” encouraging hotel booking platforms to display bedbug records publicly.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Weibo and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.title: Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
World.content:
A few weeks ago, I served as a judge on a food program in China, where I met many chefs and got a close look at how they develop new dishes. I was particularly impressed by one dish: a steamed egg custard topped with a rich crab paste made from crab roe and fat. It was a combination I had never considered before. The crab paste had a delicate aroma and a rich, oily texture, while the steamed egg custard was soft and silky, perfectly balancing its richness.

I was struck by the dish’s ingenuity, but it also raised a question: Would people be willing to pay for the recipe and instructions on how to make it?

I put this question to one of the chefs on the program. He smiled at me as though I were a child and asked why anyone would pay for a recipe. He then let me in on an industry secret: When a restaurant discovers that a competitor has introduced a new dish, it will order it and have its own chefs taste it, analyze its ingredients, cooking techniques, and seasonings, and work out how it was made. In most cases, they can reproduce it. The chef told me he had recreated other people’s dishes and had his own copied by others.

It all sounded rather cutthroat. The person who bears the cost of innovation often reaps little of the reward.

In Chinese cuisine, creating a new dish is not nearly as simple as diners might imagine. Chefs must find the right ingredients, adjust proportions, experiment with different cooking temperatures, refine textures, and continually adjust based on customer feedback. Developing a successful dish can involve dozens or even hundreds of failed attempts before it is ready to serve.

The time, ingredients, and labor costs of this trial-and-error process are all borne by the original creator. Yet as soon as the dish reaches the table, anyone can observe, taste, analyze, and even reproduce it. For a competitor, learning most of the techniques needed to make a dish may cost little more than the price of a meal.

Even more frustrating, many of these innovators lack the resources to promote their creations. A small restaurant might be the first to develop a dish but lack the advertising budget, media exposure, or network of locations to popularize it. Meanwhile, a larger restaurant can simply copy the dish and quickly introduce it to a wider audience. Since more people encounter it there first, they may assume the larger restaurant came up with it.

This suggests that the first-mover advantage does not necessarily apply in the restaurant business. Being first matters only if consumers know who created the dish and the original creator has the resources and business acumen to turn that innovation into a brand and a source of revenue. Otherwise, the creator is essentially providing free research and development while introducing consumers to a dish that benefits the entire market.

The challenge of protecting intellectual property is not unique to Chinese cuisine. It affects chefs around the world. Business schools often hold up KFC’s fried chicken recipe as a classic example of a trade secret, but the company’s real competitive advantage lies in its supply chains, restaurant network, and brand value. The law does not prohibit you from reverse-engineering KFC’s fried chicken and making it yourself, or even selling it to your neighbors, provided you don’t market it as “KFC Original Recipe Chicken.” For smaller restaurants, therefore, protecting a recipe may matter less than building the brand and reputation that give it lasting commercial value.

The celebrated 18th-century Chinese food writer Yuan Mei associated dishes with particular names as a way of preserving their origins. For example, in his influential cookbook “Suiyuan Shidan” (“Recipes from the Garden of Contentment”), he included dishes called “Prefect Wang’s eight-treasure tofu” and “Governor Yang’s tofu.” In this way, no matter how often later generations copied these dishes, their names remained tied to their origins.

However, this naming convention has its limitations. Prefect Wang, Governor Yang, and the better-known Kung Pao (of Kung Pao chicken fame) all refer to the chefs’ employers rather than the people who actually did the cooking. Only in his “Biography of Chef Wang Xiaoyu” did Yuan Mei praise a chef, elevating an obscure kitchen worker to a culinary figure remembered by later generations.

Similarly, General Tso’s chicken is familiar to almost everyone in the United States, yet few know the name Peng Chang-kuei, the chef credited with creating the dish and introducing it to America. Diners know the name of General Tso, but not the person behind the dish.

One way to recognize innovative chefs would be to give them explicit credit for their creations. For example, instead of simply labeling a dish “Chef’s Recommendation,” menus could identify the chef or team of chefs who developed it, along with the restaurant and year it first appeared. This would acknowledge the contributions of both the creators and the restaurants that invested in their work.

Chefs could also license their original recipes to restaurants and large chains. Another possibility would be to establish an industry-wide registry of original dishes, where chefs and restaurants could record development dates, launch locations, photographs, and successive versions of their recipes. That way, even if other restaurants later copied a dish and achieved greater commercial success, its creator’s contribution would not simply be forgotten.

Of course, implementing such measures would not be easy. The greatest resistance might not even come from imitators, but from within the restaurants where new dishes are developed.

For restaurant owners, naming a dish after its creator also poses risks. Chefs tend to move between jobs, and when one leaves, dishes bearing their name could become an awkward legacy, potentially even requiring a restaurant to overhaul its menu. At the same time, chefs have traditionally enjoyed relatively low social status. Within restaurants, they often have little say in day-to-day operations and limited bargaining power to protect their own interests, making it difficult to secure adequate recognition for their contributions.

These two problems are closely related. When chefs receive little recognition for their work and feel little ownership over the dishes they create or the restaurants where they work, they may be more inclined to leave. This, in turn, gives restaurants even less incentive to credit individual chefs. It may help explain why, in the rare cases in which a dish bears its creator’s name — such as Fei Da Chu’s chili stir-fried pork, sold in cities across China — the chef behind it is also the restaurant’s owner.

Protecting and rewarding the creators of original dishes, whether through naming rights or other institutional and technological mechanisms, could help raise chefs’ social status, strengthen their bargaining power, and create a more equitable relationship between chefs and restaurant owners. Restaurants, in turn, could attract diners who appreciate the work of individual chefs and are willing to pay for originality. The result could be a positive cycle of culinary innovation, recognition, and consumption.

A dish may be replicated almost perfectly, but the experience, creativity, and reputation behind it cannot. The chef who conceived the idea, the sous chefs who tested the recipe, the team members who continually refined it, and the restaurant that provided the resources and space for experimentation all contributed to the story behind the dish. Recognizing their contributions is about more than giving credit where it is due. It is also about respecting the generations of chefs who have shaped Chinese cuisine and ensuring that their knowledge, skills, and traditions continue to be valued.

(Header image: The illustration in the center depicts Yuan Mei, a Qing Dynasty poet, scholar, and artist, in a 19th-century painting by Chinese artist Ye Yanlan. Images from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone.)
