World.title: Snow blankets parts of NSW just weeks away from summer
World.content:
Parts of New South Wales have been blanketed in snow just a few weeks out from summer after a strong cold front swept along the state's coast.

David Crock from the Bureau of Meteorology said November was a "very volatile time of year", with the cold snap not that unusual, but was always "striking when it happens".

"We saw snow maybe down as low as 400 to 500 metres through parts of Tasmania yesterday, also snow on the Alps through Victoria and NSW down to about 800m," he said.

Thredbo dropped to -5.0 degrees Celsius overnight. (Supplied)

The heat in the north of the country, the senior meteorologist explained, coupled with a really cold ocean in the south was behind the change.

"So we've got that really strong temperature gradient between northern Australia and the Southern Ocean," he said.

"And that's what creates these strong cold fronts with a big push of cold air up through NSW and even into southern parts of Queensland."

On Saturday, Sydney hit 29.7C just after lunch time, dropping to 14C by the evening.

The massive drop was also experienced in Penrith, which went from 31.5C at 3pm, to 14C by late evening. Night time in Parramatta hit 13.C after sweating through 30.4 earlier in the day.

The change also brought heavy rain and storms.

'Hard to get out of bed'

Thredbo, in the state's alpine region, received a dumping of snow overnight when temperatures fell to -5.0 degrees Celsius.

It was 0C on Sunday morning and snow was still falling.

Snow resorts wind up business early after warmest winter on record An unseasonably warm and wet June brought a challenging start to the 2026 snow season and while a snow base came by July over the higher slopes, the lower alpine regions missed out on full coverage.

Madeleine McVie said while it was unexpected after a warm winter, it was "beautiful" and enough to build a snowman.

"It certainly was hard to get out of bed. It is very cold down here," she said.

"We got a little bit [of snow] a couple of days ago, and yesterday it started snowing about four in the afternoon.

" I looked out the window and it was dumping down big fat flakes. "

People who had gone hiking at Mount Kosciuszko were ecstatic, she added.

"They certainly wasn't expecting it to snow down here in November.

"And we're prepping for our mountain biking season, so we weren't expecting it either."

On Sunday, cooler temperatures hovering between 10C and 12C degrees dominated across the state.

Strong southerly winds and hazardous conditions are forecasted along the NSW coast on Monday, with the chill expected to continue.

World.title: Swans, Hawks prevail in AFLW elimination finals
World.content:
AFLW superstar Chloe Molloy has once again lifted Sydney to victory, with the Swans defeating the Western Bulldogs by 29 points in an elimination final.

League-leading goalkicker Molloy pulled off a surprise cameo down back to help the Swans claim a 7.4 (46) to 2.5 (17) win at a wet and windy Henson Park on Sunday.

Sydney will next play Geelong in an away semi-final. The Bulldogs' season is over.

Molloy's leadership in a wet-weather scrap proved the difference for the Swans, with the former Swans co-skipper finishing with one goal, 12 intercepts, and 14 contested possessions.

Tanya Kennedy was just as crucial for the Swans, locking down Bulldogs co-captain and gun midfielder Isabelle Pritchard.

Pritchard, on return from a knee injury, was kept to just 14 disposals and three clearances as Kennedy laid 17 tackles.

Fellow Bulldogs midfielder Ellie Blackburn, also returning after being rested in last week's loss to the Cats, led the visitors with 29 touches and a goal.

Swans captain Lucy McEvoy needed just 20 seconds to score the opener with a long bomb from outside the 50-metre arc thanks to the strong breeze.

A rushed behind gave the Bulldogs their sole score of the first quarter, as the hosts made the most of conditions to fire off their four unanswered goals and build a 24-point lead.

The Bulldogs could only manage one point with the breeze in the second, with Molloy helping limit the damage with five contested possessions and four intercepts as a defender.

Molloy's stint in defence forced Bulldogs coach Tam Hyett to bring defender Vaomua Laloifi into the forward line, and the pair's battle continued well into the second half.

Sunday's final turned into a slog after torrential rain came in the third quarter, with the Swans doing just enough to maintain a 25-point lead en route to victory in front of 4,325 dedicated fans.

Hawks break through for finals win over Suns

Hawthorn has broken through for their its AFLW finals victory in an 18-point defeat of Gold Coast.

A commanding third quarter paved the path for the Hawks to prevail 8.9 (57) to 6.3 (39) at People First Stadium on Sunday.

Hawthorn, who bombed out of the finals in straight sets in 2024 and 2025, will face Carlton in the first semi-final next Saturday night at Princes Park.

Eliza West (29 disposals, one goal) and Laura Stone (21, two) were outstanding for the Hawks, while Casey Sherriff, Hayley McLaughlin and Jasmine Fleming all picked up 20 touches.

Jenna Richardson was a wall in defence, with a game-high 11 marks while completely blanketing Suns forward Dekota Brown.

The Davies sisters — Darcie and Georja — impressed for Gold Coast, who were also chasing their maiden AFLW final success.

Charlie Rowbottom battled hard for her 20 disposals (18 of them handballs), a figure matched by Niamh McLoughlin and Daisy D'Arcy.

Adding injury to insult for the Suns, young gun Ava Usher suffered a serious-looking injury to her right knee in a heavy collision with teammate Maddy Brancatisano in the dying stages.

Hawthorn kicked two goals in the last 77 seconds of a high-octane opening term — through Poppy Stockwell and Jacqueline Dupuy — to lead by six points.

The Suns responded to take a three-point half-time lead, but Hawthorn raised its pressure in the third quarter and Gold Coast couldn't go with it.

The Hawks' backline repelled 11 consecutive entries from the Suns, while their midfield trampled Gold Coast at clearance and on the outside.

Hawthorn had 33 more disposals for the term, 13 more tackles and pulled ahead by 15 points at three-quarter time.

Mikayla Nurse goaled early in the fourth quarter to give Gold Coast a sniff, but the Hawks continued to pile on the pressure and exorcise their own demons.

AAP

World.title: NZ election figures tell story of disenchantment and fracturing
World.content:
If you're a fan of elections and numbers, then the New Zealand election offers a fascinating smorgasbord.

After all, it's an improbably tight result on the raw figures.

More than 2.4 million party votes have been counted so far, with just 3,650 votes separating the two major parties. Labour has 710,330 party votes compared with National's 706,680, though hundreds of thousands of special votes are yet to be counted.

That margin was somehow even tighter (about 1,500 votes) just before 10pm last night, prompting Henry Cooke, the political editor of New Zealand newspaper The Post, to marvel at the mirror columns of red and blue.

"Millions of people will vote in this election but the party vote margin between the two 'major parties' could fit in Auckland's St James Theatre," he posted on X.

Most New Zealand political observers are now (very understandably) fixated on the minutiae of the vote, the party machinations, the overhang, the special votes, and whether National will need to bring in political newcomers Opportunity in order to keep their hold on government.

Christopher Luxon told supporters on election night his party had a path to government. (Reuters: David Rowland)

National has a clear edge over Labour on seat numbers, with 42 seats projected compared with Labour's 36 seats. There's an increasingly settled view that Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has an easier avenue to power than Labour leader Chris Hipkins, who would have to navigate a much more torturous pathway to the top job.

The preliminary results do not include 400,000 or so special votes, which are yet to be counted by the New Zealand Electoral Commission. Special votes have historically boosted Labour's vote share, although election analysts say it is unclear whether they will be sufficient to push National and its coalition partners below its perilously thin majority.

Key takeaways from the New Zealand election The results in the New Zealand election are anything but clear with the two major parties — Labour and National — in the tightest of races.

After a muted speech at National HQ on election night, Mr Luxon sounded decidedly more confident when talking to journalists in Auckland this afternoon, saying his party could claim a mandate to govern.

"Ultimately, New Zealanders have given us the biggest seats in parliament, 42 seats as it stands today, and a pathway to form a government," he said.

" As a politician, would I love 50.1 per cent? Absolutely, I think everybody would, but there's no doubt about it, we've got a mandate. "

Stats tell a subterranean story

Still, if you're taking a broader view and asking what this election might tell us about New Zealand's political trajectory then there's a subterranean story that deserves as much attention as the blow-by-blow race for the Beehive.

When you pick through the latest data two figures really jump out, because they tell us a story of disenchantment and fracture in the New Zealand electorate.

Inflation, economy defining NZ's election New Zealand's coalition government faces a fragmented and increasingly disenchanted electorate.

The first: New Zealand's two major parties, Labour and National, secured only 59 per cent of the party vote between them.

This is the first time since 1996, when New Zealand embraced its MMP* voting system, that the two major parties have fallen beneath 60 per cent of the vote.

The last time this almost happened (back in 2002) it was off the back of a smashing victory by then prime minister Helen Clark, who secured more than 41 per cent of the vote while National crashed to only 21 per cent.

One commentator put it neatly last night when he mused that it was probably time to stop talking about the "major" and "minor" parties, and just talk about the "seven parties" in New Zealand.

Of course coalition politics have always been a major feature of New Zealand politics since 1996, because MMP strengthens the hand of minor players.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong addressed the party faithful at an event in in Auckland. (Jonathan Killick/Stuff via AP)

But the surge in the minor party vote, as well as the dramatic re-emergence of Qiulae Wong and Opportunity (from outside parliament too) might hint at a deeper realignment.

The contrast with 2020 is stark. Jacinda Ardern's Labour party won an outright majority of the party vote at that election, allowing it to govern alone. The current results raise questions about whether New Zealand's era of majority style politics is over.

It feels more likely that political polarisation and a fragmenting information space will continue to fuel the rise of other players, with future leaders navigating constantly coalescing, shifting coalitions between several parties.

Of course, this isn't a shift merely contained to New Zealand, look at the way One Nation has up-ended federal politics in Australia, where the major parties are also seeing a steady long-term decline in support.

The second figure worth dwelling on from this election is turnout, which dipped down to 74.6 per cent, the second lowest in New Zealand's history.

Attention is beginning to turn to the voter turnout numbers and what is behind the drop. (AP: Alex Robertson)

It's a number that might worry those tracking democracy's vital signs in New Zealand, which has a long and proud record of civic participation.

There are plenty of things that could explain this drop.

The weather wasn't exactly pleasant in New Zealand on Saturday with heavy rain and showers (particularly in the north) which may have kept people at home.

Some analysts have pointed to new enrolment rules as a possible factor after New Zealand introduced a requirement for voters to enrol 13 days before voting began.

Again, disenchantment and political disconnection are hardly unique to New Zealand.

But for leaders trying to navigate tumultuous and uncertain times, they make the hard task of building — and maintaining — a political mandate for difficult decisions all the harder.

* New Zealand uses a mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system, under which voters cast one vote for a local MP and another for a political party. The party vote largely determines how many seats each party receives in parliament.

World.title: Residents bought into communities but may end up living in 'wastelands'
World.content:
Rinnah Roque worries the view beyond her landscaped front garden will remain a construction site.

The 60-year-old committed to a growing community in Sydney's north-west when she bought a three-storey townhouse off the plan in Box Hill.

Across the road, a hive of builders were working on 47 homes as part of a project from the developer Bathla.

"I worked so hard to be able to buy a property for my mum and myself," she said.

" I was hoping that houses would be built as quickly as possible. You want to live in a community. "

Construction work on Hynds Road stopped after Bathla entered administration. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

But for the past two months, the symphony of construction noise has been replaced by silence.

"All of a sudden everything stopped, and what's so frustrating is everything was just left behind," she said.

The residential development dividing Hynds Road is one of hundreds caught up in the $3.4 billion collapse of Bathla Group.

And it is among dozens of sites that were part way through construction when the money stopped flowing.

In some cases, the private equity companies that are owed money by Bathla have taken control of the projects they invested in, and are racing to find builders that will finish them.

The Box Hill development is among hundreds caught up in the collapse of Bathla Group. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

But interviews with experts and industry stakeholders reveal that builders may be reluctant to guarantee the work of cash-strapped Bathla, posing the risk some sites could "languish".

Bathla declined the ABC's requests for interview and comment.

Hurdles to finishing Bathla's projects

The quality of the work already undertaken at Bathla's construction sites would be difficult to assess by the builders that are considering finishing the projects, said Lyndall Bryant, a leading property economics professor at Queensland University of Technology.

"If you're a builder coming into a job that's half-finished, you don't want to be warranting the work that someone else has done," she said.

"If the concrete's been poured, you don't want to be saying, 'Oh yeah, I guarantee that that concrete's been done properly.'"

Lyndall Bryant says some builders may be hesitant to take on half-finished jobs. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

She said reviewing plumbing or electrical work would be challenging if walls were already erected.

A private equity company that spoke to the ABC but declined to be named said the builders it was talking to were being cautious however, it remained confident one would be appointed.

Bathla's land deals ahead of collapse A former major lender says Bathla was expanding too quickly, leaving it vulnerable when the property market turned.

Urban Taskforce Australia, a group lobbying for developers and equity financiers, said it believed most of the projects would be completed.

"Where I would be concerned is if we were to find developments with substantial defects, where basically the cost to rectify those defects is greater than the value of the land with an approval on it," chief executive Tom Forrest said.

"I can't see that being the case in lots of occasions."

Impact on home values

Bathla was forced to stop construction at 45 sites after it was placed into administration in August, according to documents filed by the administrator Teneo to the NSW Supreme Court.

About a dozen of these sites are situated in Sydney's west, in areas such as Marsden Park, Box Hill, Rouse Hill and Pemulwuy.

Many are in new areas, clustered together.

Developments at Marsden Park in Sydney's west are among those where construction has stopped. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

Professor Bryant said the delay or failure of a project in these locations could leave communities "fractured".

"Those areas really could become almost wastelands for a number of years," she said.

"These sites attract vandalism, they're not maintained, and it just brings down the whole area.

"Unfortunately it's a negative impact on property values — and that's for the people who already live in those communities."

Ms Roque said if this scenario were to eventuate in Box Hill, it would be "a horror story".

"That will impact probably us mentally and even the whole family," she said.

Rinnah Roque (left) says it would be a "horror story" if the area become a "wasteland". (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

Urban Taskforce Australia said any drop in property values would be a "short-term blip".

"My hope is that the fracturing of the community doesn't happen because ultimately the market will come in and complete those homes," Mr Forrest said.

Councils could be left footing the bill

Two Sydney councils are among the most exposed.

Construction had stopped on eight Bathla projects in Blacktown Council, and at four sites in The Hills Shire Council.

Both councils are owed money by Bathla, and have registered as creditors with the administrator.

The councils could be left spending more money while bringing in less.

The Hills Shire Council and Blacktown Council are the most exposed from the Bathla collapse. (ABC News: Tony Ibrahim)

They might have to spend money building infrastructure such as roads and sewage that Bathla has yet to contribute to the developments, Professor Bryant said.

"Blacktown Council is at risk of having to spend significant money on infrastructure for projects that are on the fringe that might only service a few people," she said.

And they would be missing out on money they anticipated from rates, unless these developments are finished.

"I think that they should be concerned at Blacktown City Council because any major hiccup like this means delay in their cash flows," Mr Forrest said.

Blacktown Council declined a request for interview and comment.

The Hills Shire Council Mayor, Michelle Byrnes, said the collapse of Bathla was "another hit to public confidence in the construction industry".

Michelle Byrne says the public's confidence in the construction industry has been dealt another blow. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

"I'm devastated for the buyers across Sydney who have been left stranded by Bathla's collapse," she said.

Private equity investors race to recoup investments

Some investors have seized control of the Bathla sites they invested in and are racing to finish the projects.

One of them said the goal was to break even, with any profit considered a bonus.

Asian private equity company PAG has already appointed the builder ParkView to its 300-unit development in Pemulwuy.

Other private equity companies told the ABC they were in discussions with builders.

Major lender in Bathla development sells debts Private credit firms are striking deals to recover their money following the $3.4 billion collapse of property giant Bathla Group.

Ray White Capital, which owns the site in Box Hill, said it expected the site to be finished before April 2027.

Leda Group has taken control of a 240-unit development in Marsden Park, and said it was in advanced discussions with a builder.

But not all of Bathla's sites have been taken over by a creditor.

Among them is a 49-home housing estate in Lochinvar in the NSW Hunter Region.

The restructuring and insolvency firm Mackay Goodwin has been appointed to "assess available options".

World.title: Cancelled AI data centre 'victory for people power' after backlash
World.content:
Plans for another controversial AI data centre in Sydney have been scrapped, with a community group hailing the decision as a "victory for people power".

The facility, which was set to become part of a proposed logistics hub on the Cooks River at Arncliffe in the city's south, faced backlash from the local community after it was revealed in July last year.

Developers Stockland and John Boyd Properties proposed to redevelop the rezoned 18.3-hectare Kogarah Golf Club site into an estimated $3.5 billion logistics precinct including an AI data centre.

Stockland and John Boyd Properties withdrew their plans for the AI data centre. (Supplied)

Stop the Cooks River AI Project (SCRAP), which consists of hundreds of members, had been protesting against the development since forming in August.

'We were worried'

Group organiser Paddy Gibson said surrounding residents were celebrating the "very good win for people power".

"People really love this river and we're just horrified to hear that it could be threatened in this way," he said.

Mr Gibson said it would have posed a risk to the fragile local ecology around the river, which is called Goolay'yari in local Indigenous languages, which was already recovering from "industrialisation over the years".

"There's endangered plants and other animal species in the green space," he said.

"There's plenty of people trying to work on remediating what is a very polluted river, and we were worried that this would set back those efforts."

Paddy Gibson says there are endangered plants and other animal species at the proposed data centre site. (Supplied)

He also mentioned concerns about power usage and possible water contamination.

A Stockland spokesperson said the partners were now focused on building a "world class logistics precinct which does not include a data centre as part of the amended Concept Masterplan".

"The site is on the doorstep of Sydney Airport and in close proximity to Port Botany and major transport infrastructure, making it uniquely suited for a logistics hub and has potential for mixed uses, like retail and hospitality," they said.

"The project will also deliver a one-kilometre public foreshore link along the Cooks River and the future delivery of the 14-hectare Pemulwuy Park, as well as local road upgrades and improved active transport connections."

The spokesperson said the group would continue to engage openly with stakeholders as planning for the logistics precinct progressed.

'A wildlife sanctuary'

Bayside Greens councillor Peter Strong who had led council's opposition to the project said the decision was "very heartening".

Mr Strong said forums and outdoor events about the project had attracted large numbers of residents.

His main concerns were about excess energy and water use, noise, and the way AI was being "used and weaponised against the best wishes of humanity".

"That space has become a bit of a wildlife sanctuary since nothing much has happened with the old Kogarah Golf Club since they sold it," Mr Strong said.

Locals were concerned with the impact on water use and energy. (Supplied)

He said the withdrawal sent a message to the state government that "the council should have more of a veto on these data centres".

In August, the Minns government released its data centre policy framework which they said balanced the interests of households and investment in NSW.

A recent report following a parliamentary inquiry into data centres noted that the guidelines should have been in place "before developing any planning fast-track processes for these projects".

The government has until February next year to respond to the report.

Canterbury Labor MP Sophie Cotsis said she looked forward to seeing the revised logistics hub masterplan including a public foreshore link, road upgrades and improved active transport connections.

"The Minns Labor Government has established the Cooks River Consolidation Project to resolve longstanding tenure issues along the river," she said.

"As the local MP I am focused on working together with my colleagues and government agencies to see investment in the naturalisation of the river banks."

AI data centre pushback

Protesters at Merrylands rallying against a proposed AI data centre. (ABC News: Alex Lewis)

It is the latest in a series of proposed data centres to be scrapped following community opposition.

An AirTrunk data centre proposed in Lane Cove was also dropped, and another in Guildford in September.

Residents at Merrylands in Western Sydney have also rallied against the $1.1 billion Project Pluto Data Centre proposed by the Goodman Group, to be located next to the Guildford West Sportsground.

Labelled a state-significant development, locals said it was approved in July behind their backs.

The project did not receive a single submission from the public, with some locals saying they never received a letter.

Goodman Group said it had sent correspondence to more than 1,200 homes and businesses, three times.

SCRAP said it would continue campaigning against the logistics hub on the riverfront and for a ban on all new AI data centres.

World.title: Final Garage Sale Trail after 16 years of re-homing second-hand goods
World.content:
From casual beginnings in Bondi in 2010 to a nationwide annual event, the Garage Sale Trail has found a new home for more than seven million pre-loved items and, in doing so, generated $52 million for sellers.

It is a long way from what co-founder Darryl Nichols said started as a "smell of an oily rag production".

He and friend Andrew Valder called for community members in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs to host a second-hand sale.

To their surprise, 130 people signed up, and it grew from there.

The success and the impact are beyond anything they could have imagined.

Darryl Nichols co-founded the Garage Sale Trail in 2010. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

"Garage sales are a quintessential part of Australian culture," Mr Nichols said.

"They go along with Vegemite, going to the beach, watching the cricket in summer and all that good stuff.

"When the internet sort of started to kick in, in the late 90s and early 2000s, and we saw … marketplaces like eBay enter the game, maybe the humble old garage sale did take a bit of a hit.

"But we've certainly found over the years that the Garage Sale Trail provides a wonderful opportunity for people who have been thinking about having a garage sale but never sort of got around to doing it ."

More than 7.2 million second-hand items have been sold through the Garage Sale Trail since 2010. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

This year, the final event occurs across two weekends, with Sunday, November 15, to be the final day.

Mr Nichols said it was the right time to walk away.

"It's been such an incredible journey we feel like we've really made a big contribution to reuse and circularity in Australia," he said.

"Perhaps there's someone out there … that might be interested in taking on the custodianship of Garage Sale Trail … but we feel like we've made a strong contribution and we're ready for the next chapter."

Reducing landfill

According to the NSW Environment Protection Authority, Greater Sydney is on track to run out of landfill space by 2030 unless more is done to reduce waste.

In a statement, the EPA described the Garage Sale Trail as "a fantastic initiative that helps to divert waste from landfill and reduce illegal dumping by encouraging reuse as part of a circular economy."

From her garage sale at Kanwal on the NSW Central Coast, Kalie Chaney agreed.

"I honestly don't think I could work at a tip because it would break my heart seeing all the things people throw away," she said.

The NSW Environment Protection Authority says the Garage Sale Trail helped divert waste from landfill and reduce illegal dumping. (ABC Central Coast: Shauna Foley)

Ms Chaney collects items from the 1960s and 70s.

"Things were made to last back then … whether it's furniture or Tupperware or dinner plates, they are still usable," she said

"It's good to save them, because a lot of these items [would otherwise] go to landfill."

Community connection

Recycling and reuse aside, there is something about a garage sale that gets people talking.

Bill Mallie popped into Ms Chaney's garage sale for the social aspect.

"It brings neighbours together … it's a community thing," Mr Mallie said.

Bill Mallie says garage sales bring the community together. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

"At my age I need to get rid of stuff, I don't need to bring stuff in."

"[But] it's neighbours … helping each other clearing out stuff, recycling things [so] they don't wind up in the dump … what a great idea."

Mr Nichols said the social side of the movement has been almost as profound as its environmental side.

"The average person that gets involved makes about 30 new neighbourly connections through the day," he said.

Around 12,000 hosts are taking part in the final Garage Sale Trail. (ABC Central Coast: Shauna Foley)

"When you have a garage sale … people drop their guard a little bit because you're putting all this stuff out the front of your house, it kind of says a little bit about who you are and provides this lovely opportunity for people to connect."

"At the end of the day, it's the contribution it's made to keeping perfectly great stuff out of landfill and bringing local people together that probably is the real win for our nation."

World.title: One trainer was fined $50k, the other was banned for a month. This is how their cases differed
World.content:
Blinkers On SportRacingVictorian racing One trainer was fined $50k, the other was banned for a month. This is how their cases differed Danny Russell November 8, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Blinkers On is a weekly column covering the biggest issues of the spring racing carnival. On face value, Chris Waller’s $50,000 fine for a Melbourne Cup day indiscretion is a sizable whack. Chris Waller with star jockey James McDonald on Champions Day at Flemington. Getty Images Not only did the owners of his stayer Asterix miss out on a guaranteed $100,000 in prize money for taking part in the race, the trainer flew out of Melbourne with a lighter wallet. But even in racing, there are accidents and then there are accidents.



Waller’s large fine was the Freedman stable’s one-month ban. Here’s why. Related Article Updated

Racing integrity ‘Trainers are now on notice’: Melbourne Cup winners Anthony and Sam Freedman learn fate at tribunal Asterix was scratched on the morning of the Cup because it was treated with medication by a staff member on a race day; a forbidden practice, even though the anti-inflammatory oil rubbed onto the gelding’s front legs is available over the counter and not considered performance enhancing. Waller was charged and fined by stewards with breaching racing rule AR 227 (a) – engaging in conduct that has led to a breach of the rules. “I respect the decision,” Waller said on Thursday. “I think everyone will have a review of their systems post-carnival. Everyone’s doing their job, everyone’s under pressure.”



In comparison, Anthony and Sam Freedman were disqualified for a month earlier this year after breaching race-day treatment rules. Similar to Waller, they also blamed the mistake on staff. Horse trainers Anthony and Sam Freedman. Getty But they were charged by stewards with breaching a more serious charge, AR 249 – administration of medication on race day, which comes with a mandatory six-month ban except in mitigating circumstances. Two Freedman horses were found to be treated with nebulizers – a prescription-only medication allowed to be administered on non-race days via a breathing apparatus to help horses with breathing issues.



So, were the Freedmans harshly done by in comparison to Waller? We’ll let Racing Victoria explain. Related Article Victorian racing Cripps, Blues party as Birdman wins Champions Stakes; Tears as Waller speaks about Cup scratching “It is important that the stewards approach each inquiry through its own lens and maintain an open mind,” a Racing Victoria spokesperson told this column. “The stewards noted some important differences between the two cases in question. “These differences included the circumstances in which the breach was detected, the number of horses involved, the routes of administration, the products used and the potential to affect performance.”



Staff, the collateral damage Trainer Nick Ryan faces years on the sidelines if found guilty of a more serious breach. Stewards charged Ryan after allegedly discovering syringes of man-made EPO in the glove box of his car outside his Flemington stables at the start of Derby Day. All horses have been transferred from Nick Ryan’s stables. Getty Images The substance, Darbepoetin Alfa, is performance enhancing.



While Ryan was charged with AR 250 (a) – possession of a prohibited substance – the case has been deferred until the end of this month after a legal application on behalf of Ryan, who has reserved his plea. Related Article Melbourne Cup briefing

Melbourne Cup Buck of the Irish: The internationals who lit up Melbourne Cup betting But there have already been serious ramifications. Ryan has been stood down from training until the case is heard, and his horses sent to other stables. Further to that, stewards took evidence from Flemington vet Dr Luke Campbell, following “his conduct at the time” of their raid. Campbell has not been charged, and can continue working with racing stables. He did not respond to this masthead’s request for comment.



But when asked if the investigation would spread any wider, a Racing Victorian spokesperson told this masthead they would not comment on “matters our integrity team may or may not be investigating” “What we will say is that the inquiries involving trainer Nick Ryan and permitted veterinarian Dr Luke Campbell remain active, with both adjourned at this time,” the spokesperson said. “If, during the course of those inquiries or through any other means, any other licensed, registered or relevant person is found to have breached the rules of racing then we will communicate that with a stewards report announcing the charge(s) at that time, which is standard practice.” There is already considerable collateral damage in this case. Ryan’s stable staff all find themselves out of work. But stewards have to be commended for their actions over Cup week. They acted quickly and decisively in both the Ryan and Waller cases, all while keeping the public well-informed about matters of integrity.



Mega stables take control Among the back-slapping and admiration for Ciaron Maher’s record-breaking ability to train the first three horses home in the Melbourne Cup, a number of concerns were flagged. Trainer Ciaron Maher celebrates winning the Melbourne Cup with his horse Point Of Law. Getty Images Have the mega-stables become too dominant, and can it lead to team riding in big races – a prospect allowed but frowned upon by fans in sports such as cycling and F1, but banned in horse racing because of gambling outcomes? First to the Cup. Maher had seven horses in Tuesday’s 3200m staying test and filled five of the first six placings, including running the trifecta.



He did so after one of his less-fancied Cup runners, Royal Supremacy, bolted to the lead and bowled along in front. Visually, it raised eyebrows, especially considering the results. But did it set the race up for Maher? Stewards questioned Royal Supremacy’s jockey Ben Allen, but did not have an issue. After rewatching replays of the Cup, they were right. Allen set a solid tempo, but he did not cook his horse. They still held on for fifth, and he should be commended for the ride. If anyone were to blame, it was the rival jockeys. None of them reacted in time. Even the best of the best James McDonald tended to agree.



Related Article Melbourne Cup Melbourne Cup finishing order and results: From Maher’s stunning trifecta to Vauban’s lowly finish “I was on a back marker (Trustyourinstincts), so I could say I was disappointed in myself for not making a move, but that’s the situation you’re in,” he said on Thursday. “You’re not relying on others to make luck for you. You have to make your own luck sometimes, and it’s just the way the race was run.” The biggest tactical blunder was committed by Beau Mertens on Joseph O’Brien’s dour stayer Kizlyar. He led the trailing pack and should have set off earlier in pursuit of Royal Supremacy to make the race a true staying test.



Waller, Maher reign supreme The continued dominance of Maher and Waller is a worrying trend for smaller stables trying to compete, or even survive. The pair won six of the eight group 1 on offer during Melbourne Cup week – three each. Both trained trifectas in two of these events – Maher in the Cup, Waller in the Champions Mile. The two remaining group 1s were won by David Payne in the VRC Oaks, and the Freedmans in the Champions Sprint. So, is it healthy for racing? I guess it depends on who you own your horses with.



But while it becomes a monotonous storyline, the sport has a history of levelling itself out. It would be a dangerous precedent, and perhaps a breach of fair trade rules, to start imposing limits. The Coffey Cup dilemma Harry Coffey’s ability to ride Shockletz in the Melbourne Cup two days after surgery to repair a broken collarbone illustrated his bravery as well as his physical and mental toughness. Harry Coffey suffered a broken collar bone after a fall on Derby Day. Getty It must have also tested the resolve of the horse’s owners and trainer Ciaron Maher.



Heading into a $10.2 million group 1 race, even with a highly fancied lightweight runner, you need everything to go right. Sweating on a jockey’s fitness, while having concerns for his wellbeing, is not part of a usual Cup preparation. Especially when a worthy replacement, Michael Dee, is waiting in the wings. It is safe to say not all trainers and owners would have shown such faith, or taken the risk. Unfortunately for Coffey, Shockletz never had a winning chance considering the way the Cup was run – she had to drop back from a wide gate in a slowly run race. Fortunately for the connections, trainer and medical staff who cleared him to compete, Coffey delivered on his promise to ride Shockletz well. She ran home strongly to finish fifth.



Valley of dreams for Dees Melbourne Football Club has all but abandoned plans to relocate to Caulfield, but maybe it should not give up on racing. The city is visible from Moonee Valley Race Club’s construction site. Joe Armao Moonee Valley Racing Club is willing to have discussions with the Demons about sharing a home base. The Valley venue ticks a lot of boxes.



The club owns its land, is undergoing a mega rebuild, has room for two ovals on its infield, scope to incorporate offices and training facilities, and is open to business partnerships such as opening an on-site medical centre. Related Article AFL 2026 Turf war at Caulfield leaves Demons’ home base project on life support Moonee Valley originally reached out to Paul Guerra when he was the Demons CEO, but did not gain any traction, considering Caulfield was the main focus. Guerra’s dismissal by Melbourne is currently before the courts. “We have previously had discussions with the AFL about incorporating ovals in our infield,” Valley chair Adam Lennen told this column. “We are open to having further discussions with them that could involve Melbourne Football Club.”



Moonee Valley is still three years away from building a new grandstand and is under pressure to host the return of the Cox Plate next year if it can’t efficiently host a 15,000-strong crowd using temporary infrastructure. But the biggest obstacle to Melbourne considering such a move is the north-western location. It is not always palatable to cross the Yarra River from the eastern suburbs. Melbourne has been contacted for comment. Racing publican linked to election Another interesting name has popped up in the looming Victoria Racing Club election fight – popular publican Andrew Lewis.



For more than 30 years, his family ran racing’s “local”, The Emerald hotel at South Melbourne, before stepping away from the pub game three months ago. Related Article Spring racing carnival Behind the curtain of racing’s power struggle, and how it could shake up the sport Whether Lewis stands this year, or more likely next, those close to him say he has a lot to offer a race club committee such as Flemington, considering his years of experience in the hospitality world. Those who have nominated this year for a seat on the VRC board include Bill Guest, Nick Tzaferis, John Kanga, Justin O’Kane and Claire Ewart-Kennedy. All potential candidates have to be vetted before being cleared to run. The election will open later this month. Read more from our racing coverage

World.content:

George Brandis’ defence of free speech is as articulate today as it was when he addressed the parliament all those years ago on section 18c of the Racial Discrimination Act (“I will always defend someone’s right to be a bigot – it’s hypocrisy that annoys me more”, November 7). However, as he did then, he omits a critical factor from his argument – what happens when free speech becomes incitement to violence? Of course free speech is a cornerstone of liberal democracy, but we cannot reasonably insist on the right to say what we want in the public square without considering the consequences of urging violence against others, whether it be on the basis of race, religion, gender or sexual preference. Everything begins with words, and that includes violence. It is invidious to abandon all restraints, throw caution to the wind and let everyone say what they will. Where will social cohesion be then? Vic Alhadeff, Darlinghurst Senator Hanson wore a burqa into the Senate on Thursday, August 17, 2017. Andrew Meares George Brandis will always defend the right to be a bigot, as long as it does not offend him personally, as it did when his bigotry chicken came home to roost on the Senate crossbenches in the form of Pauline Hanson in a burqa nine years ago. Therein lies his hypocrisy. He thinks everyone else should be subject to random offensive bigotry without the protection of the law because offensive bigotry constitutes “free speech”. The right to feel safe from racist, sexist or other bigoted attack is surely a hallmark of a civilised society. Free speech is surely the right to express political, religious or philosophical opinions without feeling free to make bigoted personal attacks. “Freedom of political communication” does not include telling an opponent who happened to be born in another country to “pack your bags and go home”, or as Pauline Hanson said to Mehreen Faruqi in the Senate: “Piss off back to Pakistan”. June Simpson, Petersham War not genocide Plestia Alaqad repeats the genocide libel against Israel ad nauseam (“The Gaza reporter who captured the world’s eye”, November 7). It’s a war, not a genocide. Countries committing genocide don’t warn and evacuate civilians, allow millions of tonnes of food aid or provide polio vaccines, as Israel did. She claims that Israel falsely labels journalists as Hamas members, but recently Hamas has been publishing notices celebrating supposed journalists killed as “martyred” military members. The article mentions that Israel began a major offensive in Lebanon in 2024. That was only after 11 months of incessant bombing of Israel by Hezbollah. Alaqad says she refuses to appear on panels with supporters of Israel because she doesn’t want to have to debate whether she has the right to exist as a Palestinian. It’s a pity she wasn’t asked whether she believes Israel has the right to exist. The Hamas terrorists who rule Gaza and started the war certainly don’t. Shane Shmuel, Elsternwick (Vic) One Nation danger signs We’ve seen the results in the US, when billionaires bankroll unqualified and unscrupulous people into political office. Chaos, corruption, nepotism and incompetence ensue, and the rules of law, political and legal convention and ethical behaviour are discarded. If One Nation “loyalist” Sean Black warns Gina Rinehart is dictating strategy; James Ashby may be enriching himself; nepotism is rife; candidates display a lack of competence to wield power; and some insiders “don’t have a clue what democracy is”, we should all heed his warning, as he is in a better position than most to make these calls (“Secret tapes reveal turmoil for One Nation, Rinehart ties”, November 7). Add to this Pauline Hanson’s Trump-like actions in refusing to answer questions from journalists, and barring of media that she doesn’t like, and we have many danger signs that voters should not ignore. Alan Marel, North Curl Curl



Are Mar-a-Lago partygoers Gina Rinehart and Pauline Hanson ready for Trump’s celebrations of the midterm election’s outcomes? William Forbes, Medowie Gina Rinehart at Mar-a-Lago in 2024. Economically challenged I can only assume/hope that Peter Hartcher was being ironic when he asked of the Liberals, “Can you recover your standing as the most credible economic manager?” So was the profligacy of the Morrison era credible economic management (“Trump’s midterms shellacking is a gift in disguise to the Liberal Party”, November 7)? And what of the Howard/Costello changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing that has pushed up house prices 400 per cent? The liquidation of public assets and programs for tax cuts, Telstra, Qantas and all the others? Labor has to its credit the reforms of the Hawke/Keating years, the saving of the economy during the global financial crisis and finally the albeit too cautious reforms of the Albanese government. The Liberals better economic managers? In what strange parallel universe is that? Nicholas Triggs, Katoomba Peter Hartcher lets the Liberals off the hook. Sure, it’s time for them to distance themselves from toxic Trump, but there is no backbone in their economic policies. Hartcher should have nailed the usual mantra that the Liberals are the better economic managers. So, reversing tax changes, removing green energy incentives and undermining migrant workers are credible policies? When are we going to learn that negativity doesn’t equal economic management? Michael Blissenden, Castle Hill Payman owed her dues Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s refusal to allocate an adviser-level position to independent senator Fatima Payman’s office appears petty and vindictive (“From ‘token Muslim’ to a thorn in Labor’s side”, November 8). Especially when one considers every other independent parliamentarian has been granted this staffing allocation. One expects a prime minister to rise above the fray, rather than behave like a punitive factional boss. Albanese would do better to reconsider Labor’s anachronistic prohibition on its members crossing the floor. Payman’s departure from Labor followed her vote to recognise Palestine – a position the government itself subsequently adopted. Was she not simply ahead of her party? Labor’s insistence on conformity reflects its socialist traditions but is anachronistic. A truly democratic party needs to accommodate dissent, not punish it. Solidarity should not require the surrender of individual conscience. It is a mark of totalitarian governments to compel conformity, not democracies. Salvatore Sorbello, Campsie



Independent senator for Western Australia Fatima Payman in Sydney on November 2. Sitthixay Ditthavong Another “own goal” if it is true about the bribe offered to Fatima Payman, but why has she been silent for so long (“PM offered me staff in return for my vote: Payman”, November 7)? If it is true, then why tell us about it two years later. Looks like payback, and doesn’t do her own reputation and credibility any good either. Ian Ferrier, Long Jetty Bring on 2028 total detox Related Article Poultry Easy duck a l'orange < 30 mins Enjoyed the letters today commenting on Donald (Letters, November 7). Yes, it’s fabulous that the US is shedding itself of the DTs, and let’s hope withdrawal is finalised with the presidential election in 2028 and total detox.

Wendy Crew, Lane Cove North They say revenge is a dish best served cold. I can think of a better dish: lame duck a l’orange. Stephen Driscoll, Castle Hill Welcome straight bat from Uzzie



Thank goodness Usman Khawaja has come out and rescued Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft from the depths of the sandpaper scandal (“‘It was all of us’: Khawaja blows whistle on use of sandpaper”, November 7). Otherwise, the reputation of those three could have been besmirched for years. Could I suggest there should be some sort of financial reward given to Usman for pouring out his conscience to the public in such a timely fashion? Bernie Bourke, Ourimbah The publication by Usman Khawaja that the whole team knew about the sandpaper tactic is finally stating the bleeding obvious. The multitude of Australians who have played team sport have all experienced the fact that one of the joys of team sport is being in on what “today’s tactics are”. The idea that a professional team wouldn’t have shared a tactic beyond three players has always beggared belief. Well played, Uzzie. Tony Denzel, Bonny Hills Usman Khawaja has written about the sandpaper scandal in his new autobiography. Dan Peled Usman Khawaja’s sandpapergate revelation that “it was all of us” brings to mind that great line attributed to the Australian vice captain during the famous Bodyline series. To paraphrase: “Which one of you bastards called this bastard a bastard?” I mean, next you’ll be telling me the bloody Poms cheat! Phil Bradshaw, Naremburn Aristocratic touch I am exactly 100 years younger than David Jones and have some very vivid memories of visits to the store as a child (“It’s deja vu for David Jones as hard times leave it praying for a saviour”, November 7). On one occasion, just after the end of World War II, I visited the store with my mother on a well-publicised sale day. I witnessed, with the fascination of a seven-year-old, a fist fight and tug-of-war battle between two ladies over a bolt of material. I can also attest that the store treated its customers like royalty. My mother received a parcel purchased at DJs with her name typed as “The Countess E.E. Moroney”. Puzzled, she finally worked out that she must have said to the saleswoman, “The account is E.E. Moroney”. She cut out the label and kept it as a souvenir for the rest of her life. Nora Hinchen, Naremburn David Jones was for the majority of its life run as a family business. My mum was a “lady in black” in the 1960s at its flagship Elizabeth Street store, and as a 14-year-old, I worked there in the school holidays, as did many of the other ladies’ kids. Its chairman, Charles Lloyd Jones, roamed the store with his entourage of department managers. It was like being part of a big family, and service to the customer was the creed. The Jones family sold out, and the corporates took over. A different focus on profit and return on equity was their principal motive. They changed the way the store was managed and operated. This is the result. Richard Talbot, Cremorne Point



Julia Ormond, second from right, and staff in the movie Ladies in Black. Film-maker Sue Milliken’s popular film Ladies in Black is a timely reminder of the established treasures represented by David Jones. Seeing heart-breaking qualities erased by corporate forces over and over again leave our beautiful cities collectively cheapened into the bargain bins. The fabulous Sydney era, especially as represented by the ladies in black, Mark Foy’s, the Regent Theatre, the Trocadero, the Plaza Theatre, the Hotel Australia and many high-style establishments of culture and quality represents upmarket aspirant life at its functional best. The markdown fever represented by the discount grab email sees all generations diminished into silent disappointment. We had better be careful that the Capitol Theatre, Luna Park or the Steyne Ferry are not traded in for “opportunity makeovers” or the ruthless forces will wipe out our best remaining treasures. Paul Brennan, Point Clare In 1985, I met my husband in the cosmetic department at David Jones; he’d got lost trying to find haberdashery to buy a button for his CBA jacket uniform. So it goes without saying: “There’s no other store like David Jones”. It’s been our motto all these years! Wendy Bull, North Turramurra Rich can afford cuts Related Article Opinion

Household debt Six months ago, Australians were optimistic. Now, we’re cutting back on toothpaste Victoria Devine Money columnist A huge shout-out must go to your economics writer Millie Muroi for her excellent analysis of the roles of the government and Reserve Bank in managing the inflation problem (“Cutting government spending could put the economy in a worse position”, November 7). It was a measured and thoughtful article, free of bias or exaggeration, and should be required reading for all politicians and commentators, the majority of whom, I would suggest, know very little about economics. The suggestions that she quotes from the Australia Institute for cuts to private school subsidies and tax breaks for wealthy superannuants are eminently sensible, but of course any attempt to cut government spending in this way would raise a massive scare campaign from the likes of Tim Wilson, the Murdoch media, One Nation and entitled Baby Boomers, which is probably a fight Albo would be too chicken to take on. When it is all boiled down, any cuts will have to affect someone, and it may as well be those who are most able to afford them. Phil Peak, Dubbo Targeted species

World.title: Wilson makes key infrastructure vow ahead of royal commission
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Wilson makes key infrastructure vow ahead of royal commission Chip Le Grand November 8, 2026 — 6:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A political divide has opened over the management of major projects in Victoria ahead of the Big Build royal commission’s first public hearings, with Opposition Leader Jess Wilson vowing to keep and expand an independent advisory body that Premier Ben Carroll has pledged to abolish. This week’s hearings for the Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria is expected to focus on allegations that former premier Jacinta Allan helped shoehorn the CFMEU and a corrupt labour hire company into a level crossing project. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and Premier Ben Carroll are set to face off in the state election. Harry Afentoglou The Kourakis royal commission has announced that its first public hearings, starting on Monday, will examine the Gap Road project in Sunbury, a level crossing removal completed in 2023. This masthead has previously reported allegations that Allan, as the government minister responsible for the Big Build at the time, pressured the Rail Infrastructure Alliance consortium overseeing the project to side with the CFMEU in a demarcation dispute with its rival building union, the AWU.



The allegation, which Allan denies, is that her staff, through public servants working for Rail Projects Victoria, directed the consortium to “cut a deal with the CFMEU”. A subsequent agreement struck between the CFMEU and the consortium partners gave the union an industrial stranglehold over the Sunbury site. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Airport rail study doctored to ‘bake-in’ Sunshine as preferred route, commission told The CFMEU, once entrenched at the site, demanded that labour hire company BK Labour be used on the project. The company was subsequently investigated by Victoria Police and this year deregistered by the Labour Hire Authority for providing false invoices to the regulator. There are separate allegations before the royal commission, also denied by Allan, that doctored costings were included in the business case for another Big Build project, the Melbourne Airport Rail Link, and that a public service executive was threatened with the sack to ensure the proposed rail line followed the government’s preferred route. On Sunday, Wilson announced that the fate of Infrastructure Victoria – a statutory agency established early in the life of the Andrews Labor government to provide strategic advice on the state’s infrastructure priorities and appraise the merits of individual projects – would be decided by the November 28 state election.



In August, shortly after taking over as premier, Carroll earmarked the agency for the bureaucratic scrap heap. However, with it having just completed a round of structural redundancies as part of an annual budget reduction from $9 million to $6 million, Wilson announced on Sunday that she would not only retain Infrastructure Victoria, but broaden its remit. Wilson took up the cudgels for the agency during a visit to a mixed martial arts gym in Collingwood to promote a $40 million pitch to lure UFC bouts to Melbourne. In the blue corner: Wilson has taken up the fight for Infrastructure Victoria. Luis Enrique Ascui “I think it’s an important body that hasn’t been well used by this Labor government,” she said of Infrastructure Victoria. “This is a government that has been choosing projects because of politics by putting their own political interests over that of the Victorian taxpayer. So we will keep Infrastructure Victoria. We will look at how we potentially strengthen their role.”



Wilson says a Coalition government will keep Infrastructure Victoria and expand its role. Luis Enrique Ascui When it was established in 2015, the agency was made responsible for publishing a 30-year infrastructure plan for the state, one which was to be updated every five years. It was also given authority to provide advice to the treasurer when requested on any government or private sector proposals for major projects. “Government must prioritise and select the projects and reforms that deliver the highest public net benefit,” Allan told parliament at the time. “These decisions are not easy, but they should always be based on evidence and robust, transparent analysis.” In NSW, South Australia, Western Australia and at the federal level, similar bodies provide advice to governments about major projects. In some cases, this advice is provided before projects are announced and publicly committed to. However, in Victoria, the agency first learnt about the Suburban Rail Loop – the state’s largest infrastructure project – when the government announced the project via Facebook in the lead up to the 2018 election. Its advice was also not sought at the preliminary stage of the Melbourne Airport Rail Link or of any other Big Build project.



In December last year, Infrastructure Victoria was identified for the chop by the Silver Review of the Victorian Public Service. “Infrastructure Victoria has undertaken good work but now is an appropriate time to absorb its operations into a department,” the review stated. The Allan government decided not to scrap the agency, but said its operating budget would be reduced. In August this year, the Carroll government announced it would axe Infrastructure Victoria entirely to find “commonsense savings” to the budget. The announcement was slammed by key stakeholder groups who lauded the role of Infrastructure Victoria and urged the government to reconsider its decision. “With an election on the Victorian horizon, independent scrutiny of the investment pipeline is more critical than ever,” Consult Australia chief Jonathan Cartledge said. “The agency needs to be strengthened, not abolished.”



Wilson said that if the Coalition forms the next state government, it would look for ways to put Infrastructure Victoria to better use. Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Can you work with the union or not?’ Allan ‘linked’ to Big Build’s back-room dealmaking “We’re very open to looking at how we expand their remit to provide that advice to government,” she said. “We are certainly looking at how we can bring more transparency, more accountability to major infrastructure projects here in Victoria, and that’s exactly why we will keep Infrastructure Victoria.” The first block of royal commission public hearings is scheduled to run until November 20 – two days after early voting begins for the state election. During her time as premier, Allan resisted pressure from integrity experts and some of her own MPs to establish a royal commission into the Building Bad scandal. Within hours of replacing her as premier in July, Carroll announced he would call one.

World.title: Crypto’s Trump-fuelled Washington boom comes to an abrupt halt
World.content:
Analysis BusinessMarketsCryptocurrencies Crypto’s Trump-fuelled Washington boom comes to an abrupt halt Teresa Xie and Scott Patterson November 8, 2026 — 6:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Crypto’s extraordinary run of political good fortune in Washington has come to an abrupt halt. With Democrats set to control Congress following their midterm sweep, the industry faces the prospect of tougher rules and closer scrutiny of its ties to President Donald Trump. For two years, the industry enjoyed something few businesses ever get in the nation’s capital: a president who made digital assets a national priority while amassing his own crypto fortune, regulators clearing a path for wider adoption, and a Republican Congress sympathetic to its agenda. Donald Trump has given crypto a huge push in the US during his term. The New York Times Now crypto faces the harder test of becoming a lasting force in finance as its extraordinary political advantage evaporates. The Democratic sweep threatens to make comprehensive legislation harder to secure on the industry’s preferred terms and raises the prospect of congressional investigations into Trump’s crypto dealings. “Many significant figures in crypto aligned themselves with the Trump family,” said Austin Campbell, a crypto expert and former banker who is now an adjunct professor at the NYU Stern School of Business. “Those chickens are likely to come home to roost.”



Trump famously launched his own digital assets, welcomed crypto executives to the White House and made the industry’s ambitions part of his political agenda. In turn, crypto’s biggest victories became closely associated with his presidency, even as his personal financial interests complicated the industry’s efforts to secure broader political support. All that came to a head in September, when the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, which would have established clearer rules for exchanges and other digital-asset businesses. Trump’s crypto dealings became a flashpoint, though disagreements over stablecoin rewards, investor protections and banking competition also contributed to the impasse. Democratic control of Congress also brings greater power to investigate Trump’s business interests. The election is now set to change the terms of that debate. Democrats have signalled plans to demand tougher ethics restrictions, stronger consumer protections and a greater role for the Securities and Exchange Commission in overseeing digital assets. Those changes would depart from the framework many crypto companies sought under Republican control, but could also create a new path to legislation if the industry can build support across party lines.



“There’s going to be a defensive posture as the industry readjusts to new leadership, at least initially,” said Adam Minehardt, chief policy officer at Hyperliquid Policy Center. The industry’s big political bets could also have consequences. Sherrod Brown, defeated in 2024 as crypto lobby groups poured millions of dollars into the campaign against him, unseated Ohio’s Republican Senator, Jon Husted. Brown could take a top position on the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a key crypto regulator, according to researcher Capstone. Editor's pick Cryptocurrencies ‘Biggest hack in history’: Crypto giant freezes assets after $8.9b heist Democratic control of Congress also brings greater power to investigate Trump’s business interests. Lawmakers have already sought information about ventures involving the president and his family. Trump has consistently denied that his business interests conflict with his presidential duties. California Rep. Maxine Waters, a staunch critic of Trump’s crypto ties, is positioned to wield greater influence on the house financial services committee, while Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren is expected to lead the Senate banking committee.



“You’re going to have a real oversight agenda with empowered chairs,” said Minehardt. “We’re already seeing signals of it from different members’ offices. They’re going to pull all kinds of strings and see where they lead.” Still, many of crypto’s gains will be difficult to unwind. The federal stablecoin law would require new legislation to repeal, while the Securities and Exchange Commission and CFTC continue developing rules that could bring digital assets further into established financial markets. That work can proceed under Trump regardless of the election result, although future administrations could revisit agency decisions. Congress does have tools to influence regulators, such as the power of the purse, said Tyler Gellasch, chief executive of the Healthy Markets Association. It can seek to prevent agencies from spending resources on policy issues it disagrees with, a tool he said Republicans used for years to block the SEC from adopting political-spending disclosure rules. Congress can also investigate agency decisions and relationships with politically favoured firms, he said. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, was hit by a massive hack last month. Getty Images The market presents a different challenge. Bitcoin’s history of sharp boom-and-bust cycles under administrations of both parties complicates any attempt to attribute its price prospects to Washington. Bitcoin remains well below its previous highs, despite the Trump-era regulatory relief and political support that fuelled expectations of a golden age for digital assets.



The recent Binance hack underscored another challenge: security. The exchange suffered $6.3 billion in losses, but has since effectively replenished the stolen cryptocurrency, using a combination of money from its corporate treasury as well as two insurance funds. “The crypto industry needs to get these hacks out of the headlines,” said Peter Atwater, an adjunct economics professor at William & Mary. “Repetition matters. It will be interesting to see whether this propels Democrats to shift the regulatory pendulum back, with a greater emphasis on safety and soundness.” All told, crypto’s prospects extend well beyond its alliance with Trump. Digital assets now encompass investment funds, stablecoin payments and financial infrastructure involving institutions whose interests outlast any presidency. For an industry seeking customers across the political spectrum, a less partisan identity could ultimately prove an advantage rather than a setback. Industry advocates are already stressing their bipartisan ambitions. “Digital assets have always been bipartisan, and we stand ready to work with both new and returning members on both sides of the aisle,” said Ji Kim, chief executive of the Crypto Council for Innovation.
