World.title: ‘A nightmare for Pat Cummins’: Why Khawaja claims are set to dog Australia captain
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘A nightmare for Pat Cummins’: Why Khawaja claims are set to dog Australia captain Tom Decent November 8, 2026 — 6:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Among all the claims Usman Khawaja has published in the past few days – in his upcoming book and on his Instagram page – one was conspicuously wide of the mark. “I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I’m not in that team any more,” Khawaja said in a video on Sunday morning. “Now, my words don’t influence the team at all.” Loading Khawaja may no longer be a part of the Australian set-up, having retired from international cricket after the Ashes in January this year. But the Test team gearing up for the summer opener against New Zealand on December 9 features a number of players from that infamous 2018 series, including captain Pat Cummins. And as former Australian captain Mark Taylor put it on Sunday: “It’s going to be obviously a nightmare for Pat Cummins and the team leading into the summer of cricket.”



Normally, players bristle when the media brings up past controversies. This time, it is a former teammate who has reopened one of Australian cricket’s deepest wounds. If Khawaja felt the full story of “Sandpapergate”, the Australian ball-tampering scandal in 2018, had to be told, there were other ways to bring it into the public domain than through a publicity blitz while promoting a book from which he hopes to profit. That is the feeling of some influential figures in cricket across the country who have spoken to this masthead. Pat Cummins is given a cold towel by teammate Usman Khawaja during the second Test against Bangladesh in 2017. Getty After a weekend of headlines, explosive extracts and increasingly pointed responses, we still have not heard directly from the players at the centre of the original scandal. Steve Smith, who served a one-year ban, is in New York and understood to be watching the fallout closely. He will return for the first Test in Perth, and his next press conference promises to be well attended.



Khawaja claims sandpaper was used to rough up the ball near the boundary during the second Test in Gqeberha, then known as Port Elizabeth, before Cameron Bancroft was caught with it in during the next match in Cape Town. After the Cape Town incident, Smith told a press conference after play: “You can ask questions as much as you like, but I can promise you this is the first time that it’s happened.” David Warner and Usman Khawaja were long-term opening partners in the Test team. Getty Images That statement now sits in defiance of Khawaja’s version of events. David Warner, who also served a one-year ban, is in Nepal playing T20 cricket for the Kathmandu Gorkhas in the Nepal Premier League.



For one who spends so much time on social media, Warner’s silence after his childhood friend’s revelations speaks volumes. Whether he will offer his own account remains to be seen. He, too, has a book deal in his future. Warner will be in the commentary box this summer for Kayo Sports. So will Khawaja. Steve Smith addresses the media at Sydney Airport in 2018, after arriving back from the ball-tampering scandal in South Africa. Janie Barrett Joining them will be former Australian cricketer Alyssa Healy, whose husband, Mitchell Starc, has had his integrity effectively called into question by Khawaja’s insistence that everyone – bowlers, batters and staff – knew that sandpaper was being used illegally during that series. Healy will attend a Kayo Sports launch in Sydney on Tuesday. Neither Khawaja nor Warner will be there. Nathan Lyon was originally scheduled to appear, but withdrew because of the impending birth of his child, a decision made well before Khawaja’s comments.



The four main bowlers from Cape Town – Pat Cummins, Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Lyon – are standing by their 2021 statement, according to their managers. That statement rejected suggestions they knew a foreign substance had been taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball. As things stand, they will not be releasing a fresh joint statement. The bowlers are content to let Khawaja do the talking. The social media reaction to his revelations has certainly not been universally supportive. The bowlers have no desire to give Khawaja’s allegations any more oxygen, particularly after Khawaja doubled down on Sunday, refusing to retreat from his assertion that “everyone knew”.



How to sum up their mood behind closed doors? Annoyed, but hardly surprised. Will they be inviting Khawaja over for a barbecue any time soon? No. Would they have anyway? Probably not. Australia’s Pat Cummins and Usman Khawaja during a net session in 2023. Getty Images The first member of the current Test team to face the media since Khawaja dropped his bombshell will likely be NSW captain Nic Maddinson, who is scheduled to speak on Monday ahead of the Blues’ Sheffield Shield clash with South Australia on Wednesday. Maddinson had nothing to do with the 2018 South Africa tour. That won’t stop him being asked about a scandal that threatens to stick to Australian cricket like mud on a white shirt.



If he takes some wickets for NSW, Lyon may field questions after play about Khawaja’s admission that he was “pissed” that the off-spinner dropped a ball near South Africa’s AB de Villiers after a run-out during that series. Similar inquiries await Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood whenever they make public appearances leading into the first Test. Nathan Lyon drops the ball in the direction of AB de Villiers. AP Mitch Marsh is another player worth watching. He was part of the 2018 South Africa touring party and will captain Australia’s white-ball sides in upcoming matches against England, beginning on Friday. Marsh has never given a detailed account of what happened in Cape Town and was not a signatory to the bowlers’ statement five years ago. His next press conference will be worth watching.



Related Article Opinion

Test cricket Usman Khawaja remained silent for eight years. Why did he speak out now? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist Then there is Bancroft, who is weighing up if and when to speak publicly. He has already read the controversial chapter of Khawaja’s book, Sabr, which will be released on Tuesday. Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg will inevitably be drawn into the controversy, too. Khawaja claims Greenberg, then head of the Australian Cricketers’ Association, agreed with him in 2021 that the bowlers and everyone else involved in Cape Town should have accepted collective responsibility. A penny for the bowlers’ thoughts on that one. Darren Lehmann, the Australian coach at the time, suggested on Saturday that sometimes things are best left unsaid. Khawaja clearly disagrees. He believes he is doing the right thing and is entitled to tell and sell his version of events. But the manner and timing of his revelations have caused a major stir behind the scenes and ensured the fallout will dominate the build-up to the summer.



Eight years after Sandpapergate, Australian cricket is once again confronting a scandal it thought was buried. Only this time, the biggest threat isn’t coming from outside the dressing room. It’s coming from a player who was sitting inside it just a few months ago. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Only one in five voters trust Albanese now as blame sticks for cost of living
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalResolve Political Monitor Only one in five voters trust Albanese now as blame sticks for cost of living James Massola November 8, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Just 20 per cent of voters now say they trust Anthony Albanese, while the prime minister’s status as preferred leader and Labor’s two-party preferred vote are mired at record-low levels. Voters are squarely blaming the Albanese government and its latest budget for the cost-of-living crisis. With 42 per cent holding Labor responsible, the grim result demonstrates that Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ insistence that global factors were the chief drivers of inflation has failed to cut through. A quarter of respondents (26 per cent) blamed international causes such as soaring oil prices and the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran for the high cost of living, just 7 per cent of people pointed the finger at the Reserve Bank, 5 per cent blamed state governments and 3 per cent said it was the fault of businesses. Those findings suggest Albanese’s pre-emptive and thinly veiled criticism of the Reserve Bank’s latest rate hike as a “blunt instrument” has not taken the heat off Labor.



The survey of 2250 voters was conducted by Resolve Political Monitor from November 2 to 7, and came while Albanese attended a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates for the fifth time this year. All the movement in support for the parties is within the polls’ margin of error of plus or minus 2.1 per cent. The standing of the prime minister and Labor has been hit by a perfect storm of poor economic news, as interest rates rose to an 18-year-high of 4.85 per cent, September’s inflation figures came in higher than expected at 4.3 per cent, and Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock talked about Australians feeling like they were in a recession. Opposition frontbencher Dan Tehan told ABC’s Insiders that Labor should heed the lessons from the Republican rout at the US midterms last week: “Prime Minister Albanese, Jim Chalmers, and Chris Bowen should be paying very close attention [to the US midterm results]. I mean, cost of living was a key issue there that drove the change there, and I think people didn’t feel like the government, the Trump administration, was really 100 per cent focused on that. And I think it’s exactly the same here in Australia.”



In an interview with the ABC published on Saturday, Albanese pointed to the Iran war and tariffs as key reasons for the Republicans’ many defeats. Labor’s primary vote fell one point in the last month to equal a post-election low of 28 percentage points, down from 34.6 percentage points at the May 2025 election. But neither One Nation nor the Coalition directly benefited from the movement, with the Coalition also down one point to 22 per cent and One Nation steady on 25 per cent. The Greens crept 1 percentage point ahead in their primary vote for a second month in a row, rising to 13 per cent after the switch of leader from Larissa Waters to David Shoebridge. The scandal over a $6 million grant to the Marrickville Golf Club, in Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler, has also badly damaged voters’ trust in the prime minister.



Just 20 per cent of voters agreed they still trusted “what Albanese says and promises”, down 6 percentage points since September, while 22 per cent of people said they had lost trust in the prime minister. Of more concern was that 43 per cent agreed that “I did not trust Albanese before this anyway”, up a significant 9 percentage points since the question was last asked in September. The picture is worse for Labor in the contest for preferred prime minister, with Albanese down three percentage points to equal a record low of just 29 per cent, previously recorded in September, while support for Coalition leader Angus Taylor as preferred prime minister continues to inch back up, rising by 3 percentage points to 25 per cent in the past month to 25 per cent. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson status as preferred prime minister fell two percentage points to 24 per cent over the last month. Albanese’s net performance rating as prime minister – that is, the total percentage of people who said his performance has been good or very good, versus those who said it has been bad or very bad, has equalled a record low set in January this year in the wake of the Bondi massacre.



Just 34 per cent of voters said Albanese was doing a good or very good job, while 56 per cent said he was doing a poor or very poor job – delivering a net performance rating of -22 per cent. In contrast, 42 per cent of voters said Taylor was doing a good or very good job, while 33 per cent said his performance was bad or very bad and the rest were undecided, continuing a trend of small monthly improvements for the opposition leader. Hanson’s total “good” performance remained steady on 45 per cent, while the proportion of voters who rated her performance as poor increased 1 percentage point to 42 per cent.



Resolve Political Monitor pollster Jim Reed said the findings showed that “although Albanese, Chalmers and Labor are shedding personal capital at a rate of knots, their vote is holding up”. “Most damaging is that the PM is only trusted by a fifth of voters now. This is part being seen as distracted from the priority issues, like tackling inflation, but also the cumulative effect of surprise tax changes and the local grant program that have some voters questioning what’s coming next,” he said. The prime minister’s likeability rating has crashed to a record low, falling to a net negative score of minus 19 per cent, down four points in the past month. In contrast, Taylor rose 3 percentage points to plus 11 per cent – opening up a 30 per cent gap between the two – while Hanson’s net likeability score rose to plus 4 per cent. At the same time, the net likeability of the Labor Party fell another two points to minus 13 per cent in the last month and the Liberal Party’s net likeability rose 7 per cent to plus 11 per cent – a 24 per cent gap between the two major parties.



Keeping the cost of living low remains voters’ top policy priority by an overwhelming margin, as it has been all year, with 41 per cent of voters nominating it as their number one issue. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Sydney have booked a place in the AFLW semi-finals, defeating the Western Bulldogs by 29 points in a high-pressure clash at a windswept soggy Henson Park. This year’s leading goalkicker and star Swan Chloe Molly aided to her tally, banishing the Bulldogs – who fought their way into finals for first the first time since 2022 – back to the kennel by winning 7.4 (46) to 2.5 (17). Tanya Kennedy celebrates a goal with her teammates. AFL Photos The Swans asserted their dominance from the opening bounce, kicking three consecutive goals in the first quarter and leaving the Bulldogs goalless. Ellie Blackburn lifted for the Dogs in the second with a goal, but a magnificent Tanya Kennedy laid a crucial tag on Isabelle Pritchard, shutting down the Dog’s scoring capacity. When the siren blared, Swans placed raced to embrace each other, as loyal fans in red and white cheered on the boundary line, noticeably with inside-out umbrellas and soaked ponchos.



Tayla Smith competes with Alice Edmonds Getty Images This year has been an undeniably tricky year for Sydney. The women’s program has copped collateral damage from the Pullman hotel scandal and Tom Papley’s alleged drug offence, as some of the club’s men’s players continue to make headlines. But the Swans’ AFLW program has remained focused, drawing in record-breaking breaking crowds at Henson Park and continuing their finals campaign to book their spot in a semi-final against Geelong. Related Article AFLW finals

AFLW Dee-lighted: Melbourne storm back from the brink to leave Cats heartbroken; Roos smash Blues



The Cats feel agonisingly short in their qualifying final against Melbourne on Saturday, in a thrilling AFLW finals finish. Swans coach Colin O’Riordan said the team was thrilled with the win, but said the team was hungry to keep improving. “Scoreboard is important at the end of the game, but you don’t get there unless you stick to the process and you stick to what we are trying to do,” O’Riordan said. “The level of pressure thy brought across all four quarters, that was outstanding.” Hawthorn upset Gold Coast and notch breakthrough finals win



Hawthorn’s AFLW team has a complicated relationship with finals. The Hawks have had strong home and away seasons but typically run out of steam for their finals campaign, falling in straight sets over the past few years. Mikayla Williamson celebrates a goal with teammates AFL Photos But on Sunday they proved the naysayers wrong, defeating favourites Gold Coast by 18 points in Queensland to cement their first finals win. Sunday’s clash was incredibly close for the first half with both sides bringing intense pressure. As the scoreboard seesawed, Hawthorn finally broke away in the third, kicking three unanswered goals and grab a 15-point lead into the final break.



But the Suns weren’t done yet. Mikayla Nurse opened the quarter with a goal for the Suns and the home crowd roared their approval. But the Hawks held on, aided by majors from Mikaylah Antony and Mikayla Williamson to win 8.9 (57) to 6.3 (39). It was a disappointing ending to Gold Coast’s campaign. The team has had an extraordinary comeback this year after finishing last in 2025. The arrival of AFLW legend Erin Phillips as general manager of women’s football, plus the plethora of young academy talent means the Suns will likely be a deadly force next year. However for now, the team will anxiously wait for updates on youngster Ava Ulsher who has helped from the ground by medical staff after a collision with her teammate.



Hawthorn will now prepare for a semi-final clash with Carlton – the team that knocked them out of the finals last year. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: One trainer was fined $50k, the other was banned for a month. This is how their cases differed
World.content:
Blinkers On SportRacingVictorian racing One trainer was fined $50k, the other was banned for a month. This is how their cases differed Danny Russell November 8, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Blinkers On is a weekly column covering the biggest issues of the spring racing carnival. On face value, Chris Waller’s $50,000 fine for a Melbourne Cup day indiscretion is a sizable whack. Chris Waller with star jockey James McDonald on Champions Day at Flemington. Getty Images Not only did the owners of his stayer Asterix miss out on a guaranteed $100,000 in prize money for taking part in the race, the trainer flew out of Melbourne with a lighter wallet. But even in racing, there are accidents and then there are accidents.



Waller’s large fine was the Freedman stable’s one-month ban. Here’s why. Related Article Updated

Racing integrity ‘Trainers are now on notice’: Melbourne Cup winners Anthony and Sam Freedman learn fate at tribunal Asterix was scratched on the morning of the Cup because it was treated with medication by a staff member on a race day; a forbidden practice, even though the anti-inflammatory oil rubbed onto the gelding’s front legs is available over the counter and not considered performance enhancing. Waller was charged and fined by stewards with breaching racing rule AR 227 (a) – engaging in conduct that has led to a breach of the rules. “I respect the decision,” Waller said on Thursday. “I think everyone will have a review of their systems post-carnival. Everyone’s doing their job, everyone’s under pressure.”



In comparison, Anthony and Sam Freedman were disqualified for a month earlier this year after breaching race-day treatment rules. Similar to Waller, they also blamed the mistake on staff. Horse trainers Anthony and Sam Freedman. Getty But they were charged by stewards with breaching a more serious charge, AR 249 – administration of medication on race day, which comes with a mandatory six-month ban except in mitigating circumstances. Two Freedman horses were found to be treated with nebulizers – a prescription-only medication allowed to be administered on non-race days via a breathing apparatus to help horses with breathing issues.



So, were the Freedmans harshly done by in comparison to Waller? We’ll let Racing Victoria explain. Related Article Victorian racing Cripps, Blues party as Birdman wins Champions Stakes; Tears as Waller speaks about Cup scratching “It is important that the stewards approach each inquiry through its own lens and maintain an open mind,” a Racing Victoria spokesperson told this column. “The stewards noted some important differences between the two cases in question. “These differences included the circumstances in which the breach was detected, the number of horses involved, the routes of administration, the products used and the potential to affect performance.”



Staff, the collateral damage Trainer Nick Ryan faces years on the sidelines if found guilty of a more serious breach. Stewards charged Ryan after allegedly discovering syringes of man-made EPO in the glove box of his car outside his Flemington stables at the start of Derby Day. All horses have been transferred from Nick Ryan’s stables. Getty Images The substance, Darbepoetin Alfa, is performance enhancing.



While Ryan was charged with AR 250 (a) – possession of a prohibited substance – the case has been deferred until the end of this month after a legal application on behalf of Ryan, who has reserved his plea. Related Article Melbourne Cup briefing

Melbourne Cup Buck of the Irish: The internationals who lit up Melbourne Cup betting But there have already been serious ramifications. Ryan has been stood down from training until the case is heard, and his horses sent to other stables. Further to that, stewards took evidence from Flemington vet Dr Luke Campbell, following “his conduct at the time” of their raid. Campbell has not been charged, and can continue working with racing stables. He did not respond to this masthead’s request for comment.



But when asked if the investigation would spread any wider, a Racing Victorian spokesperson told this masthead they would not comment on “matters our integrity team may or may not be investigating” “What we will say is that the inquiries involving trainer Nick Ryan and permitted veterinarian Dr Luke Campbell remain active, with both adjourned at this time,” the spokesperson said. “If, during the course of those inquiries or through any other means, any other licensed, registered or relevant person is found to have breached the rules of racing then we will communicate that with a stewards report announcing the charge(s) at that time, which is standard practice.” There is already considerable collateral damage in this case. Ryan’s stable staff all find themselves out of work. But stewards have to be commended for their actions over Cup week. They acted quickly and decisively in both the Ryan and Waller cases, all while keeping the public well-informed about matters of integrity.



Mega stables take control Among the back-slapping and admiration for Ciaron Maher’s record-breaking ability to train the first three horses home in the Melbourne Cup, a number of concerns were flagged. Trainer Ciaron Maher celebrates winning the Melbourne Cup with his horse Point Of Law. Getty Images Have the mega-stables become too dominant, and can it lead to team riding in big races – a prospect allowed but frowned upon by fans in sports such as cycling and F1, but banned in horse racing because of gambling outcomes? First to the Cup. Maher had seven horses in Tuesday’s 3200m staying test and filled five of the first six placings, including running the trifecta.



He did so after one of his less-fancied Cup runners, Royal Supremacy, bolted to the lead and bowled along in front. Visually, it raised eyebrows, especially considering the results. But did it set the race up for Maher? Stewards questioned Royal Supremacy’s jockey Ben Allen, but did not have an issue. After rewatching replays of the Cup, they were right. Allen set a solid tempo, but he did not cook his horse. They still held on for fifth, and he should be commended for the ride. If anyone were to blame, it was the rival jockeys. None of them reacted in time. Even the best of the best James McDonald tended to agree.



Related Article Melbourne Cup Melbourne Cup finishing order and results: From Maher’s stunning trifecta to Vauban’s lowly finish “I was on a back marker (Trustyourinstincts), so I could say I was disappointed in myself for not making a move, but that’s the situation you’re in,” he said on Thursday. “You’re not relying on others to make luck for you. You have to make your own luck sometimes, and it’s just the way the race was run.” The biggest tactical blunder was committed by Beau Mertens on Joseph O’Brien’s dour stayer Kizlyar. He led the trailing pack and should have set off earlier in pursuit of Royal Supremacy to make the race a true staying test.



Waller, Maher reign supreme The continued dominance of Maher and Waller is a worrying trend for smaller stables trying to compete, or even survive. The pair won six of the eight group 1 on offer during Melbourne Cup week – three each. Both trained trifectas in two of these events – Maher in the Cup, Waller in the Champions Mile. The two remaining group 1s were won by David Payne in the VRC Oaks, and the Freedmans in the Champions Sprint. So, is it healthy for racing? I guess it depends on who you own your horses with.



But while it becomes a monotonous storyline, the sport has a history of levelling itself out. It would be a dangerous precedent, and perhaps a breach of fair trade rules, to start imposing limits. The Coffey Cup dilemma Harry Coffey’s ability to ride Shockletz in the Melbourne Cup two days after surgery to repair a broken collarbone illustrated his bravery as well as his physical and mental toughness. Harry Coffey suffered a broken collar bone after a fall on Derby Day. Getty It must have also tested the resolve of the horse’s owners and trainer Ciaron Maher.



Heading into a $10.2 million group 1 race, even with a highly fancied lightweight runner, you need everything to go right. Sweating on a jockey’s fitness, while having concerns for his wellbeing, is not part of a usual Cup preparation. Especially when a worthy replacement, Michael Dee, is waiting in the wings. It is safe to say not all trainers and owners would have shown such faith, or taken the risk. Unfortunately for Coffey, Shockletz never had a winning chance considering the way the Cup was run – she had to drop back from a wide gate in a slowly run race. Fortunately for the connections, trainer and medical staff who cleared him to compete, Coffey delivered on his promise to ride Shockletz well. She ran home strongly to finish fifth.



Valley of dreams for Dees Melbourne Football Club has all but abandoned plans to relocate to Caulfield, but maybe it should not give up on racing. The city is visible from Moonee Valley Race Club’s construction site. Joe Armao Moonee Valley Racing Club is willing to have discussions with the Demons about sharing a home base. The Valley venue ticks a lot of boxes.



The club owns its land, is undergoing a mega rebuild, has room for two ovals on its infield, scope to incorporate offices and training facilities, and is open to business partnerships such as opening an on-site medical centre. Related Article AFL 2026 Turf war at Caulfield leaves Demons’ home base project on life support Moonee Valley originally reached out to Paul Guerra when he was the Demons CEO, but did not gain any traction, considering Caulfield was the main focus. Guerra’s dismissal by Melbourne is currently before the courts. “We have previously had discussions with the AFL about incorporating ovals in our infield,” Valley chair Adam Lennen told this column. “We are open to having further discussions with them that could involve Melbourne Football Club.”



Moonee Valley is still three years away from building a new grandstand and is under pressure to host the return of the Cox Plate next year if it can’t efficiently host a 15,000-strong crowd using temporary infrastructure. But the biggest obstacle to Melbourne considering such a move is the north-western location. It is not always palatable to cross the Yarra River from the eastern suburbs. Melbourne has been contacted for comment. Racing publican linked to election Another interesting name has popped up in the looming Victoria Racing Club election fight – popular publican Andrew Lewis.



For more than 30 years, his family ran racing’s “local”, The Emerald hotel at South Melbourne, before stepping away from the pub game three months ago. Related Article Spring racing carnival Behind the curtain of racing’s power struggle, and how it could shake up the sport Whether Lewis stands this year, or more likely next, those close to him say he has a lot to offer a race club committee such as Flemington, considering his years of experience in the hospitality world. Those who have nominated this year for a seat on the VRC board include Bill Guest, Nick Tzaferis, John Kanga, Justin O’Kane and Claire Ewart-Kennedy. All potential candidates have to be vetted before being cleared to run. The election will open later this month. Read more from our racing coverage

World.title: Wilson makes key infrastructure vow ahead of royal commission
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Wilson makes key infrastructure vow ahead of royal commission Chip Le Grand November 8, 2026 — 6:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A political divide has opened over the management of major projects in Victoria ahead of the Big Build royal commission’s first public hearings, with Opposition Leader Jess Wilson vowing to keep and expand an independent advisory body that Premier Ben Carroll has pledged to abolish. This week’s hearings for the Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria is expected to focus on allegations that former premier Jacinta Allan helped shoehorn the CFMEU and a corrupt labour hire company into a level crossing project. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and Premier Ben Carroll are set to face off in the state election. Harry Afentoglou The Kourakis royal commission has announced that its first public hearings, starting on Monday, will examine the Gap Road project in Sunbury, a level crossing removal completed in 2023. This masthead has previously reported allegations that Allan, as the government minister responsible for the Big Build at the time, pressured the Rail Infrastructure Alliance consortium overseeing the project to side with the CFMEU in a demarcation dispute with its rival building union, the AWU.



The allegation, which Allan denies, is that her staff, through public servants working for Rail Projects Victoria, directed the consortium to “cut a deal with the CFMEU”. A subsequent agreement struck between the CFMEU and the consortium partners gave the union an industrial stranglehold over the Sunbury site. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Airport rail study doctored to ‘bake-in’ Sunshine as preferred route, commission told The CFMEU, once entrenched at the site, demanded that labour hire company BK Labour be used on the project. The company was subsequently investigated by Victoria Police and this year deregistered by the Labour Hire Authority for providing false invoices to the regulator. There are separate allegations before the royal commission, also denied by Allan, that doctored costings were included in the business case for another Big Build project, the Melbourne Airport Rail Link, and that a public service executive was threatened with the sack to ensure the proposed rail line followed the government’s preferred route. On Sunday, Wilson announced that the fate of Infrastructure Victoria – a statutory agency established early in the life of the Andrews Labor government to provide strategic advice on the state’s infrastructure priorities and appraise the merits of individual projects – would be decided by the November 28 state election.



In August, shortly after taking over as premier, Carroll earmarked the agency for the bureaucratic scrap heap. However, with it having just completed a round of structural redundancies as part of an annual budget reduction from $9 million to $6 million, Wilson announced on Sunday that she would not only retain Infrastructure Victoria, but broaden its remit. Wilson took up the cudgels for the agency during a visit to a mixed martial arts gym in Collingwood to promote a $40 million pitch to lure UFC bouts to Melbourne. In the blue corner: Wilson has taken up the fight for Infrastructure Victoria. Luis Enrique Ascui “I think it’s an important body that hasn’t been well used by this Labor government,” she said of Infrastructure Victoria. “This is a government that has been choosing projects because of politics by putting their own political interests over that of the Victorian taxpayer. So we will keep Infrastructure Victoria. We will look at how we potentially strengthen their role.”



Wilson says a Coalition government will keep Infrastructure Victoria and expand its role. Luis Enrique Ascui When it was established in 2015, the agency was made responsible for publishing a 30-year infrastructure plan for the state, one which was to be updated every five years. It was also given authority to provide advice to the treasurer when requested on any government or private sector proposals for major projects. “Government must prioritise and select the projects and reforms that deliver the highest public net benefit,” Allan told parliament at the time. “These decisions are not easy, but they should always be based on evidence and robust, transparent analysis.” In NSW, South Australia, Western Australia and at the federal level, similar bodies provide advice to governments about major projects. In some cases, this advice is provided before projects are announced and publicly committed to. However, in Victoria, the agency first learnt about the Suburban Rail Loop – the state’s largest infrastructure project – when the government announced the project via Facebook in the lead up to the 2018 election. Its advice was also not sought at the preliminary stage of the Melbourne Airport Rail Link or of any other Big Build project.



In December last year, Infrastructure Victoria was identified for the chop by the Silver Review of the Victorian Public Service. “Infrastructure Victoria has undertaken good work but now is an appropriate time to absorb its operations into a department,” the review stated. The Allan government decided not to scrap the agency, but said its operating budget would be reduced. In August this year, the Carroll government announced it would axe Infrastructure Victoria entirely to find “commonsense savings” to the budget. The announcement was slammed by key stakeholder groups who lauded the role of Infrastructure Victoria and urged the government to reconsider its decision. “With an election on the Victorian horizon, independent scrutiny of the investment pipeline is more critical than ever,” Consult Australia chief Jonathan Cartledge said. “The agency needs to be strengthened, not abolished.”



Wilson said that if the Coalition forms the next state government, it would look for ways to put Infrastructure Victoria to better use. Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Can you work with the union or not?’ Allan ‘linked’ to Big Build’s back-room dealmaking “We’re very open to looking at how we expand their remit to provide that advice to government,” she said. “We are certainly looking at how we can bring more transparency, more accountability to major infrastructure projects here in Victoria, and that’s exactly why we will keep Infrastructure Victoria.” The first block of royal commission public hearings is scheduled to run until November 20 – two days after early voting begins for the state election. During her time as premier, Allan resisted pressure from integrity experts and some of her own MPs to establish a royal commission into the Building Bad scandal. Within hours of replacing her as premier in July, Carroll announced he would call one.

World.title: Crypto’s Trump-fuelled Washington boom comes to an abrupt halt
World.content:
Analysis BusinessMarketsCryptocurrencies Crypto’s Trump-fuelled Washington boom comes to an abrupt halt Teresa Xie and Scott Patterson November 8, 2026 — 6:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Crypto’s extraordinary run of political good fortune in Washington has come to an abrupt halt. With Democrats set to control Congress following their midterm sweep, the industry faces the prospect of tougher rules and closer scrutiny of its ties to President Donald Trump. For two years, the industry enjoyed something few businesses ever get in the nation’s capital: a president who made digital assets a national priority while amassing his own crypto fortune, regulators clearing a path for wider adoption, and a Republican Congress sympathetic to its agenda. Donald Trump has given crypto a huge push in the US during his term. The New York Times Now crypto faces the harder test of becoming a lasting force in finance as its extraordinary political advantage evaporates. The Democratic sweep threatens to make comprehensive legislation harder to secure on the industry’s preferred terms and raises the prospect of congressional investigations into Trump’s crypto dealings. “Many significant figures in crypto aligned themselves with the Trump family,” said Austin Campbell, a crypto expert and former banker who is now an adjunct professor at the NYU Stern School of Business. “Those chickens are likely to come home to roost.”



Trump famously launched his own digital assets, welcomed crypto executives to the White House and made the industry’s ambitions part of his political agenda. In turn, crypto’s biggest victories became closely associated with his presidency, even as his personal financial interests complicated the industry’s efforts to secure broader political support. All that came to a head in September, when the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, which would have established clearer rules for exchanges and other digital-asset businesses. Trump’s crypto dealings became a flashpoint, though disagreements over stablecoin rewards, investor protections and banking competition also contributed to the impasse. Democratic control of Congress also brings greater power to investigate Trump’s business interests. The election is now set to change the terms of that debate. Democrats have signalled plans to demand tougher ethics restrictions, stronger consumer protections and a greater role for the Securities and Exchange Commission in overseeing digital assets. Those changes would depart from the framework many crypto companies sought under Republican control, but could also create a new path to legislation if the industry can build support across party lines.



“There’s going to be a defensive posture as the industry readjusts to new leadership, at least initially,” said Adam Minehardt, chief policy officer at Hyperliquid Policy Center. The industry’s big political bets could also have consequences. Sherrod Brown, defeated in 2024 as crypto lobby groups poured millions of dollars into the campaign against him, unseated Ohio’s Republican Senator, Jon Husted. Brown could take a top position on the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a key crypto regulator, according to researcher Capstone. Editor's pick Cryptocurrencies ‘Biggest hack in history’: Crypto giant freezes assets after $8.9b heist Democratic control of Congress also brings greater power to investigate Trump’s business interests. Lawmakers have already sought information about ventures involving the president and his family. Trump has consistently denied that his business interests conflict with his presidential duties. California Rep. Maxine Waters, a staunch critic of Trump’s crypto ties, is positioned to wield greater influence on the house financial services committee, while Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren is expected to lead the Senate banking committee.



“You’re going to have a real oversight agenda with empowered chairs,” said Minehardt. “We’re already seeing signals of it from different members’ offices. They’re going to pull all kinds of strings and see where they lead.” Still, many of crypto’s gains will be difficult to unwind. The federal stablecoin law would require new legislation to repeal, while the Securities and Exchange Commission and CFTC continue developing rules that could bring digital assets further into established financial markets. That work can proceed under Trump regardless of the election result, although future administrations could revisit agency decisions. Congress does have tools to influence regulators, such as the power of the purse, said Tyler Gellasch, chief executive of the Healthy Markets Association. It can seek to prevent agencies from spending resources on policy issues it disagrees with, a tool he said Republicans used for years to block the SEC from adopting political-spending disclosure rules. Congress can also investigate agency decisions and relationships with politically favoured firms, he said. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, was hit by a massive hack last month. Getty Images The market presents a different challenge. Bitcoin’s history of sharp boom-and-bust cycles under administrations of both parties complicates any attempt to attribute its price prospects to Washington. Bitcoin remains well below its previous highs, despite the Trump-era regulatory relief and political support that fuelled expectations of a golden age for digital assets.



The recent Binance hack underscored another challenge: security. The exchange suffered $6.3 billion in losses, but has since effectively replenished the stolen cryptocurrency, using a combination of money from its corporate treasury as well as two insurance funds. “The crypto industry needs to get these hacks out of the headlines,” said Peter Atwater, an adjunct economics professor at William & Mary. “Repetition matters. It will be interesting to see whether this propels Democrats to shift the regulatory pendulum back, with a greater emphasis on safety and soundness.” All told, crypto’s prospects extend well beyond its alliance with Trump. Digital assets now encompass investment funds, stablecoin payments and financial infrastructure involving institutions whose interests outlast any presidency. For an industry seeking customers across the political spectrum, a less partisan identity could ultimately prove an advantage rather than a setback. Industry advocates are already stressing their bipartisan ambitions. “Digital assets have always been bipartisan, and we stand ready to work with both new and returning members on both sides of the aisle,” said Ji Kim, chief executive of the Crypto Council for Innovation.

World.title: ‘A nightmare for Pat Cummins’: Why Khawaja claims are set to dog Australia captain
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘A nightmare for Pat Cummins’: Why Khawaja claims are set to dog Australia captain Tom Decent November 8, 2026 — 6:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Among all the claims Usman Khawaja has published in the past few days – in his upcoming book and on his Instagram page – one was conspicuously wide of the mark. “I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I’m not in that team any more,” Khawaja said in a video on Sunday morning. “Now, my words don’t influence the team at all.” Loading Khawaja may no longer be a part of the Australian set-up, having retired from international cricket after the Ashes in January this year. But the Test team gearing up for the summer opener against New Zealand on December 9 features a number of players from that infamous 2018 series, including captain Pat Cummins. And as former Australian captain Mark Taylor put it on Sunday: “It’s going to be obviously a nightmare for Pat Cummins and the team leading into the summer of cricket.”



Normally, players bristle when the media brings up past controversies. This time, it is a former teammate who has reopened one of Australian cricket’s deepest wounds. If Khawaja felt the full story of “Sandpapergate”, the Australian ball-tampering scandal in 2018, had to be told, there were other ways to bring it into the public domain than through a publicity blitz while promoting a book from which he hopes to profit. That is the feeling of some influential figures in cricket across the country who have spoken to this masthead. Pat Cummins is given a cold towel by teammate Usman Khawaja during the second Test against Bangladesh in 2017. Getty After a weekend of headlines, explosive extracts and increasingly pointed responses, we still have not heard directly from the players at the centre of the original scandal. Steve Smith, who served a one-year ban, is in New York and understood to be watching the fallout closely. He will return for the first Test in Perth, and his next press conference promises to be well attended.



Khawaja claims sandpaper was used to rough up the ball near the boundary during the second Test in Gqeberha, then known as Port Elizabeth, before Cameron Bancroft was caught with it in during the next match in Cape Town. After the Cape Town incident, Smith told a press conference after play: “You can ask questions as much as you like, but I can promise you this is the first time that it’s happened.” David Warner and Usman Khawaja were long-term opening partners in the Test team. Getty Images That statement now sits in defiance of Khawaja’s version of events. David Warner, who also served a one-year ban, is in Nepal playing T20 cricket for the Kathmandu Gorkhas in the Nepal Premier League.



For one who spends so much time on social media, Warner’s silence after his childhood friend’s revelations speaks volumes. Whether he will offer his own account remains to be seen. He, too, has a book deal in his future. Warner will be in the commentary box this summer for Kayo Sports. So will Khawaja. Steve Smith addresses the media at Sydney Airport in 2018, after arriving back from the ball-tampering scandal in South Africa. Janie Barrett Joining them will be former Australian cricketer Alyssa Healy, whose husband, Mitchell Starc, has had his integrity effectively called into question by Khawaja’s insistence that everyone – bowlers, batters and staff – knew that sandpaper was being used illegally during that series. Healy will attend a Kayo Sports launch in Sydney on Tuesday. Neither Khawaja nor Warner will be there. Nathan Lyon was originally scheduled to appear, but withdrew because of the impending birth of his child, a decision made well before Khawaja’s comments.



The four main bowlers from Cape Town – Pat Cummins, Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Lyon – are standing by their 2021 statement, according to their managers. That statement rejected suggestions they knew a foreign substance had been taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball. As things stand, they will not be releasing a fresh joint statement. The bowlers are content to let Khawaja do the talking. The social media reaction to his revelations has certainly not been universally supportive. The bowlers have no desire to give Khawaja’s allegations any more oxygen, particularly after Khawaja doubled down on Sunday, refusing to retreat from his assertion that “everyone knew”.



How to sum up their mood behind closed doors? Annoyed, but hardly surprised. Will they be inviting Khawaja over for a barbecue any time soon? No. Would they have anyway? Probably not. Australia’s Pat Cummins and Usman Khawaja during a net session in 2023. Getty Images The first member of the current Test team to face the media since Khawaja dropped his bombshell will likely be NSW captain Nic Maddinson, who is scheduled to speak on Monday ahead of the Blues’ Sheffield Shield clash with South Australia on Wednesday. Maddinson had nothing to do with the 2018 South Africa tour. That won’t stop him being asked about a scandal that threatens to stick to Australian cricket like mud on a white shirt.



If he takes some wickets for NSW, Lyon may field questions after play about Khawaja’s admission that he was “pissed” that the off-spinner dropped a ball near South Africa’s AB de Villiers after a run-out during that series. Similar inquiries await Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood whenever they make public appearances leading into the first Test. Nathan Lyon drops the ball in the direction of AB de Villiers. AP Mitch Marsh is another player worth watching. He was part of the 2018 South Africa touring party and will captain Australia’s white-ball sides in upcoming matches against England, beginning on Friday. Marsh has never given a detailed account of what happened in Cape Town and was not a signatory to the bowlers’ statement five years ago. His next press conference will be worth watching.



Related Article Opinion

Test cricket Usman Khawaja remained silent for eight years. Why did he speak out now? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist Then there is Bancroft, who is weighing up if and when to speak publicly. He has already read the controversial chapter of Khawaja’s book, Sabr, which will be released on Tuesday. Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg will inevitably be drawn into the controversy, too. Khawaja claims Greenberg, then head of the Australian Cricketers’ Association, agreed with him in 2021 that the bowlers and everyone else involved in Cape Town should have accepted collective responsibility. A penny for the bowlers’ thoughts on that one. Darren Lehmann, the Australian coach at the time, suggested on Saturday that sometimes things are best left unsaid. Khawaja clearly disagrees. He believes he is doing the right thing and is entitled to tell and sell his version of events. But the manner and timing of his revelations have caused a major stir behind the scenes and ensured the fallout will dominate the build-up to the summer.



Eight years after Sandpapergate, Australian cricket is once again confronting a scandal it thought was buried. Only this time, the biggest threat isn’t coming from outside the dressing room. It’s coming from a player who was sitting inside it just a few months ago. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Only one in five voters trust Albanese now as blame sticks for cost of living
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalResolve Political Monitor Only one in five voters trust Albanese now as blame sticks for cost of living James Massola November 8, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Just 20 per cent of voters now say they trust Anthony Albanese, while the prime minister’s status as preferred leader and Labor’s two-party preferred vote are mired at record-low levels. Voters are squarely blaming the Albanese government and its latest budget for the cost-of-living crisis. With 42 per cent holding Labor responsible, the grim result demonstrates that Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ insistence that global factors were the chief drivers of inflation has failed to cut through. A quarter of respondents (26 per cent) blamed international causes such as soaring oil prices and the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran for the high cost of living, just 7 per cent of people pointed the finger at the Reserve Bank, 5 per cent blamed state governments and 3 per cent said it was the fault of businesses. Those findings suggest Albanese’s pre-emptive and thinly veiled criticism of the Reserve Bank’s latest rate hike as a “blunt instrument” has not taken the heat off Labor.



The survey of 2250 voters was conducted by Resolve Political Monitor from November 2 to 7, and came while Albanese attended a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates for the fifth time this year. All the movement in support for the parties is within the polls’ margin of error of plus or minus 2.1 per cent. The standing of the prime minister and Labor has been hit by a perfect storm of poor economic news, as interest rates rose to an 18-year-high of 4.85 per cent, September’s inflation figures came in higher than expected at 4.3 per cent, and Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock talked about Australians feeling like they were in a recession. Opposition frontbencher Dan Tehan told ABC’s Insiders that Labor should heed the lessons from the Republican rout at the US midterms last week: “Prime Minister Albanese, Jim Chalmers, and Chris Bowen should be paying very close attention [to the US midterm results]. I mean, cost of living was a key issue there that drove the change there, and I think people didn’t feel like the government, the Trump administration, was really 100 per cent focused on that. And I think it’s exactly the same here in Australia.”



In an interview with the ABC published on Saturday, Albanese pointed to the Iran war and tariffs as key reasons for the Republicans’ many defeats. Labor’s primary vote fell one point in the last month to equal a post-election low of 28 percentage points, down from 34.6 percentage points at the May 2025 election. But neither One Nation nor the Coalition directly benefited from the movement, with the Coalition also down one point to 22 per cent and One Nation steady on 25 per cent. The Greens crept 1 percentage point ahead in their primary vote for a second month in a row, rising to 13 per cent after the switch of leader from Larissa Waters to David Shoebridge. The scandal over a $6 million grant to the Marrickville Golf Club, in Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler, has also badly damaged voters’ trust in the prime minister.



Just 20 per cent of voters agreed they still trusted “what Albanese says and promises”, down 6 percentage points since September, while 22 per cent of people said they had lost trust in the prime minister. Of more concern was that 43 per cent agreed that “I did not trust Albanese before this anyway”, up a significant 9 percentage points since the question was last asked in September. The picture is worse for Labor in the contest for preferred prime minister, with Albanese down three percentage points to equal a record low of just 29 per cent, previously recorded in September, while support for Coalition leader Angus Taylor as preferred prime minister continues to inch back up, rising by 3 percentage points to 25 per cent in the past month to 25 per cent. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson status as preferred prime minister fell two percentage points to 24 per cent over the last month. Albanese’s net performance rating as prime minister – that is, the total percentage of people who said his performance has been good or very good, versus those who said it has been bad or very bad, has equalled a record low set in January this year in the wake of the Bondi massacre.



Just 34 per cent of voters said Albanese was doing a good or very good job, while 56 per cent said he was doing a poor or very poor job – delivering a net performance rating of -22 per cent. In contrast, 42 per cent of voters said Taylor was doing a good or very good job, while 33 per cent said his performance was bad or very bad and the rest were undecided, continuing a trend of small monthly improvements for the opposition leader. Hanson’s total “good” performance remained steady on 45 per cent, while the proportion of voters who rated her performance as poor increased 1 percentage point to 42 per cent.



Resolve Political Monitor pollster Jim Reed said the findings showed that “although Albanese, Chalmers and Labor are shedding personal capital at a rate of knots, their vote is holding up”. “Most damaging is that the PM is only trusted by a fifth of voters now. This is part being seen as distracted from the priority issues, like tackling inflation, but also the cumulative effect of surprise tax changes and the local grant program that have some voters questioning what’s coming next,” he said. The prime minister’s likeability rating has crashed to a record low, falling to a net negative score of minus 19 per cent, down four points in the past month. In contrast, Taylor rose 3 percentage points to plus 11 per cent – opening up a 30 per cent gap between the two – while Hanson’s net likeability score rose to plus 4 per cent. At the same time, the net likeability of the Labor Party fell another two points to minus 13 per cent in the last month and the Liberal Party’s net likeability rose 7 per cent to plus 11 per cent – a 24 per cent gap between the two major parties.



Keeping the cost of living low remains voters’ top policy priority by an overwhelming margin, as it has been all year, with 41 per cent of voters nominating it as their number one issue. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Swans secure AFLW semi-final spot; Hawks break ground with first finals win
World.content:
AFLW elimination final SportAFLAFLW Swans secure AFLW semi-final spot; Hawks break ground with first finals win Hannah Kennelly Updated November 8, 2026 — 5:17pm ,first published 3:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Sydney have booked a place in the AFLW semi-finals, defeating the Western Bulldogs by 29 points in a high-pressure clash at a windswept soggy Henson Park. This year’s leading goalkicker and star Swan Chloe Molly aided to her tally, banishing the Bulldogs – who fought their way into finals for first the first time since 2022 – back to the kennel by winning 7.4 (46) to 2.5 (17). Tanya Kennedy celebrates a goal with her teammates. AFL Photos The Swans asserted their dominance from the opening bounce, kicking three consecutive goals in the first quarter and leaving the Bulldogs goalless. Ellie Blackburn lifted for the Dogs in the second with a goal, but a magnificent Tanya Kennedy laid a crucial tag on Isabelle Pritchard, shutting down the Dog’s scoring capacity. When the siren blared, Swans placed raced to embrace each other, as loyal fans in red and white cheered on the boundary line, noticeably with inside-out umbrellas and soaked ponchos.



Tayla Smith competes with Alice Edmonds Getty Images This year has been an undeniably tricky year for Sydney. The women’s program has copped collateral damage from the Pullman hotel scandal and Tom Papley’s alleged drug offence, as some of the club’s men’s players continue to make headlines. But the Swans’ AFLW program has remained focused, drawing in record-breaking breaking crowds at Henson Park and continuing their finals campaign to book their spot in a semi-final against Geelong. Related Article AFLW finals

AFLW Dee-lighted: Melbourne storm back from the brink to leave Cats heartbroken; Roos smash Blues



The Cats feel agonisingly short in their qualifying final against Melbourne on Saturday, in a thrilling AFLW finals finish. Swans coach Colin O’Riordan said the team was thrilled with the win, but said the team was hungry to keep improving. “Scoreboard is important at the end of the game, but you don’t get there unless you stick to the process and you stick to what we are trying to do,” O’Riordan said. “The level of pressure thy brought across all four quarters, that was outstanding.” Hawthorn upset Gold Coast and notch breakthrough finals win



Hawthorn’s AFLW team has a complicated relationship with finals. The Hawks have had strong home and away seasons but typically run out of steam for their finals campaign, falling in straight sets over the past few years. Mikayla Williamson celebrates a goal with teammates AFL Photos But on Sunday they proved the naysayers wrong, defeating favourites Gold Coast by 18 points in Queensland to cement their first finals win. Sunday’s clash was incredibly close for the first half with both sides bringing intense pressure. As the scoreboard seesawed, Hawthorn finally broke away in the third, kicking three unanswered goals and grab a 15-point lead into the final break.



But the Suns weren’t done yet. Mikayla Nurse opened the quarter with a goal for the Suns and the home crowd roared their approval. But the Hawks held on, aided by majors from Mikaylah Antony and Mikayla Williamson to win 8.9 (57) to 6.3 (39). It was a disappointing ending to Gold Coast’s campaign. The team has had an extraordinary comeback this year after finishing last in 2025. The arrival of AFLW legend Erin Phillips as general manager of women’s football, plus the plethora of young academy talent means the Suns will likely be a deadly force next year. However for now, the team will anxiously wait for updates on youngster Ava Ulsher who has helped from the ground by medical staff after a collision with her teammate.



Hawthorn will now prepare for a semi-final clash with Carlton – the team that knocked them out of the finals last year. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Property investor sells Seddon house for $1.25m, $50,000 below reserve
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Property investor sells Seddon house for $1.25m, $50,000 below reserve Elizabeth Redman November 8, 2026 — 4:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A property investor sold a charming red brick house in Seddon for $1.25 million after it passed in at its Saturday auction, a $50,000 discount to the published reserve price. The six-bedroom house at 14 Hobbs Street came with period details such as intricate decorative fretwork in the hallway, a stained-glass entrance and fireplaces. The property was one of 629 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 59 per cent from 416 reported results throughout the week, while 74 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. It was the first test of the market’s reaction to the Reserve Bank’s fifth cash rate increase for the year last Tuesday, to 4.85 per cent. Although the clearance rate remains at lacklustre levels, it was marginally higher than last week’s early read of 56 per cent, as many buyers already in the market may have factored the rate rise into their budgets.



The Seddon home was for sale with a reserve price of $1.3 million. Related Article Auctions Young couple snaps up inner-city Edwardian for $1,080,000 after pass in At auction, a vendor bid was placed of $1,225,000. But with no further offers forthcoming, the home passed in. Two parties showed interest after the auction and negotiations ensued. A deal was struck at $1.25 million. “It is quite a sought-after location where that house is,” Jas Stephens Real Estate selling agent Tate Moore said.



The winners are second home buyers who live locally and may renovate the house, which is set on 300 square metres. Moore said the home had previously been a rooming house and could be returned to its original state. He said there was a trend towards homes selling in post-auction negotiations, while many homes were also selling prior to auction. He said some buyers wanted to see “social proof” that others were keen on the home. “They really just want some third-party endorsement that people will put their hand up,” he said. He was unsure that the latest interest rate rise had had much impact yet, albeit that could change over time.



“Second home buyers … typically they are buying and selling in the same market,” he said. The home last sold in 2010 for $736,000, records show. The median house price in Seddon was $1.06 million over the 12 months to September, on Domain data. Elsewhere, in Hampton East, a well-kept, single-level townhouse sold for $1,361,000 to a downsizer. There were six bidders for the sunny, three-bedroom home at 2/300 South Road, which came with an al fresco entertaining area and a back garden.



Bidding began at $1.1 million, and was quickly increased to the published reserve of $1.2 million. Later, a range of increments were offered, including bids as small as $500. Related Article Victoria residential property Former ANZ CEO Shayne Elliott’s Toorak home listed for sale The winner had seen the home at the first inspection, while the underbidder had seen it only the Thursday prior, Hodges McGrath Sandringham selling agent Angus Graham said. The vendors are downsizing. He attributed the result to “realistic expectations from the owner. But it was a very well-sized three-bedroom plus study, single level, garage, which was one of those properties that is always popular.” Although he described the market as challenging, he had sold all his October auctions.



“While we are not having as many auctions, those vendors that are willing to auction are having good outcomes. Realistic sellers are getting rewarded,” he said. In the northern suburbs, a Mickleham home sold under the hammer for $590,000. The three-bedroom house at 49 Ginger Crescent was listed at the start of its campaign with a guided price range of $530,000 to $550,000, which was then updated to show a reserve price of $550,000. Four parties registered for the auction, of whom two participated.



Bidding began at $560,000, already higher than the reserve, and the price rose in a mix of $10,000 and $5000 bids. Related Article Victoria residential property What life’s like in Melbourne’s most mortgage-stressed suburb now A young first home buyer couple renting locally won the keys, while the underbidder was a man hoping to downsize. The vendor is a young man taking the opportunity to upsize. Ray White Craigieburn selling agent Adrian Prestileo thought the home’s presentation helped it stand out, as well as the affordable price point. “In times like these, price [and] presentation is the most important thing,” he said.



He also thought the rate rise would have less impact on those who were changing from one home to the next in the same market. Property alerts are now available in The Age app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.
