World.title: Tenancy Tribunal orders brother landlord to pay sibling tenant nearly $17,000
World.content:
After their mother died, one brother purchased the family home from her estate and rented it to the other.

For 17 years, neither treated the arrangement with any formality, allowing the home's condition to deteriorate, repairs to go undone and the rent to go unpaid.

The brothers, who have name suppression, ended up in the Tenancy Tribunal in October 2025, where the tenant brother was ordered to pay $19,548.57 in rent arrears and his tenancy was terminated.

That was not the end of their dispute.

A year later, the brothers returned to the tribunal, where the tenant sought exemplary damages for failures to maintain the premises and comply with Healthy Homes requirements, as well as reimbursement of fixed water charges paid during the tenancy.

This time, the tribunal sided with the tenant, ordering his brother to pay him $7000 in exemplary damages, $5000 in compensation for distress and loss of amenity, and $4966.74 to reimburse fixed water charges.

In the recently released decision, tribunal adjudicator Haamid Ben Fayed said he was satisfied there were significant failures to maintain the premises and comply with applicable Healthy Homes requirements.

"The respondent's evidence was essentially that, when his brother asked him to attend to something, he would come to the property and deal with it.

"Neither party appears to have treated the arrangement with the formality ordinarily expected of a residential tenancy."

The landlord told the tribunal this was how matters had operated between him and his brother for many years.

"That provides context," Ben Fayed said. "It does not provide a defence."

The tenant paid rent of $400 a week for a lengthy period, substantially below market rates, the decision stated.

Despite that, Ben Fayed said the breaches were significant and persisted for a substantial period, affecting the tenant's enjoyment of his home, and including matters relevant to health, safety and habitability.

The decision did not describe the home's issues.

He said there was insufficient evidence the applicant consistently notified the landlord of defects as they arose or gave him a reasonable opportunity to remedy them, which contributed to some of the issues continuing for longer than they otherwise might have.

Regarding the claim for re-imbursement of fixed water charges, the respondent's evidence was that the applicant paid the Watercare accounts directly.

Ben Fayed said responsibility for fixed water charges rested with the landlord, whose failure to meet that obligation resulted in the charges being passed on to the tenant.

The tenant also sought to revisit the earlier tribunal determinations concerning rent arrears and termination of the tenancy, but Ben Fayed declined.

The latest tribunal decision is unlikely to mark the end of the brothers' legal battles.

There is a High Court proceeding concerning ownership of the property and the circumstances in which the respondent acquired it from their mother's estate.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Starshield or nothing: NZDF moves closer to buying into Musk's satellite network for secrets
World.content:
New Zealand has moved closer to buying services from a satellite network set up by tech trillionaire Elon Musk for secret communications.

RNZ revealed in June that the NZ Defence Force (NZDF) was running a six-month trial of Starshield, the first confirmed case of a government other than America's trialling the two-year-old system that comprises hundreds if not thousands of satellites.

On Friday Defence told RNZ, "A Starshield trial has been completed and showed potential utility for the NZDF."

Starshield ran into controversy last month when Ukraine's access to it was reduced, jeopardising some combat and air defence missions, with critics warning this was the risk of relying on privately-owned systems in a war or crisis, as Time reported.

NZ Defence withheld details of the outcomes of its Starshield trial on the grounds releasing them might prejudice national security or defence or international relations.

"Any subsequent satellite communications acquisitions would follow normal capability management and acquisition processes," it said in a three-line statement.

The trial was purchased through the US government's Foreign Military Sales (FMS) system and required the defence minister here to sign an indemnity to shield the US from any damages claims, a routine requirement of the FMS.

Former Defence Minister Judith Collins. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Starshield or nothing

Judith Collins signed it last December after Defence made the case to her that it really needed Musk's system for "secure military grade" internet services and data transfer, documents and emails released under the Official Information Act (OIA) show.

Without Starshield "NZDF would have fewer satellite communications options to conduct operations", it told Collins.

"The NZDF cannot procure the deliverables from any other supplier" than the US government, it said.

The bonus was getting it at the same price and so benefiting from the US government's purchasing power, as well as from its management and technical support and "their unparalleled depth of knowledge" on a not-for-profit basis.

Any loss under the indemnity - which was unlikely - would be unlikely to exceed $10 million, Defence told her.

The NZDF already uses Starlink, Musk's network of 10,000-plus satellites used by millions of people to connect to the internet and relied on by Ukraine's military from the start of Russia's war in 2022.

Ukraine clash

Starshield's advent in 2024 gave customers an option with higher encryption and protection from the growing threat of "counterspace" attacks.

US Space Force said on Thursday it was "counting on partnerships with the commercial space industry to help it prevail against aggressive adversaries".

It rates Russia an "acute" threat and China the major (or "pacing" in Pentagon parlance) threat.

Reuters has reported the Pentagon is Starshield's largest customer and has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. The two clashed over the rising costs earlier this year.

"It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the [US spy agency] National Reconnaissance Office," reported Reuters.

Elon Musk became the world's first trillionaire after SpaceX went public on 12 June 2026. NurPhoto via AFP

Constrained from the start

New Zealand is almost entirely reliant on its Five Eyes partners for infrastructure in space but they in turn have been increasing their reliance on commercial partners.

A leading US Space Force-industry event late last month was titled 'Fielding the Arsenal of Freedom - Victory through Industrial Partnership'.

The constraints where New Zealand's space and military ambitions meet reality were evident from the start over Starshield, the OIA showed.

In an email in June 2024 headed "Expression of interest in Starshield - restricted", a capability manager asked an FMS manager at NZDF, "Is this something that you can assist us with from there?".

"I apologise for jumping around in subjects," they went on, "but when you are as hollow an organisation as we are, we have to wear many hats throughout the day."

Military bosses have repeatedly described the NZDF as "hollowed" out since the pandemic. The army at mid-2026 was still 700 personnel short "particularly in critical leadership" and instructors' ranks.

'Is there a fast track option?'

Another June 2024 email said Defence was "putting a plan together for future sustainment" and asked, "Is there a fast track option?" for Starshield.

It seemed not. "There are a few ducks we need to line up, especially as it is a service we are wanting access to; one that we have not seen any cost data on at all yet," the manager continued.

It took another 18 months for Collins to sign the indemnity in December 2025.

The Starshield trial that went ahead this year was to determine "what its uses are, if any", Defence told RNZ.

Friday's statement showed it had found some.

The government has talked about having a national mission to launch a sovereign satellite, and documents show this had come up in talks with NZ-founded, US-based Rocket Lab, but there have been few details.

Starshield has been linked to US President Donald Trump's Golden Dome. Reuters reported a $4 billion contract signed with SpaceX in May was to build a space data network "backbone" for superfast missile warning and tracking sensors. Similarly, the Dome would rely on a constellation of such satellites.

US President Donald Trump listens during the announcement about the Golden Dome missile defense shield, in the Oval Office of the White House in May 2025. AFP / JIM WATSON

'Fastest way'

Speed has been central to the directives and strategies coming out of both Washington and Wellington for buying new military tech - just on a massively different scale.

"The fastest way to get traction is to show how your idea accelerates warfighting outcomes across the architecture," the US Space Force told companies at its big open day last month.

"There are so many permutations of commercial integration across the ecosystem today that we weren't seeing even six months or a year ago."

The NZDF industrial strategy is to "deliver capability faster" including by buying or developing minimum viable products, using local small businesses or helping those businesses to partner with huge "primes" (big defence contractors, many of them American).

A big difference is the Pentagon has companies flocking to it, while NZ must go to them, as with SpaceX and Starshield. It also has to negotiate a way through US military export controls by using the FMS. AUKUS Pillar Two has removed some of those barriers between Australia, the UK and US but New Zealand has not joined Pillar Two. It has, however, signed on with several Pentagon space networks since 2020.

Spooked over US tech

RNZ is seeking from Defence any reports such as risk assessments or cost-benefit analysis arising from the Starshield trial, though the Official Information Act appears unlikely to be able to pierce the national security carapace.

In Europe last month, the disruption to Ukraine's access to Starshield spooked governments about relying on US technology.

Germany had begun evaluating 30 AI military tools but ruled out buying the US system used in the Iran war for targeting, called Maven Smart System, stating that letting a private, foreign contractor have access to national military databases was completely "out of the question" and "inconceivable".

The concerns last month prompted Maven's maker, Palantir, another tech company that has become central to Pentagon tactices, to reassure the Europeans that Maven had no "kill ‌switch" either it or the US government could use independent of NATO.

World.title: Luxon defends his leadership after 'huge loss' of senior MPs
World.content:
National Party leader Christopher Luxon is defending his leadership after the loss of multiple senior figures of his party in the election.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Luxon argued his party had done well, given global political trends that have resulted in major electoral upheaval.

"Ultimately, we've got the most seats in Parliament, and ultimately, we've been given a pathway to government," Luxon told reporters.

"When you think about global results and you look at incumbent governments, and particularly incumbent governments having to deal with a $3.60 fuel price, actually what we achieved, I think, is pretty good.

"I'd love 50.1 percent, but I'm proud of the result that we delivered last night."

Luxon said he took responsibility for the "huge loss" of four senior figures from his team.

Luxon hugs MP Paul Goldsmith on election night. Craig McCulloch.

Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee are all gone, leaving a major hole in National's ranks, including some 20 ministerial portfolios and the Speakership.

"I'm going to miss them tremendously. These are friends of mine, personal friends of mine, and we have been through a lot together over the last five years," Luxon said.

"We've lost some huge talent.

"We have been in the trenches together."

Wait for results begins

Luxon said serious coalition negotiations would not begin until the final election results were released on 27 November.

He said he might speak informally with other party leaders in the meantime, but suggested politicians, journalists and the public could all do with a break after the six-week campaign.

"Everyone's over politics. Let's all just have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," he said.

After the 2023 election they hadn't started negotiations until the final results were in, and they would take the same course of action this time, Luxon said.

"Once you know where you are you can move through those things pretty quickly, and find the common ground and areas of disagreement."

Luxon says he's unlikely to need Opportunity to govern - but he intends to build a relationship with them. Phil Walter/Getty Images

Olive branch for Opportunity?

Media challenged Luxon over his previous pledge not to work with Opportunity on Sunday afternoon.

He said he intended to build a relationship with the party, despite repeatedly ruling out working with it during the election campaign.

He maintained it was "highly unlikely" National would need Opportunity's support to govern, with the preliminary results suggesting it could continue its coalition with ACT and New Zealand First.

But he said the election result showed a need for greater cooperation across Parliament.

"I think it's entirely appropriate to build a relationship with Qiulae [Wong] and Opportunity," Luxon said.

ACT leader David Seymour said his party was planning for two scenarios - one where the existing coalition can govern, and one where they need Opportunity.

"I think it would be prudent to understand what the possibilities were in either scenario so that we can form a government as rapidly as possible," he said.

"I know people will not be very patient with parties who appear to be slowing down the government formation process."

World.title: Man arrested after nine burglaries in one week in Whiritoa, north of Waihi
World.content:
A 44-year-old man has been arrested after a string of burglaries which has been infuriating residents in a small town north of Waihi.

Police sergeant Cameron Young said in the past week nine burglaries had been reported in the town of Whiritoa.

"Whiritoa is a small community, and they understandably became increasingly frustrated with these incidents."

He said after a search warrant at an home in the town, police found "a significant amount of alleged stolen property" and took a man into custody.

"We acknowledge these recent incidents would have been incredibly unsettling for the Whitiroa community, and we hope this arrest brings reassurance that we work hard to hold offenders to account."

The man was due to appear in Hamilton District Court on Monday, charged with burglary and breach of bail.

World.title: Historic Asian firsts amid election disappointment
World.content:
Asian candidates secured a couple of notable historic firsts amid some gloomy election results on Saturday.

Opportunity's Qiulae Wong becomes the first Asian leader of a political party in Parliament after the newcomer crossed the 5 percent threshold.

Its 6 percent party vote gives Opportunity seven seats in Parliament based on preliminary results.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408085668112

National's Mahesh Muralidhar is set to become the National Party's first Indian MP to win an electorate seat based on preliminary results, defeating Labour's Max Harris by more than 5300 votes.

The Indian community must also be pleased that Muralidhar's victory in one of the party's traditionally safest constituencies doubles their recent representation in Parliament, joining ACT's Parmjeet Parmar as well as newcomer Rakesh Naidoo and sitting MP Priyanca Radhakrishnan of Labour as list MPs.

Conversely, several sitting Asian National MPs have been bundled out of Parliament based on preliminary results, with former Cabinet minister Melissa Lee, Mt Roskill MP Carlos Cheung and list MP Nancy Lu failing to retain their seats.

The result leaves Lawrence Xu-Nan of the Green Party as the only Chinese MP to have secured re-election.

Altogether, 11 MPs of Asian heritage are likely to have secured a seat in Parliament based on preliminary results - the same number that had represented the community in the previous term.

Party listings ahead of the election had suggested that this number could have grown.

Opportunity's Qiulae Wong becomes the first Asian leader of a political party in Parliament. Phil Walter/Getty Images

Wong failed to win the Mt Albert electorate, attracting just under 4000 votes and almost 10,000 less than Labour's Helen White.

As leader of the Opportunity Party, though, she's looking forward to bringing the party into Parliament.

"You guys have voted for unity over division," Wong told supporters on election night.

"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good."

With the Opportunity Party winning a projected 6 percent of the party vote, it marks the first time a party has come from outside Parliament with no previous MPs as candidates and without winning an electorate.

Mahesh Muralidhar is set to become the National Party's first Indian MP to win an electorate seat RNZ / Blessen Tom

Muralidhar secured his place in Parliament by winning the East Auckland electorate of Tāmaki with 15,330 votes ahead of Labour's Max Harris on 9974.

He managed to almost double the number of votes cast for ACT's James Christmas, who was expected to be more of a threat after former deputy leader Brooke van Velden stole the electorate from National in 2023.

Muralidhar, who describes himself as a proud Kiwi-Indian, said he wanted to make sure the Indian community's concerns were heard.

"I'll be there for the community in regards to making sure that the community is understood and heard," he said.

In Mt Albert, Lee lost her bid to snatch the Labour stronghold off White, attracting 9389 votes and falling a little more than 4700 behind the eventual winner.

Lee said she was disappointed and saddened by the prospect of not returning to Parliament.

Having served New Zealand for the past 18 years, she said she had made no plans for the next three years beyond continuing her parliamentary career.

National's Carlos Cheung poses for a photo with family members at his office headquarters on election night. RNZ / Yiting Lin

In Mt Roskill, Cheung fell agonisingly short of Labour's Michael Wood by just 262 votes.

It was nail-biting ride for the incumbent National MP on Saturday, with results showing the two candidates virtually inseparable for much of the evening and, at one point, only a solitary vote apart.

Special votes could still decide the outcome of this electorate, with the final count expected by 27 November.

Cheung acknowledged the close contest and said community safety, education and the cost of living would be his top priorities if he was able to retain his seat after special votes had been counted.

"I think continuing to serve the people in Mt Roskill would be my top priority," he said.

Lu, meanwhile, failed to make it back into Parliament, with National failing to win a single list seat after only pulling in 29 percent of the party vote. Lu was ranked 15th on National's party list.

Outging National list MP Nancy Lu poses for a photo with her supporters in Auckland on election night. RNZ / Liu Chen

Lu said she was disappointed to lose her seat, saying three years in Parliament had not been enough to accomplish what she had hoped.

"It has been a privilege to serve the country and our people for the last three years," she said.

"Three years is certainly not enough. There is still so much more I want to do to serve the country and its people."

Lu also expressed concern about the decline in Chinese representation in Parliament over the next three years, saying the number of Chinese MPs should better reflect the proportion of Chinese New Zealanders in the population.

"At the moment, it certainly doesn't," she said.

In Takinini, National's Rima Nakhle held off a strong performance from Labour's Kharag Singh, winning the seat by just under 1500 votes.

It was a compelling battle, with more than 90 percent of the votes in the electorate cast for one of the candidates from National and Labour.

Nakhle said she remained focused on serving her electorate.

Asked about ethnic representation in Parliament, Nakhle said her colleagues remained closely connected to the ethnic communities in their electorate and understood their concerns.

Labour's Kharag Singh mingles with supporters in Auckland on election night. Blessen Tom / RNZ

It was more comfortable for Labour's Vanushi Walters in Waitākere, easing past National's Agnes Loheni in the electorate race by more than 2600 votes.

In Wellington North, Labour's Ayesha Verrall fell just over 3000 votes behind Tamantha Paul of the Green Party but will return to Parliament as a list MP after being ranked sixth.

Labour's Priyanca Radhakrishnan on election night. Blessen Tom / RNZ

Labour's Priyanca Radhakrishnan failed to retake Maungakiekie from National, losing by almost 3000 votes. The MP returns to Parliament as a list MP.

Former Labour MP Naisi Chen also failed in her attempt to return to Parliament, finishing a distant third in Auckland Central behind Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick and Candace Kinser of National.

In Epsom Xu-Nan always faced a tough electorate battle against ACT leader David Seymour, National's Paul Goldsmith and Labour's Camilla Belich, attracting just 10 percent of the electorate vote and finishing fourth.

Xu-Nan, however, will return to Parliament as a list MP ranked eighth on the Greens' list.

Xu-Nan said he was determined to ensure Chinese New Zealanders' voices continued to be heard in Parliament and to hold politicians accountable for their remarks, both inside and outside the House.

"We as a country should no longer tolerate any more sort of racism that we're seeing towards our communities," he said.

Xu-Nan said he would work to amplify migrant voices and ensure the issues affecting migrant communities received greater attention nationwide over the next three years.

Lawrence Xu-Nan returns to Parliament as a list MP. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

In Kenepuru, Greens MP Lan Pham failed to make much of a dent against Labour's Babara Edmonds, who won the seat comfortably.

Pham attracted 8.5 percent of the electorate vote but returns to Parliament as a list MP ranked sixth on the party list.

Pham said protecting and restoring the environment would remain a key priority over the next three years, alongside reducing the influence of money in politics.

Pham said it was disappointing to see several Asian MPs lose their seats, stressing the importance of stronger Asian representation in Parliament.

"Greater Asian representation is absolutely critical because we know that Asian voices are a growing percentage of the New Zealand population," she said.

"I would love to see stronger Asian representation."

In Dunedin, the Greens' Francisco Hernandez suffered a heavy defeat to Labour's Rachel Brooking, attracting less than half the votes of the eventual winner.

However, Hernandez secures a seat in Parliament as a list MP ranked 10th on the Greens' list.

In Pakuanga, ACT's Parmjeet Parmar was always going to struggle to make inroads into senior National MP Simeon Brown's majority, attracting just 3.1 percent of the electorate vote.

However, Parmar returns to Parliament as a list MP ranked 10th on the party list.

World.title: Meet the surgeon saving the careers of cricket's best fast bowlers
World.content:
Fast, fearsome, and fragile were words often associated with former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond, whose promising cricket career was drastically curtailed by injury.

He debuted as a 26-year-old against Australia in Hobart in 2001, but it was in his next series, against Bangladesh, where he truly announced himself.

He took 11 wickets in two Tests at an average of 13, and it looked like the beginning of a long and lucrative career.

But Bond's back had other ideas. A stress fracture kept him out the game for almost two years from 2003.

Shane Bond is considered "patient zero" after his successful back surgery allowed him to continue his international career. (Phil Walter: Getty Images)

A meeting with back surgeon Grahame Inglis offered him hope he could overcome his injury by undergoing a little-known surgery that is now commonplace in the fast bowling fraternity.

"If I can't fix this, then the career is potentially over," Bond said of his decision to undergo pars stabilisation surgery in 2004.

"He [Inglis] talked about a procedure that he had done, one on a New Zealand high jumper and one other athlete.

" He thought that the chances I came back and bowled fast were slim, but ... I was prepared to give it a go. "

While other injuries limited Bond to just 14 more Tests before he retired in 2009, his back didn't trouble him again.

Last surgeon standing

Renowned New Zealand spinal surgeon Rowan Schouten was working with Dr Inglis at the time and said Bond was "patient zero in this whole story."

Bond took 147 ODI wickets, including a stunning hat-trick against Australia at Bellerive Oval in 2007. (AAP Image/Andrew Cornaga)

The success of that surgery laid the groundwork for a procedure that Schouten and his team have now performed on around 30 professional cricketers.

When surgeons in the UK stopped performing the procedure and Dr Inglis retired, Dr Schouten became the world's leading authority on repairing spinal stress fractures in fast bowlers.

Rowan Schouten says pars stabilisation surgery isn't a new procedure, but has recently become popular with cricketers. (Supplied: rowanschouten.co.nz)

"We were kind of left as the last man standing with experience on international fast bowlers and since then it's taken off essentially," he said.

"We're dealing with calls and connections from all around the world, from the UK, India, South Africa, Europe, Bangladesh, everywhere."

Bond still helps fast bowlers who have struggled with back issues and is often approached for advice.

He's coached Jofra Archer, Jason Behrendorff and James Pattinson, who all had the surgery and returned to play at the top level.

What is pars stabilisation surgery?

When a fast bowler is considering spinal surgery, like Australia's Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris did in 2025, it sounds like a drastic step.

Loading Instagram content

But Dr Schouten said the surgery was straightforward and "not that extreme".

It involves grafting the spine to stimulate repair, before putting screws and wires around the injured portion to provide stability.

WA quick Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris hopes to be even faster after surgery After years of back issues, Lance Morris is finally fit and firing, and the West Australian is keen to put his name in the frame for a Test call up once again.

"We've got a few little added components to it that we believe are important ... but it's a pretty standard technique," he said.

The injury, often referred to as a stress fracture, is common across sport and very prevalent in cricket.

Dr Schouten stressed the surgery is not a fusion, and most stress fractures do not need it.

"You need to preserve all that spinal motion that these guys need to be able to bowl full pace," he said.

Cameron Green opted for surgery in 2024, following several stress fractures during his career. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

If a player did opt to go under the knife, the recovery involves a six-to-nine month rehab program.

"Some stress fractures in some players become a recurring theme," Dr Schouten said.

"And then if you do that, if you have that two or three times in a row over multiple seasons, it can really disrupt a career."

World.title: Khawaja says he has thrown nobody 'under the bus'
World.content:
Usman Khawaja insists he has not thrown anyone under the bus with his bombshell ball-tampering revelations that have rocked Australian cricket.

One day on from admitting sandpaper had been used in the Test prior to Cape Town 2018 and the entire team was responsible, Khawaja defended the timing of his claims.

In a five-minute long Instagram explanation, Khawaja revealed he had planned to go public with the details days after the incident before the suspended Steve Smith talked him out of it.

Loading Instagram content

He also detailed how he made another attempt to ensure the entire team took the blame for it in 2021, before a public statement from the bowlers denied any knowledge.

But Khawaja said he had made a promise with his childhood friend David Warner to spill the details of the saga post-retirement in his book, believing Warner, Smith and Cameron Bancroft had taken the fall for the entire team.

"I haven't thrown anyone under the bus," Khawaja said.

"The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're not the victims.

"These three guys took the blame for all of us. They're the victims … people telling them that they're cheats, getting nailed by the crowd. Public humiliation."

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith were both put through the ringer. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

Extracts from Khawaja's memoir Sabr, which will be released on Tuesday, detail how an Australian player applied sandpaper to a ball in the change room in the second Test against South Africa at St George's Park in 2018.

When teammates saw how scuffed up one side became, they realised how much it would swing and Khawaja claims Bancroft volunteered to use the substance.

While Khawaja says that was initially only done at the start of sessions when entering the field, the tactic then expanded to on field in the next Test in Cape Town.

Khawaja also alleges in the book that a member of Australia's coaching staff had encouraged Bancroft to ramp up whatever he was doing with the ball, before the West Australian was caught by cameras and eventually umpires.

In the post on Sunday, Khawaja said he would "not deny" that everyone knew, and revealed how he wanted to go public in 2018 once Smith, Warner and Bancroft were suspended.

"I told Smudge [Smith] that I was going to come clean to the media," Khawaja said.

Usman Khawaja says Steve Smith talked him down from going public earlier. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

"I couldn't believe the penalties he got. But Smudge being the man and leader he was, he talked me out of it.

"He wanted to take the blame. I argued with him, but he was having none of it. That's the first time I try to come out."

Khawaja claimed he spoke extensively with then-coach Justin Langer and Todd Greenberg in 2021 about the team taking collective responsibility, with Greenberg then CEO of the players' union before becoming boss of Cricket Australia.

Lehmann claims 'everyone' was ball tampering Darren Lehmann rejects Usman Khawaja's claims the entire Australian camp knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot, but says "everyone around the world" was ball tampering up until that day.

The 39-year-old then said he never felt comfortable talking about it while back in the Australian team from 2022.

But he argued the fact he had held back the book until after Australia's Test return to South Africa last month was proof this was not a money-making venture.

"Call me a chicken or whatever you want. I didn't know how to do it because I was still in the team," Khawaja said.

"I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I'm not in that team anymore. What I say now isn't a reflection of them anymore.

"I stuck up for all cricketers in the past with the ACA [players' union] fighting for what I thought was right. This is no different.

"These three guys deserve justice and I haven't pointed fingers at anyone."

Khawaja has also been critical of Cricket Australia (CA) over its handling of the investigation into Cape Town, and that he was not interviewed.

CA has maintained it is "comfortable" with its findings from 2018 that only Warner, Smith and Bancroft knew of the idea.

Other players including bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon distanced themselves from the incident, insisting they had no knowledge "of a foreign substance" being taken on the field.

AAP

World.title: Extraordinary scenes as fog descends on 'farcical' FA Cup tie
World.content:
Does a defeat count if nobody saw it?

Altrincham fans may well be wondering that this weekend, after fog descended upon its FA Cup first round tie against Notts County at Moss Lane in Manchester.

League One side Notts County, featuring Australian former Sydney FC striker Luka Smyth, had taken a first half lead before Manchester-based Altrincham, of the fifth-tier National League, hit the front.

A late equaliser for Nottingham-based County, who won the FA Cup back in the 1893/94 season, forced extra time.

However, by that stage a heavy fog had enveloped the entire stadium, meaning extra time and penalties were played in scarcely believable conditions.

It made one slightly pity the commentators.

"I don't want to worry anyone — we can't see those dugouts at the moment because of the mist," Steve Bower said on the BBC in the closing stages of normal time, before fatefully adding that "it's getting heavier".

"We will try our best to let you know who has got the ball."

Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard said on the BBC Radio Nottingham call that "We're looking around … no-one knows where the ball is."

"We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners."

At least he was only supposed to be summarising.

"I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," his play-by-play caller Adam Hassell said.

The scenes were reminiscent of another famous foggy incident involving legendary Charlton goalkeeper Sam Bartram.

On Christmas Day, 1937, a London pea souper rolled into Stamford Bridge and completely covered the field.

In his autobiography, Bartram recalled seeing "fewer and fewer figures as we attacked steadily" over the course of the match, right up until a policeman appeared on the edge of his penalty area.

"'What on earth are you doing here?' he gasped. 'The game was stopped a quarter of an hour ago. The field's completely empty,'" Bartram wrote.

"When I groped my way to the dressing-room, the rest of the Charlton team, already out of the bath and in their civvies, were convulsed with laughter."

Fortunately, nothing like that happened in Altrincham, with the game eventually going to penalties, which took place in front of the Altrincham fans.

The Notts County fans, 100 or so metres up the other end of the ground, were left to guess what was happening based on the reactions they could hear through the gloom.

The Notts County fans didn't have the greatest view of the shootout … (Supplied)

They weren't the only ones.

"He's put it wide, I think," commentator Adam Summerton said on TNT Sports as Max Sanders stepped up for Notts County.

"It's hard to tell, I'm sorry, but it's so hard to see up here.

"No, it's in. I'm really sorry, it's so hard for us to see up here," he added as the replay was shown on his monitor.

At least Altrincham fans could see if the ball had gone in or not. (Supplied: TNT Sports)

Meanwhile, Notts County's fans started celebrating after a pause of a couple of seconds, presumably because the Altrincham fans were not.

That pattern continued all the way through the shootout, right up until the final spot kick was taken, by "I think it's [Rosaire] Longelo," Summerton said.

He scored, and Notts County was through to the second round.

At least, I suppose, nobody could see the Altrincham players' disappointment.

Don't worry Eddy Jones, I think most people couldn't see your penalty miss. (Getty Images: Jess Hornby)

World.title: Socceroos wary of Jordan friendly due to security threats
World.content:
Football Australia will continue to assess security ahead of the Socceroos' planned friendly against Jordan, with an under-strength squad named amid player concerns over safety.

Tony Popovic's squad was revealed at 10:30pm on Saturday night for upcoming friendlies against Qatar in Doha on November 13 (November 14 AEDT) and Jordan in Amman three days later.

The friendlies were initially meant to serve as preparation for the Asian Cup which has since been pushed back from January to December 2027 due to security concerns in host country Saudi Arabia.

Professional Footballers Australia (the PFA) on Friday said players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

Captain Maty Ryan and fellow veterans Jackson Irvine and Milos Degenek, plus midfielder Aiden O'Neill, are the most prominent omissions from coach Tony Popovic's squad, which includes seven uncapped players.

It is unclear whether those players made themselves unavailable for safety reasons.

As yet, there has been no movement on the Amman fixture, despite Indonesia recently cancelling their own planned friendly in Jordan.

"For the match against Jordan, we will continue to assess the security environment and provide players and staff with timely, comprehensive updates, including relevant safety advice and risk assessments," FA chief executive Martin Kugeler said.

"The safety and wellbeing of our players and staff remains our highest priority."

There are eight changes to the squad from September's friendlies against Brazil in Australia.

Diesel Herrington is one of seven new faces in the Socceroos squad. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

New call-ups are Central Coast defender Diesel Herrington, older brother of Hull City ace Lucas Herrington, Portsmouth striker Thomas Waddingham and FC St. Pauli midfielder Sam Klein.

Attacker Daniel Arzani returns after finding form at Ferencvaros, along with defender Gianni Stensness (Viking FK), who scored against Bayern Munich in the Champions League.

Stunning free kick shows Irankunda's star is aligning for Socceroos Nestory Irankunda's incredible free kick against Brazil in Townsville shows that the Socceroos have stars to rival some of the biggest and best in the world.

Striker Kusini Yengi joins brother Tete, while goalkeepers Joe Gauci (Lincoln City) and Tom Glover (RB Omiya Ardija) have been recalled.

"While the Asian Cup has been rescheduled, that does not take away from the importance of this window," Popovic said in a statement.

"We have limited opportunities to be together as a group, so every camp and every game is important.

"We will have an eye on continuing to evolve the squad for the future, with our World Cup 2030 qualifying campaign and the Asian Cup both now in the second half of 2027.

"This camp gives us another chance to work with new players and see how they fit into what we are building."

Socceroos Squad

Goalkeepers: Patrick Beach, Joe Gauci, Tom Glover*

Defenders: Kealey Adamson*, Aziz Behich, Kasey Bos*, Alessandro Circati, Jason Geria, Diesel Herrington*, Lucas Herrington, Jacob Italiano, Harry Souttar

Midfielders: Sam Klein*, Riley McGree, Connor Metcalfe, Paul Okon-Engstler, Gianni Stensness, Patrick Yazbek

Forwards: Eli Adams*, Daniel Arzani, Nestory Irankunda, Thomas Waddingham*, Kusini Yengi, Tete Yengi, Marcus Younis

(* denotes uncapped player)

World.title: Moesha Johnson's Open Water World Cup winning streak continues
World.content:
The Cancún leg of the Open Water Swimming World Cup may have been the start of a new season.

But for dominant Australian Moesha Johnson, absolutely nothing changed.

Following a stunning 2025/26 season in which Johnson won every single open water event she entered, the 29-year-old started the 2026/27 campaign with yet another double gold medal-winning weekend in Mexico, underlining a dominance rarely seen in top level international sport.

In Friday's 10km race, Johnson set out her stall early by claiming the $US1,000 ($1,455) bonus for winning the sprint lap, before easing up.

"After the sprint lap the goal was just to drop back and relax," Johnson told World Aquatics.

"I haven't got the big endurance work behind me for this season so far, so my endurance strength isn't quite there.

"I really wanted to practice my open water skills, get in the pack, just play around a little bit."

After recovering amidst the melee of the main group, Johnson made her way back to the front and powered to victory, finishing in a time of 2 hours, 3 minutes and 31 seconds, 13 seconds ahead of Japan’s Airi Ebina and Italy’s Ginevra Taddeucci.

St Peter's Western swimmer and World Cup debutant, 22-year-old Jacqueline Davison-McGovern, finished in seventh place.

After her success in the 10km, Johnson backed up to win a second gold medal in the 3km elimination race.

Johnson won the 1,500m heat, the 1,000m semifinal and the 500m final dash to make it two-from-two to start the year.

"For me this was a bit more of a closure to 2026 rather than a start to the new season," Johnson said after the 10km.

"We haven't had our normal preparation so I didn't know where I was at, but today I gave myself every opportunity to finish 2026 as my year on top.

"I know people might have come to expect [winning] from me, but it's not that easy to be on top every single race.

"It's really stressful and it takes a lot of work, and it's something that I'm really proud of now.

"Hopefully, the increasing standard keeps lifting the professionalism of our sport and the girls around us and it's just as entertaining as ever."

World.title: Wet-weather chaos in qualifying for Brazilian Grand Prix
World.content:
Oscar Piastri will start the F1 São Paulo Grand Prix from 10th place on the grid after a chaotic wet-weather qualifying session at Interlagos.

The Australian only jumped into the top 10 due to grid place penalties meted out to his rivals, however, in a wet and wild session that was twice red-flagged, and delayed by 80 minutes as torrential rain teemed down on the circuit.

Piastri was only 12th fastest in the tricky conditions, missing out on Q3.

"Today's qualifying was a very tough session," Piastri said.

"The car felt reasonable in the wet, and we've been more competitive and comfortable in the dry this weekend, so it's disappointing not to have made more of the session.

"We'll review what happened and see what the weather and final grid order bring tomorrow.

"If it's dry, we look strong; if it's wet, we're still decent, but we'll need to work hard overnight and into the race to make progress up the field."

The entire grid dealt with atrocious conditions. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

For the third year in a row, Piastri's McLaren teammate Lando Norris will start on pole.

"It's been a long day," Norris said.

"To be on pole here two years in a row… Different conditions to last year, but I am very happy.

"It was about getting two laps in, not making any mistakes and yeah, it has been a very good day.

"This was my first time driving the car in the wet, but I think I figured it out."

George Russell, who fumed at his team for telling him to back off during a flying lap, qualified second, but will start seventh after taking a five-place grid place penalty for a power unit change.

That puts world champion Kimi Antonelli on the front row of the grid after he qualified third.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was fourth fastest but has a 10-place grid drop, promoting Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson to third, with Audi's Nico Hulkenberg fourth.

Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, Oliver Bearman, Fernando Alonso and Alex Albon all made up the rest of the top 10 on track.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start from the back row of the grid after both veterans took grid-place penalties.

However, with wet weather forecast for race day, both men will back themselves to make their way through the firled to the front places.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the F1 São Paulo Grand Prix on Monday morning, with lights out at 4am AEDT.

What happened to Oscar Piastri?

Piastri was struggling on the wet-weather tyres and was delayed in changing to intermediates as the track dried during a brief window in the weather.

Then, once he changed to the correct tyres, a crash to debutant Rafael Camara meant that Q2 was brought to a premature end.

That left the Australian in 12th place and unable to participate in the final phase of qualifying.

"The track was incredibly slippery [at the beginning]," Piastri said.

"It became a little easier towards the end, but the call on tyres was always going to be difficult because I was a long way up the road and there was always a risk that an earlier red flag could change things.

"But we paid the price by missing out on Q3."

World.title: Wilson backs Wallabies to overpower mutinous England
World.content:
Harry Wilson believes the Wallabies are ready to test England's reported lack of unity at Twickenham while looking to unleash a key 'X-factor' strike weapon from their bench.

The build-up to Sunday's Nations Championship Test has been dominated by stories about unrest within the England camp at their Pennyhill Park base, leaving Australia's captain Wilson to suggest his team will be out to discover whether there's any truth in the supposed disunity.

Asked on the eve of the match whether any unrest in the opposition camp might galvanise or disrupt the hosts, Wilson said: "It could go one or two ways for them, and I guess it's on us to put them under pressure to see how close they are as a team."

But the skipper was also keen to make the point of just what a united outfit his own team has become.

"We know how close we are, how much we care for each other, and how much we love playing for our coach and coaching staff," Wilson said.

"So I'm really only worried about us, and I just want us to keep keep caring for this jersey, keep caring for every person in our group."

A report had claimed England players wanted showdown talks with coach Steve Borthwick during the July tour because of a toxic environment.

But leading England players responded with indignation this week, with Jamie George declaring they would demonstrate their loyalty to Borthwick with a stirring performance.

Yet Wilson believes his men are primed for "an epic battle in the forwards" as they seek to make amends for being outplayed at Twickenham last year.

The Queenslander is particularly enthused by the new impact role for one of their best, usual back-row starter Rob Valetini.

Last November, Australia suffered when the England second-half reinforcements came on — but now, led by Valetini, he's backing the likes of Taniela Tupou and Carlo Tizzano to fight fire with fire against the so-called 'Pom Squad'.

"It's different for Bobby, and it's just a genuine X factor coming off the bench," Wilson said.

"It's rugby now, a lot of teams have some really strong players coming off the bench, and we've got one of the best players in his position in the world coming off the bench. So he can be some genuine X factor if it's close when he comes on.

"Having a player like him coming on gives the boys a lot of confidence, and that's what England did to us last year. Hopefully, Bobby can really spark us on the bench again this year."

Harry Wilson led Australia to a famous victory at Twickenham two years ago. (Getty Images: CameraSport/Andrew Kearns)

The Wallabies' last-gasp win at Twickenham in 2024 was a breakthrough moment for Wilson himself in the early days of his captaincy, as he scored a try and had an inspirational game.

Now "comfortable" in the leadership role, he's overseeing a team which has "a lot to be excited about" and is ready to rebound from the two recent chastening defeats by a rampant New Zealand.

"We definitely want to be us. We want to play our own game," said Wilson.

"We've seen this year when we do play our style of footy how much we can hurt teams.

"In the South Africa win, when we really backed our skills and kept attacking, we really played some really good footy, and we learned some valuable lessons in those New Zealand games. We really need to take them forward."

AAP

World.title: Coach says Bancroft will 'let bat do the talking' after Khawaja bombshell
World.content:
Cameron Bancroft is being backed to let his "bat do the talking" in the wake of Usman Khawaja's bombshell revelations about the sandpaper ball-tampering scandal from 2018.

Khawaja sent the cricket world into a spin on Saturday when he said the entire Test XI knew about the use of sandpaper to alter the state of the ball on the tour of South Africa.

The comments were in stark contrast to the findings from the official investigation, which determined only David Warner, Steve Smith and Bancroft knew about the plot.

Bancroft, who was caught on camera during the Cape Town Test trying to hide the sandpaper in his pants, received a nine-month suspension, while senior figures Warner and Smith were banned for a year.

Khawaja said he had urged the entire team at the time to take collective responsibility rather than scapegoating Warner, Smith and Bancroft.

"Obviously, it didn't work that way and those three guys got crucified," Khawaja told Nine Newspapers.

Bancroft played only two more Tests once he served his ban, and recently said he was no longer as motivated to return to the Test arena as he once was.

Cameron Bancroft has been backed to let his bat do the talking. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

The 33-year-old put aside the distraction of Khawaja's comments on Saturday to score 32 off 40 balls in Western Australia's 92-run one-day loss to England at the WACA.

After the match, WA coach Beau Casson praised Bancroft's maturity in the face of renewed interest in the ball-tampering scandal.

"He's a grown man and a very mature guy," Casson said.

"I think he's handled himself with distinction in that space. I don't see it changing anytime soon."

Bancroft wasn't made available to media on Saturday to talk about Khawaja's comments, and it remains to be seen whether he will eventually address the latest revelations.

"The situation was a long time ago," Casson said.

"He's keen to move on and let his bat do the talking, and that's what we promote him to do."

Cameron Bancroft scored a colossal 186 against South Australia in the most recent Sheffield Shield match. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

Cricket Australia says it remains comfortable with the past investigation of the incident, but left the door open for new information to be considered.

Bancroft will be back in action when WA takes on Victoria in a Sheffield Shield match at the MCG, starting on Wednesday.

"We're just rapt to be able to have Cameron scoring runs for us," Casson said.

"Last week was a really good example of that [when he scored 186 in a Shield win against South Australia].

"He leaves nothing to chance. He trains hard, not only technically but physically. If he's not running miles, he's thinking about cricket.

"He's a senior player within this group, and he certainly sets the example of how to go about it to be a professional cricketer."

AAP

Tech.title: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
Tech.content:
With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.

Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem, from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both.

This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside.

I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others.

The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck.

The90 Gem’s modular design lets you detach the pendant from its necklace chain. Image: The90

The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight.

There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score.

The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score.

Previous Next

1 / 2

The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking.

My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too.

The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun.

I appreciated how the Gem encouraged me to think more about my health than simply preventing wrinkles. Photo: Sheena Vasani / The Verge

That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade.

I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary.

At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.

Photography by Sheena Vasani / The Verge

Tech.title: Discogs’ Kevin Lewandowski can’t live without his AeroPress
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Twenty-five years ago, Kevin Lewandowski founded Discogs, arguably the destination online for obsessive vinyl collectors and music nerds of all stripes. It is a marketplace for buying and selling records, obviously, but it’s also become so much more. It’s a shockingly comprehensive database that covers not just albums and singles, but all the various versions and pressings. It’s a really fun rabbit hole to disappear down when you’re trying to figure out what obscure pressing of Ministry’s The Mind is a Terrible Thing to Taste or Psalm 69 you had in high school, because you definitely blasted the cover of “Lay Lady Lay” all the time and 100 percent never owned Filth Pig.

In the years since it debuted, Discogs has grown to be much more than just a site where audiophiles go to trade rare first pressings of Beach Boys records. There are forums, groups, user-created lists, and more. It’s part eBay, part Reddit, and IMDB — just specifically for music.

With more and more people turning their back on the algorithm and rediscovering physical media, now seemed like a perfect time to check in with Lewandowski.

What is your most indispensable tool?

My AeroPress. I use it multiple times a day. In fact, I just made a coffee with it [sips coffee].

How many tabs do you have open right now?

Probably around 30 on my work computer. My personal computer is worse — probably 40 or 50.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I look at X and Instagram occasionally, but I don’t really post.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

It’s not really a gadget, but I like to tinker. Lately I’ve been playing around with Home Assistant software and built my own setup to control things like the garage door and outdoor lights. So I guess my favorite gadget is one I made myself.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

Probably a game like Rez, which came out around 2000. It’s a rhythm game where you’re almost controlling the music as you play, about as close to DJing as a video game can get. I’ve actually had an idea for my own version with a similar concept. It’s still just an idea, though.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I’ll either clear everything off my desk or change locations completely. Go to a coffee shop or sit outside. Sometimes I just need a different environment.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

Records. I was at Mint Gallery in Portland last week and picked up four. I still really like going into a record store and finding something to bring home. And I also recently picked up three reissues from the Moodsville / Acoustic Sounds series.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

The Secret Weapon.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

I don’t use memes very often, but one I was kind of proud of was putting a Discogs screen into a North Korean war room photo. I was advised that maybe it wasn’t one for the company chat.

Tech.title: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Around 7PM each weeknight, I find myself standing in front of the fridge, trying to decide on something for dinner that won’t make my husband complain, “Chicken again?” Yes, I should meal plan more, but I don’t, so this is where I’m at. A nightly battle in which the chicken usually wins.

Recently, my best weapon in this fight has been AI. Between Alexa Plus in the Echo smart display on my kitchen counter, the Samsung Food app on my fridge, and even an AI-powered cooking robot, AI has become my go-to sous chef — albeit one I need to keep a close eye on. It’s helped me swap ingredients, generate ideas, fix things when I mess up, and yes, even cook better. So I was intrigued when my go-to recipe app, NYT Cooking, introduced an AI assistant.

Many, including some NYT Cooking users and recipe purists, are skeptical of this new tool (available to subscribers on iOS only at launch), and I get why. One of the things I like most about NYT Cooking is that it features thousands of recipes from dozens of reputable sources — such as the New York Times archives, restaurants, cookbooks, and food columnists — and real people have tested them. (I’ve tried some purely AI-generated recipes and they were not good).

Another great feature of the service, which I’ve been paying for for several years, is the reader comments. Here, I’ve often found solutions to cooking dilemmas, like what to substitute for makrut lime leaves — there’s always one slightly bougie ingredient in an NYT Cooking recipe that I don’t have on hand.

I’ve used several AI tools in my kitchen and have found them mostly helpful.

However, reading through hundreds of comments to find answers at 7PM on a weeknight isn’t always practical. And this is where I’ve found the NYT Cooking assistant helpful. Among other things, it was trained on user comments, and in my few days testing it, it provided practical substitutions and solid cooking guidance for the new ingredients. It also won’t unquestionably agree to crazy requests (I tried!). As with all AI tools, it’s not perfect — it almost made me put half the required butter in my cake — but as a tool, it is useful and feels like a solid application of AI. Importantly, it doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you.

It doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you

The assistant appears in the app in a small text box on the recipe page with a prompt: “Customize this recipe…” From here, you type in a question to adapt it to your needs. This can be as simple as “What can I substitute for this ingredient?” to “Scale this recipe to feed seven people, and make it vegan and gluten-free.” The New York Times has also said the feature can suggest substitutions for cooking equipment and convert measurements; the latter option has been in the app for a couple of years.

Previous Next



1 / 3 The AI modified version of the chicken recipe. The red highlighted words are what changed from the original.

Last Friday night, instead of staring aimlessly into the fridge, I turned to the Chicken folder in my NYT Cooking app Recipe Box and found a One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger I’d been wanting to try. Only I didn’t have chicken thighs or half the ingredients.

I could have figured these steps myself, but it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible.

I typed my dilemma into the assistant box on the recipe page: “I have chicken tenders, fresh ginger, garlic, rice, broth, limes, but no chard or cilantro or scallions. I do have green beans and red onions.” Within seconds, it created a new version of the recipe, with a new title: One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger and Green Beans. It suggested a shorter browning time for the tenders, cooking the red onion alongside the chicken, and steaming the green beans on top of the rice for the last eight minutes instead of the chard. Every change was highlighted in the new recipe under a Your Version tab, and I could flip back to the original at any point.

I noticed it hadn’t adjusted for the lack of cilantro, saying it was optional. So I asked if I could use Thai basil, which I happen to have, and it agreed, highlighting how it would change the flavor. While I could have figured out a lot of these steps myself, maybe with the help of Google, it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible and nice not to have to swipe out of the app. The NYT Cooking editors say it’s been trained not to comply with requests that will taste bad.

Weeknight chicken and rice.

The resulting dish — which took the same amount of time to cook as the original — was delicious and got my husband’s seal of approval (he just had the leftovers for lunch). It was very different from the recipe Yasmin Fahr wrote, and I can see the purists’ point. But the rewritten recipe was much easier to use and produced a better dish than winging it with my own subs gleaned from the comments section, which I usually do with varying degrees of success.

I cook regularly, so I had a sense of what ingredients I had on hand that might work for the dish I wanted to make. But the assistant can also help if you have no idea what to use as a substitute. For example, I was cooking a Thai red curry and asked what I could use instead of makrut lime leaf. It replied, saying that grated lime zest would work, but “it misses the deeper floral, herbal aroma” of fresh limes. (See? Bougie.)

Previous Next

1 / 2 I tried several swaps when I was missing ingredients, asking the assistant if what I had on hand would work.

Over the weekend, I tried several more swaps, asking whether half-and-half would work instead of cream in a caramel apple Dutch baby, or if Castelvetrano olives and smoked paprika could stand in for kalamata and chile pepper in a roasted halibut dish. Swapping spices is always a bold move in any dish, as it can really ruin the flavor.

I also had the app convert the Dutch baby recipe’s metric weights to US measurements, which it did seamlessly. Then I threw in some curveballs. How about using fresh cayenne peppers with the halibut? It warned me that substituting cayenne for chile “brings significant, sharp heat.” Could I swap ladyfingers for minced beef in this trifle (à la Rachel Green in Friends)? “Minced beef cannot be used in place of the ladyfingers or anywhere in this sweet dessert trifle.” Good call.

Alexa Plus on the Echo Show 11 gave the same guidance as the NYT Cooking app. But it couldn’t show me a modified recipe.

While I was cooking, I compared the NYT Cooking assistant with Alexa Plus, Amazon’s generative-AI voice assistant I regularly use to help me cook via the Echo Show 11 smart display in my kitchen. Interestingly, it offered the same guidance as the Cooking assistant on substitutions for the chicken and rice dish, but with slightly different cooking times. Alexa pulls some recipes from the NYT app through a partnership between the companies.

However, Alexa couldn’t show the modified recipe on its screen; it could only tell me the changes while showing the original. When I asked it to walk me through them, it got confused and improvised, telling me to cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces — which wasn’t in the modified recipe. Overall, I found using the Cooking app more reliable, although messier. It would be great to be able to use voice control to navigate the app, as I can with Alexa on my smart display, rather than using my garlicky fingers.

My cinnamon roll muffins, made with AI assistance.

Time for a bigger challenge: baking.

I am typically not a baker. My cakes come out flat, and my cookies don’t crumble. Even the smart mixer I tested a few years ago couldn’t save me. I also rarely have the right equipment. So I took Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake, a recipe by NYT Cooking editor Genevieve Ko (who announced the AI feature), and asked it to turn it into muffins. (Who has a Bundt cake pan?!)

It modified the recipe’s cooking time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. But that was going to make 24 muffins, way too many for me. So I asked it to halve the recipe to get 12 muffins. This led to some smart choices, like halving five eggs to three instead of an unhelpful two and a half.

For science, I bought a Bundt pan to make the original version too. Both turned out great, but things got a bit sticky when I swapped between the original recipe and the AI version in the app. You can’t save your new recipe separately, which caused confusion when I was cooking the original. Instead of scrolling back through the recipe with sticky fingers, I asked the assistant how much butter I needed (using voice typing), and it gave me the modified recipe’s 6 tablespoons rather than the original’s three-quarter cup, without telling me which version it was using. You can delete your version, which I would advise doing to avoid issues like this — 6 tablespoons of butter would have made for a dry cake.

My AI-free cinnamon roll bundt cake.

If you already read all the comments before starting a New York Times recipe, then you will probably find this tool offers a similar experience in a more streamlined way. For everyday problems — wrong cut of chicken, no cilantro, or no Bundt cake pan — it was genuinely helpful and saved me a trip to the store. It was also smart enough to know when to say no to minced beef in a trifle.

As with every AI tool I’ve used in the kitchen, the NYT Cooking AI assistant works well as a sous chef, but it’s not the head chef — I still felt the need to double-check amounts and cooking times and cross-reference them with the original to make sure it hadn’t done something outlandish.

If you’re a purist, you can just ignore the assistant. While you can’t turn off the chat box, it’s easy to scroll past. I do think it will make me use the app more often, since I no longer need to worry as much when I don’t have makrut lime leaves on hand or the right cut of meat. For me, standing in front of the fridge with chicken tenders and no plan, it’s been a useful addition to my nightly cooking routine.

Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Tech.title: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:

Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.

What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.

Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

Tech.title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.

This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.

I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.

That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.

There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.

Hey, thanks for having me, man.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.

October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.

You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.

A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.

I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?

It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up.
